News.title: Horror as sharks circle and attack survivors of capsized boat with 11 still missing as desperate search continues
News.content:
RESCUE MISSION Horror as sharks circle and attack survivors of capsized boat with 11 still missing as desperate search continues







Next

SHARKS have picked off survivors waiting hours for rescue after their boat capsized, the US Coast Guard has revealed.

The vessel departed from Mexico and sank off the coast of Baja California on Friday with a mayday call transmitted at around 1am.



Officials are still searching for 11 people believed to be missing, with 16 Mexican nationals already taken to safety.

The Coast Guard said multiple survivors have been treated for shark bites after they were attacked in the water.



A rescue helicopter arrived at the site of the incident two hours after the distress call was made.

“Several of the individuals rescued were suffering from severe injuries consistent with shark bites, and the Coast Guard provided life-saving first aid while en route [to] San Diego,” said the agency on Saturday.

Meanwhile, a desperate search for those still missing remains underway.

The Coast Guard is being assisted by the Navy and the Mexican Navy as they scour the waters.

Multiple aircraft have also been deployed to scan from above.

A total of 27 people were believed to be onboard the vessel when it capsized.



Officials have said the incident occurred outside of US waters in a popular smuggling route that is also frequented by leisure and fishing vessels.

“We were able to help, and that’s why we launched our assets,” US Coast Guard spokesperson Petty Officer Charlie Valor said.

All survivors have been taken to San Diego and are confirmed to be Mexican nationals.

The Customs and Border Protection is investigating and interviewing them, the Coast Guard said.

News.title: Boy, 16, dies and another teen injured in horror crash after ‘car hit railings’ – as driver, 19, arrested
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

SMASH TRAGEDY Boy, 16, dies and another teen injured in horror crash after ‘car hit railings’ – as driver, 19, arrested







Next

A TEENAGE boy has died and another left injured in a horror crash – as a 19-year-old driver is arrested.

Cops were scrambled to Shaftmoor Lane in Birmingham at around 8.30pm on Saturday night following a crash involving a white Seat Ibiza.

West Midlands Police said the vehicle had smashed into railings as emergency services raced to the scene.

Despite the best efforts of paramedics, a 16-year-old boy inside the vehicle was pronounced dead.





A second passenger, a boy in his teens, was taken to hospital with a serious arm injury.

Meanwhile, officers arrested a 19-year-old man at the scene on suspicion of causing death and serious injury by dangerous driving and failing to provide a breath specimen.

He remains in custody for questioning.

A police spokesperson said: “Specialist officers from Serious Collision Investigation Unit are asking that anyone who has dashcam footage from around the time of the collision to get in touch.

“Witnesses are being spoken with and anyone who is yet to speak with us is also asked to get in contact.

Anyone with information or footage is urged to contact police quoting log 4403 of October 17.

News.title: Body of man, 53, found inside flat in UK port town in early hours – as man, 33, arrested
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

TRAGIC FIND Body of man, 53, found inside flat in UK port town in early hours – as man, 33, arrested







Next

THE body of a 53-year-old man has tragically been found inside a flat in a port town.

A 33-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of murder and continues to be questioned by police.

Cops scrambled to the scene in Holyhead, Anglesey, Wales, at 2.42am on Saturday October 17 after a body was discovered.

Despite the best efforts of emergency services, the 53-year-old was sadly pronounced dead at the scene.





A man was arrested in connection with the incident and remains in police custody.

Detective Chief Inspector Richard Sidney, North Wales Police, said: “Officers remain at the address whilst our enquiries continue.

“I would like to thank the local community for their assistance whilst officers remain at the scene.”

A spokesperson for the force said: “Detectives have been granted extra time to question a man arrested following the death of a man in Holyhead.

“Police were called to a flat at Llys Watling on London Road at 02:42 yesterday morning (Saturday, October 17) by the Welsh Ambulance Service.

“Sadly, despite the best efforts of emergency services, a 53-year-old local man was pronounced dead at the scene.

“A 33-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of murder and was taken to police custody where he remains.”

News.title: Body of singer & composer found ‘tied up’ at bottom of pool at Florida home as cops probe ‘suspicious’ death
News.content:
DEATH RIDDLE Body of singer & composer found ‘tied up’ at bottom of pool at Florida home as cops probe ‘suspicious’ death







Next

A CELEBRATED musician has been found dead at the bottom of his swimming pool in Florida after reportedly being tied up with a cord.

Venezuelan composer and pianist Gus Ormo was discovered face down in the water at his luxury home in Weston, near Fort Lauderdale, on Friday morning.



Cops have launched a homicide investigation into the mysterious death, which authorities have described as suspicious.

Officers rushed to the property on Quail Roost Drive at around 9am after receiving a 911 call reporting a possible drowning.



Chilling audio from the emergency dispatcher revealed that the man in the pool had reportedly been “tied up”.

Ormo, a singer and pianist known for his romantic compositions, was pronounced dead at the scene.



Aerial footage captured by local broadcaster WPLG Local 10 showed a long blue cord tangled across the patio of his sprawling home.

Part of the rope appeared to stretch into the swimming pool where the musician’s body was discovered.

But investigators have not confirmed whether the cord was attached to Ormo or played any role in his death.

Broward Sheriff’s Office spokesperson Gerdy St. Louis confirmed that homicide and crime scene detectives were investigating the circumstances.



Authorities have not established whether a crime was committed, while questions remain over how the musician ended up submerged in his own pool.

His body was taken to the Broward County Medical Examiner’s Office, where specialists are working to determine the cause of death.

It remains unclear who made the emergency call, how long Ormo had been in the water or whether anyone else was at the property.



The disturbing discovery has stunned residents of the quiet, gated community, where the composer had lived for several years.

Neighbours described Ormo as a private man who kept a low profile despite his successful music career.

Resident Bruno Gedikinan told NBC 6: “It’s sad what happened, and it wasn’t something I expected to happen in Weston.”

Another neighbour, Mariano Cascata, said: “It’s weird to happen. It’s not normal, of course.”

Ormo’s family have also been left searching for answers.



His sister, Antonieta Ormo, confirmed the musician’s death to CBS News Miami but said relatives had received no further information about what happened.

The tragedy comes just weeks after Ormo promoted his latest album, AGAPE, an instrumental piano collection celebrating love and human connection.

An October press release described the project as a “milestone in his career”.

It also highlighted the musician’s lifelong passion for music, which began during his childhood in Venezuela.

The announcement read: “Gus Ormo has always been a sensitive person. He recalls how, as a child, he would listen to records and feel music stirring his deepest emotions.”



Ormo had built his career around romantic melodies and expressive piano arrangements, hoping to capture feelings that words could not convey.

Speaking about AGAPE, he said: “In a world that makes us experience emotional numbness, the album is an invitation to feel without filters or need for words.

“It’s my way to give back to music all it has given me.”

Earlier this year, the composer appeared at a red-carpet event in Aventura, Florida, where he spoke proudly about his Venezuelan roots and musical career.

He had also written a tribute to his homeland, using music to explore national unity and reconciliation.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ormo said the composition reflected his deep connection to Venezuela and his belief that music could bring divided communities together.

Investigators have yet to announce any arrests or release further details about the circumstances of his death.

News.title: The sick traffickers luring women into UK’s sex trade from Thai party city & the warped tactics of Brit ‘Brothel Queen’
News.content:
Next

BLINDING neon lights, deafening music and scores of boozing tourists staggering through one of Thailand’s most notorious party cities has created a sick breeding ground for sex traffickers.

The world’s sex tourism capital is hiding a sinister shadow behind its glittering facade: a hotbed for ruthless gangs eyeing up their next target.



The grisly trade’s was laid bare when a sex trafficking gang leader dubbed the “Brothel Queen” was jailed alongside her husband last month.

Achareeya Spurr, 49, and Chin Ping, 56, were thrown behind bars for trafficking 22 women from Thailand to the UK in a single year.



The sex workers were left with eye-watering £25,000 debts despite working gruelling 14-hour days as they were paid as little as £50 per shift.

Experts fear the disturbing Brothel Queen case could just be the tip of the iceberg.

Andrew Wallis OBE, a sex trafficking expert who advised on Britain’s Modern Slavery Act, told The Sun: “That case will be replicated the length and breadth of the UK.”

Spurr is one of a new generation of trafficking kingpins bringing women to the UK from Asia to work while facing brutal conditions.

Last year, fellow brothel madam Jie Zhang, 45, was jailed after putting women to work in erotic massage “temples” and taking up to 60 per cent of their pay as part of the sexually exploitative “Cloud 9” gang.

In Thailand, the first step in a sex worker’s perilous descent into the trafficking trade can be found in Thai party towns, Matt Friedman, founder of anti-human slavery organisation Mekong Club, said.



He explained how it was one of the most effective ways recruiters lure in young women – even more than social media.

The analyst told The Sun: “You have these people who basically will go through the girl’s bars and identify somebody who they think meets a certain expectation.

“They determine the extent to which they have English… and they’ll talk them into this type of a scenario.”



The Sun revealed in August how Thai mafia gangs encourage poverty-stricken families to sell their daughters into the sex trade – some of which end up being trafficked to the UK.

Once targets are sent to the UK, they are usually met at the airport, put into a van, and stripped of their passport and phones.

In extreme cases, women are unable to leave grim prostitution dungeons for months at a time, Friedman said.

One of the main things traffickers use to keep women in check is debt.

Friedman said debts can be as high as £100,000 – but are never properly recorded to make sure they can’t be paid off.



The victims of Spurr and her husband – a Brit national originally from China – were hit with debts of tens of thousands of pounds, prosecutors said.

Friedman continued: “They don’t really tell you how much you’ve paid against the debt.

“So if you’re making money for them, it could last for years because it’s never really gonna be paid off, it’s part of the scam.



“The indebtedness is the justification, but the indebtedness allows them for the threats.”

The so-called Brothel Queen also coerced women by threatening to report them to immigration services if they complained.

Prosecutors said a total of 22 women were brought to the UK from Thailand between January and October 2025 – while two others were transported from Denmark and Scotland.

Spurr also used social media to deceive, entice and threaten her victims.

She recruited Thai sex workers for the brothels through flashy videos on TikTok, promising riches if they moved to the UK.



Wallis said: “Social media is a means of recruitment, a means of control, and a means of advertising.”

He said recruiters often threaten to send compromising material of their sex work to relatives if they don’t behave.

“So it has become the means in which to sell more, control more and deceive more,” he added.



Wallis pointed to another sinister method traffickers use – the aftermath of earthquakes or tsunamis.

“If there is a natural disaster, usually the first people on the ground are the traffickers, because they know that those people are vulnerable,” Wallis warned.

“And they will prey on vulnerable women and girls and move them.”

Experts said earthquakes and tsunamis often rip apart families and can destroy homes, workplaces and opportunities for poorer members of society.

This makes the individual vulnerable – but also desperate for cash.



“Once you start removing those things, you’re incredibly vulnerable, and traffickers just play on that vulnerability,” Wallis said.

In March last year, a huge 7.9-magnitude earthquake struck Myanmar and Thailand, killing over 5,000 people and displacing many more.

Wallis said recruiters would most likely have flocked to the scene in the aftermath to prey on women in their most desperate moments.

He stressed: “If your options are poverty, poverty, poverty, or here’s this offer of a job in the West, human nature kicks in.”

Some women are tricked into coming to the UK with promises of regular jobs, while others know they are coming for sex work.



But even those who know what to expect are subjected to much worse conditions than promised: they are controlled, paid nothing, and trapped.

In either case, it is a crime of modern slavery.

A decade ago, Britain’s Modern Slavery Act 2015 was praised across the world as a game-changing crackdown on a horrific crime.

Politicians joined forces to tackle evil human traffickers and modern-day slave masters, giving frontline charities the power to help thousands of victims escape abuse and rebuild their lives.

But 10 years later, Wallis said the uncomfortable truth is that modern slavery hasn’t been wiped out.



New official figures show referrals into the government’s National Referral Mechanism skyrocketed to a record 23,411 in 2025 – a massive 22 per cent surge in just one year.

The proportion of those who reported sexual exploitation has remained roughly the same in the past few years.

Wallis said authorities are doing less to combat it than they were a decade ago – despite the problem being just as bad if not worse.

He said: “Modern slavery used to be on the National Threat Assessment, which meant it sat as a priority on every single police force’s threat assessment… that’s no longer the case.

“I think what we’ve seen in the last nine or 10 years, is a growing scepticism by government… you have less focus on policing.



“We used to have what was called MSOIC, the Modern Slavery and Organised Immigration Crime programme.

“That’s now just Organised Immigration Crime. So that like the modern slavery aspect has been completely dropped.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The economic cost is also vast – Wallis said modern slavery costs the UK economy £60billion per year, about two per cent of GDP.

In just under a decade, the UK has gone from having a real “determination” to uncover the scale of the issue, to half-heartedly wanting to acknowledge it, Wallis concluded.

News.title: How tiny force is probing 260,000 Russian war crimes from torture & rape to deadly civilian strikes under Putin’s watch
News.content:
KREMLIN DEPRAVITY How tiny force is probing 260,000 Russian war crimes from torture & rape to deadly civilian strikes under Putin’s watch







Next

UKRAINE is struggling under the weight of 260,000 war crime cases inflicted on its land and people in the four years since Russia’s full-scale invasion.

Vladimir Putin’s soldiers and commanders are accused of raping Ukrainian girls as young as four-years-old, slaughtering families in their homes, striking evacuation routes and committing crimes against humanity.



A handful of prosecutors, investigators and police are working tirelessly to bring the perpetrators of these atrocities to justice – and their sights are set on the very highest ranks of the Kremlin.

Each day the toll of Russia’s terror ticks up, with 6,000 to 9,000 fresh cases registered by the national police force every month.



Oleksandr Ziuz, the head of the Prosecutor General’s Department for Combating Crimes Committed in Conditions of Armed Conflict, told The Sun that a single prosecutor handles 5,000 proceedings in some regions.

Zuiz expects the toll of war crimes to reach 290,000 by the end of this year.



“But we do not have an increase in capacity or staff,” he said.

War crimes include extrajudicial killings, deportation of minors, torture, sexual violence, enforced disappearances and bombings and attacks on civilian infrastructure.



Last month, the UN condemned the widespread and “abhorrent” sexual violence inflicted against Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war (POW).

A 20-page report detailed testimony from hundreds of victims. The youngest rape survivor was a four-year-old girl and the oldest an 82-year-old woman.

Veronika Plotnikova, Head of Victim and Witness Support, told The Sun: “The war will continue for some time, but after it ends there will still be victims and their trauma and the court proceedings continue.”

Her centre alone currently works with 2,500 victims with active criminal proceedings – 1,300 of whom are children.

Of these, 138 have suffered sexual violence, 300 are soldiers who have been released from captivity, 140 are former civilian detainees and 704 are victims of explosions.



The centre is also supporting 487 witnesses – more than 300 of whom are also children.

“Behind every figure is a person, their story and pain, their experience, losses and needs,” Veronika said.

One of the most challenging problems hampering investigations is Russia’s ongoing aggression against Ukraine, Zuiz said.



Access to evidence on the frontlines or in occupied territories is limited – and those tasked with collecting it often do so under live fire and the constant threat of missile strikes.

Prosecutor’s service vehicles have been attacked and police and security service personnel have been killed or injured by Russia’s relentless bombardment.

But even when evidence has been secured it remains at risk.

Just two weeks ago a Russian drone swarm targeted Kyiv, striking a building that stored crucial documents for Zuiz’s team.

He said: “Now we don’t have access to critical information. We have a lot of evidence but to preserve it is a challenge.”



Despite the mammoth task ahead of him, Zuiz is determined to “bring justice to all responsible”.

Cases can take any time from months to years to reach court or a verdict – but the vast majority are swept through court without a defendant.

Zuiz said: “Out of all suspects only 34 are prisoners of war and can take the stand. We have 1,267 suspects charged in absentia.



“This is why it is so important for us to preserve as much evidence as possible. To build a case without them here in Ukraine.”

Investigators trawl through recordings, radio dispatches, Ukrainian intelligence and eyewitness testimony to piece together a trail from each crime to a list of suspects.

But many Russian soldiers use an alias – and without a name prosecutors struggle to reach proof beyond a level of reasonable doubt.

By the end of September 2025, when the estimated number of cases was 185,000, only 446 had reached the courts.

Of these just 156 resulted in a sentence — less than one in 1,000 — according to a study conducted by the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union (UHHRU).



Executive Director Oleksandr Pavlichenko told The Sun: “Around 80 per cent of cases have been tried in absentia.

“No more than 40 people have passed through the courts. And almost 30 of those will return to Russia in exchange for PoWs.

“It is a drop in the ocean compared with what we are dealing with. And a long wait for justice without a jail sentence.”



The UHHRU’s report highlights the system’s inability to manage such a large number of crimes.

Oleksandr said: “Some cases take years to build – but pre-trial detention is capped at one year. We are trying to get this extended to two but we still don’t know.

“This is the contradiction because normally legislation would be changed. But the system has been overloaded. We are working with the legislation of peacetime – but we are in wartime.”

Faced with limited possibilities, prosecutors have changed tactics.

Zuiz said: “We are now trying to combine evidence and group these crimes against leaders – higher level perpetrators.



“We are following the chain of command to establish responsibility, not just pushed the button.”

In doing so, Zuiz believes justice can reach even the highest level of the Russian Federation – including Putin.

Zuiz said: “We are looking to create a special tribunal to try 30 or 40 of those at the highest commanding level both on the military and political side.

“It is not hard to prove the atrocities they have caused. And if we do not bring them to justice now they will continue in the future.”

The International Criminal Court has issued warrants for four high-ranking Russian commanders and officials over crimes against humanity.



These include Lieutenant General Sergei Kobylash and Admiral Viktor Sokolov, Former Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu and Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov.

In 2023, the ICC issued a warrant for Putin over the deportation and transfer of children – designated a crime against humanity by the UN earlier this year.

Ukrainian authorities claim that Russia has illegally deported or forcibly displaced more than 19,500 children to Russia and Belarus, in violation of the Geneva Conventions.



After tracking 1,205 cases of children from five Ukrainian regions, the UN found that 80 per cent of them have not yet returned to Ukraine.

In another landmark case, Ukrainian prosecutors have accused Russia of committing crimes against humanity using drones to kill civilians.

A UN inquiry found last year that Putin‘s killer drones systematically targeted civilians in Kherson, a frontline region of southern Ukraine.

At least 287 civilians have been killed in Kherson, a frontline region of southern Ukraine, over the past two years.

Many of the attacks were filmed by the drones and uploaded on social media – leading to the name of “human safari” attacks.



Some sick Russian civilians are even facing shocking claims they pay soldiers to carry out the drone attacks and catch it all on camera.

One of the most complex cases Zuiz has worked on as a prosecutor was the Russian destruction of the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant dam on June 6, 2023.

It is considered to be one of Europe’s worst ecological disasters since Chernobyl – but remains occupied by Russian forces, blocking off vital evidence to ensure an air-tight case.

The breach unleashed roughly four cubic miles of water downstream, inundating homes and displacing tens of thousands of people across Kherson Oblast.



Recent environmental studies have warned that toxins will continue leaching into the Dnipro River and the north-western Black Sea for years, threatening regional water supplies.

Zuiz said: “The disaster has affected all of Ukraine because it has contaminated our water.

“A lot of evidence needs to be collected – we will have to combine all investigators and prosecutors at all levels for this case.”

Veronika’s department was established within the Prosecutor General’s Office in 2023 – just one year after Russia’s full- scale invasion.



Victims’ needs vary dramatically case to case, from psychological support to evacuation, security, social assistance or access to legal services.

A major challenge is victims’ unwillingness to testify in court out of fear of revenge from the Russian military against themselves or loved ones held captive in occupied territories.

Many others are reluctant to face prolonged and difficult trials.

Veronika said: “Due to the significant number of victims there are difficulties in ensuring access to quality professional legal assistance.

“Material and every day needs including destroyed housing are the main immediate requests of victims. Addressing this is an urgent task which unfortunately the state cannot fully manage.”



Veronika’s office is currently building a network of victim support programmes across Ukraine with regional prosecutors offices.

There are currently 12 units in operation from bases including Kyiv, Chernihiv, Sumy, Kharkiv and Kherson.

Together they are working to implement a digital referral platform for victims to access support services and contact key services directly.

Veronika said: “It is important for us to reach as many victims as possible.

“We understand the scale of the challenge facing law enforcement and the justice system. That is why our work is aimed at not only assisting individual victims but also building a system capable of effectively addressing such a scale.”



Veronika often asks victims what justice means to them.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Their answers go far beyond holding perpetrators to account”, she said.

“It means having the opportunity to be heard and the ability to rebuild their lives after what they have experienced.”

News.title: I was dumped in a phonebox when I was born – I owe my life to passer-by – but when I found my mum again it broke me
News.content:
Next

AMONG the rubbish on the floor of a red phone box lay a newborn baby girl, her umbilical cord still attached after her mother abandoned her.

She might have gone unnoticed had a stranger not stopped to make a call and spotted what he first thought was a discarded chip wrapper one bitterly cold morning. Now, 32 years later, April Paul is telling her extraordinary story – including the heartbreaking encounter with the mum who gave her up.



April was found by kind-hearted Joe Campbell in the early hours of the morning in Forest Gate, East London.

He immediately called the police, who rushed the tiny tot to Newham General Hospital, where she was given the name April after the month in which she was born.

But while Joe had saved her life, he would spend years wondering what had happened to the little girl he had rescued.



He never forgot her, taking birthday cards, gifts and money to social services every year in the hope they would reach her.

He even asked if he could adopt her, but was turned down because he was unmarried at the time.

After years of trying to maintain contact, he was eventually told by social workers to stop.



April, meanwhile, was adopted by another family and given a new name, only learning the truth about her traumatic start in life when she was eight.

The pair were finally reunited in 2016 after a public appeal, when Joe’s colleague recognised him as the man who had found the abandoned baby decades earlier.

Since then, he has become one of the most important people in April’s life, offering the love and support she says she struggled to find elsewhere.

Now, for the first time, April has laid bare her anger towards her biological mother, accusing her of selfishly abandoning her.

She told The Sun: “My mother was so selfish.



“She neglected me and gave me the toughest start in life.”

April told The Sun she had tried to reach out to her mum years later, hoping to understand why she had been “left to die” in the phone box.

But she claims the woman slammed the door in her face, swore at her and told her never to make contact again.



She said: “Can you imagine how heartbreaking that was? What had I actually done wrong to her?

“It felt like I could have died for all she cared, she left me in the phone box on what I have learnt was a bitterly cold morning.”

April said she wanted to try to bring the family back together and reconcile with her mother, but those efforts have failed.

And she had previously kept in touch with one of her siblings, but the two have since lost contact .

She said: “Sadly though for one reason or another we are not in touch these days.



“Like I said, I have tried to unite us, and reconcile with my mum, but it just isn’t happening, she doesn’t want to know.”

Despite the pain of her childhood, April has since built a life of her own.

She works in a bank and is now a mother herself, raising a son while continuing to rely on Joe for the support she says has made such a difference.



She said: “I am now a mother to a son, I work in a bank, and I have Joe there, who is the closest thing to family, other than my son, who I can have, he actually cares about me.”

April has not ruled out a reconciliation with her biological mother, saying she would not prevent her son from having a relationship with his grandmother if the woman came forward.

She said: “If she wants to come out of wherever she is and reunite, then that is on her, she is a grandmother now and I would never stand in the way of my son and her having a relationship.”

Now in her 30s, April said she was no longer holding grudges, but still struggled to make sense of the decision that changed her life before it had barely begun.

She said: “Obviously, I am upset and putting feelings into words is not easy for me, but my message to her is where is your humanity and ultimately why?



“Why would you do this to me?”

April said she was shocked that no action appeared to have been taken despite what happened.

She said: “To be honest, I am surprised, now as an adult and a parent looking back.

“I was a newborn baby, in a phone box with my umbilical cord attached.”

“It seems crazy to me that the authorities took no action.”



While April has been left with painful questions about her past, she says she will always be grateful to the man who stopped that freezing morning from ending in tragedy.

Joe, who never gave up hope of finding the little girl he rescued, has remained a constant in her life since their reunion.

April has now launched a fundraising appeal to help him enjoy a more comfortable retirement, hoping to repay some of the kindness he showed her when she was at her most vulnerable.

She said Joe had given her a chance at life without ever asking for anything in return – and now she wants to give something back to the man who became family when she needed it most.

News.title: Urgent search for missing woman, 49, last seen wearing pyjamas in UK national park
News.content:
FIND HER Urgent search for missing woman, 49, last seen wearing pyjamas in UK national park







Next

AN URGENT search has been launched for a missing woman who was last seen wearing pyjamas in a UK national park.

Sarah, 49, vanished from Troutbeck Bridge in Windermere, Cumbria on the morning of October 18.

Cumbria Police said she was last spotted at around 8.30am and have now launched an urgent appeal for information on her whereabouts.

The force described Sarah as 5ft 3in with blonde hair while she also wears glasses.





She was last seen wearing navy and red pyjamas and may be wearing a pink fleece.

Troutbeck Bridge is a small village located within the Lake District National Park.

A police spokesperson said: “Police are concerned for Sarah’s welfare and are encouraging anyone who can help to make contact.

Anyone who sees Sarah is asked to call 999.”

Those who may have spotted the 49-year-old or have information are urged to contact the force quoting incident number 67 of October 18 2026.

News.title: Polanski says he will not overturn Green Party's 'Zionism is racism' motion
News.content:
Zack Polanski has said he will not overturn a motion passed by Green Party members that declared Zionism a form of racism.

The Green leader told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that, while he would like to make amendments, it would be party policy until 2028.

The motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month, described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".

It divided the party and sparked a major backlash from MPs, Jewish campaigners, the government and the European Green movement, with the equality watchdog writing to the party for more information on it.

The fallout from the motion overshadowed the final days of Polanski's campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, in which he came second to Labour, and threatened his leadership.

He came under criticism for not voting on the motion which was passed by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the party's 230,000 members - in Brighton earlier this month.

The motion also asserted the party's backing for "a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine", a full arms embargo on Israel and a commitment to Palestinian liberation.

Asked if he would now step in as leader to overturn it, Polanski said: "I'm not going to try to overturn it.

"At the first available opportunity, I do want to amend it - I want to move away from one state, towards saying that Israelis and Palestinians should decide that future for themselves."

He said this would not be until 2028 as "you can't [amend it] within the rules, so when you vote on something in our party conference that's then policy for two years".

Kuenssberg asked if he would therefore change the rules as leader, but Polanski said: "I think if members have made a decision, then I respect the democratic will of our members."

Polanski had previously said he would not have voted for the motion without two amendments.

The first of these would have avoided "determining there was a single democratic state", and the other would have specified that the motion should not be used to discipline Jewish Green members who attend synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.

Both of these amendments were voted down by members at the party's conference.

Green MPs, including Ellie Chowns, have called for the party's member-led decision-making procedures to be reviewed given how few people took part in the vote.

Asked if he thought Zionism was racist, Polanski said did not think this was controversial, adding: "I think what's controversial is that 75,000 Palestinians have been murdered in the last few years."

He said they were "being murdered because they're Palestinian" and said that was "very obviously a racist ideology".

Kuenssberg asked Polanski if he accepted that for many Jewish people, Zionism was the right to have a safe place to live, or homeland.

"I think that's what people think it means, but actually in practical application - which is what we're talking about here - that homeland has come to the cost of the Palestinian people," Polanski, who is Jewish, said.

"I want equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians - the practical application of Zionism has not resulted in that."

He reiterated that no Jewish Green members would be excluded based on their faith or background.

He also said being Jewish and supporting Israel were "two separate things".

Polanski's latest comments come after a fortnight of criticism from across the political spectrum over the motion.

On Thursday, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) wrote to the party asking for more information about the motion and its practical effects.

The regulator said "many Jewish people will be feeling vulnerable", but said it needed more details to assess if any parts of it could be considered discriminatory under the 2010 Equality Act, after a letter from dozens of Labour and Lib Dem MPs.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews has criticised the motion as an "attack on the Jewish community". Responding to its passing it said: "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it."

Labour has said it will end power-sharing agreements with the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disown the motion. Polanski said it was up to Green councillors to do what they saw fit.

The motion's author, Green Party member Lubna Speitan, said this week that the Labour government had been a "participant in genocide" and had "no moral high ground to talk to us about antisemitism, racism or any other matter".

The International Court of Justice is currently hearing a case that accuses Israeli forces of genocide. Israel has said the accusations are "wholly unfounded" and based on "biased and false claims".

News.title: Ending corridor care in hospitals for children a priority, says health secretary
News.content:
The health secretary has asked the NHS to draw up urgent plans to speed up ending hospital "corridor care" for children.

Yvette Cooper told the BBC there would be new standards for caring for children in A&E in England, with figures collected on corridor care by age for the first time.

She was speaking on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg where the programme highlighted the case of two-year-old Finlay Roberts who died in a hospital corridor in 2024.

The health secretary has announced Â£140m to improve urgent care in England ahead of what she said would be a "more difficult" winter than usual.

The government has already pledged to end corridor care for all patients by the end of this parliament, and now Cooper has said eradicating it for children would be prioritised.

Corridor care refers to patients receiving treatment or waiting in corridors, waiting rooms or other hospital areas due to a lack of appropriate space.

The health secretary was also asked if the government would meet a key manifesto pledge that 92% of patients would start treatment within 18 weeks of booking a hospital appointment by 2029.

"That remains our manifesto commitment and of course we're going to keep working towards it," Cooper said.

Pushed further on whether the target was achievable, she replied: "The whole point about having the targets is about having something stretching that we work towards."

The 18-week target has consistently not been met for more than a decade.

Cooper said that the NHS was dealing with a number of challenges after record A&E admissions following heatwaves over the summer.

According to the latest figures for England, an estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.

On the programme the story of Finlay Roberts, who died in 2024 after spending the final hours of his life in an A&E corridor in north London was highlighted.

Finlay's father David told the BBC the situation was a "terrible mess", with the family moved into a room with a bed before being moved back into the corridor.

"He just clung to me, as we now know, slowly dying," he said.

Liz Roberts, Finlay's mother, said corridor care "robs people of their dignity when they are at their most vulnerable". She recalled being told to administer a suppository to her son in the corridor.

Cooper apologised to Finlay's parents on behalf of the NHS, saying: "No child should be treated in a corridor. No patient should be treated in a corridor."

News.title: Watch: Police hunt for synthetic drugs in Chicago jail
News.content:
Chicago's largest jail, and the largest single use jail in America, is Cook County.

In 2023 it saw a spike in overdose deaths. The facility, which averages one or two overdose deaths a year, lost eight inmates that year to fatal seizures. Security footage shows prisoners spasming and collapsing.

Traditional drugs were usually brought into the jail in body cavities, so the jail had the same body scanners you find at airports to prevent that happening. However, a new way of drugs entering the prison was uncovered. Drugs were being mailed into the jail soaked in the paper of the pages of books and in letters.

The BBC's Quentin Sommerville joined corrections officers at Cook County as they prepared for an early morning raid on the jail's high security D block.

To understand the challenge that authorities face in tackling the problem the BBC interviewed a former inmate and dealer, who explained how synthetic drugs can be made in the US using household ingredients and how this could change the demand for drugs from outside of the country.

Read more here.

News.title: Suspects hunted after police officer injured in shooting
News.content:
Detectives are searching for two suspects who fled after a police officer was shot in Nottingham city centre.

Nottinghamshire Police said the officer had approached two suspects in Angel Row shortly before 04:50 BST on Sunday.

The officer is in a stable condition in hospital, where he is receiving treatment for a wound to his foot, the force added.

Detectives said a man and a woman had fled the scene and that a firearm, which could be seen within the cordon, had been found.

Angel Row is currently closed and a large police scene remains in place.

Police cars are parked along the road, which is lined by fast food stores and shops, and orange traffic cones have been laid out alongside items left on the road.

The cordon has also been extended to St James's Street, where an officer is standing guard.

The force said there would be a heightened police presence as the investigation continues.

News.title: Photos show luxury boat with 50m pool and water slides near Kim Jong Un's summer retreat
News.content:
An 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year.

What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end.

After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula.

This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family.

It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC.

The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size.

News.title: There's a crackdown on sports piracy but is it already out of control?
News.content:
"Football's Gone Round the Spend!" screamed The People newspaper one Sunday in July 1995. It reported breathlessly that three clubs between them were set to pay out more than Â£20m on new players.

The highlight that summer was the transfer of Stan Collymore from Nottingham Forest to Liverpool for a British record fee of Â£8.5m.

That number might not seem too impressive today, in an age when Â£100m transfers are almost commonplace. But at the time it was seismic stuff, and it symbolised the conversion of football from sport into big business.

All of this had been made possible in the early 1990s by the creation of the Premier League, and its initial TV deal with the broadcaster Sky, which paid more than Â£300m for five years of rights. The agreement put live top-tier football behind a TV paywall for the first time.

It was a lucrative model, one that other leading championships in motorsport, rugby, golf and cricket would later seek to replicate.

But now, that model is coming under pressure. Piracy has become endemic in British sports: around half of sports fans now admit to using what they might euphemistically call "alternative" means to watch paywalled material, according to the consultancy Ampere Analysis.

News.title: Braam! How the music in The Traitors plays with your emotions
News.content:
Suspicion, intrigue, treachery, Claudia Winkleman. The Traitors has it all.

But the shadowiest of the show's shadowy secrets is its music.

Have you ever noticed how the soundtrack manipulates your perception? A sinister orchestral flourish hints at a double cross. A cheeky chord injects humour into a kitchen conflab.

As ever, though, you shouldn't trust what happens in the castle. The music can provide emphasis or act as misdirection, all at the producers' behest.

Duplicity was baked into the music from the beginning.

"I remember the BBC was quite reluctant to even think about a show with murder as a main feature, so I knew I didn't want the music to go really dark," says Sam Watts, who composed the opening theme and much of the incidental score (but is not responsible for the show's haunting cover versions of well-known pop songs... more on those later).

Watts, who had previously worked on Planet Earth and The Sarah Jane Adventures, pitched to work on the programme with only a basic idea of the set-up. It was only when he learned Winkleman was the host that he settled on his approach.

"They sent me a little shot they'd done of the opening with Claudia and the castle. That's when I knew it was going to be a bit camp and high drama and all the glorious things that Claudia brings to the show. So I just went with that - dark but fun."

News.title: Man, 80, who died in light aircraft crash near Loch Lomond named
News.content:
An 80-year-old man who died in a light aircraft crash is understood to be flying instructor Ian Haggis.

He and a 16-year-old boy died when their plane came down near Loch Lomond. The teenager's identity has not been released.

The pair had flown out from Glasgow Airport at 16:17 and stopped transmitting at 16:37, a few miles north east of the village of Drymen near Stirling.

Emergency services were called to the scene of the crash at about 16:45 on Friday.

Both of them were pronounced dead at the scene.

Temporary airspace restrictions are currently in place over the area while the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) carries out its inquiries.

A road near the scene of the crash remains closed, with vehicles being turned around and hillwalkers rerouted.

News.title: NHS data breaches a disgrace, says health secretary
News.content:
NHS staff accessing the medical records of the Nottingham attacks victims and possible breaches over a man killed by a tiger is a "disgrace", the health secretary has said.

Speaking to the BBC, Yvette Cooper said she expected action to be taken against staff who have breached NHS data and privacy standards.

Her comments came after Nottingham University Hospitals (NUH) NHS Trust confirmed it had sacked a total of 15 members of staff and Yorkshire Ambulance Service said William Chapman's medical records may have been accessed illegitimately.

Dr Manjeet Shehmar, NUH medical director, previously said there was "simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason".

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Cooper said "there's got to be proper respect for patients" from NHS staff.

"Let me be really clear about this," she said. "There are proper data and privacy standards across the NHS.

Students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Valdo Calocane, who was diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

NUH said in May that it had sacked 11 members of staff for inappropriately accessing the victims' medical records and had informed the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and Nottinghamshire Police of the investigation.

At the time, the ICO told the BBC it would "assess any evidence provided by the trust in due course and consider our next steps", while police said there was "no criminal investigation".

In its update about further dismissals on Friday, NUH said it had taken action against "doctors, nurses, registered healthcare professionals and other staff" and that independent regulators such as the Nursing and Midwifery Council and General Medical Council, the ICO and Nottinghamshire Police had been informed.

NUH added a new system, currently under testing, is being implemented to protect patient records in future and alert the trust to potential breaches.

News.title: Boy, 14, stabbed in shopping centre attack
News.content:
A 14-year-old boy has been stabbed in a car park at Manchester's Arndale Centre shopping mall.

Greater Manchester Police said the boy was injured on the 9th floor of Manchester's Arndale Centre just after 15:00 BST on Saturday.

The force said his injuries were not believed to be life threatening or life changing. The Arndale was closed for several hours after the stabbing.

Det Insp Sam Jones said: "This is believed to be an isolated incident with no risk to the wider public."

The BBC understands a row with other males had taken place beforehand.

No arrests have been made in connection with the stabbing so far and inquiries were continuing.

News.title: Comedian Paul Whitehouse mugged at London cash machine
News.content:
Actor and comedian Paul Whitehouse has fought back against someone who tried to steal his card at a London cash machine, according to his wife.

Dr Mine Conkbayir posted on Instagram that her husband had gone out to get some medication on Friday, when he was mugged at a cash machine behind a Sainsbury's in Islington.

"He did fight back and retrieved his card, with the perp scuttling away empty-handed," she wrote, warning people to be "super vigilant" out there.

The Welsh comedian, 68, is known for his work on The Fast Show and BBC's Gone Fishing.

In her post, Conkbayir said Whitehouse was picking up medication for her after she had a bad reaction to some treatment.

"Well, a horrid start to the weekend, would be an understatement," she wrote, adding that she had been encouraged by her husband to make the post "in the hope that it might help folk to be more aware when out and about".

Friends and fans alike have flooded to the comments of Conkbayir's post, condemning the attack and wishing Whitehouse a speedy recovery.

Among them were fellow comedian Dawn French, who wrote that the incident in Islington was "utterly not okay", and Angela Barnes, who said it was a "horrible thing to happen" and she was "sending love to you both".

Whitehouse is best known for his work on Gone Fishing, which he presents alongside fellow comedian Bob Mortimer.

The BBC Two series began in 2018 and sees Whitehouse and Mortimer discuss life while fishing. It has been nominated six times for a Bafta TV award.

The comedian has also been cast as Hogwarts caretaker Argus Filch in HBO's upcoming Harry Potter television series.

News.title: Reform activist suspended after reportedly saying Muslims cannot be British
News.content:
Reform UK has suspended a party activist who reportedly said that you cannot be Muslim and British in footage recorded by an undercover reporter from ITV News.

It is also investigating two of its councillors who appear to have advocated for the mass shooting of grooming gang members in the footage.

The party's response follows the latest allegations from undercover filming by ITV News, external, which has led to Reform facing questions over its vetting procedures for candidates.

A party spokesperson told the BBC it was pursuing legal action against ITV and the documentary's production company which had used undercover reporting to obtain its material.

Reform said in a statement to ITV there is "no room for racism" in the party, and added that it has opened investigations where activists or members had "clearly behaved inappropriately".

In the ITV documentary Undercover: A Year in Reform - set to be broadcast on Sunday - party activist Jason Powell reportedly says: "You cannot be Muslim and British, it's like oil and water."

In the footage, Powell, who has applied to be a Reform parliamentary candidate, also says he believes migrants who arrive illegally should be kept in "concentration camps" if they cannot be returned to their country of origin.

Reform said Powell has been suspended from party membership while an internal investigation takes place.

Reform is also investigating two councillors who represent the party in the London borough of Hounslow.

In the footage, Councillor David Kerr advocates machine gunning thousands of grooming gang members.

His colleague Councillor Adam Parkins suggests if he became prime minister he would conduct Sunday morning executions in the Downing Street rose garden.

Mr Parkins told the BBC that advocating the death penalty for men who "systemically groomed and raped young girls" was a perfectly legitimate opinion.

Mr Kerr has been contacted for comment.

Reform UK has said it has prioritised and improved its vetting procedures.

On Wednesday night, ITV News broadcast undercover filming which showed some of Reform's councillors and candidates using racist, violent and sexist language.

Responding to the broadcast, Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick said all political parties had "bad apples".

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, he said he "didn't like what I heard in the documentary" but argued that the party had acted quickly, removing or suspending those in the undercover film.

News.title: Swinney's emotional explanation for his commitment to independence
News.content:
This was a more emotional speech than we are used to from John Swinney.

His voice quivered as he explained that his personal commitment to the cause is for the future of his 15-year-old son, Matthew.

Then the autocue stalled and the SNP leader is heard saying under his breath "oh, come on".

A period of silence was broken by the conference crowd who came to his rescue with a standing ovation.

Without the prime minister's name being mentioned, this section of the speech seemed to be a response to Andy Burnham's emotional appeal for the union in memory of his father at the Labour conference in Liverpool.

News.title: 'Learning to read in my 80s has changed my life'
News.content:
An 86-year-old man said learning to read has enabled him to read his and his wife's anniversary cards for the first time in 65 years.

Alan Hannay, from Dibden Purlieu, learned to read through the charity Read Easy, which helps adults across the country who struggle with the skill many of us take for granted.

Hannay told BBC Radio Solent: "It's changed my whole life, my confidence, changed my family life and everything around me.

"It's one of the best experiences I've ever had in my life."

Hannay said he now reads every morning for about an hour and a half and goes to the class twice a week.

"I enjoy it so much now," he said.

The charity said Hannay is an "inspiring example of determination and courage".

It said he asked his local library in Hythe, Southampton, about learning to read, which led him to the charity and his reading coach, Angie.

During his working life as a professional chauffeur, he relied on his memory to drive his clients around London, and at the age of 70 he attended evening classes to improve his reading.

However, he found the group situation difficult.

News.title: House that looks like boulders to be built on moor
News.content:
Plans for a house designed to look like rocks on a famous Yorkshire moor have been approved.

The contemporary structure, which has large irregular-shaped windows and a natural outdoor pool, looks similar to the landmark Cow and Calf Rocks in Ilkley, West Yorkshire.

The house will be built on green belt land which is the garden of a home off Heber's Ghyll Drive, and will be eco-friendly, to an ultra-low energy standard called Passivhaus.

Harrogate-based architects Shaw & Jagger said the scheme was eventually passed by HM Planning Inspectorate through the country house clause, which allows development on green belt for buildings of "exceptional quality".

The architect Matt Masserella-Gill was commissioned to design the home by the landowner David Rasche.

He said the design was "arguably the most complex country house application ever made in this country".

The house has been named Fomorian - meaning a supernatural race of giants in Irish mythology - taking inspiration from the mythical giant Rombald who is told to have lived on Ilkley Moor.

Masserella-Gill said: "The design approach was to propose a scheme that is intrinsically linked to the spirit of its place. Fomorian is of its place, part of the moors, its geology and its spirit.

"We took cues from local folklore, the surrounding rocks; ancient carvings, standing stones and escarpments that are synonymous with the landscape."

News.title: Sonay Kartal’s dream run to Wuhan Open final ends in defeat to Maja Chwalinska
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Sonay Kartal’s brilliant run at the Wuhan Open ended in a bruising three-set loss to French Open finalist Maja Chwalinska.

The Briton dominated the first set but was reeled back in thanks to a gritty performance from 16th seed Chwalinska, who converted her third match point at the end of a nervy final game to win 2-6, 6-4, 6-2.

The 25-year-old, who beat world No 11 Iva Jovic and six-time grand slam champion Iga Swiatek to make her first WTA 1000 final, collapsed to the court in relief as she sealed the title in two hours and 43 minutes.

While it’s a disappointing result for Kartal, this week has nonetheless been a superb step up in only her third tournament since a six-month injury layoff following a stress fracture in her back.

She had never previously gone beyond the quarter-finals at a WTA 1000 event, the level below the majors. The 24-year-old did it the hard way, dispatching three seeded players in a row in former Olympic champion Belinda Bencic, two-time major finalist Jasmine Paolini and world No 6 Elina Svitolina, before beating former French Open winner Jelena Ostapenko in the semi-finals.

Having been ranked 170th in the world after her injury lay-off, Kartal was the lowest-ranked WTA 1000 finalist since the format was introduced 17 years ago, and only the second British woman ever to make a final at this level after Johanna Konta.

She will climb to 50th in the world when the rankings are updated on Monday and replace Katie Boulter as the British No 1.

Momentum swung repeatedly over the course of the encounter, with nine breaks in the first 18 games. Kartal was superior in the first set against a flat Chwalinska but the Pole came out fighting in the second, with her unusual, crafty style, changes of pace and direction and lefty serve causing problems.

Kartal was broken in a mammoth game at 3-3 but upped her aggression to break straight back, only to be on the receiving end of a third straight break thanks to an unlucky net cord at 40-15. Chwalinska deployed the drop shot to great effect and forced a deciding set with a tidy backhand volley at the net.

open image in gallery Chwalinska fell to the ground in relief as she converted her third championship point ( Reuters )

After a run of four straight holds, Kartal was first to blink in the decider, with the Briton broken to love as she shanked a forehand wide for 2-3.

Chwalinska continued to impose herself, replying to a Kartal drop shot with a better one of her own to earn a break point at 4-2, and converting it immediately as she pushed Kartal behind the baseline, with the world No 170 firing long under pressure.

Both players were wracked with nerves as Chwalinska served for the title: Kartal missed three break points while Chwalinska spurned her first two championship points before finally converting the third as the Brit hit long.

News.title: As France burns, Macron looks like a man who has lost control
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

In his last few months as president of the French Republic, Emmanuel Macron looks more than ever a man who lost control of events, lost touch with the nation he leads, and lost the confidence of international investors with it. This is not a comfortable, confident position for any leader to be, but with a hung parliament hardly able to pass a budget and the very fabric of of the nation unravelling, this lame duck - who once promised so much with his unifying project of a radical centre - has been, and is, reacting in all the wrong ways to the malaise now enveloping his country.

Rather than through, say, a television interview or a speech delivered in person, President Macron, so inappropriately aloof, chose initially to react to the protests that have broken out across France over the weekend, sparking disorder, violence and hundreds of arrests in a rather terse statement on X: “Those who took part in the vandalism, attacked prefectures and stores, and engaged in looting, including in city hall buildings, will be brought to justice and will be punished.”

Unarguably, those who choose violence should take the consequences, but the government always had the choice between meeting the representatives of the protesters, the classic French mix of students and workers, now bolstered by the resurgent gilets jaunes, listening to their grievances and offering some sympathy and change. Instead, the Macron administration ordered the riot police to do their worst.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

Originating in a secondary school protest in the Paris suburb of school in Creteil, southeast of Paris, over a lack of teachers, and culminating in well over half a million people on the streets, many suffering life-changing injuries from police weapons, the authorities have reacted with a counter-productive brutality. A police tear gas grenade shattered a 14-year-old’s jaw and many of his teeth. A 15-year-old lost a hand in an incident involving a police stun grenade. Other adolescents have also suffered life-changing injuries blamed on police weaponry during protests.

No wonder trade unionists and others have joined the protest movement, adding the cost of living, fuel prices (as in other western countries a triggering issue) and a general sense of national pessimism and insecurity. In this way, these disturbances combine some of the themes that caused such comparable disorder in 1958, 1968 and 2005, all of which similarly drained the governments of the day of authority. More than in most democracies, direct action has always been an informal clause of the French constitution, proof that sovereignty lies with the people, rather than any essentially ephemeral institutions or haughty ruler.

This time around, there is an additional issue facing M Macron. Just as ominous as this unrest, and potentially much more far-reaching, has been the other, simultaneous challenge, to the stability of the French state - an incipient sovereign debt crisis reminiscent of the one that spread across the Eurozone fifteen years ago. Of all the major advanced economies, it is France that has suffered the most, and see the largest rise in its bond yields, and the more precipitous fall in the value of French government bonds, known as OATs (Obligations assimilables du Tresor.

open image in gallery A demonstrator carries a cardboard caricature depicting French President Emmanuel Macron as a baby holding euro banknotes and a rattle ( AFP/Getty )

As things stand the markets think that the debt issued by the likes of LVMH is more likely to hold its bake and be repaid than the paper offered by the French state. This is because the French national debt is too onerous, its economy too sluggish and its parliament and president jointly unable to get state spending down to sustainable levels - the mirror image of the complaint of the protesters, who want more spending on subsidies and schools. Hence the gridlock in policy making.

As in the earlier Eurozone crisis as it hit Greece, Italy and Spain, the eventual consequence of this devaluation of OATs will be a shrinkage in the balance sheets of the big banks, who own vast quantities of OATs. That would lead to a credit crunch and, most likely, a recession and similar “contagion” across the Eurozone, but this time with the second largest European economy at risk of default. A rescue by the European Central Bank (in practice Germany) would again demand some austerity.

The origins of these multiple crises are long and complex. However, prime among them stands President Macron’s capricious decision to call premature elections to the French parliament in 2024, at a time when he still enjoyed a comfortable majority. It was designed to renew his mandate after his party had been snubbed in the European elections. Instead, it left France with an entirely dysfunctional domestic government, and contributed to more intense political polarisation - the rise of the far right and of the hard left.

France was left rudderless. This kind of “immobilisme” is not uncommon in French history, but it rarely ends well. Apres Macron, le deluge?

News.title: Police officer hospitalised after shooting in Nottingham city centre
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Read our Privacy notice

A police officer has been injured after he was shot in Nottingham city centre.

The officer, who is in hospital with a foot wound, had approached two suspects in Angle Row shortly before the incident at 4.50am on Sunday, Nottinghamshire Police said.

The two suspects, a man and a woman, fled the scene and a firearm has been recovered by police.

Assistant Chief Constable Claire Rukas said: “This is a shocking incident and a sobering reminder of the potential dangers faced by officers as they work to protect and serve the public.

“As we investigate what happened and work to apprehend the individuals involved, my thoughts today are with the injured officer, his family and colleagues.

“I also ask that anyone with additional information shares this with us without delay. Even the smallest bit of information could make all the difference to this investigation.”

open image in gallery A firearm at the scene on Angel Row in Nottingham, after a police officer has been shot in the city centre ( PA )

Nottingham East Labour MP Nadia Whittome wrote on X: “My thoughts are with the injured police officer and his family following this truly shocking incident. We all wish him a full and speedy recovery.”

Councillor Neghat Khan, Leader of Nottingham City Council, said: “I am deeply shocked and saddened by the news of this morning’s shooting. My thoughts and full support are with the injured police officer, their family, and their colleagues across Nottinghamshire Police.

​”Nottingham City Council is working tirelessly alongside the police to support the investigation and ensure those responsible are swiftly caught and brought to justice.

​”While incidents of this nature are extremely rare, our commitment to keeping Nottingham safe is absolute. Thanks to the daily bravery of our police and Community Protection Officers, Nottingham remains a safe city, and residents can be assured that every available resource is being deployed.”

open image in gallery The officer, who is in hospital with a foot wound, had approached two suspects in Angel Row shortly before the incident at 4.50am on Sunday, Nottinghamshire Police said ( PA )

The Police Federation of England and Wales also sent its best wishes to the officer.

“This is a stark reminder of the dangers police officers face every day while protecting the public,” it added in a social media post.

“Their courage and commitment must never be taken for granted.”

Anyone with information is urged to call 101 quoting incident 106 of 18 October 2026.

News.title: Experts say ‘lymphatic walking’ can help with circulation, so I tried it for a month. Here’s how it went
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

It’s a Wednesday afternoon and I’m walking around New York City like I belong to Monty Python’s Ministry of Silly Walks.

My arms are whirling like wet noodles, my shoulders are pressed back and I’m taking long, deliberate steps. Then there’s the hitting and the breathing: I inhale deeply for five seconds before exhaling and smacking myself in the arm.

This unconventional practice is so-called “lymphatic walking “- a TikTok trend that’s supposed to improve circulation, fight puffiness, boost energy and elevate mood.

The idea appears to have germinated on social media, and hundreds of people have filmed themselves getting involved. I became a lymphatic walker for about a month, doing so nearly daily and largely in public. I walked about 20 minutes at a time, several times a day.

But does it work? Experts say there are benefits, though what I felt, mostly, was silly.

open image in gallery This exercise routine, as seen in action from The Independent’s science correspondent Julia Musto, is known as ‘lymphatic walking’ ( Julia Musto/Zack Palomo )

Lymphatic drainage has become a hot wellness topic in recent years with the popularization of jade rollers and other beauty industry tools meant to reduce facial puffiness.

The process massages the skin, seeking to relieve swelling that occurs when the lymphatic system – organs, vessels and tissues that protect the body from infection – is damaged, leading to a build up of clear fluid called lymph. These massages have real benefits, reducing excess fluids and supporting a healthy immune system. And this appears to be how lymphatic walking was born.

Hannah Campbell, a lecturer in applied human physiology at the U.K.’s University of Leeds, wrote a piece about the trend in The Conversation this past August.

There’s some science behind the idea because muscles help move fluid in the lymphatic system, she told The Independent. The more active the muscles, the more fluid that moves through you.

open image in gallery Actor John Cleese performs a silly walk in the legendary Monty Python sketch, Ministry of Silly Walks in 1970 ( Public Domain )

open image in gallery One TikTok user taps his chest while lymphatic walking on a walking pad. Swinging the arms is supposed to help fluid move through tissue that filters out harmful cells and other substances ( @bradcusworth/TikTok )

When you’re swinging your arms, you’re helping fluid move through the upper lymph nodes, areas of tissue that filter fluids in the body for harmful cells or substances, Campbell said.

The heel-toe contact of steps helps push lymph through vessels from our feet. Hitting the body is supposed to work similarly, and even breathing deeply shifts pressure in the abdomen that moves fluid around.

However, there just isn’t research supporting the trend as a whole. “In terms of generally healthy individuals, there is no evidence to support this special type of lymphatic movement or lymphatic walking,” she said.

Campbell believes the trend potentially does more good for the nervous system, coordination and motor control than it does for the lymphatic system because of the focus it requires and actions that stimulate the nerves.

open image in gallery Hannah Campbell, a lecturer in applied human physiology at the University of Leeds, says there’s some science behind the idea because muscles help move fluid in the lymphatic system ( Julia Musto/Zoom )

To benefit the lymphatic system, other forms of walking and movement work just as well, she said. “Going for walks, lifting weights, dancing. It's about trying to be more active, or just generally move more,” said Campbell.

I definitely felt more active the first few times I did it. The exaggerated movements were more of a workout than an average walk. However it was hard to tell if it made any difference to my body’s fluid retention.

However, Campbell says - at day’s end - it’s not necessarily about the trend, but what movement does for your body.

open image in gallery One TikTok user swings her arms while lymphatic walking. Experts say just getting up and moving is the key to regulating the lymphatic system ( @organic_girlx/TikTok )

That’s a conclusion Rebecca Faria, the founder of Beverly Hills lymphatic massage clinic Detox by Rebecca, agrees with.

“Your heart is a pump. It pushes your blood around your body all day and you never think about it. Your lymphatic system does not have a pump. There is no motor inside,” Faria, who lists actor Anne Hathaway and singer Miley Cyrus among her clients, explained to The Independent. “It only moves when something moves it, and your muscles can do that.”

Unfortunately, Americans’ increasingly sedentary lifestyle raises their risk of painful lymphedema, swelling that occurs when there’s a blockage in the lymphatic system, UCSF Health notes.

Up to 10 million Americans suffer from the condition, according to the Lymphatic Education and Research Network. The condition can raise the risk of deadly skin infections, such as cellulitis.

open image in gallery Just using muscles can help fluid flow throughout the body. Sedentary lifestyles leave people at risk of lymphedema, a painful swelling condition ( Julia Musto and Zack Palomo )

A lot of people don’t have control over how long they sit if they have long commutes or are desk-bound most of the day.

To help keep the lymphatic system functioning well, Faria advises 10-20 minutes of walking after sitting for a while. Lying down and putting your legs up against a wall for a similar period of time also helps drain any stagnant fluid, with gravity doing the work.

Investing in a pair of compression socks may work, too. They typically sell for at least $25 a pair.

“Compression socks work on the same idea. They give your legs a constant, even hug, so the fluid does not have space to pool down there. Your calf muscles are pumping all day, and the socks help them do that job better,” Faria said.

News.title: Leeds vs Man United LIVE: Score and updates from crunch Premier League clash
News.content:

( Reuters )

Leeds United play host to old rivals Manchester United this afternoon in a crucial Premier League contest for both teams.

Daniel Farke’s side have begun the season in superb fashion and sit seventh in the table following two wins and three draws from their first five matches. Last time out the suffered their first league defeat of the season as Premier League champions Arsenal came from behind to clinch a 2-1 victory at the Emirates Stadium after James Justin had given the Whites the lead. Yet despite the result Farke was pleased with his team’s performance and he will take confidence into today’s clash against a struggling Man Utd.

Michael Carrick’s team have won only once in the league so far – against Ipswich in August – and pressure is mounting on the manager to turn around their form. The noise around the club only increased during the week following a bombshell interview from Lisandro Martinez, which he has since apologised for, in which he took aim at the United hierarchy for a lack of investment.

Carrick knows the only way to quiet outside noise is to secure positive results on the pitch and he and his team will attempt to do so at Elland Road today.

News.title: UK to France ferry route closes early after more than 40 years
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Brittany Ferries has discontinued a historic ferry route connecting the UK and France after more than four decades.

The direct Poole to Cherbourg, Normandy, service set sail for the final time on Monday, three weeks earlier than the ferry operator had planned.

Served by the Barfleur since 1992, the operational change will see the vessel moved to cover Rosslare to Cherbourg sailings from 12 October.

The last crossing was originally planned for the end of the month.

Contentin, the vessel formerly used on the Rosslare route, has been sold by Brittany Ferries and was required to be withdrawn from service by mid-October.

A potential backup vessel, the Commodore Clipper, suffered a “significant technical problem” with a gearbox failure earlier this month, forcing its withdrawal from the fleet pending remedial work.

The gearbox problem pushed the early closure of the Portsmouth to Le Havre route, with Barfleur moved early.

According to Brittany Ferries, bookings on the Poole to Cherbourg had “already weakened” ahead of the route closure.

Brittany Ferries began operating on the Poole to Cherbourg route in 1985 following its acquisition of Truckline Ferries, which originally established the route as a freight service in 1973. Barfleur’s first sailing from Rosslare to Cherbourg departed on 12 October.

The company has apologised to all affected travellers, offering alternative travel from Portsmouth or a full refund.

Christophe Mathieu, CEO of Brittany Ferries, said: “The reality is that, post Brexit, Rosslare/Cherbourg has become a strategically significant route for Brittany Ferries, carrying nearly 25 per cent of all freight traffic, so we must prioritise.

“I know there will be disappointment with this operational change, and I apologise to all those travelling from Poole in the latter half of October. We shall of course refund tickets or provide alternative travel on routes out of Portsmouth.

“It has been a privilege to serve the Poole-Cherbourg route since 1986. But we should be clear that we will still sail to Guernsey and onto France in our fast craft from Poole, even if we must say an early adieu to a much-loved vessel and direct services from Poole to Cherbourg.”
