News.title: I worked on death row for 18 years. This is why the livestream execution was cancelled
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Since the US Supreme Court reinstated capital punishment in 1976, state and federal authorities have executed 1,684 individuals.

For half a century, this violence has been conducted with clinical distance – shrouded in quiet, standardised procedure.

When defence secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan would be broadcast live to the world, that bureaucratic veneer dissolved.

Labeled by the United Nations as “tantamount to a public execution” – a spectacle unseen in American justice for nearly a century – the Pentagon’s proposal transformed state-sanctioned killing into primetime political theatre.

Donald Trump has since backtracked, reversing the decision to stream the execution following international condemnation and internal political friction.

But for Dr Asim Qureshi, director of CAGE International, who has spent two decades navigating the legal mechanics of America’s death row, viewing this retreat as a victory for human decency is to misunderstand how the Trump administration operates. ‘

The policy balloon has been floated, the precedent logged, and the public appetite tested.

open image in gallery Pete Hegseth announced the decision to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan by firing squad earlier last week ( AFP/Getty )

“Mine was quite a reaction of horror,” Dr Qureshi says, reflecting on the initial announcement of the live streaming. “It’s presented as accountability, transparency, justice – but at the heart of it, it is this fascination with wanting to show power. This administration is built on the optics of projecting power.”

When a government seeks to broadcast a state killing, it relies on a specific, fragile logic: that absolute dominance can be demonstrated through controlled violence.

The White House’s sudden U-turn exposes the inherent risk of that calculation. Unfiltered spectacle is a political “wild card”, which, once broadcast, cannot be controlled.

“I think one of the main reasons it was cancelled is that the Trump administration has discovered that livestreaming horror doesn’t really work,” Dr Qureshi explains, pointing to the shift in global consciousness over recent years.

“For the past three years, we’ve watched a livestreamed genocide. And because of it, opinions toward Israel – across both the Democrat and Republican parties – are at an all-time low.”

In criminal defence, “mitigation” is the methodical reconstruction of a defendant’s life to understand the factors that brought them to the moment of their crime. In bringing a camera into the execution chamber, the state unwittingly invites the public to conduct its own act of mitigation.

“To livestream an execution would force people to mitigate and reassess the case of Nidal Hasan,” Dr Qureshi states.

“When it comes to it, Nidal Hasan’s issue was with American malfeasance across the world – his reasons were rooted in American foreign policy in Afghanistan and Iraq. And I don’t think Trump, or anyone in his administration, wants people asking those questions.”

This creates “a bizarre duality” for the White House: where the desire to punish Hasan for his actions must be reconciled with the possibility that Americans may interrogate what led to them.

open image in gallery The livestreaming of Nidal Hasan’s execution may encourage viewers to conduct their own act of mitigation, cautions Dr Qureshi ( Bell County Sheriff’s Office )

But even in the cancellation of the livestream, the proposal has already changed the course of American justice. By floating the idea of a televised execution, the state has expanded the boundaries of what violence can be considered “just”.

“If you want to shift public opinion, you need to bring the most egregious act to the table,” Dr Qureshi explains. “And bit by bit, the mainstream narrative will move toward the next, slightly less egregious thing.

“It’s worked, because everybody is talking about whether Nidal Hasan’s execution should be livestreamed, but nobody’s talking about why he is being executed in the first place.

“And in doing so, it has made a future livestreamed execution a much more realistic possibility.”

But this baseline has never been a just one.

“We are looking at a country where 98 per cent of criminal defendants are coerced into plea deals, where one third of Black men face the shadow of incarceration, and where children lose years of their lives to wrongful convictions,” explains Dr Qureshi.

“This is not a system suffering from administrative flaws. It is an unjust system.

“This livestreamed execution is not indicative of anything other than the direction that American justice is barreling toward.

“And there will be no justice without a fundamental rethink.”

News.title: Ruthless Daniel Dubois dispatches Fabio Wardley in just two rounds
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Daniel Dubois vs Fabio Wardley.

When Wardley dragged himself out of the ring at Manchester’s Co-Op LIVE Arena, the physical damage was obvious, but the psychological sting was far deeper. Wardley had Dubois severely hurt early on, flooring the Londoner twice and teetering on the verge of a career-defining stoppage. Instead, he let the knockout slip away, allowed Dubois to find his rhythm, and was ultimately broken down and halted in the 11th round - surrendering his WBO heavyweight belt in a dramatic comeback victory.

Now, just five months after that gruelling night, the two heavyweights meet again at London’s O2 Arena in an immediate rematch that carries potentially massive implications for the entire division.

For Wardley (20-1-1, 19 KOs), the decision to trigger his rematch clause was instant. Dismissing concerns over the severe punishment he absorbed down the stretch, the Ipswich man is motivated entirely by redemption and the belief that his early success proved Dubois is beatable.

Dubois (23-3, 22 KOs), however, views things very differently. Entering as The Ring’s No. 1 heavyweight contender and a proven two-time world champion, Dubois has brushed off Wardley’s power, claiming his rival “punches like a baby” and insists Wardley threw away his one and only chance at glory in Manchester.

With Oleksandr Usyk approaching the final chapter of his career and the Anthony Joshua vs. Tyson Fury blockbuster looming just eight weeks away, this London clash is far more than a personal grudge match. The winner won’t just walk away with the WBO strap; they will stake an undeniable claim as the torch-bearer for the heavyweight division’s next era if they can land another title fight in short order.

News.title: Newcastle jeers tell Matthias Jaissle his ‘vertical’ football is not working
News.content:
Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

News.title: Liverpool’s £400m front line clicks but win at Brentford turns on red card
News.content:
Only time will tell if Liverpool’s £400m front line can ever justify the extraordinary amount of money that was spent on them, but this was at least a significant step in the right direction. In a gritty victory away to Brentford, all four of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Victor Muñoz either scored or assisted goals.

Admittedly, the task was made significantly easier by the major turning point of this game: a red card for Brentford’s Yehor Yarmoliuk. At the time of Yarmoliuk’s “headbutting action” towards Liverpool defender Jeremy Jacquet, the visitors were trailing 1-0 and looking worryingly short of ideas in attack.

But as the context of the match changed, so did the level of threat from the visitors. Against 10 men, with more space in which to operate, Liverpool’s forwards looked increasingly dangerous. Wirtz began to pull the strings, Barcola started to cause problems, Muñoz stretched the Brentford defence and Isak became a lurking menace.

News.title: Steely Chelsea triumph despite losing Martinez to head injury
News.content:
This was the afternoon when Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea went from swashbuckling to stoic, thrilling to tenacious.

For all Alonso’s attacking vigour at the start of his reign, there can have been no more symbolically satisfying victory under the new coach than this resolute win at Everton – the most vivid example of an increasingly impressive transformation.

This was what Alonso described as “winning in a different way”. A triumph amid the adversity of losing goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez to what appears to be a serious injury after a head collision with Jarrad Branthwaite is just one facet of why the joyous visiting supporters might consider this an early turning point.

Where recently they wilted, on Saturday they thrived in securing a first Premier League clean sheet for nine months.

Much more of this and the adjectives which were splattered across Chelsea during the golden years of José Mourinho – solid, robust and dogged – will be part of the Stamford Bridge lexicon once more.

“Just one day,” Alonso warned, both acclaiming the importance of the win while wisely preaching caution. “It will be key when we manage 10 clean sheets, even though this one feels good. We need to repeat it again and again, but the mentality was very good. Sometimes it is not to play nice, it is to play good – to win second balls, and to be efficient. We needed one of these: a clean sheet and a win.”

Asked about Martinez’s condition, Alonso said: “It was a concussion, but beyond that I do not know. I have only seen one clip of the incident, so we need to wait.

“What we know is that he left the stadium conscious and is now in hospital undergoing precautionary tests.

“We need to wait. Hopefully it will not be too serious, but at the moment we just have to wait.”

News.title: Wallabies humiliated in ‘unacceptable’ thrashing by New Zealand
News.content:
New Zealand blew Australia off the field in an extraordinary first-half display in Sydney as they claimed a 13th successive win against the Wallabies and completed a 2-0 Bledisloe Cup clean sweep.

The annual series had already gone New Zealand’s way for a 24th successive year at Eden Park last weekend, but Australia did enough in a highly competitive first half in Auckland to suggest they could give the All Blacks a game on their home turf. And in a breathless opening six minutes in Sydney, it looked as if they might.

The ball-in-play time during that opening spell was incredible as both teams committed to fast, attacking rugby, offloading from everywhere. Like two heavyweights going toe-to-toe in the opening round of a boxing contest, throwing haymakers to see who would get knocked out first.

Ryan Lonergan produced an excellent turnover for the Wallabies to trigger an Australia counter, and the irrepressible Peter Lakai responded with one for the visitors, as the ball travelled from one end of the pitch to the other in one long unbroken spell.

But after New Zealand wing Josh Moorby finally crossed the whitewash, it was Australia who found themselves out on their feet, punch drunk.

News.title: England’s Rugby League World Cup hopes in tatters after Tonga defeat
News.content:
McDermott was full of credit. “They’re a big team, a strong team,” he said. “They’ve got some tremendous players in there, and I thought we stuck toe-to-toe with them for nearly all the game.

“They scored some tries through kicks, which are always hard to defend, and then towards the back-end of the game we made some errors chasing the scoreboard.”

It should be factored in that this was McDermott’s first match in charge and strides have clearly been made since England were woeful in losing the Ashes 3-0 last year.

“I thought we opened up Tonga in that first 20,” McDermott added. “Whether we went through the middle or the edge, we found ourselves in a good ball position, but we had some scrappy finishes to the good ball sets. It was too erratic. We wanted to put a load of fatigue into Tonga, but credit to them. I thought they were terrific defensively.”

Having been beaten by Samoa in the World Cup four years ago, England must face up to the burgeoning conviction that they are no longer among the top three countries in international rugby league. There was the palpable sense of the old order being changed in a stadium packed with the red shirts of Tonga.

As Williams said in the build-up, this is a “mad” format, with only the top two from the combined six-team group of Pool B and C going through to the semi-finals, but now it is very simple as far as England are concerned. They must beat France and Papua New Guinea in their remaining two matches, and do so heavily, then pray that Tonga can beat Samoa in the last match of the pool stage. However, Samoa thumped France 78-4 on Friday, so even that potential avenue appears blocked. McDermott has no other option but to look ahead.

“We know what’s in front of us now, we’ve got to win the next two games and improve on the things we need to improve on,” he said. “But I’ve seen enough tonight that is telling me we’re heading in the right direction.

“It would be tremendously disrespectful to either France or PNG to suggest we’re going to rack up points. I can start looking at points difference and start working out our strategies, but the road will lead us back to winning those two games, and winning them in a strong way.”

Team details

England Radley, Pearce-Paul, Nsemba (King 62), Thompson (Harvard 29, Currie 69), O’Neill (Litten 58); Brimson (Nsemba 79), Young, Savala, Farnworth, Eckersley, Williams, Smith, King (Walters 33, Thompson 76).

Tonga Frizell (Vaimauga 28, Taumalolo 64), Wong (Olakau’atu 41), Olakau’atu (Fonua-Blake 38, Utoikamanu 66), Taumalolo (Halasima 31), Foketi; Hopoate, Watene-Zelezniak, Koula, Toia, Fifita, Fainu (Lolohea 17), Katoa, Fonua-Blake (Utoikamanu 21, Wong 52).

Referee Gerard Sutton (Australia).

England’s Rugby League World Cup challenge could well be over, just 80 minutes after it started.

Brian McDermott’s hopes of qualifying for the semi-finals were all but shattered in his side’s first pool match in a brutal encounter in which Pacific Island physicality and passion ultimately earned Tonga a famous victory.

England displayed huge attacking courage with their offload strategy – in all, they made 26 – but their adventurous intent could not find the finishing touch and was not enough to topple a ferocious opposition defence in Perth. Despite excellent performances from captain George Williams and Dom Young, they were ultimately blown off HBF Park.

On their seventh attempt, this was Tonga’s first win over England and although this intense contest was for, so long, much closer than the scoreboard finally showed, there can be no doubting the excellence of Kristian Woolf’s team and the ruthlessness they displayed in the last quarter in which they never stopped tackling refused to stop coming.

News.title: ‘The boats don’t stop’: The deadly coastline that has become a trafficking superhighway
News.content:
The dangers were illustrated earlier this month, when a boat carrying more than 300 migrants sank near Obock on its way to Yemen. At least 139 people drowned, including 15 children. There were 700 drownings or people lost at sea on the route in 2025.

“The boats don’t stop, day or night,” the local coastguard chief told the Telegraph as he looked out at the waterway, walkie-talkie in hand, one day earlier this month.

The chief, who declined to be named, pointed to skiffs and fishing boats moored in a lagoon outside his outpost, that he had confiscated from smugglers and traffickers.

The world has become familiar with the 18-mile-wide Bab el-Mandeb strait as one of the globe’s most congested and strategically important maritime choke points.

Sitting to the south of the Suez Canal, the East-West artery flowing through the strait carries approximately 12 to 15 percent of global maritime trade.

What is less well known is that there is also a migration superhighway running across the strait, linking Africa via Djibouti to Yemen and the Gulf beyond.

Many tens of thousands of people cross the waterway each year and while Yemeni refugees fleeing the Houthi offensive have made headlines in recent weeks, the majority of those braving the waterway are heading the other way.

This maritime migrant route out of Africa has recently been busier than all the crossings across the Mediterranean into Europe, according to the International Organisation for Migration (IOM).

The IOM estimates there were nearly 64,000 crossings across the Bab el-Mandeb in the first four months of 2026, compared with a total of just over 23,000 across the Western, Eastern and central routes of the Med.

The vast majority heading east are Ethiopians so desperate to find work in the Gulf that they are prepared to trek through war-torn Yemen, which has been tipped into a humanitarian crisis by its civil war.

The IOM recorded some 202,000 migrant trips into Djibouti from Ethiopia in 2025 and by early October, the figure for 2026 had already hit 177,000.

The reignited war in Ethiopia’s Tigray region is expected to increase the numbers wanting to leave, yet the exodus is also being held up by escalating fighting along Yemen’s coast between Houthis and the government.

Fewer are now able to get across the strait, leaving them stranded on the western side, or forced to take more dangerous routes.

News.title: Asia’s vaccine self-sufficiency drive gets $650m boost
News.content:
An “innovative” partnership to boost vaccine security across Southeast Asia will inject up to $650 million into regional manufacturing, in a bid to reduce reliance on imported shots.

The five-year initiative, announced at the annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok on Friday, will see major lenders, non-profits, and the private sector come together to invest in the region’s vaccine industry.

Currently Southeast Asia’s production base remains limited and exposed. The majority of shots are imported, and any capacity the region does have is highly concentrated – one analysis this year estimates 60 to 90 per cent sits with a single vaccine manufacturer.

Even before Covid-19 hit, this vulnerability was recognised. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), a regional bloc of 11 countries, endorsed a vaccine security and self-reliance initiative in 2019, driven by Thailand’s National Vaccine Institute (NVI).

These concerns have mounted since the pandemic, but up until now investment as well as political will has been lacking. The partnership announced on Friday, led by NVI, hopes to remedy this, and develop a model that can be copied worldwide.

​​“If we can do it here in Asia, then that really provides a model for the world,” said Aurélia Nguyen, deputy CEO of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (Cepi), a a vaccine research non-profit. “We can build it out in Africa, in Latin America, and that really gives us the resilience that we want the next time we have a major epidemic.”

Cepi has committed up to $20 million of “catalytic funding” for the programme, which is backed by the World Bank as well as organisations like the Singapore-based AVPN investment network.

In all, the package of loans and grants will include at least $174m in public financing, and up to $460m in private capital mobilisation for regional vaccine manufacturing. Further details, including recipients, have not yet been announced.

But Paschal Donohoe, the managing director and chief knowledge officer of the World Bank Group, told a panel in the Thai capital that “we believe this has the ability over time to mobilise up to $650m of finance”.

He added that the group would use public loans and grants alongside investments by its private-sector arm, the IFC, while its guarantee arm, MIGA, would help cover investors against risk.

“It’s really important because each element of the World Bank Group is involved in it,” Donohoe said. “We’re not just talking the talk, but walking the walk.”

Speaking to the Telegraph after the event, Nguyen added: “Innovative models and partnerships like this, where we’re each bringing a piece to de-risk scientific technology, [allow us] to leverage larger quantities of capital.

“But I think what’s also helpful in this model is, beyond the financing, [we] have a sort of coordinating umbrella through Asean,” she said. “So you can be smart and [avoid] duplicating investments, which brings commercial sustainability and resilience for health systems.”

Nakorn Premsri, the director of NVI, added that the investment model will help “build a more sustainable and resilient regional vaccine ecosystem, to meet both routine needs and the demands of health emergencies”.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

Sports.title: ‘What have we just witnessed?’ – Brighton star Diego Gomez scores from HALFWAY LINE in Crystal Palace derby clash
Sports.content:
Next

FOOTBALL fans could not believe their eyes after Brighton star Diego Gomez smashed home a goal from the HALFWAY LINE.

It was a nightmare start for Crystal Palace against their rivals after young defender Jaydee Canvot turned home an own goal after just four minutes.

But things took a turn for the spectacular just three minutes later when Paraguayan midfielder Gomez launched an audacious effort from the halfway line.



Surrounded by Palace shirts, he elected to leather an effort at goal, floating above backup Eagles keeper Walter Benitez and dipping under the bar to double his side’s advantage.

Sports.title: Jose Mourinho makes astonishing admission about Arsenal’s failed summer transfer pursuit of Vinicius Jr
Sports.content:
Next

JOSE MOURINHO has admitted he would have forced his way out of Real Madrid if he were in Vinicius Jr’s shoes.

The Brazilian superstar has found himself at the centre of another storm at the Bernabeu after a difficult start to the season, with his place in the team now under threat.



Vinicius was heavily linked with a blockbuster move to Arsenal over the summer in a deal that would have sent shockwaves around Europe.

But he ultimately committed his future to Madrid by signing a new contract running until 2032.



Mourinho, however, believes his winger could have benefited from a fresh start away from the Spanish giants.

The Portuguese boss said: “If I were (Vinicius), in his place, I probably wouldn’t be here.



“Last summer I would have forced my exit to a league, to a country, to clubs and stadiums where they’d respect him.

“But because he’s a Madrid fan, he has love for the club and the city, he believes things can always improve, he renewed, and he’ll keep that smile.

“I think there’s nothing or no-one that can take that away, that joy for living and working. He’s a great boy.”

“When he signed that contract, he signed it because Madrid is his home, and Real Madrid is his home. He’s one of the main sources of joy in that dressing room.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“What I said before was that I doubt I’d be able – as a player with lots of options – I doubt whether I’d be able to have his psychological strength, to hold on.”

Mourinho’s comments come amid growing uncertainty over Vinicius’ role in his Madrid side.

The winger was hauled off after an hour during their clash away to Roma on Wednesday, with Madrid trailing 3-1.



Mourinho brought on Endrick, and the substitute helped turn the game around as Madrid eventually claimed a dramatic 4-3 victory, with Carlos Espi also scoring after coming off the bench.

After Vinicius’ substitution, Mourinho said: “I don’t care what he thinks about the decision. Did you see the game after he came off?

“I’m the coach here. I decide who plays and who doesn’t. If Vini isn’t performing, it’s my responsibility to take him out of the game. That’s part of my job.”

The decision has raised further questions over Vinicius’ place in the starting XI, particularly with the Brazilian also facing a four-match LaLiga ban.

He was sent off during the 1-0 win over Villarreal last weekend after pulling Nathan Saliba’s hair, before receiving a two-match suspension for the incident and another two games for his “aggressive” reaction.



The comments come after a turbulent period at the Bernabeu, where player power was a major talking point last season.

Vinicius and Kylian Mbappe were both accused of undermining Xabi Alonso during the first half of the campaign, with the current Chelsea boss eventually losing his job.

The problems continued under Alvaro Arbeloa, now in charge of Fulham, as Madrid endured a trophyless campaign.



Mourinho is now tasked with restoring order, but results have not entirely eased the pressure.

Los Blancos have won eight of their ten matches in all competitions this season, yet have looked far from convincing compared with Hansi Flick‘s rampant Barcelona side.

The Catalan giants have won all 11 of their matches, scoring 48 goals, and sit nine points clear of Madrid, who have a game in hand.

Madrid face Sevilla tonight before travelling to the Camp Nou for next Sunday’s Clasico.

If they lose, it would leave Mourinho under immediate pressure despite only taking charge over the summer – a reminder of just how unforgiving the Real Madrid job can be.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi, 39, scores TWO solo wondergoals then taunts rival with provocative celebration as Inter Miami beat Atlanta
Sports.content:
Next

LIONEL MESSI proved his class to the world again as he scored two stunners to help Inter Miami to a win – and to get revenge on an opponent.

The Argentina legend started in his side’s MLS clash with Atlanta on Sunday, alongside the likes of Luis Suarez and Casemiro.



Winger German Berterame opened the scoring for the side moments before the half time break.

But the second period belonged to Messi, who doubled his team’s advantage in the 56th minute.



The former Barcelona star picked the ball up near the halfway line and drove into the opposition’s final third, playing a neat one-two with Berterame before firing a strike under the Atlanta keeper.

He struck again four minutes later, as he was played in by Suarez with only defender Junior Alonso to beat.

Messi twisted and turned and left the Paraguayan defender in his dust, before clipping his finish in at the far post.

The pair of goals took Messi to 25 goals from 26 matches this MLS campaign, five more than the next most prolific finisher in the league.

And his second finish will have been that little bit sweeter thanks to who it was against.

Messi had a bone to pick with Alonso after a confrontation occurred during the sides’ last encounter.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Messi had two chances to latch on to a loose ball in the box in that match, but ended up seeing his shot blocked by an Atlanta defender.

Alonso then stood up and excitedly screamed and pumped his arms in the football GOAT’s face.

The 39-year-old clearly didn’t forget the incident, and got his own back by walking directly in front of the star before celebrating towards the Miami fans alongside Rodrigo De Paul.

He was also spotted on the broadcast appearing to make a spinning gesture towards the defender with his finger, possibly poking fun at him failing to keep up with the attacker for the second goal.

Sports.title: Chelsea star Emi Martinez ‘back in a few weeks’ as star breaks silence after operation to fix fractured jaw
Sports.content:
Next

EMI MARTINEZ has given a positive update on his health after his grisly clash of heads against Everton.

The Argentina international was stretchered off the field against the Toffees on Saturday after suffering a nasty clash of heads in the second half.



He contested the ball with Jarrad Branthwaite before they smashed into each other, with the Blues man coming off worse.

He was placed on a backboard and transported to hospital, with Mike Penders coming on to replace him.



But now the star and his wife have revealed that his surgery on a fractured jaw has been successful and that the outlook is a positive one, claiming he will be back in action in just weeks.

Martinez’s wife Mandinha first wrote on Instagram on Saturday night: “Thank you all for the lovely messages and for checking in on Emi.

“He’s doing fine, it’s nothing serious, and he’ll soon be back to his usual self.

“Thank you from the bottom of my heart for so much love and support.”

It was revealed on Saturday that the star was set to undergo surgery on his jaw following the scary incident.

But himself Martinez then spoke out in the early hours of Sunday morning to confirm the procedure had been successful.



He also shared a snap of him giving a gesture from his hospital bed.

He said: “Thanks to everyone for the messages. The surgery went well.

“The most important thing is that we won and kept a clean sheet.

We’ll be back in a few weeks.”

Chelsea also confirmed the operation had been a success.



A club statement said: “Goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez has undergone successful surgery on a fractured jaw.

“Martinez was injured following a collision midway through the second half of our 2-0 victory over Everton at the Hill Dickinson Stadium on Saturday.

“Martinez was taken to hospital for further assessment, which confirmed a fractured jaw that required surgery.

“Everyone at Chelsea wishes Emi a speedy recovery and will support him throughout.”

In the aftermath of Chelsea’s 2-0 win at Everton, Blues boss Xabi Alonso revealed the 34-year-old World Cup winner was in hospital.



He said: “As far as I know he left the stadium conscious. Right now he’s in the hospital doing precautionary tests, so let’s see. But this is what I know so far.”

Chelsea’s veteran midfielder Jordan Henderson also said: “He’s very important. It looked pretty bad actually so I hope he’s okay.

“All the lads and everyone will be thinking of him and texting him so fingers crossed it’s nothing major and he can be back with us pretty soon because he’s a really important figure not only on the pitch but around the dressing room too.”

Saturday afternoon’s win marked Chelsea’s first Premier League clean sheet in nine months as they rose to fourth ahead of Brentford on 13 points.

Sports.title: Botham reopens war of words with Stokes over Ashes fallout
Sports.content:
England lost the last Ashes series 4-1 and Ian Botham criticised England's preparation for the series; Ben Stokes said that 'has-beens' did not have the same factors at play as his England side did when they got ready for the Ashes

We take a look back at an extraordinary summer of Test series which saw Ben Stokes retire, a new England captain, the end of Bazball, and a series sweep of Pakistan.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Lord Ian Botham has reopened his war of words with recently retired England captain Ben Stokes.

The pair have criticised each other in the media in the past year following England's poor performance in the Ashes in Australia.

Botham criticised England's lack of preparation ahead of the Ashes series last winter, which led to Stokes calling him and Michael Vaughan "has-beens".

England lost the series 4-1 amid off-the-field issues over late-night drinking sessions and breached curfews.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ben Stokes, just 5 weeks on from his retirement that shocked the sporting world, sits down with old teammates Stuart Broad and Jos Buttler on the For Love Of Cricket podcast.

Botham, who scored 5,200 runs and took 383 wickets in 102 Tests, was asked whether he liked the way Stokes resigned as captain in the middle of a Test match against New Zealand.

"No, I didn't and I stand by what I said," Botham said.

"You have got a situation, starting from the beginning when he had a go at myself and Michael Vaughan in Melbourne because we said they had not prepared properly.

"They played two and a half days of cricket in the build-up to taking on Australia in Perth.

"But to be absolutely honest with you, we had a go at them saying that's ridiculous, no one knows what they are doing, the slip fielders have to practice, very, very difficult."

When Stokes was asked by journalists for his views on the criticisms, he replied: "We've not been preparing for this tour over the last three weeks, we've put a lot of thought and process into this for a few years now.

"There's quite a few factors that play into why we can't prepare how the has-beens maybe prepared in the past."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at some of the best batting innings from Ben Stokes as he announces his international retirement.

Botham, who was part of two victorious tours of Australia in 1978-79 and 1986-87, was speaking at the Cheltenham Literature Festival to promote his new book, Seasons.

"So that's open warfare and I'm quite happy with that because I just think he let himself down," Botham said.

"He's a bloody good cricketer and he played well but he let himself down in those final couple of months.

"The team going 2-0 down in Australia, one of them in two days.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ben Stokes announces his international retirement inside England's dressing room during their Test series against New Zealand.

"For me to be then seen at Noosa, one of the most popular places in Australia to holiday and, we have got five days off on the lash.

"I just thought that was poor. Curfews, well, they were set and they were broken.

"In the book, I just said that right at the end, a throw away line, 'Well, well, well, Ben Stokes, you are now a member of the has-been team'.

"Didn't go down too well, not that I'm bothered."

Botham said that during the Ashes tour of 1986-87, which England won 2-1, the players would go to Australian wineries to drink and socialise between matches.

"That's out of visual and we were actually winning, so we could have paraded ourselves around a bit if we wanted, but we didn't," Botham added.

Sports.title: Chacarra earns third win of year to move top of Race to Dubai standings
Sports.content:
Eugenio Chacarra won the DP World India Championship by two shots with the Spaniard's third victory of the season moving him top of the Race to Dubai standings, above Patrick Reed and Rory McIlroy, with three events remaining.

Chacarra carded a two-under final-round of 70 in New Delhi to reach 21 under as he followed his back-to-back triumphs in June at the KLM Open in Amsterdam and the Italian Open in Turin with another success and secured a fourth DP World Tour title overall having clamed his maiden win at the Hero Indian Open in 2025.

The former LIV player, who took a five-stroke advantage into the final round following a nine-under 63 in round three, picked up shots at two of his first three holes before a bogey at six and then some clutch par putts preceded a birdie at 11.

Pressure was applied by Australia's Daniel Hillier (19 under) - when Hillier birdied the last, Chacarra's advantage was cut to two with three holes remaining - Chacarra's fellow Spaniard Angel Hidalgo (15 under) and Poland's Adrian Meronk (15 under) but the leader held firm to rise to to 4,092.89 points in the Race to Dubai.

The 26-year-old, who has knocked Reed off top spot for the first time in seven months, could become the third Spaniard, after Jon Rahm (2019) and six-time winner Seve Ballesteros, to be crowned Europe's No 1 golfer.

Image: Chacarra formerly competed on the LIV Golf tour

Chacarra said afterwards: "I know what I'm capable of. I was one of the best amateurs in the world and I want to be one of the best professional players in the world.

"It would mean the world to [win the Race to Dubai]. Rahm and Seve are heroes for me. Seve did everything for European and Spanish golf and Rahm is a guy I look up to.

"Hopefully I can put my name on that trophy, too."

Chacarra targets spot at 2027 Ryder Cup Eugenio Chacarra, speaking after his win at the DP World India Championship “I told [European Ryder Cup captain Luke Donald] that I want to be on the team, not as a pick but one of the [automatic] six spots. "That is one of the goals. That is still a year away but I know I am a good player. I just want to keep getting better and keep winning."

Where did Reed and McIlroy finish in Delhi?

Reed (eight under) and McIlroy (four under) finished joint-23rd and joint-42nd respectively in India.

The major winners sit second and third in the Race to Dubai standings, with Casey Jarvis and Aaron Rai rounding out the top five ahead of next week's Genesis Championship in South Korea.

The tour is set to move to the United Arab Emirates for the final two tournaments - the Abu Dhabi Championship from November 5 and the DP World Tour Championship in Dubai a week later.

Image: Rory McIlroy finished 17 strokes behind Chacarra in India

McIroy, looking to equal Colin Montgomerie's record of eight Race to Dubai titles, began his the final round in Delhi 13 shots back after completing an even-par third round of 72 earlier on Sunday, with play having been halted on Saturday evening due to fading light.

The world No 2 got off to a promising start in his closing round, birdieing the par-five first, only to then double bogey three and drop another shot at four before a birdie at eight was followed by a bogey to finish his back nine.

McIlroy registered two birdies and two bogeys coming home, with a gain at the par-five 18th seeing him sign for a two-over 74.

Reed, aiming to become the second American, after Collin Morikawa in 2021, to claim the Race to Dubai, rounded off his week with a three-under 69.

Image: Patrick Reed has been knocked off top spot in the Race to Dubai

Chacarra: Two of the best are coming for me now

Chacarra is now in pole position to claim the Harry Vardon Trophy in a season in which his three victories have come around five other top-five finishes, including tied-second at last week's Open de Espana in his native Madrid.

The Spaniard added on pursuing the Race to Dubai crown: "It is not going to be easy.

"Rory always plays good in Dubai, so it will be a big battle. Patrick, too - two of the best in the world are coming for me."

England's Tommy Fleetwood notched a top-five in India with a final-round, four-under 68 elevating him to 13 under, while Scotland's Robert MacIntyre and Northern Ireland's Tom McKibbin ended up in the top 10 on 12 under.

Sports.title: Van Gerwen suffers another early exit as Van Veen makes history
Sports.content:
Dutch favourite Michael van Gerwen suffered a shock second-round exit at the Dutch Darts Championship on Saturday, losing 6-5 to Irishman William O'Connor.

The defeat extends Van Gerwen's poor run of form, having lost his opening match at four European Tour events this season before arriving in Maastricht: the European Darts Trophy, German Darts Grand Prix, Flanders Darts Trophy and Swiss Darts Trophy. It marks his most first-round exits in a single season since the tour began in 2012.

O'Connor produced a superb display, firing in three ton-plus checkouts of 136, 131 and 121 to seal his victory and book his place in round three.

Elsewhere on Saturday, Gerwyn Price's return to the stage ended in glory as he beat Scott Williams 6-3, while Gian van Veen broke the European Tour record average.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Earlier this year, Laura Turner and Chris Murphy reviewed Van Gerwen's limp loss to Dirk van Duijvenbode at the World Matchplay and suggest he's becoming like Manchester United

Martin Schindler and Stephen Bunting also jumped into the qualification spots for Dortmund.

Van Veen averaged a staggering 120.24 in whitewashing Sebastian Bialecki, breaking the previous record of 118.66 by Dave Chisnall.

Schindler sealed his spot at the European Championships later this month with his victory over Karel Sedlacek.

Bunting left it late to secure his place at the European Championship, beating already-qualified Cameron Menzies 6-2 to book his spot. The former Masters champion needed a strong finish to get over the line.

The 41-year-old pinned six out of ten attempts at the outer ring in his victory over the Scot, and jumped into the qualifying places, knocking Kim Huybrechts out of the running.

Image: Dutchman Gian van Veen broke the European Tour record average on Saturday

Brendan Dolan remains the only player capable of pushing Sedlacek out of the European Championship qualifying spots after beating Heine Uuldriks 6-4. The Northern Irishman had led 4-1 before being pegged back.

Nathan Aspinall ended Michael Smith's hopes of qualifying for Dortmund with a dominant 6-1 victory. The World Grand Prix semi-finalist averaged over 102 to dispatch the former world champion.

Wessel Nijman and Danny Noppert also secured their places in Sunday's action, with the Dutch pair defeating Jeffrey De Graaf and Dave Chisnall respectively.

Niels Zonneveld edged a last-leg decider against Krzysztof Ratajski, hitting seven maximums for the second consecutive match to book his place in round three. Fellow Dutchman Jermaine Wattimena also progressed, beating Host Nation Qualifier Jimmy van Schie 6-2.

Sports.title: Williams stars as Golden State Valkyries beat Atlanta Dream in WNBA Finals Game 1
Sports.content:
Gabby Williams converted two free throws with 1:18 left to put Golden State ahead, two more with 4.1 seconds to go, and finished with 26 points as the Valkyries held off the Atlanta Dream 68-64 in Game 1 of the WNBA Finals.

Williams scored 16 of her points in the second quarter and no other Valkyries reached double figures as they shot 32.1 per cent and seven of 33 from three-point range.

"We always knew we were going to find a way somehow," Williams said on the microphone postgame as fans chanted "Gabby! Gabby!"

Sports.title: Dubois wants Usyk trilogy fight: 'We're coming out on top this time!'
Sports.content:
Daniel Dubois, the WBO heavyweight world champion, believes he would defeat Oleksandr Usyk if they had a trilogy fight.

Twice Dubois has boxed the imperious Ukrainian, and twice Usyk, an unbeaten and two-time undisputed champion at heavyweight, has stopped the Londoner.

But after a stunning two-round victory in his rematch with Fabio Wardley on Saturday, Dubois is convinced he has reached a new level and can beat Usyk.

No heavyweight, Dubois is adamant, can stand up to the punches he hit Wardley with.

"No. Fabio's got a great chin. He's known for taking punishment but I was going through him. I just had to pull myself back and reset. I want to know who's next!" Dubois declared.

Image: Dubois finishes Wardley in a corner

He would welcome a potential trilogy fight with Usyk. "Definitely, definitely, I'd love that," Dubois said. "We're coming out on top this time. We've made our mistakes and we're coming out on top."

Promoter Frank Warren said: "Daniel in my opinion he's not the same fighter he was even a year ago. He's a totally different fighter now.

"When he's doing what he's doing at his best, you've got to be some fighter to be standing and being able to take those shots. He's a tremendous puncher. When he gets you in trouble, you are in trouble. He's a good finisher."

Usyk vacated all the world titles he held, allowing Dubois to claim the WBO belt ahead of his first fight with Wardley, Filip Hrgovic to pick up the IBF strap after beating Moses Itauma, and Agit Kabayel to be elevated to WBC heavyweight world champion.

Image: Dubois' jab hurts Wardley

Next year Dubois is looking to add more championships to his collection. "I've heard talk about Kabayel but I'll fight whoever's next in line. Whoever pays the most cash," Dubois said.

"The future's looking bright."

Promoter Frank Warren thinks it will take 18 months for a new undisputed champion to be crowned, but expects a wave of heavyweight unifications to get under way in next year.

"I think it'll happen in about 18 months because of the timings of it all," Warren said. "We will make them as soon as we can, I expect in the first quarter we'll have at least one of those unifications on. If we get it on, somebody's going to be holding two belts.

"Filip's got a mandatory against [Frank] Sanchez," Warren noted. "We've got Agit, who's fighting in November in Germany and we've got Tyson [Fury] and AJ fighting in December [for the WBA 'super' title]. So they're all busy but we'll be out, don't worry about that.

Image: Dubois has his hand raised in victory. (Photos: Leigh Dawney/Queensberry Promotions)

"The good thing about it is everybody wants to fight. They're fighting men.

"We want the best fighting the best to find out who is the best," the promoter continued. "Get Usyk back in it.

"There's all sort of permutations. One thing for sure is 2027 is going to be a phenomenal year.

"[Dubois] wants the four belts. So do all the other guys. That's what's going to be so exciting."

Sports.title: Leeds United v Manchester United: Premier League – live
Sports.content:
36s ago 09.22 EDT 18 min: Gudmundsson is the next in the book for a late tackle on Santos, catching the Brazilian high on the ankle with his studs. “A bit more force and that could be a red card”, says Gary Neville on Sky Sports commentary. One yellow card for each team. This match is not going end with a full complement of players, if things carry on like this. Share

3m ago 09.19 EDT 16 min: Darren England is letting a lot go, with the referee waving play on despite both sets of players diving into tackles. Bruno Fernandes is VERY late on Muharemovic but play continues, with Stach wasting a good opportunity to either cross or shoot on a Leeds counter-attack. When the ball goes dead, England does caution Fernandes for the challenge. The Manchester United captain can really have no complaints, but he is giving the referee an earful about something. Share

7m ago 09.16 EDT 14 min: No goals here but a quick glance at the other 2pm BST kick-offs: Bournemouth lead Sunderland by a goal and Brighton are 3-0 up against rivals Crystal Palace! Diego Gómez has just scored from the half-way line for the Seagulls! Share

10m ago 09.13 EDT 12 min: Ampadu with a nasty challenge on Mbeumo, 30 yards from the Leeds goal. The Welshman popped his studs straight into the ankle of the Manchester United man. Ampadu escapes a booking. Share

11m ago 09.11 EDT 10 min: Tanaka is late on Santos and Leeds send every player back to defend the set piece. Fernandes completely overcooks the delivery and Calvert-Lewin mops things up at the back post. Share

13m ago 09.10 EDT 8 min: Looks like Fernandes and Mbeumo are interchanging, the latter switching from from the left wing to striker, then back out again to the flank. Share

14m ago 09.09 EDT 6 min: Baleba is so important to Manchester United today, particularly with the visitors missing the physicality of Mainoo. The Cameroonian outmuscles Stach, rides a couple of challenges before running into Leeds traffic. A good start, though from the Manchester United No 20. Share

17m ago 09.05 EDT 4 min: Baleba is sent flying in midfield by a strong challenge from Stach. Exactly the sort of tackle we would expect from a fixture of this magnitude. Share

18m ago 09.04 EDT 2 min: Bruno Fernandes played off the right wing for Manchester United in midweek against Atlético. It looks like the Portuguese is playing centrally today as a false nine. Mbeumo off the left, Amad off the right. So a completely new-look attack for Carrick. Share

21m ago 09.01 EDT Elland Road is bouncing, of course it is. “I don’t understand why Justin and Bogle are not in the discussion for England right-back,” emails Gary Stover. “That Farke has found a way to start them both must be a key to Leeds success. What do you think?” Justin and Bogle are very good footballers. I’m not sure they would win England the European Championship in 20278. Reece James, Nico O’Reilly, Trent Alexander-Arnold and Lewis Hall might. Share

36m ago 08.46 EDT Daniel Farke, Leeds manager, is the next to speak to Sky Sports: double quotation mark We have to make sure we give them nothing. We want to make sure the ball belongs to us, to press them high, to have possession. Share

38m ago 08.44 EDT “Just had great fun reading the Joy of Six article,” emails Richard Hirst. “My abiding memory of the 1972 Leeds 5-1 win is not the olé period at the end, but that the goals all seemed to be scored from inside the six yard box: they were wonderful team goals which ripped Man Utd to shreds. The fact that Allan Clarke, my hero from his Fulham days, was on the end of them only made it better.” Share

40m ago 08.43 EDT A bit more on those teams: Leeds are unchanged for the fifth game in a row. That’s hardly surprising, given their excellent form. Daniel Farke’s team were unlucky to narrowly lose at Arsenal last weekend. Manchester United make two changes from the Champions League defeat at Atlético. Harry Maguire returns in place of Ayden Heaven, and Amad Diallo comes into the side instead of Marcus Rashford. Carlos Baleba makes his first Premier League start, while Matthijs de Ligt is in the squad for the first time since November 2025. Share

42m ago 08.41 EDT Michael Carrick was as dull as dishwater in his pre-match interview, but maybe that’s the point after a turbulent week. He spoke for a few minutes and these were the most exciting quotes: double quotation mark It’s a fantastic game. We’ve come here to try and win the game. It’s a challenging place to come. I think we’ve got good balance throughout the team. Mainoo and Shaw were close-ish [to being fit] but not close enough. Share

51m ago 08.32 EDT Leeds’ Ethan Ampadu, who captains the club for the 100th time, speaks to Sky Sports: double quotation mark We know what this game means. We know that they are not too happy at the moment but we know that they might show a reaction. But we know what we need to do to win this game. Share

Sports.title: James and Carpenter lead Chelsea surge as sorry Spurs hit for six in WSL again
Sports.content:
Two goals each from a rampant Lauren James and battling Ellie Carpenter helped Chelsea cruise past Tottenham and keep the pressure on Manchester City at the top of the Women’s Super League table.

It was a thrilling show and a statement from the home team, a game laden with stunning goals after a frustrating first half that allowed Tottenham more of the ball than Chelsea would have been happy with.

James’s first was cancelled out by Matilda Vinberg’s first-half equaliser, before Carpenter restored Chelsea’s lead and James added her second. Sjoeke Nüsken and Maika Hamano powered in the fourth and fifth before Signe Gaupset pulled one back and Carpenter converted for the second time.

Following Tottenham’s 6-1 defeat to London City Lionesses Martin Ho said he was the “most frustrated” he has been during his time at the club. Spurs looked lightweight against the Bromley-based side, despite going into the game unbeaten.

At Stamford Bridge heads were up and it had looked like it would be a different story after a strong start by the visiting team. The concession of the opening goal in the 25th minute was a cruel reminder of their defensive issues. It was Toko Koga who was uncharacteristically caught out, the Japan defender turned her back on James, who dispossessed her and drove towards the near post before she fired in at the far post from the tightest of angles.

View image in fullscreen Lauren James squeezes in Chelsea’s opener from the tightest of angles. Photograph: John Walton/PA

The bright play of Ho’s team did not evaporate, though, with Kadeisha Buchanan on hand to steer the ball out for a corner just ahead of Cathinka Tandberg. A deserved equaliser arrived just before the break when Vinberg converted Julie Blakstad’s pinpoint ball towards the far post with a bullet header.

If there was hope that Spurs would end their run of 20 WSL games against big four opposition without a win, securing four draws and suffering 16 defeats in that time, they were well and truly crushed in the second half.

It wasn’t so much a Spurs collapse as Chelsea putting their foot on the gas, channelling any anger and frustration felt at a less than dominant first-half performance into one laden with gut-busting intensity in the second half.

Just before the hour mark Sonia Bompastor’s side retook the lead, when Alyssa Thompson drove into the box from the left before sending an angled cutback for the arriving Carpenter to power in.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Chelsea retake the lead in the second half thanks to Ellie Carpenter’s first goal. Photograph: John Walton/PA

Four minutes later James extended their lead, collecting the ball from Lucy Bronze in the centre circle before she powered towards the box, wrongfooted Koga and curled her effort past Lize Kop. Chelsea’s fourth was as stylish as the rest; Keira Walsh flicked the ball to the substitute Nüsken and she blasted a rising strike six minutes after entering the game.

Hamano found herself in acres of space for the fifth, sending a curling effort into the top corner. Walsh was at fault for Spurs’ late second, waiting for the ball into her feet which Gaupset saw, pounced on and then fired a low effort in. Unwilling to let the game finish on a down note, Carpenter swapped the ball from her left foot to her right as she turned and fired in her second.

It was a chaotic finish to a thrillingly end-to-end match and Chelsea continue to assert their status as serious title contenders.

Sports.title: Europe is a blast – but more a curse than a blessing if you are not a Premier League super-club I Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
The sun shone. The temperature was in the high 20s. There was a mood of great conviviality. If you were struggling with the official allocation, it turned out you could just email the president of Torreense and he’d sort you out. Were these “Nuno-tickets” real? It turned out they were. Not only that, but you could sit anywhere you wanted in a stadium too big for the game and, if you happened to have gravitated to the comfortable hospitality seating at the back of the lower tier, the beer was inexplicably free.

Locals in Leiria seemed bewildered but could hardly have been more accommodating. A beer pump had been installed outside a patisserie on the Praça Francisco Rodrigues Lobo, whose owner soon found fans happy to help stack empty barrels if that facilitated the free flow of Sagres. “There was a meeting at the town hall to explain these are not hooligans,” said the owner of a radical leftist flammkuchen restaurant between the square and the cathedral. “They told us the club comes from the labour movement and I found that very interesting.” And how had she found the fans? “Noisy, but with a quirky sense of humour.”

This was everything Sunderland fans could have wished for from their first European away game in 53 years and more. They had seen other fans experience these things, and now they could tick off the checklist: complicated travel to a pretty foreign town they would otherwise never visit, a fussy Albanian referee and a great sense of togetherness and community. There was even an injury-time winner from, miracle of miracles, Noah Sadiki.

Ask any of the 5,000 or so Wearsiders who made the trip to Portugal if the Europa League was worth it and the answer would be unanimous. Bournemouth, Crystal Palace and Brighton fans would surely say something similar: European football, especially for clubs who are unfamiliar with it, is a joy and an adventure. It generates experiences that will be remembered for ever, and if the cost is that the risk of relegation goes up, that’s a price worth paying. Others at those clubs may see things differently.

View image in fullscreen Sunderland fans enjoyed a trip they will remember for ever when they played Torreense Photograph: Paulo Cunha/EPA

The four Premier League clubs involved in the lesser two European competitions play each other on Sunday. Brighton are thriving; the other three are not. Palace were 12th before the weekend fixtures but not playing well. Bournemouth against Sunderland is a battle of third- and fourth-bottom. Whether the Europa League football can yet be blamed is debatable. Brighton surely can’t be bucking the trend just because of the lesser demands of the Conference League. Thursday’s was only the second round of Europa League league games, and the clubs involved bypassed a round of the Carabao Cup; fatigue may come but it shouldn’t be an issue yet.

There are other factors at play. Sunderland have already played Manchester City, Arsenal, Brighton and Brentford, the top four going into this weekend. They could easily have been a couple of goals up by half-time at Brentford. They missed a penalty to go ahead against Arsenal. They registered an xG of 2.72 in losing 5-3 at Manchester City. Only in the defeat to Brighton last weekend have they really disappointed. In the equivalent six games last season (substituting Ipswich for Burnley), Sunderland took only one point; in that sense, they are actually three points better off this campaign.

But that can’t alter the fact that four points from six games leaves them beginning to fret. There is pressure on this next run of fixtures: after Bournemouth, they are home to Leeds, then away to Coventry. Sunderland’s transfer business left a major question on the right of the forward line that has yet to be resolved. A lack of depth in certain areas has been exposed by injuries to Brian Brobbey and Habib Diarra, although both players were on the bench on Thursday.

Bournemouth have also lost key players to injury. Eli Junior Kroupi, who scored 13 league goals last season, has not played this campaign. Neither has Amine Adli, although he came off the bench on Thursday, as did Justin Kluivert, who had been out for a month. Most damagingly of all, perhaps, after impressing for England against Croatia, Alex Scott has been ruled out with a thigh injury.

The transition away from Andoni Iraola was always likely to be disruptive and, while Saturday’s 5-1 defeat at Chelsea was a jolt, their other losses this season were to Manchester City and Liverpool. There has been a sense of margins going against them, of draws that might have been wins. The concern, as with Sunderland, comes if that affects morale, and decent displays that have yielded disappointing results curdle into disappointing performances.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Álvaro Rodríguez scores Bournemouth’s third goal against Sturm Graz, but they have found domestic assignments tougher. Photograph: Tony O Brien/Reuters

Palace are in a slightly different position. Other than City, their fixture list has been relatively kind. Seven points from six games would constitute comfortable survival if extrapolated over the season as a whole, but Opta’s expected points table, which has Bournemouth ninth and Sunderland 10th, has them 18th. A new manager is settling in, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Múñoz were sold over the summer, while Jean-Philippe Mateta hasn’t played since the opening weekend.

For none of those three sides can unsettled starts be blamed entirely or even primarily on Europe. That said, the evidence is clear: over the past five years, teams who did not play in Europe the previous season see their league position fall when they do play in Europe: Palace dropped from 12th to 15th, Nottingham Forest from seventh to 16th, Newcastle from fifth to 12th, Brighton from sixth to 11th, West Ham from sixth to seventh. Of those examples, only Forest even came vaguely close to relegation, but the fear nags away.

Although winning the Europa League would bring the vast rewards of Champions League football, losing in the final would probably bring in not much more than £20m for a Premier League club, plus gate receipts and whatever intangible benefits there might be from increased exposure. To put that in context, that’s roughly the difference between finishing ninth and 14th in the Premier League.

Which is to say that while fans revel in trips to Milan, Prague or Lyon, for club executives a few nice mini-breaks do not balance out the potential financial headaches.

Sports.title: ‘I suffer a lot’: Villarreal owner Fernando Roig on not enjoying games and the prospect of Liverpool
Sports.content:
The first time Fernando Roig watched Villarreal play as their president, he sat in the stand at a tiny whitewashed ground that had concrete fever and was half empty. It was a Sunday night in the second division, they lost 3-0 to Badajoz, and he didn’t enjoy it much.

But then, he doesn’t ever enjoy it much. Even on Tuesday at Anfield, he will not: into his 30th year, the longest presidency in Europe, that is about the only thing that hasn’t changed. More than 1,000 games and still it happens. “I don’t get nervous. It’s worse: I get worried, very anxious,” he says. “I suffer a lot.

“It’s emotional to play Liverpool. This will be the fifth time we have faced them, the third at Anfield. The other two were European semi-finals. I’ll watch the morning training session, travel with the team. We’ll go and eat; everywhere we go we get treated very well and we treat them well back. The next day I’ll watch the under-19s in the morning, that I do like. And then the game, which I don’t. Then we’ll fly back here very, very late. It’s very stressful.”

It is the morning after Villarreal have beaten Napoli in the Champions Leagueand Roig is in an office at the headquarters of Pamesa, the ceramics company he owns, on the edge of town. He is better now, the tension subsided. They needed that victory, their first in the competition going back to before they last faced Liverpool, in the 2022 semi-final, and, besides, he is always better the next day.

A cabinet holds pictures, mementoes, footballs, a basketball too. Three paintings by his wife, Elena Negueroles, fill the far wall. He has been talking a short while when two people join him, at the long table, in front of the cabinet. He introduces them as Villarreal’s consejero delegado, CEO, and Pamesa’s director of communications; they are also his son, Fernando, and daughter, Elena, named after their parents.

“I can enjoy it today, the day after, tomorrow and the day after that,” the 79-year-old says. “Until Elche comes on Saturday and it’s time to suffer again. And then the Liverpool day. It’s very stressful for me.”

So why do it? “Because when the game ends, there’s that satisfaction, that feeling the town, the province, have enjoyed it, that they admire their team. It’s about community. It costs people money to come and watch a game. What they want is to enjoy it and what we want is to give them that.”

They have done that, come a long way. “I remember that Badajoz match, thinking ‘so this is how it starts’,” he says. “We didn’t have a training ground. We trained on any patch of grass we could find. The stadium held fewer than 4,000 people. The first thing was to try to build a squad that could go up, find a pitch to play on, a decent dressing room, create an academy.”

It was May 1997 and Roig describes the offer to buy the club as an opportunity, but it was more like a plea. For survival and stability, not success: asking for Anfield would have been absurd.

Villarreal had spent most of their history in tercera, reaching the regionalised Segunda B nine years earlier, and had never played in primera. In the second division for the first time, they had barely 1,500 members, were struggling to stay afloat and Pascual Font de Mora, the former player and current president, was seriously ill. His family were looking for someone to take on the club and assume a debt near €80m.

The man they entrusted to find a buyer was José Manuel Llaneza. One day, Llaneza came to these offices. Roig had money and experience with sports: Valencia Pamesa basketball club. His brother Paco owned Valencia’s football team.

View image in fullscreen Fernando Roig with his daughter, Elena, and son, Fernando. Photograph: Villareal CF

So why take on another club? And why in Villarreal, an hour up the coast? “All my factories are here: here, in Almassora, Onda, L’Alcora; 98% of all the ceramics made in Spain are made here in a 50km radius around the town. We knew a lot of people in Villarreal, in the province of Castellón. This was our place, where we could give something back.

“And the owner wanted to sell; it was an opportunity. They came to us. I had been at Pamesa Valencia since 1986. We had been in the second tier and taken them to the ACB [the top professional basketball division in Spain], so I had some experience. I still watch them. Yesterday, after the [Napoli] game, I watched them against Olympiacos on the tablet.

“I was president of both for a while, but you couldn’t combine them. I remember winning the Copa del Rey in basketball at the same time as we were playing at Numancia.”

Another of Roig’s brothers, Juan, continued at Pamesa Valencia. Alongside Llaneza, manager general, consejero delegado and vice-president, he began building at Villarreal. “In a city of 52,000 people, we did something we can be proud of,” he says. What they did is barely believable, although investment was heavy and Roig keeps insisting there was never any doubt. This, he says, is exactly as they imagined it.

Well, maybe not exactly. “We went up, probably before we were really ready, then came straight down again. Went back up. We got into Europe, reached a Champions League semi-final in 2006. We’ve been promoted three times, been relegated twice.

“The second relegation in 2012 was terrible: really, really awful. We started that year in the Champions League, but didn’t win a game and went down in the last minute of the final game. We were in the second division for one second all season, but it was the last second. We had to sell players, rebuild. I had to ‘compensate’.”

That was a warning they heeded. Roig sold a 2.4% shareholding of the 9% stake he had in the supermarket Mercadona to balance the books. Villarreal had in effect been part of the Pamesa group, but they were separated, only the sponsorship remaining, the whole model restructured. Now he says the first thing every year is survival – “42 points and it’s time to raise a toast” – even if ambitions, and indeed the model, see Europe as a minimum.

The size of the club does, too. How much have you invested over the years? “I couldn’t say. Maybe about €200m. There has been a lot of investment: the training ground, another training ground, the stadium.”

Roig looks at his son. “€180m, maybe? I haven’t calculated it all, but Villarreal is worth more than all of it. We can’t compete economically with the biggest clubs, the state clubs. We can’t have salaries of €10m, €12m, €15m, €20m. Our policy is clear: be sustainable, spend what we can generate. We’re not a selling club, but if someone offers the right amount maybe we sell, for two reasons: one, economics. And two, we won’t curtail a player’s career.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Fernando Roig lifts the Champions League trophy in 2021. Photograph: Villareal CF

“We keep growing: we’ve extended the stadium: over 23,000. Very nice, very comfortable, very yellow. We’re constantly reforming.”

There’s another glance across the table, something Roig repeats often. “The consejero delagado does everything now: he’s the one that decides, leads and executes,” he says. “He has us on a good path. I don’t do anything any more. All I do is suffer during games. We think we have done something important, but what really matters is what’s next. In 30 years we’ve spent 27 seasons in the first division, 19 in Europe.”

If Anfield offers a symbol of how far they have come, so do Liverpool’s rivals to the east. “When we went to sign Diego Forlán from Manchester United, I said to Llaneza: tell them to come and play a friendly here, make it part of the deal. And they said: “Where? Villarreal?” Roig says. “I said: ‘Don’t worry, they’ll come next year … and they’ll do it for free.’ And then next year, or maybe the year after, they came in the Champions League.

“Diego wasn’t playing much, but we looked after him, gave him affection, and he was a great player. He won the golden boot here. Because he was at Villarreal, no one talked about it much. When he won it again, at Atlético, then they talked about him.”

“If you want, you can call us a family club; we admit it. It’s a club with no pressure, not much media attention, none of the toxic surroundings other clubs have. We have to create the pressure ourselves, the demands. Above all, we create an ecosystem.”

It works. It started with investment on established players, particularly from South America. But they searched among emerging footballers as well and bit by bit the academy, built on an old orange grove, bore fruit. Mention Santi Cazorla, who joined as a teenager, and Roig’s eyes light up. “An excellent player and an excellent person. He came as a kid. Real Madrid wanted him, but we convinced him to stay.

“He overcame so much with those injuries, then came back for at the end. He didn’t know if he would be able to play again, but we welcomed him back, were pleased to give him that opportunity and he gave us three more superb years.”

“And we had a Ballon d’Or winner here. Rodri was with us for five years. He wanted to progress and we weren’t going to stop him: he went to Atlético Madrid, from Atlético to Manchester, and won the Ballon d’Or. We have great memories of him, a good relationship. It fills me with pride to see him win the World Cup.

“Not just him: Álex Baena came to Villarreal at 11. He had those first years of melancholy, not being back at home in Almeria, but he grew up here. Yeremy [Pino] came very young. Borja Iglesias too. That’s an example of what we want to be.”

View image in fullscreen Rodri is honoured by his former club’s president before the Champions League match between Villarreal and Manchester City in 2025. Photograph: Magara Press SL/Alamy

Ask Roig for a player from all those who have been at Villarreal and beyond Juan Román Riquelme or Robert Pires, Marcos Senna, Bruno Soriano and Gerard Moreno it is Pau Torres that comes to mind. “He’s born in the town and triumphed here, won a European title,” he says, “which was the only game I couldn’t go to.”

All those matches and Villarreal’s president missed that one. The 2021 Europa League final, the greatest, most epic victory of all, the one that completed a journey and belonged to everyone, their first trophy. Football can be cruel.

“I had Covid the week before,” Roig says. “I got certificates from every lab in Villarreal: they all showed I was negative. But as I was in the team bubble, Uefa demanded some other certificate. There was no time. We tried to argue, put some pressure on. It was no good. But it filled me with pride. And when Pau dedicated the win to me, it meant so much. He even came back from Poland and gave me his medal.”

It is here, a simple gold disc on black ribbon, around a match ball in the cabinet behind Roig’s son and daughter. “Pau won it there. As for me, I had to fly back and watch the final calmly at home with my wife. Well, ‘calmly’? I suffered there too, terribly.”

4h ago 04.48 EDT From the archive: Leeds United v Man Utd classics double quotation mark Leeds United 1-0 Manchester United (FA Cup semi-final replay, 31 March 1965); Leeds United 0-1 Manchester United (Division One, 17 April 1965) Here’s where the stags really begin to rut. Don Revie’s side, freshly promoted, were on course for the Double. Only problem was, so were Matt Busby’s men. The pair were drawn in the semi-final of the FA Cup, and spent 90 minutes at Hillsborough kicking seven colours out of each other, Jack Charlton, Billy Bremner, Nobby Stiles, Denis Law and Paddy Crerand enjoying themselves like the proverbial pigs. Good luck if you found yourself in the middle of that. Brouhahas broke out on the terraces as well, and did so again four days later during the replay at the City Ground. The on-field behaviour was much improved, though. According to Big Jack, Manchester United put on a performance as stylish and dangerous as they ever were under Busby, but Leeds somehow held on, wrested the ascendency, and nicked it in the last minute, Bremner twisting in mid-air to steer home an outrageous curling header. Bremner was missing 18 days later when Manchester United came to Elland Road in the league. Had they won, Leeds would have gone five clear at the top with four games left. They went into the game as favourites, Busby’s side having failed to find the net against Leeds in both Cup games and the earlier league match at Old Trafford, which the visitors won 1-0. That particular lean spell ended after 14 minutes – or 284, if you like – when John Connelly drove home. Leeds failed to respond, despite the best efforts of the newly crowned Football Writers’ player of the year, Bobby Collins, and went down again in their next Bremner-less match, a 3-0 hosing at Sheffield Wednesday. Busby’s third great side won their first title; Revie’s team, not quite ready yet, lost the Cup final as well. 4h ago 04.21 EDT Dominic Booth If the 2013 FA Cup final represented a blip for the Sheikh Mansour-era Manchester City in their quest for total domination of English football, it was a historic moment for their conquerors, Wigan Athletic. Memories of that famous day at Wembley still endure for Latics’ supporters despite the relegation from the Premier League that followed. Yet watching the modern-day Wigan, who remain bottom of League One despite a 1-0 win over Reading on Saturday, makes the toppling of City in a Cup final seem an epoch ago. The club, perhaps understandably, continue to hark back to their halcyon days. Last season they brought back Gary Caldwell – club captain in 2013 – for his second stint as manager, having led the club to promotion from this division in 2015-16. Choosing to swap Exeter for a return to the Latics last season was seen as a risky move by Caldwell, considering the shoestring budget imposed upon him by Mike Danson, the owner who is keen to sell. Finances are ultra-tight at the Greater Manchester club amid dwindling crowds and losses on the pitch and on the balance sheet. The local businessman Danson and his family saved Wigan from liquidation in June 2023 after mismanagement from previous owners brought a points deduction and relegation from the Championship. Three successive mid-table finishes in League One under their stewardship have brought a semblance of stability, but this season they have plummeted. The problem is the Dansons have been unable to find an ambitious buyer to take the club to the next level. Now the prospect of a first season in the fourth tier since 1996-97 is a distinct possibility, although victory against Reading – the Latics’ second league win of the campaign, sealed by Scott Hogan’s 71st-minute strike – made the picture a little rosier. 5h ago 03.28 EDT Jonathan Wilson The sun shone. The temperature was in the high 20s. There was a mood of great conviviality. If you were struggling with the official allocation, it turned out you could just email the president of Torreense and he’d sort you out. Were these “Nuno-tickets” real? It turned out they were. Not only that, but you could sit anywhere you wanted in a stadium too big for the game and, if you happened to have gravitated to the comfortable hospitality seating at the back of the lower tier, the beer was inexplicably free. Locals in Leiria seemed bewildered but could hardly have been more accommodating. A beer pump had been installed outside a patisserie on the Praça Francisco Rodrigues Lobo, whose owner soon found fans happy to help stack empty barrels if that facilitated the free flow of Sagres. “There was a meeting at the town hall to explain these are not hooligans,” said the owner of a radical leftist flammkuchen restaurant between the square and the cathedral. “They told us the club comes from the labour movement and I found that very interesting.” And how had she found the fans? “Noisy, but with a quirky sense of humour.” This was everything Sunderland fans could have wished for from their first European away game in 53 years and more. They had seen other fans experience these things, and now they could tick off the checklist: complicated travel to a pretty foreign town they would otherwise never visit, a fussy Albanian referee and a great sense of togetherness and community. There was even an injury-time winner from, miracle of miracles, Noah Sadiki. Ask any of the 5,000 or so Wearsiders who made the trip to Portugal if the Europa League was worth it and the answer would be unanimous. Bournemouth, Crystal Palace and Brighton fans would surely say something similar: European football, especially for clubs who are unfamiliar with it, is a joy and an adventure. It generates experiences that will be remembered for ever, and if the cost is that the risk of relegation goes up, that’s a price worth paying. Others at those clubs may see things differently.
