World.title: Sixteen Months On and Still Unresolved: Lungu Remains Draw Forensic Demand
World.content:
A South African pressure group has asked police in that country to carry out a DNA test to confirm the identity of the person reported to have died as former Zambian President Edgar Lungu. The demand opens a new front in a dispute over his remains that has run for more than 16 months, with no burial yet publicly confirmed.

The Progressive Forces of South Africa (PFSA) made the request in a seven-page letter to the South African Police Service (SAPS), citing concerns over the identity of the deceased and the circumstances surrounding his death.

PFSA President Mthetho Ngcukayitobi asked SAPS to preserve the remains, arrange forensic examinations and investigate the circumstances of Mr Lungu’s reported death.

The letter is the latest chapter in a story that began on June 5, 2025, when Mr Lungu, Zambia’s sixth President, who governed from 2015 to 2021, died in Pretoria while receiving medical treatment.

In the days that followed, the Government and the family negotiated over funeral arrangements. On June 15, 2025, the two sides reached an agreement under which the body would be repatriated on June 18 and buried in Lusaka on June 23.

That deal did not hold. On June 18, the family halted the repatriation, accusing the Government of breaching the terms of the agreement. A day later, President Hakainde Hichilema ended the national mourning period early, citing the impasse.

The family then announced plans for a private burial in Johannesburg, saying Mr Lungu had made clear before his death that his successor and long-time political rival should play no part in his funeral.

The Government responded through the courts. On June 25, 2025, the day of the planned private funeral, the High Court in Pretoria issued an order stopping the burial hours before it was due to take place.

In August 2025, the High Court ruled in the Government’s favour, ordering that the body be handed over for repatriation and a state funeral. The court said a former President’s personal wishes, or those of his family, could not outweigh the right of the State to honour him. A grave had already been prepared at Embassy Park in Lusaka, the official burial site for Zambia’s former Presidents.

The family’s attempt to go directly to the Constitutional Court was dismissed on procedural grounds, without a ruling on the merits. The case then moved to the Supreme Court of Appeal.

While the appeal was pending, control of the remains changed hands. In April 2026, the Government announced that it had taken custody of the body, before a court ordered it returned to the family.

The family accused the Government of conducting a post-mortem while the body was in its possession, without a court order and without any relative present. The remains were then moved to a mortuary agreed upon by both sides, with access limited to the family.

On June 23, 2026, the Supreme Court of Appeal overturned the 2025 order. It ruled that the family, not the Government, had the right to decide where and how Mr Lungu would be buried.

The court found that the Government had failed to prove that a binding agreement had been reached over a state funeral, and that it had no legal right under South African law to override the family’s wishes. It also ordered the Government to pay the family’s legal costs.

The appeal had been brought by the former President’s widow, Esther Lungu, and seven other family members, who want him laid to rest at Fourways Memorial Park in Johannesburg.

Two days after the judgment, family spokesperson Makebi Zulu said the family was holding internal consultations, had not reached a final decision on the burial site and had not set a burial date.

The PFSA letter now raises questions of a different kind. Mr Ngcukayitobi said reports in the media, legal correspondence and posts on social media had raised concerns about who the deceased was, what caused his death and how the remains had been handled administratively and diplomatically.

He said the group’s request was grounded in South African laws governing police investigations and inquiries into deaths that occur under unusual or unexplained circumstances.

The group also cited allegations that the deceased had been admitted to hospital under an alias. Mr Ngcukayitobi argued that the circumstances described in those reports brought the matter within the scope of the Inquests Act and the investigative responsibilities of SAPS.

He set out why the group believed action could not wait.

“Because of the combination of disputed identity, allegations of foul play, and the international dimension, urgent forensic steps are necessary,” Mr Ngcukayitobi said.

The PFSA called on state forensic pathology services to conduct whatever medico-legal examinations were required, warning that any delay could result in evidence being lost or contaminated.

Its demands extend well beyond a DNA test. The group asked police to secure hospital admission and medical records, staff rosters, CCTV footage and digital records from hospitals in Pretoria and Johannesburg reportedly involved in the patient’s treatment.

It also sought the preservation of relevant immigration records and diplomatic communications, and asked investigators to interview hospital personnel, administrators and funeral parlour staff.

On timelines, the PFSA asked SAPS for written confirmation of the action taken, together with an investigation case number, within 72 hours of receiving the letter. It also requested a public statement on the matter, including the status of any post-mortem examination.

Mr Ngcukayitobi said the group was ready to provide further information to investigators.

The claims in the letter are the group’s allegations and have not been tested by any investigating authority. The letter does not challenge the Supreme Court of Appeal ruling; it asks South African police to treat the death itself as a matter requiring forensic confirmation.

SAPS had not commented on the letter at the time of publication. The family’s most recent public position remains the one given after the June judgment: consultations continuing, with no burial site or date announced.

World.title: Hichilema to Open 2026 Mining Insaka as DRC and Botswana Send Presidential Envoys
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema is expected to open the 2026 Zambia Mining and Investment Insaka (ZAMII) in Lusaka on Monday, with more than 1,500 participants due to attend the five-day gathering, including special envoys of the presidents of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and Botswana.

The event runs from October 19 to 23 at the Mulungushi International Conference Centre. It will bring together Government, mining companies and development partners to explore investment opportunities and strengthen regional cooperation in the mining sector.

Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development Permanent Secretary Hapenga Kabeta said the presence of the two presidential envoys showed the Insaka’s growing standing as a platform for regional trade and investment.

Dr Kabeta made the remarks at a press briefing at the conference centre, where he was joined by Butella Investment Holdings Chief Executive Officer Happy Mbulo and the company’s Director of Sponsorship and Resource Mobilisation, Inonge Mpupuni.

The guest list extends well beyond the region. Dr Kabeta said representatives of the World Bank, the European Union and the African Development Bank would take part, alongside business people from Australia, China and the United Arab Emirates.

That mix of multilateral lenders, foreign investors and neighbouring governments reflects the twin purpose organisers have set for this year’s edition: attracting capital into Zambia’s mines while building closer mining ties with countries across the region.

This year’s Insaka is held under a theme built around regional value chains, shared prosperity and empowering communities. Dr Kabeta said discussions would concentrate on three priorities: adding value to minerals, creating jobs and strengthening mining value chains across the region.

Beyond the conference sessions, the meeting is expected to produce business deals and joint ventures. Organisers have tied those outcomes directly to the Government’s Grow Zambia Agenda.

The most prominent target under that agenda is copper. Government aims to raise annual copper output to three million metric tonnes by 2031, and Dr Kabeta said the Insaka would support that goal.

The copper ambition sits within a wider set of 2031 production targets now being turned into implementation plans. The Presidential Delivery Unit (PDU) is running Delivery Labs through October, bringing Government institutions, private sector players and development partners together to draw up roadmaps for eight priority areas of the economy, one of which is mining.

For readers catching up, the Insaka has become the mining sector’s main annual meeting point between the State, investors and industry. Its value lies in placing policymakers and those with capital in the same room, where commitments on new projects, expansions and partnerships can be negotiated directly.

The attendance of envoys from Kinshasa and Gaborone gives this year’s edition a stronger regional character. Dr Kabeta’s emphasis on regional value chains signals that Zambia wants mining cooperation with its neighbours to move beyond trade in raw ore towards shared processing and supply arrangements.

Value addition has been the recurring thread in the Government’s message on minerals. Processing more of what is mined, rather than exporting it in raw form, is presented as the route to more jobs and higher earnings from the same resources.

Development finance institutions will also be watched closely during the week. The participation of the World Bank and the African Development Bank places lenders capable of backing large infrastructure and mining-related projects at the table alongside private investors.

Job creation sits beside value addition on the Insaka’s agenda. Dr Kabeta said the meeting would focus on employment as one of its core outcomes, linking the expansion of the mining sector to opportunities for Zambians.

Community empowerment, part of this year’s theme, places mining-host communities within the discussion. The question of how those communities share in mineral wealth is expected to run through the sessions alongside the investment talks.

The President’s opening address on Monday is set to frame the week. Delegates will then spend four further days in sessions and deal-making before the Insaka closes on Friday, October 23.

World.title: Five-Day Regional Crackdown Nets K23.3 Million Haul as 72 Illegal Immigrants Held in Lusaka
World.content:
Zambian security agencies have seized smuggled goods, wildlife products and stolen vehicles worth K23.3 million and detained 72 foreign nationals in Lusaka during a five-day operation against cross-border crime, carried out alongside police forces across Southern and Eastern Africa.

The operation, code-named USALAMA-12, ran from October 5 to 9 across Lusaka, Copperbelt, Eastern, Southern and Western provinces. Fourteen people were arrested for various offences, while the 72 foreign nationals were held in the capital for being in the country illegally.

Inspector General of Police Graphel Musamba released the results in a statement, saying the exercise was designed to strengthen regional security by dismantling criminal syndicates and other transnational crime networks. Usalama, he explained, is the Swahili word for security.

The crackdown brought together a wide coalition of state institutions. Officers from the Zambia Police Service worked alongside the Immigration Department, the Cyber Crime Agency, the National Anti-Terrorism Centre, the Department of National Parks and Wildlife (DNPW), the Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA) and the Zambia Environmental Management Agency (ZEMA).

Zambia’s effort formed part of a wider regional task involving the Southern African Regional Police Chiefs Cooperation Organisation (SARPCCO) and the Eastern Africa Police Chiefs Cooperation Organisation (EAPCCO), with support from the International Criminal Police Organisation (Interpol). The arrangement places the operation within a regional framework built to pursue crime that does not stop at national borders.

By value, smuggled consumer goods made up the overwhelming bulk of the seizures. The joint team confiscated 14,147 bricks of assorted cigarettes worth more than K14.1 million and 60,528 bottles of assorted alcoholic beverages valued at more than K8.3 million.

Together, those two consignments are worth upwards of K22.4 million, roughly 96 per cent of the entire haul. Smaller quantities of groceries were also recovered, including 29 cases of hot chocolate valued at K15,678 and 54 boxes of pasta worth K21,600, along with a further consignment valued at K10,800.

Six vehicles were also taken off the road. On the Copperbelt, the team impounded three vehicles that Interpol records show were stolen outside Zambia: a white Toyota Hilux double-cab, registration BLB 9684; a grey Toyota Fortuner, registration BCD 9210; and a white Ford Ranger, registration ADE 6634.

In Lusaka, investigators found a Volkswagen suspected to have been smuggled into the country. Two Mercedes-Benz vehicles were also flagged after officers discovered their temporary import permits had expired.

Wildlife crime accounted for some of the most striking arrests. In Lusaka, a man was detained for possessing a pangolin valued at K340,000, the single most valuable wildlife item recovered during the five days.

Further arrests followed the discovery of a dried leopard skin valued at K120,000. In Chibolya township, two men and a woman were picked up after officers found them with 221 kilogrammes of buffalo, hippopotamus and warthog meat worth K178,000.

Elephant ivory surfaced in two separate cases. One man was found with tusks weighing 13 kilogrammes and valued at K103,341, while in Zimba another was caught with pieces of ivory weighing 44.5 kilogrammes and worth K115,000. Between them, the two cases removed 57.5 kilogrammes of ivory from circulation.

In Mumbwa, three men were arrested for possessing the carcass of a Kafue lechwe valued at K10,000. Taken together, the wildlife seizures carry a combined value of about K866,000.

The immigration sweep in Lusaka netted nationals from nine countries. Burundians formed the largest group at 33, close to half of those detained, followed by 18 Congolese and 14 Tanzanians.

The remainder comprised two Malawians and one national each from Zimbabwe, Nigeria, China, Somalia and Rwanda.

The spread of the seizures, from cigarettes and spirits to ivory, bushmeat and foreign-registered vehicles, reflects the range of illicit trade the multi-agency team set out to target. Each category fell under a different agency’s mandate, which explains the presence of revenue, wildlife, environmental, immigration and cyber crime officers within a single operation.

The three Copperbelt vehicles remain impounded on the strength of Interpol records, while the 14 suspects arrested during the operation are being processed for the offences linked to their seizures.

For now, the USALAMA-12 results stand as one of the clearest measures yet of the scale of contraband moving through Zambia, with K22.4 million in cigarettes and alcohol alone intercepted in under a week.

World.title: Entertainment: Kazadi gives The Pawn his blessing and tells Zambians to watch Mwamba’s film
World.content:
Filmmaker Mr David Kazadi urged Zambians to watch Mr Wyclif Mwamba’s new feature film, The Pawn, praising its storyline, cast and cinematography in a candid Facebook review that turned what social media had cast as a bitter feud into a public show of respect between two of the country’s best-known screen names.

Mr Kazadi said he absolutely loved the storyline and described Mr Mwamba as a phenomenal storyteller, calling that gift a core talent and creative strength nobody can take away from him.

“If you haven’t watched The Pawn yet, you definitely should check it out and support the vision,” he wrote.

The verdict landed barely a week after Mr Kazadi publicly took aim at the film’s troubled premiere, where more than 1,000 film lovers were left unable to watch the screening because of technical issues. In that earlier post, he criticised a culture in which local creators take on every role in a production themselves, and warned that one badly executed project damages the trust of audiences, sponsors and investors for everyone who follows.

“Leveraging someone else’s skills, knowledge, or expertise doesn’t make you weak, it makes you stronger,” he wrote at the time.

Many of his followers braced for a demolition job. What they got instead was a balanced, generous review from a producer who had clearly sat through the whole film and found plenty to like.

Mr Kazadi did not pretend the film was flawless. He said Mr Mwamba may not have the best interpersonal skills and lacks some exposure to certain technical and directing disciplines, but added that his passion for the project comes through clearly on screen, making it obvious why he was so determined to bring The Pawn to life.

On production, he pointed to areas common to most independent films. Dialogue could have been polished further, he said, and some on-set audio recording and volume transitions needed balancing to lift the viewing experience.

Those were small blemishes in his view. The sound glitches, he wrote, do not overshadow the film’s strengths. The cast delivered impressive performances, and several moments of striking cinematography caught his eye.

His warmest praise went to what Mr Mwamba has built beyond the film itself. Launching his own streaming platform, Capstone, was in Mr Kazadi’s words “a stroke of genius”, a smart, forward-thinking move for distribution and creative control in a country that usually suffers from exactly that problem.

He closed the review with a line written in capital letters for emphasis: “NOT ALL CRITIQUE IS SYNONYMOUS WITH HATE!”

The comment section quickly filled with surprise and approval. Mr Luckson Chilambwe Kalambulwa admitted he had expected Mr Kazadi to dismiss the film outright, and said the review showed the value of creatives building one another up.

Mr Tinozye Marvin Ndolo called it maturity at its highest, while Ms Nancy Siame described the review as very mature. Nthombz DanieLz Ngoma tagged Mr Mwamba and told him to take his flowers.

Writing in Bemba, Mr Felix Siya Mukonda marvelled at how quickly the beef between the two men had been settled, joking that Mr Kazadi had ended it in the blink of an eye.

Not everyone overlooked the criticism. Mr Mwewa Juma said the point about interpersonal skills matched his own view exactly, though he too gave credit for a storyline he loved. Mr James Maxmillan Makalani Banda put it simply: “In all honesty, it’s a good movie.”

The loudest call in the thread was for the two filmmakers to work together. Ms Glory Sampa said combining Mr Mwamba’s storytelling with Mr Kazadi’s technical experience could open doors to great things, a view echoed by Mr Kunda Chisenga and Ms Chipo Francine Kapoma.

Mc Heiz framed it in national terms. “We want to see you people working together on certain projects, the win for you guys is the win for the whole Zambia,” he wrote.

For Mr Mwamba, the endorsement arrives at a useful moment. The Ndola-based writer, director and producer rose to prominence with the soapie City on Fire for Zambezi Magic, and his credits also include Payback and Contravene. His Facebook page carries more than 930,000 followers.

He launched The Pawn’s trailer in Lusaka on 30 August before an audience of musicians, filmmakers and producers, and announced plans to feature more musicians in his future productions. The trailer hinted at a story built on power, betrayal and survival, the kind of drama Zambian audiences have long asked local filmmakers to deliver.

For viewers still on the fence, the case is now hard to dispute. A storyline praised even by a rival producer, a cast singled out for strong performances and a home-grown streaming platform built to keep Zambian stories in Zambian hands add up to a film worth an evening of anyone’s time.

Viewers can watch The Pawn on Capstone, Mr Mwamba’s own streaming platform. To find the right link and viewing details, fans should go through Mr Mwamba’s official Facebook page, Wyclif Mwamba, rather than unofficial uploads or forwarded links.

Fans who bought tickets for the disrupted premiere at Levy Mall have not lost out. Mr Mwamba said every ticket bought for that night remains valid and that a new screening date would be announced.

“You shall watch The Pawn,” he told fans.

Anyone searching online should check they have the right film. An American thriller from 1999 with the same title appears on several international streaming services, including Amazon Prime Video and Pluto TV. It is not the Zambian production, which stars Ms Mwaka Mugala and veteran actor Mr Clive Mwape in the leading roles.

Mr Kazadi is also preparing his own red-carpet event on 14 November, for which he said tickets reached 60 per cent capacity in just four days. That gives Zambian film fans two homegrown productions to back before the year closes.

Captain Alassane Diarra became the hero in Ndola, firing a late winner as Red Arrows edged South African giants Kaizer Chiefs 1-0 to keep alive Zambia’s hopes in CAF club competition.

Diarra struck inside the box from a corner to settle a tense CAF Confederation Cup Second Round first leg at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium, handing the Airmen a slender but crucial advantage ahead of the return leg in South Africa.

In a match where national pride was at stake, Arrows were the dominant force from start to finish, creating numerous chances in both halves while a cautious Chiefs side sat deep and relied on counter attacks.

It should have been more comfortable for the home side.

Arrows star Ackim Mumba will go home kicking himself after squandering two golden opportunities just before the break.

Twice Mumba was denied by Chiefs goalkeeper Renaldo Leaner, who produced stunning saves to keep his side alive.

But persistence finally paid off late on when Diarra pounced from close range after Arrows’ pressure from a corner, sending the Ndola crowd into raptures.

Arrows head coach Chisi Mbewe hailed his team’s performance, admitting he knew it would not be easy against a side with Chiefs’ continental maturity.

“I knew it wasn’t going to be an easy game playing against Kaizer Chiefs who have a lot of maturity in this competition. I’m so happy with the way the boys performed despite missing numerous chances,” Mbewe said.

“A 1-0 victory gives us advantage but we know the return leg in South Africa won’t be easy. So we have to prepare and go to South Africa to fight. Sometimes football can be like that, you create many chances but you end up scoring one goal,” he said.

For Chiefs, it was a sobering afternoon in Ndola. Coach Fernando Da Cruz conceded his side lacked aggression in the first half but insisted the tie is far from over.

“We played a tough first half with no aggression. In the second half we played better, we didn’t create many chances but had a better second half. We want to congratulate Red Arrows for this win,” Cruz said.

“Now we are focusing on the return leg at home. We know that we can win the match at home,” he said.

The victory means Red Arrows remain Zambia’s sole surviving representative in CAF club competitions this season, carrying the nation’s flag into the most difficult of assignments – a second leg away in Johannesburg where Kaizer Chiefs will be desperate to overturn the deficit in front of their massive home support.

But for now, the Airmen can savour a night when Zambian resilience overcame South African pedigree.

World.title: Councils implored to actualise economic expansion agenda
World.content:
Government has challenged local authorities to translate the Grow Zambia Agenda into practical and measurable results at community level.

Northern Province Acting Permanent Secretary, Beauty Undi-Phiri, underscored the need for councils to take a leading role in actualising economic expansion agenda.

Ms Undi-Phiri said this when she officiated at the installation ceremony for Kasama Mayor, Peter Yuda, held at Civic Centre grounds yesterday.

She noted that Kasama is well-positioned to contribute significantly to the realisation of the Grow Zambia Agenda through sectors such as agriculture, livestock production, trade, tourism, and small-scale enterprise development and that the council should take leading role in actualising opportunities.

“Kasama is well positioned to contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda, I therefore encourage the council to work closely with stakeholders to support farmers, improve market infrastructure, promote value addition, attract both local and foreign investment and create an enabling environment for business growth,” Ms Undi-Phiri stated.

She further appealed to Mr Yuda and councilors to serve the people of Kasama with diligence regardless of their political affiliation.

“Let the interests of Kasama and its people always take precedence over individual and partisan considerations,” she said.

And the Acting Permanent Secretary has urged the council to spearhead constructive engagement with traders and provide practical solutions that promote lawful economic activity while ensuring orderly urban development.

And delivering his maiden speech, Mr Yuda pledged to work with the government through constructive and collaborative engagement.

He observed that Kasama residents are yearning for development hence the need to put politics aside and provide the much needed services.

“Development knows no political colour, bad roads affect every vehicle; poor sanitation threatens every family and economic hardship touches every household regardless of how they voted,” Mr Yuda said.

He added that there is need for the municipality to work with all stakeholders and come up with practical ideas aimed at increasing the revenue base.

The Mayor further called for the construction of key infrastructure in the district, among them, a modern abattoir and a dry port.

Kasama has 19 Councilors spread across the three Constituencies in the districts with three more Councilors elected under the Proportional Representation Electoral System.

World.title: Lavushimanda DC urges residents to go for HIV testing
World.content:
Lavushimanda District Commissioner Terries Kunda, has encouraged residents in the district to go for HIV testing services and know their HIV status.

‎

‎Speaking during the launch of the commemoration of HIV Testing, Counseling and Treatment (HTCT) Day held at Lukulu Health Center, in a speech read on his behalf by District Health Human Resource Management Officer, Oliver Chanda, Mr Kunda said Knowing one’s HIV status is a critical step towards protecting individual health, safeguarding families, and building healthier communities.

‎

‎Mr Kunda added that effective treatment is available for people who test positive for HIV, noting that early initiation of treatment, good adherence to medication and regular clinical follow-up, people living with HIV can live long, healthy and productive lives.

‎

‎“HIV is not a death sentence; it is an opportunity to take control of one’s health,” he said.

‎

‎He further emphasised the need to fight stigma and discrimination, noting that no one should be discouraged from seeking healthcare services for fear of being judged or rejected.

‎

‎Mr Kunda encouraged community members to create an environment where people can freely access HIV services, receive support and live with dignity.

‎

‎The District Commissioner also commended health workers for their continued commitment to improving the health of communities.

‎

‎He urged them to continue providing quality counselling, safeguarding clients’ confidentiality and treating every client with compassion and respect, noting that more efforts are needed to improve healthcare service delivery.

‎

‎Meanwhile, speaking at the same event, Mpumba Rural Health Centre Right to Care Zambia Professional Counsellor, Kennedy Bwalya, urged community members who test positive for HIV to adhere to their medications in order to improve their health

‎

‎Mr Bwalya explained that taking medications will reduce the spread of the virus as well as maintain better health.

‎

‎“When you go for HIV testing at health facilities and test positive, ensure that you start taking your medication. The medication will improve your health,” he said.

‎

‎This year’s 2026 HIV Testing, Counseling and Treatment Day is being commemorated under the theme “One Door, Many Services: Integrated Health for a Sustainable Future.”

World.title: Nigeria: Nigeria's Hunger Crisis Takes an Emotional Toll on Caregivers #WorldFoodDay
World.content:
Fatima Ibrahimâs 23-month-old daughter, Aisha, was admitted to the Nilefa Kiji nutrition facility in Maiduguri after battling meningitis and repeated convulsions. The three weeks spent in hospital were filled with conflicting emotions. While grateful to see her daughter improve, Fatima could not stop thinking about the eight children she had left at home.

As millions of people across northern Nigeria face severe food insecurity, children continue to bear the consequences of a deepening malnutrition crisis. But the impact is far beyond the children in treatment. This can be a source of significant anxiety, exhaustion, and emotional distress for parents and caregivers, particularly those who spend weeks in the hospital when a child is severely malnourished and are concerned about starving children at home.

The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) estimates that 34.7 million people in Nigeria are in crisis levels of food insecurity during the lean season, while more than 5.4 million children are acutely malnourished. In northern Nigeria in 2025, MSF teams provided treatment to 425,634 children who were suffering from acute malnutrition.

The food crisis has particularly affected Nigeria's northeastern states of Borno, Adamawa and Yobe. It is estimated that by 2026 nearly 5.8 million people will be severely food insecure. In Borno State, conflicts, climate shocks and displacement are interfering with people's means of livelihood and damaging local food production, putting about 15,000 people at risk of suffering from catastrophic hunger.

The World Food Programme (WFP) has warned that ongoing insecurity is worsening hunger by forcing communities to flee their homes, preventing farmers from accessing their land and restricting the delivery of humanitarian assistance.

Monica Genya, Association Director at Doctors Without Borders (MSF) Southern Africa, described the "situation as critical," with medical teams treating children suffering from severe acute malnutrition and related illnesses.

In MSF nutrition facilities such as Nilefa Kiji in Maiduguri, she said, teams see intensive care units full of children fighting severe acute malnutrition. Many arrive severely wasted, and because malnutrition weakens their immunity, many also have illnesses such as measles, diphtheria and malaria, she said.

"It is severe, and it is life-threatening for many children," said Genya.

In 2025, MSF treated 353,989 children for severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and 90,723 for moderate acute malnutrition (MAM). She said that SAM is the most dangerous form that continues to claim young lives in the region. Children are severely wasted, and their immune systems are weakened. Some arrive at treatment facilities already suffering from diseases such as measles, diphtheria and malaria. Treatment can last anywhere from a week to more than a month, leaving caregivers facing prolonged separation from the rest of their families.

Genya said MSF treated 41.8 per cent more children for acute malnutrition in 2025 than in the previous year, reflecting a worsening crisis. Admissions have risen steadily since 2022, driven by insecurity, displacement, food shortages, disease outbreaks, economic hardship and cuts to humanitarian funding.

"These pressures compound one another, so more families are pushed to the edge each year," she said.

The rising number of children requiring treatment also raises questions about whether humanitarian resources are keeping pace with the need. MSF supports the state Ministries of Health in Zamfara, Katsina, Kebbi, Borno, Bauchi, Sokoto and Kano.

Abba Adamu Musa/MSF Inside a ward of MSFâs facility, Nilefa Kiji, in Maiduguri, Borno State, northeast Nigeria. Here, MSF provides care for children suffering from malnutrition.

Supporting caregivers as part of treatment

Genya said that the emotional burden carried by caregivers is often overlooked in discussions about child malnutrition, where attention tends to focus on medical treatment, admissions and recovery rates.

"Medical statistics capture admissions and recovery rates, but they cannot measure the emotional burden carried by the person at the bedside, who is most often the mother," she said. Caregivers endure fear, anxiety, guilt, uncertainty and emotional exhaustion, and some develop symptoms of depression."

The consequences extend beyond their own wellbeing. This matters for the child's recovery too. A caregiver's emotional wellbeing influences how engaged they stay in treatment, whether they follow medical advice and how well they can care for the child after discharge.

"Caring for the caregiver is part of caring for the child," she said.

The competing demands on caregivers are evident in the experiences MSF counsellors encounter at its nutrition facilities in northern Nigeria. "Caregivers are pulled in two directions," said Genya. "Many arrive with a critically ill child while having left other children at home, sometimes with no one to look after them and little to eat."

Their worry does not stop when treatment begins. Genya recalled the experience of a mother in Maiduguri.

"One mother in Maiduguri told us she had left eight children at home, and when she heard one had a fever and there was no money for treatment, she cried and could not eat. Another was asked by her eldest son when she was coming home, because the children were hungry without her," she said. In another case, counsellors met a mother of six who had to leave the hospital because her husband had left the children with neighbours and she could not bear to stay.

"These stories show how guilt, worry and separation can put a child's treatment at risk, which is why we listen and respond," she said.

Recognising the emotional toll of malnutrition, MSF incorporates mental health and psychosocial support into its nutrition programmes.

At Nilefa Kiji, caregivers receive psychological first aid on arrival, followed by individual counselling and group sessions where they can share experiences, express their fears and learn coping strategies. Caregiver education helps families understand and manage the emotional and behavioural challenges that can arise during and after treatment. Children take part in structured play activities that help restore a sense of normalcy during recovery.

"The support is also practical," she said.

Counsellors help distressed caregivers reach relatives by phone, and in some cases supervised home visits let a caregiver briefly check on their family before returning to finish their child's treatment. She said that this helps caregivers cope, builds their confidence, supports treatment adherence and contributes to better recovery. "Many regain hope as they watch their children get better, and some come back after discharge just to show how healthy their children have become," said Genya.

Beyond treating malnutrition

For MSF, addressing the crisis requires more than treating children after they have become severely malnourished. Families must also be reached earlier, before food insecurity and other pressures push children into life-threatening conditions.

Abba Adamu Musa/MSF MSF counsellor-educator Keturah John engages Adamaâs daughter, Fatima, in a play therapy session at MSFâs facility, Nilefa Kiji, in Maiduguri, Borno State, northeast Nigeria. Fatima is an inpatient and has been receiving treatment for malnutrition.

"Treating children once they are already severely malnourished saves lives, but we also need to reach families before they get to that point," she said.

Insecurity and displacement, disease outbreaks and economic hardship continue to undermine families' ability to provide adequate food and care. Genya said prevention and treatment must go hand in hand, alongside support for caregivers who bear much of the responsibility for children's recovery.

She added that the pressures pushing children into malnutrition, including insecurity and displacement, food insecurity, disease outbreaks and the economic crisis, are not easing. Sustained funding is needed not only for nutrition services but also for mental health and psychosocial support, she said. Governments and humanitarian organisations must work to ensure families can access essential assistance before children reach the point of severe malnutrition.

"This is why MSF's work focuses on both prevention and treatment, and why we care for the whole family, including the caregivers at the bedside, through counselling and psychosocial support. This work depends on public support," she said. "Donating to MSF's humanitarian efforts helps our teams keep reaching children across northern Nigeria, treating them early and supporting the families who care for them."

With over 5.4 million children acutely malnourished this year, every contribution makes a difference, she said.

As the world marks World Food Day, the experiences of families in northern Nigeria underline the need to recognise the human cost of food insecurity beyond the physical effects of hunger.

Genya said that addressing the crisis requires supporting caregivers alongside treating children. She said that there is a need to support caregivers through mental health and psychosocial services. She said that behind every child in our facilities is a caregiver, most often a mother, living with fear, anxiety, guilt and exhaustion. Many are worried sick about children left at home without enough food. Their emotional wellbeing shapes whether they can stay engaged in treatment, follow medical advice and keep caring for their child after discharge.

"Recognising and supporting caregivers is therefore key to ending this crisis, not a side issue," she said.

She urged donors to reconsider humanitarian funding cuts and sustain investment in nutrition care, including mental health and psychosocial support, to ensure children and their caregivers receive the help they need. "Behind every statistic is a caregiver's mental health impacted by malnutrition," said Genya.

The fear of losing a sick child, combined with guilt over being separated from other family members, can take a significant toll on their mental well-being. "A mother sits at a hospital bedside, grateful that her child is improving, while worrying that her other children at home have nothing to eat. She is afraid of losing the child in front of her, and guilty about those she can't be with," she said. "These are people showing extraordinary resilience under immense strain, and their stories rarely get told."

"Healing is not only about restoring a child's weight," said Genya. "It is also about restoring hope and resilience to the person who sits at the bedside every day."

World.title: Nigeria: Aircraft Loses Door Mid-Air, Makes Emergency Landing in Abuja
World.content:
The aircraft, a CL60 with registration number T7-SEI and flight identification DWC052, was departing Abuja for the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos, when the incident occurred.

An aircraft operated by Triton Aviation made an emergency landing at the Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport, Abuja, on Thursday after its crew reported that a door had opened mid-air shortly after take-off.

The aircraft, a CL60 with registration number T7-SEI and flight identification DWC052, was departing Abuja for the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos, when the incident occurred.

According to a serious incident report, the aircraft took off from Runway 22 at 4:17 p.m. Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) and, about three nautical miles from the airport, was climbing at 3,000 feet when the crew issued a distress call at 4:20 p.m.



The crew reported an open door in flight, prompting air traffic controllers to direct the aircraft back to Abuja for an emergency landing.

Airport fire and rescue personnel and the medical team were subsequently alerted and placed on standby in preparation for the aircraft's return.

The incident report stated that at about 4:29 p.m. UTC, the crew asked the Abuja control tower to confirm whether the door was open.

The duty air traffic controller attempted to observe the aircraft with binoculars but could not establish the door's condition because of the aircraft's position.

The crew was informed that the controller could not visually confirm the situation.

The aircraft landed safely on Runway 22 at approximately 4:34 p.m. UTC, about 14 minutes after the Mayday call.

After landing, the controller observed that the aircraft's door was missing from the fuselage.

The aircraft was subsequently taxied to the international apron extension, where it was parked with the assistance of a marshaller.

Meanwhile, a video circulating on social media appears to show the aircraft's missing door. In the footage, an unidentified man said some farmers found the door while returning from their farm in the Abuja area.

He suggested that it had fallen from an aircraft but did not provide further details about the discovery. The circumstances surrounding the reported discovery have not been independently verified as of the time of filing this report.

The cause of the incident and the circumstances surrounding the door's detachment have not been established.

The number of people on board is also not immediately available.

The Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau (NSIB) confirmed that the incident occurred and said investigators have been deployed.

"Yes, it happened. The investigators are there. We will be releasing an official statement shortly," the bureau's media team said.

Close 

The Director of Public Affairs and Consumer Protection at the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA), Michael Achimugu, also confirmed the incident but said the NSIB has jurisdiction.

However, Triton Aviation could not be reached for comment when this report was filed.

World.title: South Africa: Lions Player Dies From Suspected Cardiac Arrest in French Hotel
World.content:
A Lions player has apparently died in a hotel room in France, where the South African team has been preparing for the Champions Cup debut against La Rochelle.

French media are reporting that a Lions player has died in a hotel room on the Île de Ré, where the South African team has been preparing for the Champions Cup debut against La Rochelle.

Île de Ré is an island off the western coast of France, and connected via a bridge to the mainland city of La Rochelle.

According to media reports in France, the player was found unresponsive in a shower cubicle.

Paramedics attempted to resuscitate him but were unsuccessful. He was pronounced dead. The player, in his thirties, was in cardiac arrest when emergency services arrived shortly before 10.30am.

Sources have independently confirmed the news to Daily Maverick, but the player's family have yet to be informed, so his name cannot be released.

It is unclear at this stage whether the Champions Cup match against two-time champions La Rochelle will go ahead, originally scheduled for Saturday, 17 October 2026. DM

President Tinubu urged the Senate to expedite the nominees' confirmation in view of the forthcoming general elections next January.

World.title: Africa: Ebola Spread Raises Fresh Urgency for Africa's Domestic Health Funding
World.content:
Bulawayo — An Ebola death last week in Kenya is highlighting the urgency of Africa's public health emergency preparedness and how the continent's governments are committing their national budgets to the health sector.

The Kenya case is serving as a call to arms in the fight against Africa's public health emergencies and how locally coordinated efforts are adequately equipped to contain the spread of communicable diseases.

"Health emergency preparedness gives us a head start, and Kenya has put important outbreak control measures in place," Janabi said in a 6 October media brief, which was in stark contrast to concerns raised in the DRC that life-saving medical supplies only arrived ten days later from neighbouring countries, effectively allowing Ebola to leave a trail of death.

As the disease surges at its north Kivu epicentre in the Democratic Republic of Congo, questions have returned about how the shuttering of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) has devastated public health emergency responses across Africa.



Last week, Doctors Without Borders warned that the current Ebola strain was spreading so fast for emergency health workers "it was like fighting a megafire," further raising concerns over how the DRC and neighbouring countries will tackle the crisis amid increasingly limited resources.

Despite being often cited as having vast mineral wealth, the DRC's Ebola response has been plagued by an under-funded health sector where international humanitarian agencies are struggling to provide basic medical care.

As the new Ebola strain took root in the DRC's east, Amadou Bocoum, CARE International's DRC Country Director, lamented that "with proper funding, we would have had prepositioned stock and begun distributing critical supplies like PPE from day one, but instead, we started with nothing and lost 10 days."

These funding concerns would be raised weeks later by the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (UNECA) at the 76th Session of the WHO Regional Committee for Africa in Addis Ababa in August.

UNECA noted that "Africa's health financing model remains structurally fragile," with governments failing to allocate adequate budgets for the health sector.

African governments and other health sector players have already raised alarm over the Trump Administration's decision to ice the USAID, which triggered a continent-wide shortage of anything from condoms to malaria and HIV/AIDS drugs.

At the WHO Regional Committee conference, UNECA raised concerns that "external health assistance was down almost 30 per cent," and as Ebola spreads, the effects of that deficit are being felt with catastrophic consequences.

The impact of the reliance on overseas development assistance was made clear by Aboubakri Diaw, who leads UNECA's Sustainable Financing Initiative, who told the gathering that "Africa does not have a reform deficit. It has a sustainable financed-reform deficit."

"Health financing strategies sit on shelves. Insurance schemes are legislated but struggling to be capitalised. Benefit packages are defined but not costed into medium-term expenditure frameworks. A reform without a budget line does not constitute a policy," Diaw said.

Yet it is a commitment African governments made in 2001 at the Abuja Declaration to allocate 15 percent of national budgets to health, but countries have fallen short, with some allocations ranging between as little as 2 percent and 12 percent, according to the World Health Organisation.

To address the public health funding crisis, UNECA says what remains crucial is "a fundamental reset in how African governments and their finance ministries fund health systems" in a continent where millions lack access to and cannot afford basic medical care.

"External aid covered more than 30 per cent of health expenditure, and in some 13 countries the ECA has looked at, households pay more for health than their own governments do," Diaw said, adding that "many countries on the continent now spend more on servicing debt than on public health."

Amid these challenges and competing public spending priorities, it is not yet clear how governments will navigate these new public health funding realities, as pressure from international lending institutions for African countries to repay billions of loans still remains.

Close 

Analysts however see the funding crisis as part of Africa's broader political architecture where short-term planning by sitting governments prioritises projects closely linked to the election cycle.

"Governments have to balance health against infrastructure, security, education, social protection and other priorities," said Pakhani Mhazo, a public health researcher based in South Africa.

"However, health preparedness often produces benefits that are not immediately visible to voters. For example, if you invest in disease surveillance, laboratories and emergency systems and successfully prevent an outbreak from becoming a crisis, there is no obvious event that voters can see as the result of that investment," Mhazo told IPS.

Meanwhile, without any clear or immediate sources to fill the funding gaps left by international aid, African governments have their work cut out, and as Claver Gatete, UNECA Executive Secretary, reminded African ministers during the High-Level Forum on Sustainable Health Financing in April this year, "Health is not expenditure; it is investment - in people, in productivity and in prosperity."

IPS UN Bureau Report

World.title: Kenya: Image of Kenyan Senator Edwin Sifuna Asleep At Public Event Is Doctored
World.content:
Image of Kenyan senator Edwin Sifuna asleep at public event is doctored

IN SHORT: An image posted on Facebook purportedly shows the Nairobi senator drunk and asleep alongside veteran broadcaster Fred Machoka. But inconsistencies between the image and footage from the event suggest it was manipulated.

A Facebook post claims that Edwin Sifuna, the senator for Kenya's capital Nairobi, became drunk at a public event. It includes an image appearing to show him asleep in a chair next to veteran broadcaster Fred Machoka, who also appears to be asleep.

The image shows Sifuna wearing a white shirt and black trousers, sitting next to Machoka, with several bottles of alcohol and glasses on a table in front of them.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Another image shows Sifuna awake, sitting with his arms folded.

One image is labelled "Mlevi Sifuna", Kiswahili for "Sifuna the drunkard". The post describes him as "drunk and disorderly" and a "fake" presidential candidate.

Sifuna, an opposition politician who has declared his intention to run for president in Kenya's 2027 elections, launched the Equitable Party on 4 October 2026.

The image circulated shortly after Machoka celebrated 50 years in broadcasting at an event in Nairobi on 10 October. Sifuna attended the celebration, which featured performances by several musicians, including Congolese star Koffi Olomide.

On 14 October, president William Ruto mocked Sifuna's new party and referred to his appearance at the celebration, where bottles of alcohol were visible on a table. Ruto also questioned Sifuna's presidential ambitions.

The image has also been posted here, here and here.

But does it really show Sifuna and Machoka asleep after drinking too much? We checked.

Doctored photo

Royal Media Services, Machoka's longtime employer, published a video of the celebration. We examined it and compared it with the circulating image.

Both men appear in the footage, but neither is shown asleep.

We also found several inconsistencies. Videos from the event show Sifuna wearing a black wristwatch, which is missing from the circulating image.

Additionally, the man presented as Machoka in the image also has different facial features from those seen in the event footage. His red outfit lacks the black shoulder detailing visible in the video.

Close 

These differences suggest the image was manipulated.

We also analysed the image using Hive Moderation's AI content detector, which returned a 99.8% likelihood of AI-generated content. Such tools are not conclusive, but the result adds to the evidence that the image is inauthentic.

Sifuna attended Machoka's anniversary celebration, but the circulating image purporting to show the two men asleep appears to have been doctored.

World.title: The one lesson every parent should teach their child after the Bend school shooting
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Three children and a teacher were killed on Oct. 15 at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, just 20 minutes from our home in central Oregon. Four precious lives were stolen, leaving families facing a grief no parent, spouse, or loved one should ever have to endure. Children who should be coming home to their families will never walk through those doors again. A teacher who devoted a life to educating and caring for children is gone.

Among the critically injured is 7-year-old Saylor, a child who had previously been honored in Bend as a "Sparrow" through a program that supports children facing serious medical challenges. Already familiar with adversity, she is now fighting for her life after being shot in the face. Our hearts break for Saylor and for all the other victims of this devastating violence.

Our community and our nation are in mourning.

ARMED BYSTANDER FATALLY SHOOTS SUSPECTED TEEN GUNMAN AFTER 3 CHILDREN, 1 ADULT KILLED AT OREGON SCHOOL: FEDS

As an anti-bullying specialist and expert witness, I've witnessed more than 20,000 students around the world publicly apologize for bullying and related behavior. Some of these apologies have helped prevent students from harming themselves or others.

We don't know the motives of the 16-year-old shooter. We don't know whether he was bullied at Silver Rail or any other school. But this tragedy raises questions about a destructive pattern that requires entire communities—not just teachers and schools—to confront bullying. After all, bullying is a cultural problem, not merely a "school problem."

The Secret Service's report, "Protecting America's Schools," examined 41 targeted school attacks. Among the 35 attackers whose backgrounds were analyzed—all male—80% had experienced bullying. For 57%, that bullying was persistent.

There is no evidence at this point that bullying played any role in the Silver Rail attack. But research into past targeted school attacks shows why bullying remains one of the behaviors communities should take seriously.

Each time our nation reels from another school shooting, a dangerous misunderstanding is often treated as fact: The shooter must be severely mentally ill. Yet most people with severe mental illness are not violent. Equating psychiatric diagnoses with dangerousness stigmatizes people who need care and distracts from the specific behaviors that should concern us.

HERO DAD WHO TOOK DOWN OREGON SCHOOL SHOOTER IDENTIFIED ALONG WITH TEACHER, STUDENT BOTH KILLED IN ATTACK

Having worked with countless targets of bullying for more than 25 years, I've witnessed how persistent abuse can leave children emotionally inflamed. Some turn their pain inward, while others express it outwardly through anger, aggression and sometimes violence. Too many are expected to endure a level of persistent abuse that no adult would tolerate.

Telling a child to ignore cruelty is not intervention. Admonishing a child to "turn the other cheek" in the face of relentless abuse is one of the most tortured applications of Scripture. Requiring an apology without checking whether the abuse has stopped is not accountability. Moving the targeted child to another classroom or school—an all-too-common practice—while leaving the aggressor unchecked only deepens the injustice and resentment.

POLICE DISPTACH AUDIO RELEASED AFTER OREGON ELEMENTARY SCHOOL SHOOTING

Students need trustworthy adults and clear reporting options, including anonymous reporting. They also need protection against retaliation. When reporting makes life worse, children learn to remain silent precisely when adults most need information.

What most people don't understand is that bystanders possess the greatest potential power in the theater of bullying. Bullies often seek an audience, and that audience can either reward their cruelty through laughter, encouragement, or silence—or help stop it through courageous action. When witnesses intervene safely, they can shift the balance of power in favor of the targeted child.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

To help break the connection between persistent bullying and the risk of school violence, we need a national commitment that begins at the dinner table. We must expand our family values to include a simple pledge: When our children witness bullying, they will take at least one of three actions:

1. Comfort the targeted child afterward.

2. Report—not tattle—what they saw or heard.

3. Intervene directly, when safe, using assertive but nonviolent words.

Have this conversation with your family today.

Because right now, while adults cry, mourn, and thank God their own children are safe, thousands of other children are carrying emotionally inflamed hearts. They, too, are precious to God. Compassionate bystander intervention can help ease their suffering, reminding them that the cruelty they endure is undeserved, that they are not defined by it, and that they are loved.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

We won't stop every school shooting. But we can stop complacency. That begins when we teach our children that witnessing bullying carries a responsibility to act safely and compassionately.

Bullying does not have to be an ordinary part of growing up. And standing against it should become an ordinary part of raising our children.

World.title: The nine key races that will decide who controls the Senate, and where they stand
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Democrats have expanded their once-narrow path to reclaiming the Senate majority with just over two weeks until Election Day, but they'll need to win several competitive races to take control of the chamber.

If Democrats ride a massive blue wave in the midterm elections, they could end up with 52 or even 53 seats in the next Senate. But if Republicans out-perform the polls, they could hold their majority, which currently stands at 53-47.

Here's a look at the current battlefield and both parties' routes to securing a Senate majority in the midterms.

The latest Power Rankings point to Democrats and Republicans each taking 47 seats in the midterms, leaving six races rated as true toss-ups. Additionally, three races are rated as leaners — one step shy of a toss-up. These nine showdowns will likely determine whether the Democrats make a net gain of four seats to win control of the Senate or if the GOP holds the majority.

DEMS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP SENATE SEATS BUT GOP'S MASSIVE CASH ADVANTAGE AN OBSTACLE

"Nine races will determine control of the Senate, and on the polling alone, you could call any of them toss-ups," said Remy Numa, a Fox News contributor who steers the network's Power Rankings.

The GOP is fighting political history, as the party in power in Washington has traditionally lost seats during midterm election years. Republicans also face a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and President Donald Trump's increasingly negative approval ratings.

With Republicans controlling the seats in six of the nine competitive races in the Power Rankings, the GOP is playing more defense than the Democrats.

The six toss-up states are Alaska, where Sen. Dan Sullivan is seeking re-election against Democratic challenger and former Rep. Mary Peltola; Iowa, where Rep. Ashley Hinson is trying to keep retiring Sen. Joni Ernst's seat in GOP hands against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek; and Maine, where longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins is running for re-election against former state Senate President Troy Jackson, the Democratic challenger.

DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING - HERE ARE THREE FACTORS THAT COULD STOP IT

Also on the list is Ohio, where appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted is running to serve the final two years of the term won in 2022 by now-Vice President JD Vance. He's facing former longtime Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown. And in Texas, state Attorney General Ken Paxton is battling Democratic state Rep. James Talarico in the race to succeed longtime GOP Sen. John Cornyn, who was ousted by Paxton in a bitter Republican primary.

Democrats are playing defense in Michigan, the sixth toss-up, where nominee Abdul El-Sayed is trying to keep party control of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters' seat, as he faces former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Democrats are also on defense in New Hampshire, where Rep. Chris Pappas is aiming to keep retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen's seat blue against former GOP Sen. John E. Sununu. The Power Rankings rate the race "Lean Democrat."

It's a similar story in Minnesota, where Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is trying to keep retiring Sen. Tina Smith's seat in party hands.

But the Power Rankings this past week shifted the race in the blue-leaning state toward the GOP, from Likely Democrat to Lean Democrat, as Republican nominee Michele Tafoya appears to gain traction.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Meanwhile, the GOP is on defense in red-leaning Kansas, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces a difficult re-election fight against Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton, a pastor. The Power Rankings rate the race Lean Republican.

Numa, pointing to Kansas, Minnesota and New Hampshire, said that "the voter profiles and histories of those states are keeping them at 'Lean D' and 'Lean R' on the forecast, but this map has expanded, and with the exception of the North Star State, mostly into red territory."

Meanwhile, two states are now pretty much off the table for the GOP.

Georgia was a top Republican target when the 2026 cycle began, but Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff holds a solid lead over GOP challenger Rep. Mike Collins in the southeastern battleground. Republican outside groups have cut their spending significantly in Georgia, and the Fox News Power Rankings rate the race as Likely Democrat.

In neighboring North Carolina, Republicans appear to have conceded the seat held by retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis. Republican groups have pulled the plug on spending on behalf of GOP nominee Mike Whatley, who trails former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee, in polling. The Fox News Power Rankings also rate this race as Likely Democrat.

The Democrats win the majority if they run the table by holding Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire, and flip North Carolina as well as at least three of the five GOP-controlled toss-up states.

"Senate Democrats are in the strongest position yet to win the majority – with multiple paths to flip GOP-held seats and growing momentum across the map," Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee chair, touted in a recent statement.

Conversely, Republicans would keep control of the chamber by holding at least three of the toss-ups where they're playing defense. A 50-50 Senate would remain in GOP hands, thanks to the tie-breaking vote of Vice President JD Vance.

Gillibrand's counterpart, National Republican Senatorial Committee Chair Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, remains optimistic.

"I think it's going very well for us," Scott said Thursday in an interview on Fox News "America Reports." "The momentum, frankly, is with us, not against us."

The GOP majority could be bolstered if the party goes on offense. While chances of Sununu flipping New Hampshire appear to be receding, Republicans are optimistic Rogers can top El-Sayed in Michigan. Trump is expected to hold a rally with Rogers in the Great Lakes battleground later this month.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Meanwhile, Scott has his eyes on a flip in Minnesota.

"Michele Tafoya is running a very independent campaign, lots of traction," he told Fox News. "I think we close that gap. And if there's an October surprise, Minnesota goes Republican."

World.title: William Shatner finds answer to 'What the f--- is heavy metal?' after forming new band at 95
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

William Shatner is showing no signs of slowing down as he prepares to front a heavy metal band at age 95.

In addition to his decades-long career as an actor, Shatner is also an accomplished musician, who has released 11 studio albums encompassing a wide range of genres including spoken word, rock, progressive rock, Christmas and country releases.

During an interview with Fox News Digital, Shatner, who recently partnered with over-the-counter hearing aid maker Audien Hearing for a new campaign, shared his reaction when his music label Cleopatra Records first approached him earlier this year about making a heavy metal album.

WILLIAM SHATNER SAYS HE'S 'TAKING CARE OF BUSINESS' AT 95: 'THE LEAST OF ALL I WANT DO IS DIE'

"I said, ‘What the f--- is heavy metal?’" the "Star Trek" icon recalled.

"And that's the title of the album, ‘What the F is Heavy Metal,’" Shatner added.

COUNTRY MUSIC SINGER SHANE SMITH PUTS HIS OWN SPIN ON JOHNNY CASH'S ICONIC 'HURT' COVER

Shatner told Fox News Digital that he teamed up with his longtime creative collaborator and friend, author Robert Sharenow, for the project. The two previously worked together on five albums featuring autobiographical lyrics and spoken-word performances.

"So we wrote six songs for the album," Shatner said. "And I laid down my track."

WATCH: WILLIAM SHATNER, 95, ANSWERS ‘WHAT THE F--- IS HEAVY METAL?' WITH NEW ALBUM

In addition to six original songs, Shatner said that "What the F is Heavy Metal" will feature covers with contributions from more than 50 musicians,

"We've got one number in the album that's gonna be out in the wintertime called ‘What the F is Heavy Metal,’" Shatner said. "All of a sudden, 50, I'm told 50 heavy metal musicians all volunteer to be on this album."

PAUL MCCARTNEY REVEALS HOW A 'HAPPY' TEEN HITCHHIKING TRIP WITH GEORGE HARRISON DELIVERED A SHOCK

The musicians included Queen's Brian May, who performed a guitar solo for one of the album's tracks titled "Rage." Shatner explained that "Rage" features the famous line "Rage, rage against the dying of the light" from the 1951 poem "Do not go gentle into that good night," written by Welsh poet Dylan Thomas.

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Shatner recalled that he was later invited to perform at Riot Fest, an annual three-day punk rock music festival held at Douglass Park in Chicago, Illinois. In a July social media post, the organizers of Riot Fest announced that Shatner would debut his heavy metal band The *uckers at the festival, noting that they had tried to book him for over a decade.

ROD STEWART CONFIRMS FINAL TOUR AFTER HEART PROCEDURE AND HEALTH SCARES

The "Boston Legal" alum said that his label tapped five musicians to form his new heavy metal band. The all-star rock and heavy metal lineup includes guitarists Marcus Nand and Britt Lightning, bassist Phil Soussan and drummer Fred Aching.

"They put together a group of fabulous musicians," Shatner said. "We call ourselves The *uckers for, you know, ‘What the f--- is heavy metal.’'"

BRET MICHAELS CANCELS REMAINING 2026 TOUR DATES HOURS AFTER 'COMEBACK' PERFORMANCE DUE TO HEALTH SCARE

The band made its live debut in Chicago on Sept. 19 and performed at Riot Fest the following day. The *uckers played original songs including "Rage," "Sky" and "One Fear" alongside covers of Ozzy Osbourne's "Crazy Train," Motörhead's "Ace of Spades," and Metallica's "Enter Sandman."

"We went to Riot Fest … and was a huge success, huge," Shatner recalled. "They were cheering and the reviews and the people…so it proved to me the viability of ‘What the F is Heavy Metal.'"

‘A MAN WITHOUT LOVE’ SINGER ENGELBERT HUMPERDINCK CREDITS UNDERWATER WORKOUT FOR KEEPING HIM ‘ALIVE’ AT 90

After performing with The *uckers and making his heavy metal album, Shatner said he has an answer to his original question.

"It is the beat of life," he said. "It is such an energetic way of doing music. It enlivens your life. It stirs you up. It makes you pay attention."

WATCH: WILLIAM SHATNER SAYS HEAVY METAL ‘ENLIVENS’ HIS LIFE AS HE FRONTS BAND AT 95

Shatner explained that his approach to heavy metal extends beyond the music itself. For the album, he said he incorporated fresh takes on the lyrics of several classic songs, including Metallica’s "Enter Sandman," which he believes contains darker themes beneath its familiar melody.

"I've reinterpreted even the cover songs," he said.

Shatner said his version of "Enter Sandman" focuses on the sinister implications of the song’s lyrics rather than treating the Sandman as a harmless bedtime figure.

"It's a total reinterpretation of the Sandman," he said. "It is amazing."

While Shatner is embracing the volume of heavy metal, the project also connects to a more personal issue. The actor is partnering with Audien Hearing on a campaign about hearing health after experiencing tinnitus and hearing loss himself.

Shatner recalled that his hearing challenges began decades ago on the set of "Star Trek." During the filming of an explosion scene featuring him alongside his co-star Leonard Nimoy, the stage doors were accidentally left closed, preventing the blast from dissipating properly.

He told Fox News Digital that the two actors were taken to a doctor after their ears began ringing. Shatner said that he did not immediately realize that the noise had become permanent. The Canada native recalled that while walking on the beach one day, he noticed that the hiss of the retreating waves never completely disappeared.

"I heard the hiss, but the hiss never went away," he said. "It was always hissing."

Shatner said he eventually learned to live with the tinnitus through a process known as habituation. He also estimated that he has lost roughly 20% to 30% of his hearing and said hearing aids have helped him rediscover everyday sounds.

"The dog claws on the floor, the creak of this rocking chair — all the panoply of sounds that go to make up the richness of the world around us, we’re using hearing," he said.

Shatner's hearing challenges have not stopped him from playing heavy metal. However, he said the loud music can temporarily intensify the tinnitus, which he noticed after performing at Riot Fest.

"Now I'm fitted with earphones, right? And the sound would have been blasting in anyway, but it's heavy metal sound," he said. "I'm blasting in on my tinnitus."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"So there is this noise," Shatner continued. "Either I'm going to perform with the noise or I'm not going to perform."

"And my tinnitus is just coming back down now," he added. "It was hissing so loudly being subjected to that sound."

WATCH: WILLIAM SHATNER SAYS HE PERFORMED THROUGH ‘LOUD’ TINNITUS DURING HEAVY-METAL DEBUT AT 95

Despite the challenges that come with performing through tinnitus, Shatner said he is moving ahead with the album. He told Fox News Digital that the tracks have already been recorded, but he plans to listen to the completed music and determine whether he needs to make any changes to his performance.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"In effect, the album has been made, but I'm going in a week or two to listen to it to see how much of an adjustment in my performance I need to do with these musicians, who are playing in an area that I really don't know," he said.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"I want to see if my performance needs to be adjusted to their tempo and their meaning of the heavy metal," Shatner continued. "So that's what's going to happen."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"This is going to be a major thing in heavy metal," he added. "'What the F Is Heavy Metal,'" with 50 of the greatest people, including Brian May, on the album."

World.title: Former NFL QB Sean Salisbury wants officials to face postgame questions just like players and coaches
World.content:
NFL players and coaches have to answer questions after games, usually while they're still angry about whatever went wrong. Former NFL quarterback Sean Salisbury wants officials getting that same treatment when they're the ones who made the mistake.

REDZONE HOST SCOTT HANSON DEFENDS NFL OFFICIATING, CALLS LEAGUE 'BEST OFFICIATED' IN AMERICA

"I want to know what they saw on the field immediately after the game, when their emotions were up, just like the players and coaches," Salisbury told OutKick.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

We talked about missed calls, but also about the recent confrontations between officials and players. Watching some of those exchanges, I wondered why the people responsible for keeping things under control were getting so worked up themselves.

"It's like officials are instigating certain situations," Salisbury said.

Salisbury wants officials explaining what they saw after games

Salisbury doesn't want to wait for somebody at the league office to explain a missed call the next day. He wants to hear from the person who made the decision, while the game is still fresh.

The NFL has what's called a pool interview process where reporters covering a game can request an explanation of a particular call. A designated pool reporter asks the questions, and a transcript of the answers is distributed to the rest of the media. That's where some of the referee explanations you read in game stories come from.

But I'd like to see officials take questions on camera after games as routinely as players and coaches do. If a quarterback has to talk about why he threw a crucial fourth-quarter interception, or a coach has to face a grilling about a questionable fourth-down decision, then a referee can explain why he missed an obvious call.

Salisbury repeatedly expressed respect for the job officials do. But he's frustrated by mistakes he believes should be obvious without somebody needing to slow down a replay and draw circles on the screen.

"You can't miss the ones that the naked eye can see," he said. "You just can't. That's their gig."

He also wondered whether replay has made some officials more hesitant to make a call themselves. Salisbury described it as a "security blanket," suggesting that knowing there's another opportunity to get something right can affect the initial decision.

Salisbury pointed to the NFL’s recent suspensions of two officials as an example of the league holding them accountable. On Oct. 5, it suspended line judge Jeff Seeman for two games and referee Adrian Hill for one following separate Week 4 confrontations with players.

SUPER BOWL CHAMPION BRUCE ARIANS RIPS 'OUT OF CONTROL' NFL REFS AFTER TWO SUSPENSIONS

Seeman was caught on video appearing to yell "F–k you" at Cardinals tight end Trey McBride during Arizona's game against the Giants. Hill yelled at Vikings linebacker Eric Wilson after Wilson was accidentally knocked into him during Minnesota's game against Miami. Wilson later said Hill accepted his apology and explanation.

Keeping your emotions out of it is part of the job

During our conversation, Salisbury said officials are held to a higher standard. I told him I'd describe it a little differently.

Players should be held to a high standard, too. They're on television in front of millions of people and they make a lot of money to play football. But an official has a different responsibility when an argument starts, because he's supposed to be the person who can settle it.

I umpire high school baseball during the spring, and I've had plenty of parents chirp at me about calls. Do people say things that get under your skin? Of course. I don't get to start cursing at them because I've decided I've heard enough.

Dealing with that frustration is part of the job I agreed to do.

That's why I don't find "officials are human" to be much of an explanation for these confrontations. Sure, they're human. So am I. Being annoyed doesn't relieve you of the responsibility to keep your own emotions out of the game.

Salisbury agreed with that distinction.

"Your job is not there to pour gasoline," he said.

He said the best officials know how to settle a confrontation before it gets worse. Sometimes that means calming a player down, and sometimes it means being firm. Either way, the official has to keep the game moving without turning a disagreement into something personal.

And getting into it with a player can follow an official long after that particular argument ends. Salisbury pointed out that the next disputed call might then look personal to the team that was just arguing with him.

"You start to think, well, if you miss a call later on against the team, well, he had it in for us," he said.

Salisbury also brought up gambling and the conspiracy theories that come with disputed calls. Fans who think an official just cost them a winning bet are already going to question what happened. Watching that official get into a shouting match with a player gives them something else to point to.

I'd much rather hear the official explain what he saw than spend the next day watching people guess at his motives. Put him on camera after the game, while the coach is still answering questions about the loss. And if the official got it wrong, he can say that, too.

"We hold players accountable. I think officials need to be held accountable," Salisbury said.

World.title: Human vs. ChatGPT NFL Week 6 betting picks: AI goes all-in on totals after another weekly win
World.content:
OK, this is getting annoying.

ChatGPT beat me in NFL betting for the second straight week, going 3-2 while I finished 2-3. The robot added 0.94 units to its total, while I gave back 1.26. It also won our only head-to-head matchup, backing San Francisco while I took Seattle. That's three straight losses for me in games where we picked opposite sides.

NFL WEEK 5 SUNDAY TAKEAWAYS: RODGERS DEFIES FATHER TIME, COEN GETS BAILED OUT, 49ERS SURVIVE UGLY PERFORMANCE

Apparently, telling the robot I was proud of it last week was a mistake. Now it has confidence.
