Before GPT gets too excited, though, I'm still the only one making money this season. I'm sitting at 13-11-1 and +1.26 units, while the machine is 11-14 and down 3.87 units. Yes, my lead is shrinking. No, I don't particularly want to talk about that.

What I would like to talk about is the Eagles covering as my latest "plug your nose and hit place bet" pick. Apparently, the bets I hate making are the ones I should be making more often (4-0 this year). There's probably a lesson in there somewhere, but knowing me, I'll ignore it.

Anyway, we've both got five more picks for Week 6. Let's see if I can give humanity something to celebrate again.

Both of us get five selections from the same odds board, with a maximum price of -120.

The stakes are adjusted so every winning bet produces one unit of profit. For example, -110 requires risking 1.10 units, while +110 requires 0.91 units. A push returns the stake and counts as zero units.

Odds were captured Thursday at 8 p.m. ET.

Before we get to the Week 6 picks, let’s review last week.

Week 5 NFL Betting Results

Dan’s Week 5 NFL Betting Picks (2-3, -1.26 units)

Philadelphia Eagles +7½ (-110) ✅ (+1 unit) Minnesota Vikings-New Orleans Saints Over 42 (-107) ❌ (-1.07 units) Las Vegas Raiders-New England Patriots Under 45 (-109) ❌ (-1.09 units) Denver Broncos-Los Angeles Chargers Under 42 (-108) ✅ (+1 unit) Seattle Seahawks -3 (-110) ❌ (-1.10 units)

The Eagles coasted to an easy cover in a game where they never trailed by more than 7 and would have won the game outright if not for Nick Sirianni's terrible late-game decision-making. Basically, my Sunday peaked before the early-afternoon games started and never really got better.

I was way wrong about the Saints offense, as Tyler Shough threw for 96 yards in the loss. And I was even more wrong about the Patriots, who matched the entire 45-point total on their own. I stand by the Seahawks pick, and I’m still mad about Mike Macdonald calling an outside zone run from Seattle’s own 4-yard line with 18 seconds left in the first half. George Holani fumbled, and San Francisco recovered in the end zone.

GPT’s Week 5 NFL Betting Picks (3-2, +0.94 units)

Tampa Bay Buccaneers +9 (-105) ✅ (+1 unit) Chicago Bears-Green Bay Packers Under 46 (-110) ✅ (+1 unit) Las Vegas Raiders +3½ (-104) ❌ (-1.04 units) San Francisco 49ers +3 (-102) ✅ (+1 unit) Buffalo Bills-Los Angeles Rams Under 54½ (-102) ❌ (-1.02 units)

GPT nailed Thursday Night Football as the nine-point underdog Bucs went into Dallas and upset the Cowboys. But it whiffed badly on the Raiders, who lost by 28. Yes, it got me on the 49ers-Seahawks bet, and I'm still mad about that fumble recovery in the end zone to close the first half.

Not to keep tooting GPT's horn, but since its abysmal 2-8 start (including 0-5 in Week 1), the robot is now 9-6 over the past three weeks.

SEASON REPORT CARD

DAN: 13-11-1, +1.26 units

GPT: 11-14, -3.87 units

Dan’s Week 6 NFL Betting Card

Chicago Bears-Atlanta Falcons Under 52½ (-108) Los Angeles Chargers +7½ (-110) Las Vegas Raiders +5½ (-110) Dallas Cowboys Moneyline (+101) Washington Commanders +7½ (-110)

1. Chicago Bears-Atlanta Falcons Under 52½ (-108)

Chicago Bears at Atlanta Falcons, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET

Dan’s analysis:

I just think this total is too high. Caleb Williams is back, but I think he's going to be cautious coming off his hamstring injury and not use his legs as much. I also think the Bears staff wants to keep him healthy by establishing the run early and often. The Falcons have been putting up points since Michael Penix Jr. returned from injury, but I think their offense is due for a step back. I can see both teams running the ball a ton and keeping the clock moving, so I'll take the under.

GPT’s analysis:

The high total and both teams’ rushing production give your under a credible foundation. Chicago has also converted just 42.9% of its red-zone trips into touchdowns, making an efficient shootout less dependable. My concern is the defensive personnel: Chicago is missing Montez Sweat, Dayo Odeyingbo and T.J. Edwards, while Atlanta’s cornerback injuries give the Bears a favorable passing matchup. Those absences create scoring opportunities on both sides. I see the under argument, but the competing injury effects kept this outside my five.

2. Los Angeles Chargers +7½ (-110)

Los Angeles Chargers at Kansas City Chiefs, Sunday at 4:25 p.m. ET

Dan’s analysis:

This is the official "Dan Z.’s Plug Your Nose and Hit 'Place Bet' Bet of the Week" (that's trademarked and don't you dare try to steal it from me). I just can't quit the Chargers. I refuse to believe that a team led by Justin Herbert is completely incapable of scoring points. Also, the Chiefs are 4-0 and a team the public generally likes to bet. So, I'll fade the likely public money and back the Chargers (again), even though it's going to feel terrible hitting that "place bet" button.

GPT’s analysis:

Getting more than a touchdown is the strongest argument for Los Angeles, especially with a defense performing better than its 0-5 record suggests. Kansas City is also missing Rashee Rice and Josh Simmons. My concern is the Chargers’ depleted offensive line and turnover problems against a rested Chiefs team. Stalled possessions and short fields could help Kansas City build separation without consistently beating that defense. I prefer under 41.5, but your +7.5 still cashes in a 24–17 Chiefs victory. The hook makes this considerably more appealing than +7.

3. Las Vegas Raiders +5½ (-110)

Buffalo Bills at Las Vegas Raiders, Sunday at 4:25 p.m. ET

Dan’s analysis:

I’m not sure if I can have two "plug your nose" picks in one week, but this is another one that could easily qualify (I mean I make the rules so I can whatever I want, but I digress). Basically, I've decided I'm just fading the best teams in the NFL this week (this theme isn't done). The Raiders came out firing at 3-0 before suffering a heartbreaking loss against the Chiefs in Week 4 and then getting boatraced by the Patriots in Week 5. But this is more about the Bills. Buffalo is coming off a thrilling overtime win over the Los Angeles Rams on Monday Night Football. It's tough to recover on a short week after an overtime game. Plus, the Bills are playing back-to-back games out west in the Pacific Time Zone. I think Las Vegas can keep this close enough to cover.

GPT’s analysis:

Buffalo’s vulnerable pass defense gives Kirk Cousins and Brock Bowers a route to keeping Las Vegas competitive. The Bills are also coming off a Monday night overtime game, strengthening the home underdog’s case. My hesitation is Las Vegas’ defense, which allows 140.6 rushing yards per game and faces Josh Allen and James Cook. Buffalo could score efficiently without needing its questionable receivers at full strength. I prefer over 53.5, which can cash whether the Raiders keep this close or Buffalo creates separation.

4. Dallas Cowboys Moneyline (+101)

Dallas Cowboys at Green Bay Packers, Sunday Night Football

Dan’s analysis:

In all honesty, this is all about fading public perception. Dallas is coming off an ugly Thursday Night Football loss to a previously winless Tampa Bay team starting rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels. On the other side, the Packers smashed a shorthanded Chicago Bears team. Basically, everyone thinks the Cowboys are bad and the Packers are good. The answer lies somewhere in the middle, so I'll take the plus money with Dallas because I think they're going to win this game.

GPT’s analysis:

Dallas’ productive offense and three extra rest days offer the best case for your pick. Green Bay has also lost defensive tackles Javon Hargrave and Jonathan Ford to injured reserve, creating an opportunity for the Cowboys’ running game. My concern is Dallas’ defense, which ranks last in EPA allowed per play. Jordan Love and Green Bay’s receivers have a favorable matchup at home. The Cowboys can win this, but their defensive problems make the outright victory difficult to trust. I lean Green Bay -1, although neither side made my five.

5. Washington Commanders +7½ (-110)

Washington Commanders at San Francisco 49ers, Monday Night Football

Dan’s analysis:

I told you I was fading the best teams in the NFL this week, and this one certainly qualifies. Yes, San Francisco is coming off a big win over Seattle, but it was not the team's best performance. The 49ers turned the ball over three times and committed 8 penalties for 70 yards. They really only won because the Seahawks somehow managed to play worse (including one of the most puzzling coaching decisions of the year by Mike Macdonald). Washington is coming off a brutal tie against the Giants (a game that somehow had even worse coaching) and, yes, the overtime hurts. But the Commanders have an extra day to recover, which helps. I'm a big Jayden Daniels believer and I think the team is going to be motivated by last week's debacle. Motivated enough to keep it within a touchdown, at least.

SEAN MCVAY IS 'SICK' ABOUT HIS OVERTIME CALL AS ANOTHER SUPER BOWL COACH PUBLICLY REGRETS END OF GAME DECISION

GPT’s analysis:

Getting 7.5 gives Washington valuable protection against a seven-point loss. Jayden Daniels’ mobility provides a way to sustain drives, and San Francisco is without Deebo Samuel while Mike Evans and Christian Kirk remain questionable. My concern is Washington’s defense, which has allowed 95 second-half points through five games. Brock Purdy’s efficient offense is positioned to exploit that weakness as the game progresses. The hook helps, but Washington’s defensive inconsistency and the absence of leading rusher Jacory Croskey-Merritt kept this outside my five.

GPT’s Week 6 NFL Betting Card

For full transparency, I used GPT-6.1 Sol, and set the thinking effort to Ultra (highest available). Then, I fed it the OddsChecker board as it appeared Thursday at 8 p.m. ET and gave it the following prompt:

"Pick your five best bets for Week 6 based on the odds provided. No bet can be priced worse than -120. Review every spread, total and moneyline that falls within those parameters and determine whether it belongs among your five picks. Explain exactly why you’re selecting each of the five bets. Also explain exactly why you’re passing on the eligible bets you don’t select. Use at least 10 different sources for each game so you have a broad understanding of everything surrounding each game. Before delivering the results, do a fact-check and ensure that everything is correct."

After nearly 10 minutes of thinking, here’s what it came up with:

Carolina Panthers-Philadelphia Eagles Over 39 (-107) Tennessee Titans-Indianapolis Colts Under 44½ (-108) New York Jets-New England Patriots Under 43½ (-108) Buffalo Bills-Las Vegas Raiders Over 53½ (-108) Los Angeles Chargers-Kansas City Chiefs Under 41½ (-110)

1. Carolina Panthers-Philadelphia Eagles Over 39 (-107)

Carolina Panthers at Philadelphia Eagles, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET

GPT’s analysis:

Carolina averages 30.3 points per game, while Tanner McKee gets DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks available against a Panthers defense missing both starting cornerbacks. Philadelphia’s offensive-line injuries and Saquon Barkley’s absence are the biggest concerns, but 39 doesn’t require a shootout. Carolina’s productive passing game can supply much of the scoring, and McKee has enough receiving help to contribute. I prefer the over to laying three with the Panthers because it can cash regardless of which team wins.

GPT’s projected score: Panthers 24, Eagles 17

Dan’s analysis:

Not gonna lie, I kind of love this pick. It's like GPT is taking a page out of my playbook: fade the obvious bets. I have to think the public is going to actually like the UNDER because of the Eagles losing Jalen Hurts, but the team's offense is actually returning several key players. Tanner McKee is capable enough to lead the Eagles to at least 20 points and if he does, I think this game probably does go OVER.

2. Tennessee Titans-Indianapolis Colts Under 44½ (-108)

Tennessee Titans at Indianapolis Colts, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET

GPT’s analysis:

Tennessee has managed just 58 points in five games, and both Cam Ward and Daniel Jones average 5.8 yards per attempt. The Titans also allow only 3.54 yards per rush, giving them a way to limit Jonathan Taylor and force Indianapolis to rely on its struggling passing game. Tyler Warren’s questionable status adds receiving uncertainty. Indianapolis’ poor defense is the biggest concern, but 44.5 leaves room for Tennessee to improve without producing a high-scoring game. I prefer the under to trusting either offense against the spread.

GPT’s projected score: Colts 24, Titans 16

Dan’s analysis:

I don't have a lot to say here. The Titans offense has been abysmal and the Colts aren't lighting up the scoreboard. Plus, divisional games tend to be lower-scoring and more tightly contested. So, I guess I kinda like this bet?

3. New York Jets-New England Patriots Under 43½ (-108)

New York Jets at New England Patriots, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET

GPT’s analysis:

New York averages 18.6 points and will be without Breece Hall, Adonai Mitchell and Dylan Parham, leaving an already limited offense with fewer options. Christian Gonzalez’s return helps New England contain Garrett Wilson, while the Jets’ pass rush presents a challenge for Drake Maye. A.J. Brown’s return and Maye’s effectiveness against blitzes are the strongest opposing arguments. Still, 43.5 offers room for a Patriots victory without another offensive outburst. I prefer the total to choosing which team covers the seven-point spread.

GPT’s projected score: Patriots 23, Jets 17

Dan’s analysis:

I mean, following my logic from the previous GPT under, I guess I kinda like this one too? The Patriots put up a ton of points the past two weeks, but their offense couldn't do anything in Weeks 1-3. The Jets are... the Jets. They haven't scored more than 24 points in a game this season and the Patriots defense is pretty good.

4. Buffalo Bills-Las Vegas Raiders Over 53½ (-108)

Buffalo Bills at Las Vegas Raiders, Sunday at 4:25 p.m. ET

GPT’s analysis:

Buffalo averages 32.8 points and faces a Las Vegas defense allowing 140.6 rushing yards per game, giving Josh Allen and James Cook a favorable matchup. The Raiders have their own scoring route through Kirk Cousins and Brock Bowers against Buffalo’s vulnerable pass defense. Buffalo’s questionable receivers and short turnaround after Monday’s overtime game are concerns. However, both defenses allow more than 25 points per game, and the indoor venue removes weather disruption. I prefer the over to needing Buffalo to create separation.

GPT’s projected score: Bills 31, Raiders 27

Dan’s analysis:

This total is way too high for me to back the over. Not loving this pick, GPT.

5. Los Angeles Chargers-Kansas City Chiefs Under 41½ (-110)

Los Angeles Chargers at Kansas City Chiefs, Sunday at 4:25 p.m. ET

GPT’s analysis:

Los Angeles averages 16.8 points and has a depleted offensive line, making consistent touchdown drives difficult to expect. The Chargers’ defense has played considerably better, giving them a way to limit Kansas City’s scoring. The Chiefs will also be without Rashee Rice and left tackle Josh Simmons. Kansas City’s explosive running game and the Chargers’ turnover problems are the main risks. Still, 41.5 allows a 24–17 game to cash. The offensive limitations and potential defensive resistance make this my fifth selection.

GPT’s projected score: Chiefs 24, Chargers 13

Dan’s analysis:

I like this because if this game goes under the total, it makes it more likely that the Chargers will cover the 7½-point spread. I also tend to think this is going to be a lower-scoring game, so I don't hate GPT's play here. But it's pretty crazy that GPT is going all-in on totals this week. The robot has been OK on totals this season (4-3), so maybe this is a smart move. I guess we'll see.

World.title: Trump tries different approach with Russia to bring Americans relief amid ongoing war with Ukraine
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

President Donald Trump is easing some of the economic pressure on Russia in hopes of bringing Vladimir Putin closer to a peace deal — a gamble that will test whether economic incentives can move Moscow where years of sanctions have not.

The administration's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel has drawn opposition from Republicans on Capitol Hill and skepticism over whether the move will meaningfully lower prices for Americans.

Meanwhile, Russia has offered few public signs of concessions in return.

Six Republican senators joined Democrats this week in urging Trump to reverse the decision, while five House Republicans signed a separate bipartisan letter Thursday seeking to revoke the Treasury authorization.

The resistance comes as Washington approaches an Oct. 18, 2026, deadline to begin implementing a sweeping new sanctions law Congress overwhelmingly approved to increase economic pressure on Russia.

BIPARTISAN SENATORS DEMAND TRUMP SCRAP RUSSIA DIESEL DEAL, CALL IT 'BETRAYAL' OF US ALLIES

The administration argues that allowing Russian diesel back onto global markets could help bring down prices for American consumers while demonstrating the economic benefits Russia could gain through improved relations with the United States.

Trump has defended the agreement as a way to add supply to a global diesel market strained by high prices, stressing that the Russian fuel does not necessarily need to come state side to benefit American consumers.

"That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market because the world market suffers with high prices," Trump told reporters Tuesday.

But energy analysts have questioned whether the volumes involved would meaningfully affect prices. Russia, meanwhile, continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure after Trump declared an immediate energy ceasefire Sunday.

John Hardie, deputy director of the Russia Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, argued the diesel agreement would make more sense as part of a reciprocal deal under which Moscow and Kyiv both stopped attacking energy infrastructure.

"The Ukrainians could stomach it if it were part of a mutual energy truce where both Russia and Ukraine don't strike each other's infrastructure," Hardie told Fox News Digital.

Instead, Hardie said, Trump pressed Ukraine to halt its refinery strikes without securing the same restraint from Putin.

"The better solution is to go back to the Kremlin and try to get that two-way solution," he said.

Trump announced the diesel agreement Oct. 9 after a phone call with Putin, saying Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the "American and Global Marketplace," followed by another 500,000 tons in November, 1 million tons shortly thereafter and eventually another 3 million tons depending on the condition of its refineries.

TRUMP RUSSIA DEAL COULD FUEL PUTIN'S WAR, EX-NATO COMMANDER WARNS AS ZELENSKYY SAYS 'NYET'

Treasury issued General License 135 the same day, temporarily authorizing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027.

The diesel dispute has become part of a broader strain between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Trump has repeatedly pressed Kyiv to halt refinery attacks, while Zelenskyy has criticized the diesel deal and accused Russia of ignoring Trump's energy ceasefire. Ukraine resumed attacks on Russian oil infrastructure this week after saying Moscow had failed to observe the pause.

Russia, meanwhile, has intensified attacks on Ukraine's energy system as winter approaches. A major missile and drone attack Wednesday damaged dozens of energy facilities and left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power, according to Ukrainian officials.

The White House says the deal serves two purposes: adding supply to global fuel markets and showing Moscow some of the economic benefits that could come with improved relations.

Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed the agreement with Ukrainian officials as part of an effort to revive peace negotiations, Reuters reported. One person briefed on the talks said the deal could help "soften" Moscow's position by signaling that Trump remains open to doing business with Russia.

But analysts question how much genuinely new diesel Russia can provide.

"The amount of diesel Russia can provide would be a drop in the bucket compared to global demand," Masha Kotkin, a fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told S&P Global.

"If you are asking about US diesel prices, I don't think it's going to make a difference," she said.

Sergey Vakulenko, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center and former Russian oil executive, similarly cautioned against treating the roughly $7 billion value of the diesel contemplated under the agreement as new revenue for Moscow, noting that Russia was already exporting substantial quantities despite Western sanctions.

He estimated the sanctions relief could instead benefit Russian exporters by roughly $30 to $40 per ton through better commercial terms and lower shipping costs — tens of millions of dollars per month, only part of which would reach the Russian state through taxes.

At the same time, Ukrainian strikes have sharply constrained Russia's ability to increase supply. Vakulenko said Russian diesel available for export fell from roughly 3 million tons per month in April to about 325,000 tons in September, leaving both Russia's additional financial benefit and the deal's potential impact on global prices more limited than the headline figures suggest.

Hardie said signs of division between Washington and Kyiv could encourage Putin to increase military pressure rather than compromise.

"That message of irresolution and of division between Washington and Kyiv only encourages Putin to intensify military pressure, kind of seeing that opportunity," Hardie said.

He said the administration had previously presented sanctions relief and renewed economic ties as benefits Russia could unlock through a negotiated settlement. Offering some of those benefits beforehand, he warned, could undermine that incentive.

"It'll lead Putin to kind of digging his heels in on maximalist demands," Hardie said.

The debate comes as Congress is moving in the opposite direction.

Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law Sept. 18, giving the administration new authorities to target Russian officials, financial institutions and entities helping sustain the war. Its first 30-day implementation deadline arrives Oct. 18.

Six Republican senators — Thom Tillis, Susan Collins, Alan Armstrong, Lisa Murkowski, Mitch McConnell and John Cornyn — joined six Democrats Tuesday in calling on Trump to rescind the diesel agreement and implement the new sanctions law.

The senators acknowledged the need to bring down energy costs but argued the Russian diesel would have a "negligible impact" on prices while generating additional revenue for Moscow.

A separate bipartisan group of 22 House lawmakers called on Trump Thursday to revoke the diesel authorization and fully implement the Graham law.

The White House has stood by the agreement, arguing Trump's priority is lowering costs for Americans while continuing to pursue an end to the war.

Hardie questioned whether economic incentives would carry enough weight to change Putin's calculations.

"Putin cares much more at this point about Ukraine and his legacy, and this broader kind of cocktail of grievances that led him to this war than he does about, you know, clearly Russia's GDP or well-being, or else he never would have done this in the first place," Hardie said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The diesel agreement now puts Trump's theory of leverage to an early test: whether giving Putin a glimpse of the economic benefits available through improved relations can draw him toward a settlement, or whether Moscow will see easing pressure before a ceasefire as a reason to hold out for more.

World.title: WATCH: Virginia cops crawl through burning house to save man trapped in fire
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

As police officers raced up to a wooden house in the town of Culpeper, Virginia on the evening of Oct. 3, heavy smoke billowed out of the windows.

Residents who lived in separate apartments in the house stood outside, according to the Culpeper Police Department.

But one man hadn’t come out, they told police. They worried that he might be inside.

MYSTERY STRANGER VANISHES AFTER FAMILY SAYS FRANTIC WARNING SAVED THEIR LIVES DURING DEVASTATING HOUSE FIRE

Officer Ashley Sain didn’t wait. She rushed toward the house and went in without protective gear and began checking doors, searching for anyone who might still be inside.

Moments later, Officer Neal Coffey joined her.

SHERIFF'S DEPUTY SAVES MAN FROM FIERY WRECK AFTER HIGH-SPEED CHASE ENDS IN CRASH

Body-worn camera footage shows one officer running up stairs, past "No Smoking" signs with red lettering posted on the walls.

On the second floor, the duo found a door that was locked from the inside. Smoke slipped through through cracks above and below.

MARINE VETERAN AND BOSTON FIREFIGHTER DIES AFTER RESCUE EFFORTS AT MASSIVE HOUSE BLAZE

Body-worn camera footage shows Coffey crawling on his hands and knees, then flat on the wooden plank floor, searching the room with a flashlight.

He inched forward on his chest, feeling around through the smoke. Suddenly, he found a man lying unresponsive on a bed.

A team of firefighters carried the man out of the burning building, and extinguished the fire.

World.title: Poll: Americans are anxious, pessimistic and deeply unhappy with Trump ahead of the midterms
World.content:
Weeks ahead of Election Day, 71% of U.S. adults think the country is on the “wrong track.” It’s the highest share yet in President Donald Trump’s second term, illustrating the grim national mood his party faces in the midterm elections, according to a new NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey.

Poll respondents expressed deep unhappiness over economic conditions and widespread distrust toward both major political parties, but Trump and Republicans bore the brunt. For the first time in Trump’s second term, the poll has found the “right track” sinking into the 20s. A majority of Americans view the president’s administration as uniquely corrupt, even as they look skeptically at corruption in both parties. And they say Trump is failing to improve their material financial conditions.

Trump’s approval rating slipped to 34% among U.S. adults, a second-term low in this poll, while his disapproval rating rose to 66%. In another warning sign, the poll found a majority (51%) of respondents “strongly disapprove” of his performance, a second-term high.

Trump’s approval rating is slightly better among registered voters, 39%-61%. Registered voters said they prefer Democrats over Republicans to control Congress by a 55%-45% spread, another sign that the GOP’s House and Senate majorities are in danger in the Nov. 3 election.

Yet despite the sinking ratings for the party in power, Americans continue to hold a negative view of Democrats, too. Among adults, just 43% view the Democratic Party favorably, while 57% hold an unfavorable view.

The survey found that 37% have a favorable opinion of the Republican Party, while 63% view it unfavorably.

The president’s approval rating is 76% with Republican adults. That represents a drop from his previous numbers among members of his own party, fueled by a decline among Republicans who consider themselves more a supporter of the party than a supporter of the MAGA movement. Meanwhile, Trump’s approval rating sits at 21% with independents.

Among men under 30 — a group Trump won by 1 point in 2024 exit polling — his approval rating sits at 28%. And among Latinos, who also shifted toward Trump in 2024, his approval rating is 31%.

The poll highlights the tricky balancing act facing Republican candidates in competitive states and districts as they simultaneously try to energize GOP voters who continue to support Trump without alienating Americans who disapprove of the administration.

Among adults, 58% said Trump’s policies are hurting the country, while 28% said they are helping the country. Another 14% said they aren’t making a difference.

When broken down by issues, Trump’s approval rating is 27% on handling the cost of living, 29% on handling the war with Iran and 33% on his handling of AI. On his best issue, border security and immigration, 43% of adults approve.

Economic concerns are at the center of the sour national mood, with the economy once again topping the list of most important issues at 31%. While 18% of Americans said their financial situation is better off today than a year ago, 38% said it’s about the same and 44% said it’s worse now.

The results provided detail on how rising inflation, which last month rose to 3.7% year over year, has weighed on Americans’ daily lives.

Gas prices were described as a “very serious” or “somewhat serious” problem by 67% of respondents. Majorities said economic conditions have caused them to change what groceries they buy to live within their means, and to cut back on spending to afford necessities.

Pluralities also said they’ve cut back on electricity use, changed or canceled travel plans or delayed a major purchase as a result, according to the poll.

Trump has sought to appeal to voters by promising $5,000 payments if Republicans win the 2026 midterms. But the new poll showed that most U.S. adults aren’t buying it: Just 14% said they “definitely” or “probably” expect to receive such a check if the GOP keeps control of Congress, while 71% think they “definitely” or “probably” won’t.

Self-identified Republicans are among those who don’t appear to buy the president’s pledge, with 47% saying they don’t expect to receive the $5,000 payment Trump promised, while 28% do.

Corruption also registered as a major concern, with Americans harboring skepticism about both parties.

More than half (52%) of U.S. adults said in the poll that they find his administration “more corrupt” than previous administrations, while about 1 in 4 said it’s less corrupt and another 1 in 4 said the current administration is about as corrupt as predecessors.

A 56% majority also said corruption is equally bad in both parties, while another 25% said it’s a bigger problem inside the GOP and 17% said it’s worse among Democrats.

The dissatisfaction may be reshaping what Americans want in a politician. In another edition of this poll one year ago, Americans said by a 16-point margin they prefer an insider with the experience to get things done over an outsider who shakes up the system. That margin narrowed to 4 points in the new poll.

Among Democrats, the survey also found indicators of diminishing trust in the party’s establishment and an openness to different kinds of candidates.

When asked to pick one or the other, 52% of self-identified Democrats said they’re more of a supporter of progressive causes and the progressive movement, while 48% said they’re more of a supporter of the Democratic Party.

Among Democratic-aligned adults, 42% said they consider themselves to be democratic socialists, while 58% said they do not.

And despite Trump’s unpopularity, the country was split almost evenly on whether a potential Democratic-led House should begin impeachment proceedings: 52% said it should, while 48% said it should not go down that path.

The NBC News Decision Desk Poll powered by SurveyMonkey surveyed 19,135 adults online from Sept. 28 to Oct. 12 and has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.6 percentage points.

World.title: U.S. taking Putin’s side would be a ‘historic mistake,’ says Zelenskyy
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that the U.S. formally siding with Russia’s Vladimir Putin would be a “historic mistake,” but said he still sees President Donald Trump as an ally despite a series of moves that have unsettled his country and its friends on Capitol Hill.

“We want to trust him,” Zelenskyy told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday, referring to Trump. “I hope that he will change his decisions, because I think that it’s all mistakes, and it will not help us, and it will not help United States.”

Trump on Friday waived sweeping new sanctions against Russia passed by Congress, saying in an executive order that the move “is in the national interests of the United States.” Passed with bipartisan support and signed by Trump last month, the sanctions were intended to target Russia’s revenue streams by punishing global buyers of Russian oil and gas.

The waiver came days after a deal with Putin to release hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market as fuel prices soar.

At the same time, Zelenskyy said, U.S. intelligence sharing was briefly “blocked,” blinding Ukraine to incoming ballistic missiles, while limits have been placed on Starlink technology critical to intercept jet-powered drones.

Zelenskyy told moderator Kristen Welker that Ukrainian officials believe the decision to limit Starlink, imposed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, came in response to a “message from American government.”

The U.S. has been Ukraine’s most significant backer across four and a half years of war, but personal relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have appeared severely strained in recent weeks, with each offering public criticisms of the other.

Asked about Trump’s remark this week that the Ukrainian leader was “more difficult to deal with than Putin,” Zelenskyy said he was “very honest” with Trump.

“Maybe it’s not very polite,” he said, but it is “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face.”

Zelenskyy, who accused the U.S. of betraying Kyiv last week, said that his feelings have not changed. He warned that Trump’s diesel deal with Russia “will strengthen Putin in his will to occupy us.”

Announcing the deal week, Trump expressed hopes that it would go some way to address soaring fuel costs.

But Zelenskyy said the deal wouldn’t have “a real influence” on the price of oil in the U.S. because the rising prices were due to the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, not Ukraine.

“I don’t know all the reasons why President Trump makes such deals,” he said.

Of the prospect of the U.S. more formally siding with Russia, he said: “If these two countries will be together ... we will not prevail, and we will not be able to stand.”

Zelenskyy said it was a “pity” Trump had waived the sanctions in a bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who he said was “a great supporter of peace and of Ukraine.”

“He invested his life and time because he really believed in Ukraine,” he said.

In a separate interview on “Meet the Press,” Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., defended Trump’s decision to lift the Russia sanctions.

“He’s trying to walk this fine balance between trying to be able to put pressure on Russia, but also to be able to help the American people, so he is choosing the American people first is what he’s doing,” Lankford said, pointing to high gas prices.

Asked whether Trump’s moves indicate the president is siding with Putin, Lankford said that Trump was “siding with the free people of Ukraine,” adding later that Trump was working to get the two countries “to the table to be able to negotiate.”

The war has seen little recent movement on the frontline, with Russia continuing to occupy around a fifth of Ukraine. Trump had vowed to end the conflict within days of his second term, but peace talks have effectively stalled, with Ukraine saying that Russia has rejected a short-term ceasefire and that Putin’s terms for peace are tantamount to a full surrender.

Meanwhile, another difficult winter looms for Ukrainian civilians, with a critical munitions shortage limiting Zelenskyy’s ability to defend infrastructure against Russian strikes.

Zelenskyy said he was due to speak to U.S. negotiators by phone later Sunday and was still hopeful of a meeting in the days ahead. “I’m very open for this, even with all the difficult circumstances,” he said.

He cited some progress after a multiday interruption to U.S. intelligence about incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which he said has now been “deblocked.”

“We are very thankful for this,” he said. “Now it works.”

European and Ukrainian officials previously told NBC News they believed that a move to limit sharing intelligence, coming only days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia, were most likely aimed at pressuring Kyiv into making concessions at the negotiating table amid a stalemate in peace talks.

While Zelenskyy indicated that the intelligence problem has been resolved, he said that Ukraine was still facing an ongoing speed restriction on its use of Starshield, the military version of the Starlink service.

Asked if he thought Trump or Musk had directly made the decision to limit Starlink, Zelenskyy said that he didn’t know but thought “both” were involved. He said that if Trump decided tomorrow to lift the restriction, “it will immediately work as it was before.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: ‘The house was toast’: Surf swallows California homes
World.content:
LONG BEACH, Calif. — It was 3:30 a.m. on Oct. 9 and the unthinkable was happening all around Shawn Curtis: The boardwalk in front of his two-story beachfront apartment building was gone. The 25-foot-wide sand beach was gone. Salt water poured in from all sides. And now the building was slanting down into the ocean.

Curtis couldn’t make sense of what he saw. “The doorframe was crooked. The window was crooked, and then I saw a big wave crash,” he told NBC News on Thursday.

The surf crashed all the way up to the second floor. Neighbors across the street said they could see water cascading down onto the roof of Curtis’ home of nine years. Booming waves were loud enough to wake him and shake his apartment as though an earthquake rippled through, he said.

World.title: Two people, including a child, killed after woman drives through youth soccer game in Kansas
World.content:
A 6-year-old boy and 35-year-old man were killed, and 10 others were injured, when a woman drove a truck through a youth soccer game at a city sports complex in Wichita, Kansas, Saturday afternoon, police said.

The 34-year-old driver, from Garden City, Kansas, was in custody, though it wasn’t immediately clear whether the incident at the Stryker Sports Complex was intentional, police said.

“She has been cooperative up to this point in the investigation,” Wichita Police Capt. Aaron Moses said at an evening news conference.

Wichita Police Capt. Aaron Moses speaking outside the Stryker Sports Complex during a press conference in Wichita, Kan., on Oct. 17. NBC News

Both of the dead were from the city of McPherson, Moses said, but were not related to each other.

The injured include five children, ranging in age from 5 to 9 years old, as well as five men and women between 28 and 68 years old, he said.

“Those injuries span from minor injuries, like bruises, to extremely severe injuries,” the captain said. “But at this point, we believe those to be non-life-threatening.”

An additional patient, a 61-year-old woman, was hospitalized with “non-traumatic medical issues,” he said.

People began calling 911 shortly before 3:30 p.m., Moses said, “reporting that a vehicle had driven through a soccer game at Stryker Soccer Complex.”

First responders, including Kansas Highway Patrol officers, Sedgwick County sheriff’s deputies and police from nearby Bel Aire, found the boy and the man dead at the scene, he said.

They also saw bystanders tending to the injured.

“They saw community members and citizens rendering medical aid to those who were injured,” he said.

The driver was still in the truck, as were two children, Moses said. One of the women’s children had a game at the complex, though at a different field from where the crash occurred, he said.

Wichita Mayor Lily Wu said on her personal Facebook page that the incident left her filled with sorrow.

“I’m heartbroken by reports of a tragic incident at Stryker Sports Complex,” she said. “My thoughts and prayers are with everyone affected, especially the children and families involved.”

Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly said in a statement that she’s monitoring the situation and has offered state resources to Wu.

“My condolences go out to the families of the victims, the survivors, and all those impacted by this event,” she said, adding that she was “very grateful” to first responders.

The Stryker Sports Complex is a city facility with 11 turf fields used for “all sports,” it states on its website. The city of Wichita said all events at the facility have been canceled for now.

The Kansas State High School Activities Association said its scheduled flag football state championship has been suspended, along with any other of its matches through the weekend.

An investigation into the incident was ongoing, police said.

In a statement posted to Facebook, the Wichita Police Department asked anyone with video of the incident to upload it so investigators could take a look.

World.title: The inseparable legacies of Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner
World.content:
The old farmhouse in the hamlet of Springs, N.Y., is easy to miss, if not for the sign for the Pollock-Krasner House and Study Center. Here, on the east end of Long Island, is where Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner moved in the winter of 1945. And it was here where the Abstract Expressionists would send a seismic tremor through the art world.

The Pollock-Krasner House and Study Center on Long Island. CBS News

It was their home and workplace. The married couple moved into a house with no plumbing or heating. "It was really a choice that they made to come out here, to go into isolation almost to really focus on the work," said the Center's director Matthew K. Ward.

Now an historical site run by Stony Brook University, the Pollock-Krasner House looks much as it did when Krasner died in 1984.

Ward showed us the custom-made speaker system that Pollack himself wired through a crawlspace. It has paint all over it. "Yeah, a lot of stuff here has paint all over it!" Ward laughed.

Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner in the Long Island studio, 1950. Photograph by Hans Namuth; courtesy of Pollock-Krasner House and Study Center, East Hampton, N.Y.

Krasner worked in an upstairs bedroom – small, but with a view of Accabonac Creek. Pollock painted in the barn out back, but without an easel. "No – that's kind of Jackson's thing," Ward said.

Pollack stretched his canvases out on the floor, and would pour, drip, and splatter paint from above down onto the canvas. The floor is a work of art in itself. Ward said, "The way Pollock worked was so physical. I think we feel him through the floor."

Inside the barn that was Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner's studio. CBS News

The entire art world changed right here. In fact, Ward said, "The most modern work anybody had ever seen was made in this rustic space."

In 1949, Life magazine famously asked of Pollack, "Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?"

And yet, many people who might show up at the Pollack-Krasner House may ask, "Who's Lee Krasner?" After a new show at New York City's Metropolitan Museum of Art, no more.

In "Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous," for the first time the two artists' careers are considered together. "We hopefully prime you for this idea of creative adjacency, two careers in parallel," said co-curator Brinda Kumar.

Early in the exhibition, you see Krasner's work on the left wall, and Pollock's through a portal. "You automatically understand, hopefully, how this dialogue is happening across the studio, across the lawn," Kumar said.

A view of the exhibition "Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous," at New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art. CBS News

Pollock was born in Cody, Wyoming. Krasner was the child of Jewish immigrants in Brooklyn. So, why did they hit it off?

"A very good question!" said co-curator David Breslin. "I think for Pollock to meet someone who had that degree of sheer intelligence, bravado, I think her connections weren't a bad thing."

As to what attracted Krasner to Pollock, Breslin said, "I don't know if she needed him. She was drawn to his work. Who the man was who could have made that work almost became a riddle that she wanted to solve."

That riddle proved confounding. Pollock drank heavily, and had affairs. "She has this great line that says something along the lines of, 'Unfortunately, I have the fortune of being married to Jackson Pollock,'" said Breslin.

But in the mid-1950s, Krasner left for Paris. Jackson moved his girlfriend, Ruth Kligman, into the house and, said Breslin, "things kind of went to hell."

In 1956, Pollock died in a car crash. Kligman, also in the car, survived, but a friend did not.

Krasner went back to the house in Springs. She would aggressively promote Pollock's legacy as a painter, but she now took over his studio.

According to Breslin, "He dies; she's unleashed."

Kumar said, "Moving into the barn after Pollock's death allowed her to work on an unprecedented scale as well."

In the Sixties, she'd paint "Through Blue," "Right Bird Left," and "Combat."

"Through Blue" by Lee Krasner (1963). Oil on canvas. Currently on view in the exhibition "Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous," at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York City. Private Collection; © 2025 Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York.

"These are painted directly on the wall," Kumar said. "There's a kind of ferocity. And today if you go to Springs, you'll see the kind of ghostly outlines [from the canvases]."

Krasner lived and worked here for another 28 years after Pollock's death. Ward said, "This home is filled with ephemera that belonged to both of them. Lee wanted Jackson's legacy to live on just as her own, and she wanted them to live on together."

In effect, the exhibition "Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous" tries to rewrite history and change the mythology about these artists. Breslin said, "Our exhibition really has been an effort to say she's an equal."

An installation view of "Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous," at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. Anna-Marie Kellen/Metropolitan Museum of Art

World.title: The inseparable legacies of Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner
World.content: The inseparable legacies of Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner In the 1940s and '50s, Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner sent a seismic tremor through the art world. But Krasner has long been eclipsed by the shadow of her husband, even after his death in 1956. Now, correspondent Anthony Mason reports on the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York's landmark show that rewrites the story of Krasner and Pollock, two artists whose work and legacies were – aesthetically and personally – bound together. World.title: California's proposed billionaire tax: How does it add up?
World.content:
When California voters head to the polls next month, they'll be asked whether to adopt a new proposal that calls for billionaires to be taxed like never before. Jo Ling Kent shares what Proposition 40 is all about:

"There's never been a proposal like this anywhere in the world, so it's a novel idea," said healthcare workers union leader Dave Regan. "We are facing an emergency."

An emergency that began, according to Regan, with President Trump's so-called "One Big Beautiful Bill," which includes cuts targeting federal funds to Medicaid over the next few years.

"What we're trying to do is restore $100 billion worth of health care cuts," Regan said. "Three-and-a-half million people lose health insurance. Hospitals, clinics, and emergency rooms will close." They could also cost jobs in Regan's own union, SEIU United Healthcare Workers West.

So, to bridge the gap, Regan and the union led a petition drive to put on the November ballot a one-time, 5% state tax on the net worth of California's 200 or so billionaires, known as Proposition 40.

How confident is Regan that it will pass? "Pretty confident," he replied.

Regan's tactics are controversial. His behavior? Under scrutiny. But if the wealth tax passes, he expects the state will collect $100 billion over five years, with 90% specifically earmarked for healthcare.

"We're not trying to pretend that it's a permanent solution," Regan said, "but a five-year solution is better than no solution. And that gives the state of California an opportunity to figure out what's the right permanent solution."

Asked if a five-year tax is a solution, Regan replied, "Absolutely. Ask the three-and-a-half million people who are going to lose healthcare coverage."

Competing Propositions

Since the wealth tax was proposed, some billionaires have left California, including venture capitalist Peter Thiel, and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin. Brin is spending more than $100 million to oppose the measure.

And California being California, there are two other opposition-backed proposals on the ballot, Propositions 41 and 42. If either one receives more votes than Prop 40, that effectively nullifies the wealth tax.

And the billionaires have some strange bedfellows: several other major unions and big-name Democrats agree with them on voting no, including California Governor Gavin Newsom (who calls Prop 40 "a flawed initiative"), and former Democratic Congresswoman Katie Porter.

"I generally, as a progressive, have fought to make sure that the ultra-wealthy pay more," Porter said. "But this tax doesn't do that correctly, causing these people to pick up and to leave. We want billionaires to create jobs here, to start companies here. …

"You don't get a second bite at tax policy," she continued. "A tax that you pass has enduring consequences. When somebody leaves California, we can no longer tax them. That is a permanent problem. It is much harder to get tax base back than it is to grow it in the first place."

Here's where taxes get complicated: billionaires can pay a lot in income, property and capital gains taxes. But most of their wealth is typically growing in stocks, which aren't taxed until they sell.

"It's a system in which essentially the richest Americans have been written out of the tax system, much like the aristocracy of pre-revolutionary France," said Ray Madoff, a professor at Boston College Law. "People who have enough money to live on their investments and inheritances legally don't have to pay any taxes."

Madoff says Prop 40 spotlights a "deeply broken" tax system, and believes it can be beneficial. "My feelings about Prop 40 are that meaningful change has to happen at the federal level," she said. "And I think that to the extent Prop 40 creates an incentive for meaningful change to take effect on the federal level, then I'd say it would be helpful. On its own, it obviously can't do anything; it's just patching a temporary hole, right? But I think that there is a certain amount of symbolic value of Prop 40."

"California is America's coming attraction"

As for how this turns out, the polls are tightening, with voters now more divided. A "Yes" voter told us, "To me, it's bigger than Prop 40. It's a fight back against the Trump administration."

A "No" voter said, "We really are concerned about people leaving the state."

No billionaires contacted by "Sunday Morning" wanted to talk to us about Prop 40 … except for one. "I don't mind paying taxes; the more you make, the more taxes you pay, so I'm okay with that," said Jensen Huang, the founder and CEO of the American chipmaker Nvidia, headquartered in Silicon Valley. "I don't like tax dollars wasted. But I also support all that this country represents."

Huang's first job was as a dishwasher at Denny's. Today, Forbes lists his net worth at about $200 billion, making him the seventh richest person in the world.

"I am the ultimate American dream," Huang said. "If not for this country, the education, the ability to create a new company, pursue your dreams, I wouldn't have met all the people that made Nvidia possible. I love this country in every possible way. And it's not perfect, but it's incredible."

Even if you end up paying perhaps $8 billion over five years? "The fact that I can afford to pay $8 billion in taxes over five years is a privilege," Huang replied. "I'm not afraid of paying taxes. I'm just afraid of being poor."

Whether you're poor or rich, for or against the billionaire tax, its architect, Dave Regan, is already looking beyond November – and beyond California. "Other states around the country are going to start looking to follow California's lead, just like it's happened so many times in the past," he said. "California is America's coming attraction, and this is coming to a state near you after we pass it on November 3."



Story produced by Dustin Stephens. Editor: Emanuele Secci.

World.title: More than 1,800 arrested in France after protester violence erupts
World.content:
Police arrested at least 1,800 people across France after violent groups clashed with officers and looted shops during nationwide demonstrations that drew hundreds of thousands who denounced rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.

Authorities said masked groups on Saturday set fires and attacked public buildings, including city halls, in several cities.

In Limoges, a city in central France, flames engulfed the 19th-century City Hall, causing its roof to collapse. Haute-Vienne prefect Maurice Barate told LCI television that the fire was deliberately set and nearly destroyed the building. The fire was under control Sunday.

French President Emmanuel Macron will hold an emergency meeting with top government officials on Sunday afternoon, before addressing the nation at 8 p.m., according to his office.

French Republican Security Corps (CRS - Compagnies Républicaines de Sécurité) stand guard during a demonstration to protest against the "high cost of living," in Lille, northern France, on Oct. 17, 2026. Sameer AL-DOUMY /AFP via Getty Images

"The right to protest is a fundamental right. Deliberately and collectively sowing disorder through violence is not," Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez wrote on X, pointing to the looting of hundreds of businesses in many cities including Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux.

About 550,000 people took part in protests across France, according to authorities, while organizers counted about 800,000. More than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters were injured, Nuñez said.

One person died of a heart attack, Paris police said in a statement, without providing details. Paris prosecutors' office said it was investigating.

"Stunned by the level of destruction"

Around Paris' Place de la République on Sunday morning, dislodged cobblestones, shattered storefronts and broken glass marked the aftermath of the events. Looting and damage were reported around the square and in some other tourist and shopping areas in the city center.

Paris police said Sunday that 855 people were arrested in the French capital region alone. The Paris prosecutors' office said that 557 of them were kept in police custody.

"I am actually stunned by the level of destruction and violence that was expressed," Marie Peyreigne, a 57-year-old government employee, said, wondering what led to the mayhem.

People look at charred cars the day after a demonstration against rising living costs, joining students' grievances, in Paris, on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026. AP Photo/Emma Da Silva

Inspecting the damage, many Parisians took photos of the partially dismantled base of the central monument at Place de la République — a statue of Marianne, a symbol of France.

Jean Foissy, 74, said he wanted to join the protest but found "a wall of riot police and fires everywhere," and went back home.

"I was very scared," he said. "I've been a Parisian since I was born, so when I got here, it almost made me want to cry because I find it so bad, it hurts me."

Margaux Eude, 26, said she supports the protest movement but "didn't think it would escalate like this."

"It's the troublemakers who came, and it breaks my heart because it delegitimizes the movement," she said.

Political leaders trade blame

Political leaders across the spectrum sought to parlay the fallout of Saturday's riots into political capital, looking ahead to next spring's presidential election.

Far-right leader and presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen lashed out at far-left rival Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who joined the Paris march. "Looting, ransacking, destroying and attacking law enforcement: Rioters have again spoiled the Oct. 17 demonstrations for the protection of purchasing power," Le Pen wrote on X.

Her running mate, Jordan Bardella, said on X that "if the silent majority of French decide it, we will reestablish order for the long term."

Mélenchon, for his part, traded barbs with the prime minister, accusing Lecornu of "playing with fire" and alleging that "by banking on degradation, you have only succeeded in uniting all youths and workers' unions."

A protester holds a board with a photo of French president Emmanuel Macron in front of a burning tourism office during a demonstration against rising living costs and in solidarity with students' grievances in Lyon, France, on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. AP Photo/Laurent Cipriani

Mélenchon insisted that "my message is clear: those who share our fight have no business in looting or destruction."

U.S. President Trump posted "France is burning!" on his Truth Social platform, apparently linking the unrest to "the immigration of people from an entirely different world."

"Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!" he wrote.

French authorities and police have not linked immigrants to the rioting and have repeatedly attributed some of the violence to "radical far-left groups" and other people who joined to loot.
