World.title: Doing the dishes and riding the subway? Why the royals keep trying to look relatable
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It all seemed a bit prosaic, really, chatting about doing the dishes with her husband or riding on the subway with her daughter.

But there was Catherine, Princess of Wales, telling seniors how she and Prince William share the washing-up duties, and a few days later, taking a trip on the London Underground with Princess Charlotte.

Beyond that glimpse into their everyday lives, though, these recent moments reflect an attempt to deal with a longstanding and more fundamental challenge that is a priority for the monarchy: how to appear relatable to a public that lives far beyond royal walls.

"The monarchy isn't trying to convince us that William and Catherine are ordinary people," royal historian Justin Vovk said in an interview.

"It's about trying to convince us that despite extraordinary circumstances, they experience the same human concerns as everybody else."

Efforts to do that convincing have long been a priority for monarchies throughout Europe.

Catherine, Princess of Wales, right, sits with residents onboard a West Sussex Minibus, a volunteer-led community transport group, during a visit to Pulborough, southern England, on Sept. 30. (Arthur Edwards/AFP/Getty Images)

"Since … the political upheavals of the 19th century, which saw various monarchs … losing their thrones … there was a real consciousness that you no longer needed just the support of the elite, you needed to be relatable," said Judith Rowbotham, a social and cultural scholar and visiting research professor at the University of Plymouth in southwestern England, in an interview.

"Queen Victoria writes her highland journal — suitably sanitized — but that's an attempt to make herself relatable."

What's thought of as relatable nearly 200 years ago differs from what William and Catherine and other working royals may try to do or show today. But the overall significance is the same, Rowbotham suggests.

"Relatability is something that modern monarchies, certainly modern European monarchies, see as genuinely important," she said.

"Particularly at a time when people are worried about money, when people are questioning government actions over taxes … the fact that yes, they live in a lavish house, but they live ordinary lives in a lavish house … that's the impression they want to give, that they don't have live-in staff, they're not surrounded by flunkies and footmen."

As much as there is that desire to appear relatable, there is little to suggest it can ultimately eliminate the actual separation between the monarchy and the public.

This 1969 photo is one of a series taken to show the informal life of Prince Charles, centre, as he sits with Queen Elizabeth, background centre, Prince Philip, second from left, Prince Edward, left, Princess Anne, background, and then Prince Andrew, right, at Sandringham House, in Sandringham, England. (The Associated Press)

"There will always be distance between the monarchy and the people," said Vovk.

"But all of [it], stretching from Queen Victoria up to William and Catherine is about trying to close as much of the distance as they can that is within their control."

And there's a basic reason behind that, Vovk suggests.

"The monarchy's relevance, its viability, is now predicated on its perceived relatability and accessibility," he said.

"People don't want a Royal Family that is distant and isolated and feels unfamiliar. They want a Royal Family that they feel they can connect with, that they feel like if they were to bump into them on the street, they could just go up to them and talk to them."

That, however, creates something of a paradox.

"If you strip away all of the pomp and the pageantry and some of the mystique around royalty, it raises the question of what makes it so special, anyway? Why have it at all?" Vovk said. "So it is a balancing act."

Pomp and pageantry are on full display as King Charles, left, and Queen Camilla, right, make their way along the Mall following their coronation on May 6, 2023, in London, England. (Charles McQuillan/The Associated Press)

Other factors can play into the monarchy's focus on relatability at any given time.

Queen Victoria's seclusion, particularly after the death of her husband, Prince Albert, drove concerns about relatability during her reign. Rowbotham sees another circumstance closely connected to the monarch at play right now.

"We don't know how long Charles is going to be around, given that he's in his 70s, given that he is still being treated for cancer," she said.

"This time, it's a question of assuring the monarchy's survival by making it clear that there is an heir who is well-prepared and ready to take over the duty.

"That's why I think … they're paying so much attention to the whole issue" of relatability, Rowbotham said.

Vovk sees a greater level of transparency from the current royals compared to previous generations when it comes to relatability.

"We're seeing the curtain being pulled back on the aspects of royal life that are no different or at least have minimal difference from the average person — so, you know, siblings bickering, not liking doing chores, spouses sharing domestic responsibilities."

On the constitutional or political side of the monarchy, however, he sees less revelation.

"There's still some degree of gatekeeping going on here with what amount of royal life is being disclosed and what isn't. That will always be the case with something that is connected with the political life of the nation."

Passing a robot controller to a prince

Benjamin Santiago, left, teaches Prince Edward, right, how to drive a robot using a controller at Queen's Park in Toronto on Oct. 2. (Grant and Martin Curtis/Duke of Edinburgh's International Award — Canada)

Benjamin Santiago had never had an experience like it.

"It's not every day that you get to give a robot controller to royalty and teach them how to drive it," the Grade 12 student at St. Joseph's Catholic High School in London, Ont., said in an interview.

Benjamin, a 17-year-old member of the school robotics team, had that opportunity earlier this month when he passed the controller to Prince Edward, the Duke of Edinburgh, at an event in Toronto.

The gathering that drew education leaders, school board representatives, industry partners and students to Queen's Park highlighted the recent announcement by the provincial Ministry of Education to expand access to the Duke of Edinburgh Award program to schools across Ontario. That comes as the award, founded by Edward's late father, Prince Philip, is evolving and working to blend trades and skills-based experiences into public education to boost opportunities for young Canadians.

"It was amazing. I'm super grateful," Benjamin said of his opportunity to meet Edward. "The prince was super enthusiastic and really just interested about who we are and what our goals were as Ontario students."

In the royal encounter, Benjamin saw the potential to boost support for an area of education close to his heart.

Benjamin says Prince Edward was 'super enthusiastic and really just interested about who we are and what our goals were as Ontario students.' (Grant and Martin Curtis/Duke of Edinburgh's International Award — Canada)

"If someone like the prince can feel the controller and feel how it is to be an engineer in high school and then later on become an engineer in post-secondary … the funding towards programs like robotics may increase."

Edward has had a longstanding interest in youth and promoting opportunities for them, something that has been a frequent focus on his visits to Canada.

"He really took the time to really focus his attention on the students, which is something that I really personally admired about this, but also to make sure that every student felt seen and heard," Laura Briscoe, senior director for business development, communications and experiential education for the Duke of Edinburgh's International Award — Canada, said in an interview.

"He wants to know the realities of youth in Canada and how the award can support their lifelong learning and development, and I found him to be very responsive and open to hearing feedback, whether it's constructive feedback, what are the barriers, where are the gaps, what are we missing?"

The Queen's Park gathering was a "wonderful experience" for everyone there, said Kathy Cepo, Benjamin's chemistry teacher and one of his robotics coaches.

"The prince was so engaged with these students and they felt like they were the only people in the room," she said in an interview.

"He was praising them the entire time and so proud of them."

They meet again

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left, speaks with King Charles, right, during an audience at Buckingham Palace in London on Wednesday. (Aaron Chown/Getty Images)

Few world leaders have shaken hands with King Charles as often as the president of Ukraine.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy was back in the U.K. this week, meeting Charles at Buckingham Palace on Wednesday.

"I thank His Majesty King Charles III for the audience," Zelenskyy posted afterward on X .

"It is important for me to have the opportunity to personally thank him for his unwavering support for Ukraine. We appreciate all the assistance provided by the United Kingdom."

It was his third meeting with the King this year, and came as the U.K. doubled down on support for Ukraine and called for its international partners to increase pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin to respect the U.S. call for an energy ceasefire.

The King meeting with Zelenskyy "on a bit of a consistent basis is a way of … reaffirming Britain's overall support for Ukraine, even though governments are changing," said Vovk.

"It's a way to reassure President Zelenskyy that the United Kingdom stands with Ukraine."

While a monarch is meant to be above politics, meeting with Zelenskyy would also come at the request of the U.K. government.

"The King isn't being party political, taking sides. He's doing his constitutional duty," said Rowbotham.

Prince Harry and Meghan step out in Nottingham

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, left, and Prince Harry, right, greet well-wishers as they arrive at the Community Recording Studio, a youth and community charity that offers a wide range of creative activities, sports, mentoring and youth development programs, in Nottingham, England, on Thursday. (Christopher Furlong/Getty Images)

They aren't official working members of the Royal Family anymore.

But the casual passerby could be forgiven for being a bit confused Thursday as Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, carried out events connected with their private charitable interests in the city where they did their first public outing as an engaged couple nearly a decade ago. It was their first joint appearance in public since they returned to the U.K. from California in late August.

"It's great to be back," Harry said. "Wonderful and great to be back ⁠in Nottingham, too."

They began by visiting a recording studio run by a youth and community charity that has received support from a 1.1-​million-pound ($2.1-million Cdn) donation announced by Harry last year.

At their next stop at the Himmah charity, which tackles food poverty, Meghan was reunited with ​four contributors to a charity cookbook released to raise funds in the wake of London's 2017 Grenfell Tower fire disaster. She had donated 10,000 pounds ($18,800 Cdn) from the book's proceeds to help the Himmah hub.

Thursday's visit was the first pre-arranged and advertised occasion since their return, Rowbotham said, but it was not an official royal event.�

WATCH | Prince Harry and Meghan are returning to Britain: Harry and Meghan moving back to the U.K. | Duration closed caption 2:06 Prince Harry and his wife Meghan are moving back to the United Kingdom with their children, Buckingham Palace has confirmed. The couple will remain non-working royals and live as private citizens.

"However, it was carefully arranged to ensure media reportage and a suitable turnout of sympathetic public by choosing a location — Nottingham — which was … where they were for their first post engagement royal visit."

But it was on a much different scale, she said.

"No local dignitaries were there in official capacity."

Vovk saw the visit as their first outing as part of "the new Sussex court."

He also sees the potential of a "problem of optics" for the monarchy where "Harry and Meghan are engaging in activities that to the average observer look really more or less the same [as] what the monarchy does."

Prince Harry and Meghan, Duke and Duchess of Sussex, visit the Himmah Hub in Nottingham, England, on Thursday. (Annabel Lee-Ellis/The Associated Press)

Vovk expects to see an escalation in public appearances and informal events from the senior working royals.

"I think the monarchy is now going to have to pick up the pace in terms of the kinds of engagements and public accessibility they're doing just in order to keep that clear distinction between Harry and Meghan [having] titles but they are technically private individuals from a legal, constitutional perspective," he said.

The biggest danger and concern for the royals, he said, is "that the brand itself could be misappropriated, misrepresented, in a way that has never really been a factor before."

Rowbotham doesn't see a threat to the institution itself, although she expects it will be discussed as such.

Royally quotable

"We like sitting quietly and reading. Occasionally, when I'm deep in a book, I'll hear him roaring with laughter about something."

— Queen Camilla, in a television documentary, offering some insight into the reading habits of her and her husband, King Charles.

Royal reads

Catherine, Princess of Wales, third from left, and Prince William, third from right, help behind the till during a visit to an Ikea store in Belfast, Northern Ireland, on Oct. 9. (Phil Noble/Getty Images)

British police say search ‌warrants they secured to search properties linked to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor had been issued unlawfully and must be quashed, but said the investigation into King Charles's younger brother was ongoing. [CBC]

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor faced a 1.8-million-pound ($3.4-million Cdn) bill to cover repair and restoration of his former Royal Lodge home in Windsor after the lease was officially surrendered. King Charles reportedly covered some of the costs. [The Guardian]

King Charles spoke of his " special connection" to Wales while delivering an address to the Welsh Parliament. [The Independent]

Zara Tindall has opened up about the tough-love upbringing she received from Princess Anne and Mark Phillips — including being told she would get no help when she decided to follow her parents into top-level equestrian sport. [Daily Mail]

The Prince and Princess of Wales met hundreds of royal fans in south Belfast as part of a surprise visit to Northern Ireland. [Belfast Telegraph]

Prince William brought traffic to a halt just down the road from Buckingham Palace to play cricket with some of the game's biggest names. [The Independent]

World.title: Should Alberta separate? Here's why these Canadians feel the way they do
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On Oct. 19, Alberta will have a referendum on many questions, including separation.

Specifically, the ballot will ask: should Alberta remain a province of Canada or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?

CBC News asked Albertans — and Canadians with a personal connection to Alberta — to share the personal experience that shaped how they will vote in the 2026 referendum. We had a large volume of responses to our online callout and also went into the community to ask people to contribute.

We've selected several of them — five Albertans and two Canadians with deep connections to the province — to share their perspectives with you, in their own words. Among the writers are an engineer, a radio host, an oil and gas worker, a social worker. They represent perspectives from across the political spectrum — from ardent supporters to remain within Canada to moderate separatists and those convinced independence is the answer.

You might disagree with some of the authors. But perhaps after reading their pieces, you might understand why they intend to vote the way they do.

Keep in mind, these First Person columns should not be taken as endorsements of any particular political party or political stance by CBC News. Rather, they are expressions of the writers' points of view at the time of publication, and a look at how those perspectives came to be formed. CBC News was involved in fact-checking and editing their writing efforts. For more background, check out our website and the First Person FAQ here.

We'll be publishing these columns throughout the months of September and October. Check back here to read them all.

To my family, Brexit seemed laughable. Now I don’t think the threat of Alberta separation is funny

Rosie Costen moved from the U.K. to Calgary as a child and watched Brexit from afar. Now she's seeing similarities with the Alberta independence movement. (Elise Stolte/CBC)

Rosie Costen’s family moved to Canada from the U.K. ahead of its vote to leave the European Union. For her, the similarities between that vote and the upcoming referendum in Alberta are a source of worry. Read her story.

I was pushed to be self-sufficient. I want my province to stand on its own, too

Vicky Bayford lives in Innisfail, Alta., and works in the oil and gas sector. Her support for separatism grew out of a sense of frustration with the way society has changed. (Submitted by Vicky Bayford)

As a young mom, Vicky Bayford was denied social assistance in an Alberta that valued small government and self-sufficiency. That experience shaped her view of the debate on separatism and her hopes for an independent Alberta. Read her column.

I'm an Indigenous entrepreneur fighting to keep my business. Alberta needs change, but not separatism

Mike Deranger is an Indigenous entrepreneur in Fort McMurray. He is pictured here beside the Athabasca River on September 15, 2026. (Vincent McDermott/CBC)

In Fort McMurray, Mike Deranger built a successful oil and gas service company during a heyday of support for local Indigenous business. But so much has changed, he writes, and the independence movement is not offering solutions. Read his column.

Hosting a radio show taught me immigrants came for Canada, not a separate Alberta

As the host of Red FM, Rishi Nagar has heard from many listeners who, like him, are immigrants to Canada and don't want Alberta to separate. (Submitted by Rishi Nagar)

As the host of Red FM, Rishi Nagar has heard from many listeners who, like him, are immigrants to Canada and don't want Alberta to separate. Read his column.

My mom’s funeral showed me Alberta is more complicated than its stereotypes

Sarah Beley, executive director of Working Gear is pictured in Vancouver, British Columbia, on Wednesday, September 16, 2026. (Nav Rahi/CBC)

At Sarah Beley’s mother's funeral, Alberta was more than a political identity. Nobody stopped to sort the separatists from the federalists before deciding who would clear the tables. Read more.

I don't know many committed separatists. But I know people who are angry and hungry for change

Matthew Morin lives in Calgary and spends his free time hiking in the nearby Rocky Mountains. He says the experience of precarity in daily life influences his views on separatism. (Submitted by Matthew Morin)

Matthew Morin is a Calgary resident who is drawn toward Alberta separatism because daily life feels more precarious and he feels those on top don’t seem to care. Read more.

Living in Calgary showed me Albertans don't realize how good they have it, but their grievances are real

Chris Regier spent a decade living in Alberta before returning to Saskatchewan. His experience has given him an understanding of the separatism debate from both inside and outside Alberta. (Chris Regier)

As an engineer from Saskatchewan, Chris Regier was taken aback by some of the opulence he saw in Alberta's oil and gas sector.

He says his decade of experience in the province showed him two things can be true at the same time: Alberta is better off than other provinces and yet there are legitimate concerns about equalization. Read more.

Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.

World.title: Could this 93-year-old sprinter's muscles hold clues to healthy aging? Scientists think so
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At 93, Emma Maria Mazzenga still gets the jitters before a race.

"On race day, I'm very tense," she said. "People ask to interview me, and I tell them: Don't come near me until I've run."

Over the last four decades, Mazzenga has won 11 world titles, 31 European championships and 115 Italian races. She currently holds the 200-metre world record in the women's over-90 category: 50.33 seconds, set in 2024, when she was 91.

Now she is giving scientists a rare look at just how much of the physical decline we associate with aging may not actually be inevitable.

Mazzenga ran as a university student in Padua, in northern Italy. She then stopped for three decades while she taught high school biology and raised two children, largely on her own after her husband died.

In 1986, when she was 53, the president of her old university running club rounded up former athletes for the growing field of masters competitions, for those over age 35.

"One by one, my friends quit," she said. "I kept going."

In this 2024 file photo, a then-90-year-old Mazzenga shows her membership card for the Italian Athletics Federation, ahead of a race in San Biagio di Callalta, Italy. It shows her birthdate: Aug. 1, 1933. (Remo Casilli/Reuters)

She still trains three times a week, mostly short repeats of 50 to 200 metres. Slow jogging bores her.

What drives her isn't winning, Mazzenga said. In Italy, she has no rivals in her age category. "I come first because I have to. I'm the only one," she said. "I can't get any emotion out of that."

So she races the clock instead. "If I win with a mediocre time, it gives me no satisfaction."

Her proudest moment is still her first world title, the 400-metre W75 race at the World Masters Athletics Championships in Sacramento, Calif., won in 2011.

"There were just a handful of us Italians. I found myself alone on the podium," Mazzenga recalled.

WATCH | Watch Mazzenga compete in 100m race in Florence, Italy, last month: Watch Emma Mazzenga, 93, compete in 100-metre race | Duration closed caption 0:38 Italian sprinter Emma Mazzenga, 93, competes in a women's 100-metre race in Florence, Italy, in September. Mazzenga is an accomplished runner whose athletic performance is providing new insights into human aging.

From VO2 to muscle fibres

But eventually, her performances drew a different audience: Scientists.

Two years ago, Antonio La Torre, a scientist at the University of Milan and technical director of Italy’s athletic federation, tipped off two researchers who were studying how the body ages.

"We were told there was this woman who was able to run 200 metres in a very short time," said Martino Franchi, an associate professor of human physiology at the University of Padua. "But it was her age that we were really interested in."

Mazzegna became the most extreme case in a broader, two-year project called Trajector-Age, which tracked how muscles, nerves, heart and metabolism change in people over 50 to see whether exercise can slow decline.

Researchers from several Italian universities and the University of Wisconsin-Madison put Mazzenga through a gruelling cycling test and took biopsies from her thigh.

Mazzenga, then 90, competes in the 100-metre W90 category race in San Biagio di Callalta, Italy, on May 4, 2024. (Remo Casilli/Reuters)

Franchi says Mazzenga's maximal oxygen consumption is comparable to that of someone in their 50s. Also known as a VO2 max, it represents the greatest amount of oxygen a body can take in and use — a key measure of cardiovascular fitness.

"And she's 90," he said. "This is fantastic."

The bigger surprise was inside her muscles, said Franchi. Mazzenga has lost some of the fast-twitch fibres used for explosive movement, although fewer than expected. But her slow-twitch fibres — the ones that resist fatigue — are extraordinary.

"They are as big as a girl in her 20s," he said. "That's unique."

Martino Franchi gestures toward a screen showing a microscopic view of muscle fibres at his lab at the University of Padua, in Italy. (CBC)

Researchers think those unusually large fibres may help her hold her pace and compensate, at least partly, for the fast fibres lost with age.

Aging has happened, Franchi said, "but in a slower way." And so many years of training means that her body runs almost on auto-pilot when her feet hit the track.

The research was published earlier this year as two cases in the Journal of Applied Physiology, with a rendition of a Mazzenga landing on the cover . Lead scientist Marta Colosio received an award for the work at the American Physiology summit.

The team is now analyzing a second round of biopsies, along with genetic and molecular data, trying to tease apart what Mazzenga inherited versus what decades of training may have preserved.

Mazzenga walks with Martino Franchi, one of the researchers who has studied the 93-year-old's muscles and athletic performance to glean new insights into human aging. (CBC)

'A bit of a rarity'

Mazzenga has her own theory. "I always say that if I had been sitting on the sofa, I would have aged differently."

With the running came fame — eventually. "No one paid much attention to me in my 80s, but after 90, yes," she jokes. "They look at me as a bit of a rarity."

She now speaks regularly at public events, most recently at la Repubblica's Festival di Salute, an annual health festival that draws Nobel laureates, scientists and sports champions.

As friends die and family members get busy with their own lives, Mazzenga says those connections — along with her masters teammates — matter almost as much as the training.

Mazzenga shows off her first pair of track shoes, when she first took to racing in her early 50s, at her home in Padua, Italy. (Megan Williams/CBC)

Franchi has his own reason for pushing exercise.

During the COVID-19 lockdowns, he noticed his father, then in his 70s, struggling to get up from the sofa. So Franchi printed out graphs linking inactivity to mortality.

"I said, 'Dad, I study sarcopenia. This is it,'" said Franchi, referring to the loss of muscle mass, strength and function with age. "He got scared, so he went back to the gym."

Today, Franchi's father can pull off full lunges and hikes several times a week.

Franchi likes to tell the story to his students, telling them that physical activity is important — but be sure to keep doing it when you're older.

Asked what she'd tell someone 80, or even 90, thinking about taking up a sport, Mazzenga laughs. "You'd want to start a little earlier."

For those still able, she says, see a doctor, find a coach and match your body to the effort.

She herself has no plans to slow down. At a recent club final, she ran faster than she had two years earlier. "I was very pleased."

World.title: How AI is making it harder to book on Airbnb; Is junk food bad for your brain?: CBC's Marketplace Cheat Sheet
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Miss something this week? Don't panic. The CBC's Marketplace rounds up the consumer and health news you need.

Want this in your inbox? Get the Marketplace newsletter every Friday.

Behind the lens: How Marketplace uses hidden cameras

(CBC)

This week's episode features an inside look at our hidden camera investigations, ranging from driving schools to real estate to social experiments.

Find out how we decide when to go undercover, why we do it and what it takes to uncover the truth — straight from some of the journalists who bring you the stories.

Watch the full episode anytime on YouTube or CBC Gem .

AI photos are making it harder to know what you're booking on Airbnb. Here's what to look out for

When booking his trip to Montreal, Wells found extremely polished-looking photos of hosts appeared in numerous Airbnb listings, leading him to suspect they had been generated using AI. Short-term rentals in that city are subject to strict rules aimed in part at protecting the city's housing supply. (Josh Wells/Reddit)

Josh Wells, a college student from Iowa, was excited to explore Montreal on his first trip outside the U.S. But as he scrolled through Airbnb listings in search of a place to stay, he began to notice something that didn't seem quite right.

Several of the hosts renting out their properties had profile pictures that Wells suspected were generated by artificial intelligence.

"Your average person taking an iPhone photo, there's obviously like a little bit of imperfections," Wells told the CBC's Cost of Living. "The AI photos, they just looked too perfect."

Still, Wells kept browsing. He was even close to booking one of the properties when a final look at the listing's photos raised another red flag.

He zoomed in on a piece of wall art depicting two halves of faces joined together. At the top, the artwork appeared to read "Picasso." But in another photo of the same room, taken from a different angle, the artwork looked different.

"The text was all warped and funky," he said. "I'm just like, 'Yeah, OK, this is AI."

That was enough to put Wells off the listing — and ultimately using Airbnb for this trip. Unable to tell whether the photos showed a real place or an AI-generated version, he opted for an apartment-style hotel instead.

"The fake profile picture is one thing, but listings of the actual place that you're staying at and spending thousands of dollars was an immediate no for me.”

Wells isn't the only traveller to question whether the photos found on Airbnb or similar short-term rental-style platforms accurately reflect reality.

As AI makes it easier to alter photos, experts say travellers may find it increasingly difficult to know whether Airbnb-style listings accurately reflect reality, raising questions about consumer trust and protections in Canada.

In a statement to CBC News, Airbnb said its rules require listings to be "accurately represented" and that the company may ask hosts to remove content that uses AI or other digital technology to "edit flaws, hide damage, add amenities or attributes that are not part of a listing, or otherwise materially misrepresent the listing."

The company further said it encourages guests to report misleading listings and that those who find a property that doesn't match its description can contact its 24/7 community support team. Under AirCover, Airbnb added, it may help guests find a similar place or provide a refund if the host can't resolve the issue.

Read more from the CBC’s Catherine Zhu.

We know junk food isn't healthy, but scientists are trying to determine if it's also bad for our brains

Ultra-processed foods could damage your brain: study | Duration closed caption 2:00 New Canadian research suggests that eating too many ultra-processed foods, such as soda, chips and processed meats, could damage your brain. Researchers urge Canadians to cut down on such products.

Most people have food in their fridges and cupboards that they know isn't the healthiest choice.

A box of chocolate chip cookies you grab for a bedtime snack. Instant noodles for when you can't be bothered to make dinner. Or that bag of ketchup chips you grabbed on a late night stroll home from the bar.

But it's not just guilty pleasures. Nearly half of the calories Canadians consume — 45.7 per cent on average, according to Statistics Canada — comes in the form of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and includes everything from breakfast cereals to frozen meals.

Over the years, research has shown that UPFs can negatively impact everything from our weight to our cardiovascular health , and could even be linked to some types of cancer .

But a new study co-authored by two professors at Hamilton's McMaster University, published Thursday by JAMA Network Open , signals that our brains could also suffer as a result of consuming too many foods produced to be cheap and ready-to-eat.

The authors say that the people with the highest intake of UPFs in their diets may face an increased likelihood of experiencing changes to the brain that could serve as precursors for stroke, dementia and cognitive decline.

People wouldn't necessarily be aware of these potential harms, says study co-author Russell de Souza, an associate professor at McMaster's Mary Heersink School of Global Health and Social Medicine.

But he says the findings could encourage people to shift their eating habits now, before experiencing serious consequences later in life.

Read more from the CBC’s Nick Logan.

Marketplace needs your help

(David Abrahams/CBC)

Have you ever wondered what personal data you might be giving away when you use apps on your phone? If you're curious and willing to be on camera, drop us a line at marketplace@cbc.ca.

World.title: ‘Our river is almost dead’: What’s killing an iconic Miramichi fishery?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Every veteran salmon angler, guide and outfitter in the Miramichi watershed remembers their first encounter with a striped bass.

For Rip Cunningham, a member of the storied Black Brook Salmon Club, it happened at the junction of the Main Southwest Miramichi River and the Cains River.

“I caught what I thought was a salmon, and I was going, ‘This fish isn’t jumping. This is odd,’” he said. He reeled it in.

“The guides who live on the river, who’d been fishing on the river for years, said ‘What’s that?’ They had no idea whatsoever.”

It was a striped bass, a fish Cunningham believes now represents an existential threat to the Miramichi’s most iconic species: his beloved wild Atlantic salmon.

Byron Coughlan, who runs the County Haven fishing lodge near Blackville, was guiding two salmon anglers from New England about 15 years ago when they caught two bass.

“They said, ‘Your river's done,’” he recalled. “‘The bass is going to eat everything.’ They said, ‘Eventually you won’t have any salmon.’”

LISTEN | The saga of salmon, striped bass and the Miramichi: Atlantic Voice 26:10 A tale of two fish on the Miramichi How much do you meddle with Mother Nature? Atlantic Salmon and striped bass have always lived in the Miramichi watershed, but with populations of each out of whack - the salmon waning, and the bass surging - anglers, scientists and politicians are weighing in about what to do. Wade into a world with no easy answers, and no shortage of opinions, in Jacques Poitras' documentary, Two Fish Stories.

The community of anglers, guides and outfitters in the Miramichi watershed fear that prediction is now on the verge of coming true.

Juvenile salmon, they say, are being gobbled up on their migratory trek to the ocean by a growing striped bass population.

“We have a crisis facing Atlantic salmon and other species on the Miramichi,” Alex Mills, an angler who is part of lawsuit against the federal government, told the House of Commons standing committee on fisheribes and oceans this month.

In 1996, the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans closed the commercial striped bass fishery to halt a collapse in stocks caused by overfishing.

The salmon anglers say the closure allowed the bass population to grow to an unsustainable level, moving upriver from its traditional home in tidal waters and throwing off the Miramichi’s delicate balance.

Bradford Burns, background, fly fishes for Atlantic salmon on the Southwest Miramichi River. Burns, an American, has been coming here from the U.S. to fish for decades. The angler in the foreground is Dawson Hovey. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)

DFO blamed for ‘a big mess’

The anglers say the growth of the striped bass is killing the fabled recreational salmon fishery, once an economic lifeline for small communities along the river.

DFO officials “have done essentially nothing” to curb the bass boom “and created this big mess,” said Bradford Burns, a Maine business owner with a salmon camp on the Southwest Miramichi.

The bass population is now north of 500,000 — some estimates are much higher — while salmon returns were below 5,000 in 2025, DFO numbers indicate.

Burns, Cunningham, Mills and two other anglers have filed a lawsuit in federal court hoping to force DFO to resume a commercial bass fishery to reduce the population and give more smolts a chance to reach the ocean.

“This extraordinary level of predation is completely unsustainable and is on the verge of extirpating Atlantic salmon from what has long been considered the greatest salmon river in North America,” the group wrote in a letter to the federal fisheries minister in 2024.

Salmon are so tied to the identity of the Miramichi region, highway signs depict the fish. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)

On its website, DFO says bass eat “variable numbers” of smolts every year, and “it is not clear whether this natural predator-prey dynamic is limiting the number of returning adult salmon to the Miramichi river.”

‘A direct correlation,’ outfitter says

Brock Curtis, who operates an outfitter store in Blackville that is an essential destination for anglers and guides, says the cause and effect are clear.

“Our numbers are dropping as the bass numbers are increasing, and there's a direct correlation there,” he said.

The Atlantic salmon is so tied to the river’s identity that its image is used on provincial road signs identifying the Miramichi river route. Curtis says what’s at risk is a unique fishery that puts a premium on patience, practice and a calm state of mind.

“We live in a world where a lot of people are used to immediate gratification,” he said.

“This sport isn't like that. It's a skill, and you put your time in and you will be rewarded in the end.”

Brock Curtis runs a salmon-angling outfitting store in Blackville. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)

Striper success

By contrast, the abundant striped bass has spawned a two-day frenzy of immediate gratification that unfolds downriver every May.

Hundreds of anglers crowd into the city of Miramichi for the Striper Cup, a bass tournament with a seemingly bottomless list of prizes and giveaways.

"We’ve always had fish,” participant Barry Hay said in an interview over the side of his boat during this year’s tournament. "We’ve never won, but we’ve always had fish, two a day."

Dwayne Ogilvie of Salisbury said he loves the “aggressiveness” of the bass.

The Striper Cup launched in Miramichi in 2015 and has turned into one of the city’s biggest tourism draws. Paul McGraw, the city’s economic development officer, said the success of the event is “one hundred per cent” attributable to the booming bass population.

A striped bass is weighed during the Miramichi Striper Cup, an annual catch-and-release tournament for the fish. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)

“We never, ever imagined that it would grow and develop the brand that we have with the Miramichi Striper Cup as quickly as we have done it,” he said.

McGraw would not comment on the debate involving salmon.

“We'd be naive to think there wasn't a controversy,” he said, “but that's not what we're into.”

At the cup's opening ceremony in May, pro angler Jeff Wilson, a co-founder of the tournament, urged participants to lobby politicians against a reopened commercial striped bass fishery.

“It’s really important that you folks talk to your politicians and protect this resource for our kids,” he said.

“It’s been here for millennia. They’re not bad. They’re good. Bass are good.”

Anglers pose with the first striped bass caught during the 2026 Miramichi Striper Cup. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)

A detour for juvenile salmon

The anglers taking DFO to court estimate a commercial fishery of 300,000 to 400,000 bass would reduce the population to about 100,000 — enough, they say, to give the salmon a chance.

Ottawa approved a First Nations striped bass fishery of 50,000 in 2018 and increased the allowable catch to 175,000 six years later.

That maximum has not been reached, and anglers say letting non-Indigenous anglers catch that quota would be a good start.

In the meantime, the Atlantic Salmon Federation, the Miramichi Salmon Association and Anqotum Resource Management, a Mi’kmaw conservation agency, are doing what they can.

The Atlantic Salmon Federation, the Miramichi Salmon Federation, and Anqotum Resource Management are collecting juvenile salmon, known as smolts, in large spinning drums to be tagged, counted, and transported downriver in an effort to keep them safe from bass predation. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)

In the spring, their teams descended on the northwest branch of the Miramichi at Wayerton to collect and tag salmon smolts and truck large numbers of them downriver, around and past the hungry bass population, so they could make it to the ocean.

“Concept-wise, it works,” said David Roth, an Atlantic Salmon Federation biologist who called the operation an emergency measure. "It's really just about the numbers that you can catch in total.

“It's not like we want to transport fish for decades to come. Where the population currently is, everything helps.”

Salmon angler Rip Cunningham calls it “a good experiment” but unlikely to make a dent in the problem.

“You cannot get enough of them in tanks and move them around to make any reasonable difference to this river,” he said.

DFO biologist looks for ‘larger mechanisms’

Roth and Joe Augustine, a biologist from Metepenagiag First Nation, said there’s no doubt the bass boom is the biggest cause of the salmon’s decline.

Roth said fewer than 10 per cent of migrating smolts in the Miramichi reach the ocean, compared to 80 per cent in other nearby rivers.

The difference? “It's definitely the massive population of striped bass that we do have in the Miramichi,” Augustine said.

Federal scientists say other factors can’t be discounted, because the decline is also happening in other rivers with fewer or no bass, including in Europe.

Joe Augustine, left, of Metapenagiag First Nation works with Anqotum Resource Management. David Roth, right, is a biologist with the Atlantic Salmon Federation. Both men and groups are involved with the smolt trucking project. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)

“We don't say that striped bass do not eat juvenile salmon,” said Cindy Breau, a DFO biologist based in Moncton.

“What we are saying is that if we want to answer the question about why salmon are not returning to our rivers, we need to look at larger mechanisms and try to unravel the mechanisms involved with that.”

Breau suggested one reason Miramichi returns are lower may be the little tracking tags the conservationists insert in the smolts — weighing them down as they try to outrun hungry bass.

Climate change is also warming rivers beyond what cold-water salmon can tolerate and may be disrupting the food chains they rely on when they migrate to the ocean, Breau said.

But Mills said DFO’s science “flies in the face” of research done by conservation groups, providing the department a “half-baked justification for doing nothing.”

“It’s not climate-related. It’s not habitat-related. It’s striped bass-related, and if DFO does not see that, they are blind,” he told the House of Commons fisheries committee.

Katie Patles of Anqotum Resource Management tags a smolt as part of the conservation project to save some young salmon from being eaten by striped bass. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)

MP says larger bass fishery an easy fix

Some anglers also point to industrial logging practices that may increase runoff into the rivers and reduce shade that blocked the sun’s heat.

Acadie-Bathurst MP Serge Cormier says some illegal net fishing may also play a role. But Cormier, an avid angler, said the striped bass clearly have “a big impact.”

Cormier is a member of the House of Commons fisheries committee, and he persuaded his colleagues to hold hearings this year on the Atlantic salmon.

“We need solutions. Enough talk,” he said.

While other factors DFO has identified are complicated to address, the MP said reducing the striped bass population with a revived commercial fishery “is the easiest piece to do right now.”

Paul McGraw, an economic development officer with the City of Miramichi, makes announcement's during the Striper Cup, a striped bass fishing tournament that's become a big tourism draw. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)

Ottawa is spending $81.7 million on a 12-year Atlantic salmon strategy that includes climate-resilience measures, Indigenous partnerships and more transparent monitoring of stocks.

Federal Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson visited New Brunswick in August and met with the the Atlantic Salmon Federation and Miramichi Salmon Association.

"Let's understand that science is the backbone of what we do, but we also pay attention to the people who are closest to the resource,” Thompson said in an interview.

“And then if there's a disconnect, as there is in this instance, what is it that we need to do to find and strike that balance?"

'Is it our job to intervene?'

The Striper Cup has its own science championing the striped bass.

Dockside at the Striper Cup in May, a team of biologists from Acadia University ran the weigh station for the tournament.

Competitors returning to Ritchie’s Wharf watched the team rush their fish up to a table and submerge them in a tank before weighing them.

This year’s winning bass was 9.4 kilograms, or almost 21 pounds, the largest of almost 700 bass caught and released.

Salmon anglers say that abundance shows the species could withstand a regulated commercial bass fishery.

“We are not saying that we want to eradicate an entire striper population,” Augustine said.

“They're a native species, and it's important that they stay at decent levels as well, because they're meant to be here as well.”

But the Acadia team said it’s too soon after the bass’s near-collapse to take a chance.

“We should be able to long-term monitor before making big decisions,” said Leah Creaser, a Mi’kmaw biologist and Acadia researcher.

“Like, ‘that species is doing great, that one is not doing great,’ so there’s a game of picking and choosing because of a lot of social pressures.”

Leah Creaser, left, a researcher and student at Acadia University, checks striped bass during the weigh-in at the Miramichi Striper Cup. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)

Trevor Avery, the Acadia professor and biostatistician who leads the team, said it’s “really hard to pit one species against another” when the ecosystem is more dynamic than a simple “smoking gun” scenario.

Creaser said the rebound and growth of the striped bass on the Miramichi may be an example of evolutionary history unfolding in real time.

“Is it our job to intervene? I’m not sure.”

A changing camp on a changing river

As the debate continues, some salmon outfitters have resigned themselves to a different Miramichi.

Wilson’s Sporting Camps, a lodge that dates back to 1855, has branched out into canoeing, tubing, corporate retreats, weddings, and, yes, even striped bass fishing.

“It's to the point now where our river is almost dead,” co-owner Karl Wilson said.

“There’s very few fish out there … and it doesn't seem like anybody's really doing anything about it.”

Everyone is “pointing the finger at one another” while waiting for Ottawa to act, Wilson said.

“In my opinion, it's almost too far gone.”

Karl Wilson, who runs Wilson's Sporting Camps, says he's seen declines on the river that have forced his business to pivot to include other outdoor sports and experiences beyond salmon angling. (Jacques Poitras/CBC)

Joe Augustine, though, remains optimistic.

His community’s long history with the Atlantic salmon runs through his great-grandfather, who could catch enough salmon in a day to feed his entire family for a summer.

Augustine said his father, as a child, “could hear the salmon run coming up the river to spawn. It would keep him up at night.”

There’s no choice but to be optimistic, he said.

“You have to believe that the salmon numbers are going to come back," he said. "Or then what are we doing this work for?”

“They’ve hit critical levels, but we've seen striped bass hit critical levels 20 to 25 years ago, and now look at them back in our river. It’s crazy, the amount — maybe, definitely, a little too much.

“But if it can be done with striped bass, why can't it be done with Atlantic salmon?”

World.title: He was imprisoned and tortured by the Houthis. He’s counselling diplomacy, not war
World.content:
Article content

I called someone I have known since the late 1990s. Hisham Al-Omeisy, 47, was born in Sana’a and was among the first of about 100 students chosen, on merit, for a Nexen scholarship program I helped design. He studied at the University of Calgary, went home, worked for the U.S. State Department in Yemen, and stayed after the Houthis seized the institutions of government in 2015. In August 2017 the Houthis picked him up and held him for five months. He was released in January 2018 and got out of the country. He is now a senior adviser at the European Institute of Peace in Washington, which is a polite way of saying he spends his time trying to get people who would rather shoot each other into the same room.
