World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Colombia’s first lady promises transparency over earthquake donations
World.content:
Colombia’s first lady, Ana Lucia Pineda, vowed to reveal how much money she collected and spent in response to the August 10 earthquake that affected hundreds of thousands of people.

Amid mounting public pressure about where the money had gone, Pineda went on the morning program of public television channel Nuestro Caribe to promise that her foundation, Luz y Sonrisas, will take its finances public on Friday.

Carrying a white folder, the wife of President Abelardo de la Espriella stressed that “in the foundation’s accounts rest all, absolutely all of the monies from the donations we received during the ‘Colombia One Single Heart’ campaign” that was announced on August 12.

“A lie is not going to tear down the truth of who I am or what I represent, or how my children recognize me,” said Pineda.

Luz y Sonrisas was one of three NGO’s that were promoted by the De la Espriella government to collect contributions for victims of the earthquake.

Pineda’s foundation was the only one that could receive contributions from abroad.

Earlier in the week, news program Noticias Uno revealed that her foundation that was founded on July 7 lacked the tax exemption that would allow it to accept donations, a process that usually takes months.

In a press statement, tax office DIAN subsequently said that it had granted the tax exemption to the first lady and that she could legally accept financial contributions.

Pineda did not say how much money she had received, but said that she stopped supporting the initial relief efforts “because the humanitarian aid was sufficient, it was huge.”

The first lady vowed she had saved the donations for the reconstruction phase “because I have also taken the initiative to build and return to the victims a house that is durable for the families who lost everything.”

World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Colombia declares official start of El Niño, warns of strong impacts
World.content:
Colombia’s meteorological institute IDEAM officially declared the arrival of El Niño, and warned that the climate phenomenon could trigger water shortages and forest fires.

In a press statement, the IDEAM said that its “confirmation reflects the sustained warm conditions in the Pacific Ocean, which, according to the latest measurement, broke records, reaching a sea surface temperature anomaly of +3.49°C.”

The meteorological institute said it expected that this year’s “Godzilla El Niño” could continue to disrupt local climate patterns until March next year.

Initially, the weather phenomenon is expected to reduce rainfall between October and December, which is normally the rainy season in large parts of the country.

“Given this situation, and in light of the alerts issued since the beginning of the year, the national government launched an interagency response,.. with specific instructions for the responsible agencies to have their contingency plans formulated and activated by November 30 at the latest,” said the President’s Office in a statement.

The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) coordinates response capabilities across the country and enhances the monitoring of wildfires using satellite technology. For its part, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is taking steps to protect strategic ecosystems, water sources, and the most vulnerable areas. President’s Office

The Mining Ministry “is implementing an emergency plan aimed at ensuring the country’s energy security by strengthening thermal power generation, securing fuel supplies, and implementing efficiency and conservation measures,” according to the President’s Office.

EPM, the local utilities firm in Medellin, has been testing the effectiveness of water rations as they fear the lack of rain could affect the hydro-electric power plants that provide the northwest of Colombia much of its energy.

Before leaving office on August 7, former President Gustavo Petro ordered the mass purchase of solar panels to reduce the pressure on the electric grid.

World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: De la Espriella announces first $309M in aid for earthquake reconstruction
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella announced that his Miracle Fund received COP1 trillion ($309 million) for the reconstruction of western Colombia, which was hit by a 7.4M earthquake on August 10.

The announcement followed announcements by the press, which reported that the Finance Ministry allocated ($192 million) COP625 billion to the fund almost two months after the disaster.

Thank you for your patience, but please understand that the government’s bureaucratic inertia and the situation we’ve inherited are extremely complex. However, we’re working to resolve the issue, and the Milagro Fund is now up and running, thanks to God and the efforts of all the officials in this administration. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“In November, the government will move forward with contracting another COP2.7 trillion ($835 million),” Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo told Caracol Radio.

The money is the first of an estimated COP30 trillion ($9.3 billion) that would be needed to rebuild the damage to airports, roads, hospitals and other public works.

The fund will be managed by De la Espriella’s general secretary, Carlos Rios, and a handful of businessmen with ties to the administration.

The announcement followed increased unrest about the government’s lack of response to the earthquake, which affected more than 400,000 people in the Valle del Cauca and Choco province, and the coffee region.

The government’s initial response was delayed because De la Espriella suspended the process to transfer power a month before he took office on August 7.

World.title: Colombia seeks to expand definition of terrorism in draft “counterterrorism statute”
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella will present Colombia’s Congress with a comprehensive “counterterrorism statute,” which would give authorities enhanced powers to fight designated terrorist organizations.

A 116-page draft bill, which was leaked to Caracol Radio, would facilitate a military approach to combat illegal armed groups and organized crime groups, for example through air strikes.

The Antiterrorism Statute would additionally create a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors, which would make it easier to freeze the assets of suspected terrorists and their financiers.

Last but not least, the bill creates a presidential Terrorism Commissioner and a special prison regime for leaders of designated terrorist organizations.

Broader definition of terrorism

The bill seeks to change Colombia’s criminal law and define terrorism as any individual or collective conduct that produces “fear, panic or terror, creating risks, threats or the use of violence.”

A technical body of the National Security Council (NSC) will advise the council on the inclusion of organizations or individuals that ought to be included to its public National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors.

Anyone who believes he was falsely put on the terror list can challenge this decision before the NSC and the Council of State, Colombia’s top administrative court.

The bill additionally seeks that “the Council of State shall hear, in the first instance, constitutional protection lawsuits filed against the President of the Republic or against defense authorities for acts or omissions related to operations by law enforcement agencies to preserve national security.”

This would make the suspension of military operations more difficult for citizens, who now can seek legal support to protect their constitutional rights at lower courts.

The bill also creates new crimes and modifies the penalties for conduct related to “terrorism,” such as the use of drones, illegal mining, oil theft, the extraction and sale of gold, kidnapping, smuggling, human trafficking, drug trafficking, extortion, cybercrimes, election crimes, riots, and attacks on critical infrastructure.

In the case of riots, “the penalty shall be increased by up to double when the riot is directed against law enforcement units conducting operations; or is carried out in conjunction with listed terrorist organizations.”

The bill also allows Colombian authorities to investigate and prosecute terrorism, terrorism financing or providing material support for terrorist organizations abroad.

High Counterterrorism Commissioner

The bill additionally seeks to expand presidential powers to create the Office of the High Counterterrorism Commissioner.

The expanded power would additionally give De la Espriella six months to regulate the powers of this new advisory office and to appoint its first commissioner.

World.title: Tesla’s new Roadster uses compressed air and fans to jump and drive upside down
World.content:
Tesla’s new Roadster uses compressed air and fans to jump and drive upside down

18th Sunday, October 2026 - 12:31 UTC Full article

In the demonstration, held at SpaceX’s test site in McGregor, the prototype drove up a ramp, turned upside down, separated from it and completed a rotation before touching the ground

Tesla unveiled on Thursday in Texas a redesigned version of its Roadster electric sports car, developed with SpaceX, which combines suction fans and compressed-air thrusters to climb near-vertical surfaces, drive upside down and flip in the air. The company plans to begin production in 2028.

In the demonstration, held at SpaceX’s test site in McGregor, the prototype drove up a ramp, turned upside down, separated from it and completed a rotation before touching the ground. According to Tesla, the vehicle uses two systems. Fans reduce the pressure under the chassis so that outside air pushes it onto the track, producing up to 4,700 kilograms of downforce that boosts grip even at standstill. In addition, two carbon-fibre tanks holding 600 litres of compressed air feed ten nozzles that provide thrust to accelerate, jump and correct the car’s position, with no combustion.

Do a kickflip! https://t.co/DJ1Bq1yu8m — Tesla (@Tesla) October 16, 2026

The company announced thrust of more than 80 kilonewtons and acceleration from zero to 97 kilometres per hour in 0.81 seconds. “It can basically fly like a rocket. It can do flips, crazy gymnastics, whatever you want really,” said Elon Musk, who acknowledged: “This is not necessarily a car optimised for safety.” The stored air allows only bursts of a few seconds, not sustained flight.

Tesla will offer three versions. Performance and Thrust, two-seaters, are already taking reservations with deposits of US$50,000 and US$250,000 respectively. Rocket, a single-seater with thrusters around the body, will be available by invitation only and is not approved for use on public roads. The company has not given dates for driver testing or explained how manoeuvres that lift the vehicle off the ground will be regulated.

Musk first unveiled the Roadster in 2017, with deliveries promised for 2020 that never materialised.

World.title: Bolsonaro and Lula head into the final stretch of Brazil’s campaign in a statistical tie
World.content:
Bolsonaro and Lula head into the final stretch of Brazil’s campaign in a statistical tie

17th Saturday, October 2026 - 06:23 UTC Full article

Both polls were conducted before the Senate approved on Wednesday a cut in the working week from 44 to 40 hours, one of the flagships of Lula’s campaign

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva are heading into the final days of the campaign for the October 25 runoff in a statistical tie, according to two new polls. A Datafolha survey released on Thursday night gives Bolsonaro 51% of valid votes and Lula 49%, compared with 52% and 48% a week earlier, with a margin of error of two points.

A Quaest poll published on Wednesday puts Bolsonaro on 46% of voting intentions and Lula on 44%, also within the margin of error. Some 9% will vote blank or spoil their ballot and just 1% are undecided. Rejection rates are similar: 54% say they would never vote for Bolsonaro and 53% would never vote for Lula. Asked which they fear more, Lula’s re-election or the Bolsonaro family’s return to power, respondents split evenly at 43% each. Lula leads in the northeast and among recipients of the Bolsa Família programme; Bolsonaro in the south and among evangelicals.

Both polls were conducted before the Senate approved on Wednesday a cut in the working week from 44 to 40 hours, one of the flagships of Lula’s campaign, which Bolsonaro also voted for.

In an interview with TV Globo, Lula said he supports lowering the age of criminal responsibility for the most serious crimes, a proposal until now championed by his rival, who wants to reduce it from 18 to 16. “My opinion, as a Brazilian citizen, is that for any heinous crime I am in favour of lowering the age of majority,” he said. The president also took responsibility for his high rejection rate: “If I failed to make people understand the government I formed, I cannot blame anyone, the fault is mine.”

Bolsonaro, who won 47.03% of the first-round vote against Lula’s 45.16%, has secured the backing of almost all right-wing and centre-right parties, and has promised to maintain the current government’s social programmes and create a Ministry of Prosperity. The two candidates will face each other on Sunday in their first debate, on the Band network.

World.title: Brent touches US$110 for the first time since May on Middle East tensions
World.content:
Brent touches US$110 for the first time since May on Middle East tensions

17th Saturday, October 2026 - 06:17 UTC Full article

Attacks around Hormuz have intensified over the past ten days, with Iran saying it is responding to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions imposed last month

Brent crude reached US$110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May, driven by fears that escalation in the Middle East could further tighten supplies and by doubts over how much diesel Russia can supply to the market. Brent settled 3.7% higher at US$109.86, its highest since May 19, while US benchmark WTI rose 3.5% to US$101.41.

Over the week, Brent has gained 4.9% and WTI 10.4%. Prices rebounded after the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched towards Yanbu, the Red Sea port the kingdom uses to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Initial reports indicated no damage to its facilities.

Attacks around Hormuz have intensified over the past ten days, with Iran saying it is responding to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions imposed last month. “Intensified Iranian attacks drove Gulf crude flows sharply lower,” consultancy Kpler said, forecasting a slow and uneven recovery in the absence of a political deal.

The war in Ukraine is adding to the pressure. President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire on energy sites announced on Sunday by US President Donald Trump, and criticised his willingness to strike deals with Moscow. A day later, a drone attack forced the suspension of a distillation unit at Russia’s Ryazan refinery. “It’s questionable how much diesel fuel Russia can actually deliver to the markets,” said Dennis Kissler of BOK Financial. Trump announced last week a deal with Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply some 4.8 million tonnes of diesel.

To ease the market, the International Energy Agency agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of fuel, and the US Department of Energy offered an exchange of up to 17 million barrels from its strategic reserve. According to the International Monetary Fund, higher energy prices benefit Latin America’s commodity exporters and hurt importers.

World.title: Trump drops his new press secretary after a week of controversy
World.content:
Trump drops his new press secretary after a week of controversy

16th Friday, October 2026 - 21:50 UTC Full article

She admitted that, although she graduated in law, she had not passed the bar exam, despite presenting herself as a lawyer for years

Katie Zacharia will leave her post as White House press secretary just five days after taking it up, according to advisers to President Donald Trump quoted by several US media outlets, following a widely criticised first briefing and the revelation that she had presented herself as a lawyer without passing the bar exam.

A White House official said Zacharia was “transitioning out” of the role. Before leaving for a campaign rally in Georgia, Trump told reporters he had suggested she reconsider staying on: “Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider. Katie, do you need this?” The president said she had been treated “very unfairly” by the media and that many people wanted the job.

Zacharia, appointed on October 9 to succeed Karoline Leavitt, held her first and only briefing on Tuesday, lasting 14 minutes, in which she was unable to answer a question about whether the United States had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. Days later she admitted that, although she graduated in law, she had not passed the bar exam, despite presenting herself as a lawyer for years.

Her tenure is shorter than the 11 days Anthony Scaramucci spent as Trump’s communications director in 2017.

World.title: Rodrigues-Birkett, UN leadership hopeful: “Not choosing a woman would send a very negative message”
World.content:
Rodrigues-Birkett, UN leadership hopeful: “Not choosing a woman would send a very negative message”

16th Friday, October 2026 - 21:50 UTC Full article

Guyana’s ambassador to the UN, Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, one of the best-placed candidates to succeed António Guterres at the head of the organisation, has warned that not choosing a woman “would send a very negative message to the world”, in an interview with the newspaper El País published on the day the Security Council holds its first informal colour-coded straw poll, which reveals whether any of the five permanent members opposes each candidate.

“I am not running because I am a woman; I am running on the basis of my ability and my competence. But if there is one place that should set an example on equality between men and women, it is the UN,” said the former Guyanese foreign minister, 53, who is of Arawak Indigenous descent. “The women taking part in this process have stepped forward. I do not believe that, at this stage, the world has concluded that none of us has the right profile.”

Rodrigues-Birkett called for respect for the principle of rotation, under which it is now the turn of a candidate from Latin America and the Caribbean, and for any new contender to be subjected to “the same level of scrutiny” as the current ones. She also warned that reaching January 1 without a successor “would be one of the best ways to undermine the credibility of the UN”.

The candidate slipped to third place in the last informal poll, on October 7, after articles recalled her criticism of Israel over the war in Gaza. “If defending the Charter and international law is going to work against me in this race, I choose that without hesitation,” she said, adding that she was aware of “other efforts” against her that she would discuss “at the right time”.

According to leaked results of that poll, Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan received 9 encourage and 6 discourage votes; Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, head of the International Atomic Energy Agency, 6 encourage, 7 discourage and 2 no opinion; and Rodrigues-Birkett 5 encourage, 9 discourage and 1 no opinion. To be recommended to the General Assembly, a candidate needs at least nine votes in favour and no opposition from a permanent member. According to the specialist outlet PassBlue, the United Kingdom would oppose Grossi because of Argentina’s claim over the Falklands.

Seven candidates remain in the race, four of them Latin American. No woman has led the UN in its more than 80-year history.

World.title: Kast and Paz open the way in La Paz to normalising Chile-Bolivia relations
World.content:
Kast and Paz open the way in La Paz to normalising Chile-Bolivia relations

16th Friday, October 2026 - 21:50 UTC Full article

“President Paz, today we stop turning our backs on each other. We did not come just for a gesture, we came to begin making history,” Kast said after the bilateral meetings

Chilean President José Antonio Kast and his Bolivian counterpart Rodrigo Paz pledged on Friday in La Paz to move towards normalising diplomatic relations “at the highest level”, broken off since 1978, during a visit the Chilean government described as historic as the first official bilateral visit by a Chilean president to Bolivia in more than seven decades. The two governments signed economic integration and border security agreements, although they did not announce the restoration of embassies.

“President Paz, today we stop turning our backs on each other. We did not come just for a gesture, we came to begin making history,” Kast said after the bilateral meetings. Paz replied that the two countries have “historical differences” and that the claim to sea access is enshrined in Bolivia’s Constitution, “but Bolivia understands that this history cannot hold back its development. Problems of the past must be resolved.” Kast invited Paz on a state visit to Chile in 2027.

Ministers from both countries signed agreements on mining integration, electricity interconnection, bi-oceanic corridors, border security and the migration status of Bolivians living in Chile. They also discussed reviving the Arica-La Paz railway, provided for in the 1904 treaty between Bolivia and Chile, 24-hour operation at the Tambo Quemado-Chungará border crossing and the fight against smuggling. According to the Oruro customs post, more than 76% of Bolivia’s foreign trade passes through the Chilean ports of Arica and Iquique.

Bolivia’s claim to sovereign access to the sea, which it lost at the International Court of Justice in 2018, was not on the agenda. “We are not going to renounce our historical claim, but it is also clear that we have to address a fundamental agenda,” said Bolivia’s Minister of the Presidency, Fernando Aramayo.

The rapprochement comes at a time of alignment between the two governments, which this year joined the Shield of the Americas, the US-backed regional security alliance. The Bolivian opposition, however, criticised the visit over the destruction in Chile of part of a seized shipment of Bolivian timber over alleged traces of drugs. “The situation is tense, we cannot be hypocrites,” said deputy Elena Pachacute of the Unidad alliance.

World.title: Royal Navy urged to replace defective Ice Patrol HMS Protector
World.content:
Royal Navy urged to replace defective Ice Patrol HMS Protector

16th Friday, October 2026 - 13:59 UTC Full article

HMS Protector role helped to maintain a sovereign, reassuring, and versatile presence in the South Atlantic and the British Antarctic Territory

The Royal Navy's only ice patrol vessel has been towed into Devonport, reportedly with a double engine failure, raising fresh concerns over how the news will be interpreted by Argentina. HMS Protector fulfils an icebreaking role to monitor the demilitarized Antarctic and support safe navigation for scientific research in challenging conditions.

According to the UK’s Defense Investment Plan and the Royal Navy, she is due to be replaced by a more modern variant.

However, the document also highlighted the importance of the military's now-missing ice patrol capability to “maintain this essential presence and support Government activities in the Arctic and around the British Antarctic Territory”.

Speaking to BFBS Forces News, retired Royal Navy Commodore Steve Prest assessed the geopolitical significance of the vessel's woes given Argentina's continued claim to the Falkland Islands.

“In those territories down in the South Atlantic, there is still some contestation over their sovereignty, and we've seen a resurgence of some of those claims from Argentina in recent weeks and months, emboldened by the political situation in America,” he said.

“Let's not forget that it was the withdrawal of one of the previous ice patrol ships that was down there, HMS Endurance that was one of the precipitating factors of the invasion of the Falklands in 1982.

”It was seen as a signal that the British weren't interested in the South Atlantic in quite the way they previously had been. So these things are important, not only in terms of the work that they do, but also the signaling that they send geo-strategically.“

Considering the international discourse, the timing of HMS Protector's defect, as described by the Royal Navy, demands new context applied to any concern over South Atlantic security.

The withdrawal of the previous icebreaker in the 1980s was seen as a retreat of the UK from some of its overseas territories and interests, Cder. Prest explained.

”I don't think we're in that situation at all now,“ he said. ”I think we're absolutely crystal clear in terms of the UK Government's policy around the sovereignty of the British South Atlantic territories, the Falkland Islands and so on.

“We have significant military assets down there, not least fast jets and air defense teams and infantry companies. So the Islands are well defended, far better defended than they were in 1982.”

He added: “I don't think we should be too alarmed. The diplomatic and Foreign Office signaling is unambiguous with regard to sovereignty of the Falkland Islands. So I don't think there's going to be the same miscalculations.

”I don't think we need to worry about that. But these ships, HMS Protector and her predecessors, had a job of work to do down there. And that job of work will need to be done.

“And we should, in my view, both for reasons of doing that job of work, but also signaling that we still take our maritime responsibilities in that part of the world seriously, replace the ship as quickly as possible.”

A Royal Navy spokesperson said: “HMS Protector has returned to her home port of Devonport while investigations into a defect take place.

”As part of the Defense Investment Plan, HMS Protector will be replaced with a more modern variant to maintain the ice patrol capability. She remains part of the fleet, and any decisions on her immediate future will be made in due course.”

World.title: The Falklands dispute threatens Argentina’s bid to join the trans-Pacific trade pact
World.content:
The Falklands dispute threatens Argentina’s bid to join the trans-Pacific trade pact

16th Friday, October 2026 - 10:07 UTC Full article

The possibility was raised in the House of Commons by Conservative MP Wendy Morton, who urged the government to prepare to oppose Argentina’s application if threats over the islands continue

The escalating dispute between Argentina and the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands has spilled into trade: London, a member of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, has not ruled out using its position to stall Argentina’s bid to join the pact, which requires the consensus of all its members. The British government says Buenos Aires’s conduct raises “very serious questions about its reliability as a partner”.

The possibility was raised in the House of Commons by Conservative MP Wendy Morton, who urged the government to prepare to oppose Argentina’s application if threats over the islands continue. Overseas Territories Minister Uma Kumaran replied that the UK does not comment publicly on accession discussions and does not speculate on possible sanctions, though it will continue to consider “all appropriate measures”. She added that Argentine attempts to obstruct economic activity in the archipelago “damage legal certainty”.

Argentina submitted its accession request on June 2. The pact brings together Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Peru, Singapore, Vietnam and the United Kingdom, the only country to have joined since its creation. Opening accession talks and issuing the final invitation both require the consensus of all members, so any one of them can block the process. Uruguay, which applied in December 2022, has been in formal negotiations since November 2025 in a working group chaired by Chile.

According to Argentina’s foreign ministry, the country’s exports to the bloc’s members reached US$16.329 billion in 2025, with a surplus of US$8.93 billion. Staying out would not halt that trade but would deprive exporters of the pact’s tariff preferences and common rules. The separate bids by Argentina and Uruguay have also caused friction in Mercosur, where Brazil has questioned their departure from joint negotiations with third countries.

The warning caps a week of escalation. On Tuesday, Argentina asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to order a halt to Sea Lion, after the United Kingdom on October 11 rejected its claims and refused to adopt the measures it had demanded. The tribunal has yet to set a hearing date. The same day, London announced it would use its protection of trading interests legislation to prevent British companies and citizens from having to comply with Argentine sanctions; according to the British press, the measures would be in force before the end of the year. Navitas Petroleum, the project’s operator, welcomed the British backing and has said it is replacing two contractors that withdrew under Argentine pressure.

The Argentine government rejects the reliability argument. “Reliability is shown by honouring the international commitments one has undertaken,” Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno said earlier this month, arguing that the United Kingdom is exploiting disputed resources in breach of UN resolutions calling on both countries to negotiate.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Guadalajara water protest fallout, IMSS demands and another Pacific hurricane
World.content:
Listen to this article

Protests over contaminated water in Guadalajara and over pay and medicine shortages at IMSS, along with another hurricane approaching the Pacific coast, set the agenda in Mexico the second week of October. Clashes between police and protesters in Guadalajara on Sunday left dozens hurt and 39 arrested, and the National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) is now investigating alleged police abuses. IMSS workers demonstrated in nearly every state, rejecting a 2.9% pay offer and demanding 10%.

On the Pacific coast, Hurricane Trudy is forecast to pass by Colima and Jalisco over the weekend, as coastal states continue to recover from a close brush with Hurricane Simon and deadly flooding after Tropical Storm Rachel touched down in Baja California. The week also brought mixed news on the security front: Homicides continue to trend down, but organized crime notched a win after Morelos exchanged an alleged criminal leader to save three kidnapped police officers.

Exports hit a record in the first eight months of the year, but trade talks with the U.S. reportedly stalled over tariff disagreements.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Guadalajara: Police response under investigation as water crisis persists

A march demanding clean tap water ended Sunday in clashes outside the Jalisco governor’s residence, where police used tear gas and water cannons. State authorities put attendance at about 10,000, while University of Guadalajara researchers estimated about 21,400. The state blamed the violence on roughly 400 people, while human rights advocates accused police of excessive use of force and arbitrary detentions.

On Monday, Sheinbaum condemned “repression” and said Jalisco authorities must explain their use of force, adding that her government does not support privatizing Guadalajara’s water service. Governor Pablo Lemus said Tuesday that all 39 detainees had been released and that police used excessive force and made “unjust arrests.” By Thursday, Sheinbaum said the CNDH was investigating the use of water cannons and gas, and allegations that police tortured some detainees.

Residents across the Guadalajara metropolitan area have reported cloudy, foul-smelling tap water for months, with poor water quality affecting at least 342 neighborhoods. Governor Pablo Lemus has blamed deteriorating infrastructure and irregular discharges into a canal that feeds the Las Pintas dam. Earlier this month, the state stopped drawing water from the dam for an estimated six months. Water is expected to be rationed through rotating service cuts by neighborhood, and some areas may need tanker deliveries.

IMSS: Workers reject pay offer as government prepares new proposal

Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) workers protested in nearly every state on Tuesday, including about 7,000 in Mexico City. They are demanding a 10% increase in base pay, rejecting an offer of a 2.9% pay increase plus a 3.9% increase in benefits. Workers are also calling for an end to medicine shortages and for higher staffing levels at hospitals. Sheinbaum acknowledged medicine distribution problems at her Tuesday morning press conference while rejecting claims of a “crisis.”

After workers voted down the offer on Wednesday, Sheinbaum said on Friday that IMSS director Zoé Robledo is evaluating a “comprehensive program” with a larger raise “within the limits of what’s possible” and the regularization of positions. She did not say whether it would meet the 10% demand.

Pacific coast hurricanes: Rachel’s toll rises as Trudy approaches

On the heels of Hurricane Polo, Rachel weakened into a Tropical Storm but still caused significant loss of life in Baja California. The death toll rose to eight people this week, with at least four people missing after heavy rains caused flooding and mudslides. Earlier in the week, the army rescued 32 people stranded outside Ensenada by a mudslide, and Hurricane Simon killed a 71-year-old man in Guerrero and caused significant property damage in coastal communities.

Warm waters off Mexico’s southwest coast continue to generate an onslaught of hurricanes, with Hurricane Trudy reaching Category 3 southwest of Acapulco on Friday morning. Fabián Vázquez, head of the National Meteorological Service, said it would pass about 65 kilometers off the coast of Colima and Jalisco on Saturday night or early Sunday, adding that “any movement to the right or the left can change meteorological conditions a lot.” But like the storms before it, Trudy has behaved unpredictably. Friday afternoon, the storm unexpectedly weakened to Category 1.

#AvisoMeteorológico #Trudy se localiza a 220 km al sur de Manzanillo, #Colima, como #Huracán categoría 1 en la escala Saffir-Simpson. Toda la información en https://t.co/ooqhgp4eqF https://t.co/MIIUi38h3p — CONAGUA Clima (@conagua_clima) October 17, 2026

Security: Baja California tops homicide ranking

Federal figures showed Baja California recorded 1,092 homicides from January to September, just ahead of Guanajuato’s 1,089. Nationally, homicides averaged 42.2 per day in September, down 30.6% from a year earlier. The government says this shows its strategy is working, though analysts and NGOs have questioned whether some homicides are being reclassified as other crimes.

In Morelos, authorities freed alleged Pueblos Unidos leader José David Vergara hours after his arrest to secure the release of three kidnapped police officers. Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said the decision was meant to save lives. Four officers died in a crash while responding to the ensuing unrest.

In other security news, a U.S. State Department-affiliated advisory council reported the CJNG has not fragmented since El Mencho’s death, though some structural weakening may have occurred.

Trade and economy: Stalled talks and a lowered outlook

The Wall Street Journal reported that U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s opposition to tariff cuts has stalled trade talks on the 25% vehicle tariff and the 50% levy on steel and aluminum. Officials from both countries denied the talks had stalled. According to the Financial Times, another factor might be at play: President Donald Trump pressed Sheinbaum on energy deals, contributing to the delay of the next round of formal talks.

Mexico exported a record US $549.4 billion in the first eight months of the year, up 29.3%, which Sheinbaum attributed partly to electronics. Nonetheless, the new World Economic Outlook rated it unlikely that Mexico will reach the top 10 by 2030, projecting 12th place and average annual growth of 1.7% during Sheinbaum’s term.

The week included several major developments in the business world. Grupo Televisa and Fintech Holdings agreed to buy AT&T’s Mexican mobile business for US $2 billion, with closing expected in the first quarter of 2027. It also came out that Mexico’s antitrust commission is expected to approve the Viva-Volaris merger before year-end, concentrating 73% of domestic air traffic in one company.

Looking ahead

The coming weeks will show whether Mexico and the U.S. can restart trade talks that have hit a wall over tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminum, which Mexico has named its top priority. At home, IMSS and its union are working on a new pay proposal after workers rejected the first offer, and workers have said protests could intensify if their demands aren’t met. The rest of the country is preparing for the cultural and economic phenomenon that is Día de Muertos. Mexico will host millions of tourists and visitors, as families and communities remember loved ones who have passed with food, flowers and ofrendas.

More news from across Mexico

World.title: From the archive: AI won’t solve your language learning problems
World.content:
I won’t say I’m a complete expert at spotting the work of artificial intelligence (AI) in creative writing, images or videos. Especially as it becomes more sophisticated, I feel fairly certain I won’t be able to.

But as someone who actually spends quite a bit of time writing and reading, I am still usually able to spot what’s written with AI and similar tools. And I’m definitely aware of the limitations of AI when it comes to nuanced, complicated tasks like translation.

For some things, AI is helpful. A friend of mine uses it to practice her Spanish — nice and slow, everything written. Another friend, an experienced teacher, uses it to reduce lesson-planning time.

Sometimes you can use it as a thesaurus: “What’s a better word for ‘throb’ that doesn’t sound weird and sexual?”

Sure, AI will make up sources that don’t actually exist, but most people don’t seem overly concerned. When it comes to the environmental impact of the gigantic power grid-draining data centers AI must use, though, I fear we’ll only react properly once it’s too late. Or maybe people will think it’s a fair price to pay for all this convenience.

Admittedly, most of my relationship to AI has not been all that positive and I’m glad that Mexico doesn’t seem to be diving headfirst into the techngology as quickly as the U.S.

As a “service” none of us voted to have, which, on top of that, is using all of our data to “learn,” I feel pretty defensive.

And none of us are protected from its effects. We’ve all been tossed into the Wild West without seatbelts or helmets. Even AI company leaders admit that AI “might” end up destroying humanity, but they “have to” move forward.

Do they? Do they have to move forward? I personally heard no booming voice from the sky, and I’ll gladly just go back to using thesaurus.com. Really, it’s fine.

An endless retraining loop

So when I hear people say that they’re using AI to learn Spanish, I bristle somewhat.

My first bristling instinct is admittedly selfish: Nearly every skill I’ve learned while living in Mexico that can actually keep me surviving in the economy is ripe for the AI picking. I’m still a writer, but writing doesn’t pay the bills. Teaching English did for a while. Translating did for a good while, though all that work has now dried up too.

Currently, I’m an audio description writer (kind of like making subtitles for the blind), a job that I love. But I know that it’s only a matter of time before AI gets good enough to swipe that one away too.

How many times can a person be expected to retrain while also juggling all of life’s other requirements? With some predicting that AI will soon be able to do the job of anyone who works in front of a computer, a lot of us might be about to find out.

For now, I’m hanging on as well as I can.

What AI can and can’t do

I keep hearing the same platitude when it comes to jobs: “You won’t be replaced by AI, you’ll be replaced by someone who works with AI.” Cute.

And in the language field, that’s kind of true, I guess? Usually, the “someone who works with AI,” though, is the company itself working with AI so that it doesn’t have to pay anyone.

As someone who’s been involved in many of these human-to-machine transitions, especially in the language field, there are a few things I can say with confidence:

1. AI is not a good transcriber

One of my many professional hats over the years has been legal transcription editor. In many courtrooms these days, AI transcription services are being used to get what was said into printed words. And let me tell you, it does not do a good job, not even the professional-grade software you pay for.

Accents, mumblings, people following the natural cadence of speech all mean that if you want an AI transcript to be legible, you’d better have an experienced editor on hand who can listen closely and write a clean copy. And to use those cool services like a translation app or the new AirPods, people will have to speak slowly and clearly in complete sentences to be understood.

Now, if you and the other person don’t speak each other’s languages at all, I suppose it’s better than nothing. Still, it’s not the miracle it’s made out to be, and misunderstandings are bound to occur.

2. AI is a pretty good translator… if it’s all transcribed properly (it’s not)

If you’ve got a well-written text with proper spelling and grammar, most AI software will do a fairly good job translating it. What it won’t do is translate style.

Spanish writing, I’ve long said, is the king of the run-on sentence. “Break things up,” I’d advise new translators. “English speakers can’t stay focused reading a sentence that goes on for more than three lines.”

When there’s a dual AI job — transcription and translation — things get stickier. After most of my subtitle translation work dried up, I would occasionally get assignments to “proofread” AI’s translations. Most of the time, it wound up being more work than doing it from scratch would have been, and for far less money. If the transcription was bad, then the translation was bad, and it became quite a bit to untangle.

3. There’s nothing like actually talking to people to learn how to talk to people

For all my grouchiness about AI, the point is not to discourage you from using it as a tool to help with your Spanish learning. Whatever helps you communicate is good, and whatever helps you learn is good. But AI companies are trying to convince us in so many areas that AI is just as good as or better than other humans.

When it comes to language learning, it’s simply not.

While AI might be able to explain every detailed grammatical rule that you like, it can’t build a relationship with you. It can’t be your friend or tell you about its personal experiences, always intrinsically linked to the culture and language around the tellers.

So if you’re able, use the tools you need, but try to learn the language and make friends the old-fashioned way. It’s worth it.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Why are fewer Mexicans having children? Financial strain, security concerns and fears for the future
World.content:
Mexico’s national statistics agency, INEGI, recently released the results of the 2025 Intercensal Survey, showing that the country’s population has surpassed 130 million. The findings also reveal a striking trend: fertility rates have fallen considerably nationwide, with Mexico City recording the lowest rate, at just 0.8 children per woman.

Mexican families have changed over the decades. In earlier generations, larger families were more common, partly because of limited access to contraception and family planning services, lower levels of education among women and a more rigid division of labor. Men were generally seen as breadwinners, while women handled most household and caregiving responsibilities.

In an exploratory survey conducted by Mexico News Daily, 13 of 35 respondents said they did not want children. Participants were men and women ages 25 to 35 who were single, in relationships or married, and lived in nine cities: Mexico City, Toluca, Monterrey, Querétaro, León, Ensenada, Cancún, Guanajuato and San Miguel de Allende. They were contacted through social media and asked one open question: “Do you want to have children? Please explain your answer.” The sample is not nationally representative, but it highlights recurring concerns: insufficient income, housing, public safety, health, the climate crisis and the lack of a stable partner.

Financial strain and absent support systems

Luis, 34, lives in Querétaro with his girlfriend. He explained why he has not considered having children:

“I had a privileged upbringing. I went to private school, had enough to eat and never lacked anything. But today, I can’t provide those things for someone else, so bringing a child into the world feels unfair. There’s no guarantee of a stable future, either. My job doesn’t guarantee a steady income or the pay raises I would need to live without financial hardship. And the outlook is bleak: water shortages, housing problems, rising costs and so on.

“Another issue is that we both work, and our families live in Toluca, so we don’t have a support network to help us care for our children. We would have to rely on daycare and extracurricular activities, which would mean additional expenses. Finally, I don’t want to repeat the way I was raised. I had everything I needed materially, but not emotionally, and I’m not ready to break those patterns yet.”

Of the 22 respondents who said they wanted children or were considering having them in the future, some said they had not yet found a stable partner or wanted to become more financially secure first. Three people in this group reported health or fertility problems that had prevented them from conceiving.

Vanesa, 29, lives in San Miguel de Allende and has been married for two years.

“Yes, I want to have children, but first I would like to own a home so I can feel more secure,” she said. “I’m also afraid of global warming. I worry that by the time my child is 15, there could be a water crisis.”

Reasons behind decisions to remain child-free

The 13 respondents who did not want children cited financial pressures, insecurity in Mexico and global problems as their main reasons. Many said they did not earn enough to support a family. Others felt that conditions in the country would make it difficult to raise children in a healthy, safe environment. Wars, global warming and water shortages also influenced their decisions. A smaller number said they did not feel ready to become parents or lacked the patience or skills to care for a baby.

Milé, 34, is single and originally from Querétaro.

“I don’t think I have the skills or resources to be a mother,” she said. “Finding a man my age who wants to share that responsibility would also require me to be honest with myself and able to contribute equally. My jobs haven’t provided social security coverage, either, and I wouldn’t have the financial means to support children. I think bringing children into the world under these conditions would be selfish and irresponsible.”

Respondents who already had one or two children said that number was enough to provide a decent standard of living and, above all, give their children the attention they deserved. Some mothers said they did not want to experience pregnancy and its hormonal changes again because of the physical toll. Fathers said their incomes barely covered the cost of raising one or two children.

One respondent pointed to limited living space, describing a three-bedroom home with one room for the parents and one for each of two children. Housing constraints were another reason not to have more children. Some respondents also said that both parents needed to earn an income to support the family, making a return to paid work an economic priority for mothers.

Why parents are stopping at two children

Paul, 31, is married, has two children and lives in León. He explained why he and his wife decided not to have more:

“My wife and I decided to stop at two children, and it wasn’t a decision we took lightly. When you imagine starting a family, you often don’t think about numbers, square footage, school fees or how many chicken nuggets fit on a baking tray. You just think, ‘I want a lovely family.’ Then adulthood comes along and says, ‘Yes, that’s lovely. Now do the math.’

“That’s when we began to realize that having children involves much more than loving them with all your heart. There’s food, clothing, school, doctors, activities, vacations, birthdays, toys, transportation and all those little things that stop being little once you have children.

“We want to give our children a good life, but we also want some financial peace of mind rather than constantly calculating how to make it to the end of the month. We also believe that having two children allows us to give them time, attention and energy in a way that works for our family. We don’t want more children simply because there’s ‘room’ for them. We want to enjoy the children we have, support them, watch them grow, be present and give them the best we can within our means.”

Raising a family of four

How much money does a family of four need to live in Mexico?

The answer depends on where the family lives and its lifestyle. For this report, we focused on five of the cities where respondents lived: Mexico City, Querétaro, León, Monterrey and San Miguel de Allende.

Drawing on the National Household Income and Expenditure Survey (ENIGH), labor-market information from Data México and reference prices, Mexico News Daily estimated that a family of four living in an owner-occupied home in these cities needs between 29,500 and 48,000 Mexican pesos per month. This budget covers everyday needs such as food, clothing, public school expenses, transportation, personal hygiene products, utilities, communications and health care, while setting aside money for emergencies.

The following table breaks down expenses by category and compares costs across the five cities included in this article. Monterrey has the highest basic utility costs, while León has the lowest overall costs among the cities examined.

How do average wages compare?

Data México reports average monthly earnings in these cities, including both formal and informal employment.

The comparison reveals a gap between average earnings and the estimated budget for a family of four. Even two average incomes combined fall short of the amount needed to cover the projected expenses and save for emergencies. To make up the difference, some families seek additional income by selling products through catalogs or preparing food for sale. Others cut spending on health care, food and recreation.

Insecurity in Mexico

Safety concerns weighing on parents

Eduardo and Ana are married but have not yet decided whether to have children. They live in Metepec and regularly travel to Toluca for work.

“I don’t want children for one simple reason: insecurity,” Eduardo said. “The country gets worse every year, and more people go missing every day. If I’m already worried about the situation, I can’t imagine being responsible for a little person. I would rather avoid that worry.”

Perceptions of insecurity also emerged among respondents’ reasons for not having children. The 2026 National Survey of Victimization and Perceptions of Public Security (ENVIPE) does not measure an individual’s risk of becoming a crime victim, nor does it replace crime-rate data. It does, however, show that 74% of adults considered their state unsafe during the survey period.

The highest proportions were recorded in Estado de Mexico, at 90%; Morelos, at 88.7%; Tabasco, at 87.6%; Guanajuato, at 85.9%; and Puebla, at 83.3%. The lowest were in Coahuila, at 27.8%; Yucatán, at 35.5%; and Aguascalientes, at 41%.

Rising crime and missing persons statistics

The 2026 ENVIPE, which covers crimes committed in 2025, reported the highest estimated crime incidence rates in Mexico City, at 68,154 crimes per 100,000 inhabitants; Puebla, at 41,876; and Mexico State, at 40,915. The survey’s crime categories included theft and robbery, fraud, extortion, threats, assault, kidnapping and sexual offenses.

According to a report by the Mexican Institute for Human Rights and Democracy (IMDHD), Mexico’s national missing persons registry listed 134,257 people as missing as of May 16, 2026. That number rose to 135,048 by June 16. The report recorded 12,632 disappearances in 2024 and 12,373 in 2025, and indicated that the trend in 2026 pointed toward similarly high numbers.

As of May 16, 2026, the five states with the largest cumulative numbers of registered missing persons were Mexico State, with 14,648; Tamaulipas, with 13,787; Jalisco, with 12,765; Michoacán, with 7,782; and Nuevo León, with 7,476. Together, they accounted for 42% of the national total, according to Red Lupa’s analysis of the National Registry of Missing and Unlocated Persons (RNPDNO).

Mexico recorded 11,586 victims of intentional homicide from January through August 2026, according to figures reported by the federal Security Cabinet and the Executive Secretariat of the National Public Security System. Although President Claudia Sheinbaum highlighted a decline in homicides earlier in the year, safety concerns remain part of many Mexicans’ daily lives.

Motherhood as a choice

The evolution of women’s roles

Women have always worked and played an important role in society. The Industrial Revolution, which began in the mid-18th century, expanded their participation in factory work and paid employment. During World War I and World War II, their roles in industry became even more prominent as many filled jobs left by men who had gone to fight.

Over time, advances in labor rights, greater access to higher education and the availability of contraception expanded women’s opportunities and their ability to make decisions about their lives, including whether to become mothers, when to have children and how many to have.

Motherhood is now a choice, not an obligation. Women may pursue a career, raise a family or do both. For some of the mothers interviewed, returning to work was both a financial necessity and a professional choice.

Personal perspectives on motherhood and career breaks

Zayra, 32, lives in Monterrey with her husband and their two children.

“At first, I only wanted one child so I could give them the attention and care they needed for their development. But six months later, I became pregnant again,” she said. “It was a shock because I didn’t know how I would manage twice the expenses. I had my second child, but I decided to undergo sterilization so I wouldn’t have any more.

“I made that decision because I struggled badly with hormonal changes during both pregnancies, and there were concerns about preeclampsia. Having children is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you, but it’s also a lot of work and very tiring. Finances also play a role in deciding not to have another child.”

Kiev, 32, is from Querétaro, married, and has two daughters.

“Yes, I’ve thought about having one more, but I’ve practically ruled it out, mainly for financial reasons. Babies are very expensive,” she said. “On top of that, my house only has two bedrooms, and we would need to expand it sooner to live more comfortably.

“Then there’s the career break I’m taking. I wanted to look after the house and the babies myself, with the intention of returning to work once they’re a little older. Having another baby would add more years to that break.”

Rejecting social scripts and facing future challenges

Marcela, 34, lives in Querétaro with her partner and has decided not to have children.

“I don’t like children. I’ve never known how to interact with them or spend time with them, so having one seems strange to me, and I find it difficult to play with them. I don’t have a maternal instinct,” she said.

“I also don’t want to feel obligated to follow a social script of getting married and having children. I firmly believe children should be fully wanted and planned for, not something you have ‘just because’ or because it’s the next step.

“The third reason is the situation in Mexico and the world in general. The thought that having a child would mean never feeling at ease again because of the country we live in and its insecurity — especially if the child were a girl — is a major factor.

Wages, security and the environment

“There’s also the economic situation. Wages make things difficult, and building financial security keeps getting harder. Add the environmental situation, the wars happening now and tensions with the United States, and I can’t picture a bright future for a child.”

Declining fertility poses long-term challenges for Mexico. An aging population will require more health care, caregiving services and sustainable social protection systems. But the answer is not to pressure people into having more children. For those who want to start a family, the challenge is to create conditions that make raising children compatible with stable earnings, affordable housing, childcare, safety, reproductive health care and a more equitable division of caregiving responsibilities.

The interviews in this report do not represent Mexico’s entire population, but they reveal a shared tension. For many people, the question is no longer simply whether they want children, but whether they can have them without sacrificing their stability, health, careers or peace of mind.

María Ruiz is the Director of Digital Marketing at Mexico News Daily. She enjoys photographing her hometown of San Miguel de Allende in her spare time.

World.title: Spider-Man 2099 has a Día de Muertos secret in his origin story
World.content:
There may not be another superhero who is more globally renowned or imitated than Spider-Man (sorry, Superman and Batman, but you can sit this one out).

In my neighborhood’s main square, there is a man who regularly dresses up as Spider-Man and web-thwips his way into photos for a few pesos. Driving around Mexico, I’ve seen motorcyclists wearing Spider-Man-themed helmets. There’s even an official spinoff Spider-Man character, nicknamed Arácnido Jr., who hails from Mexico City and has a luchador father.

Just learned that Marvel has a Mexican Spider-Man named Arácnido Jr. who is the son of a luchador & protects Mexico City. He appeared in one of the “Spider-Verse” comics & was created by Enrique Puig & Francisco Herrera. He’s been around since 2015. Can’t believe I didn’t know 🇲🇽 https://t.co/h38pTyT9m8 — Carlos Aguilar (@Carlos_Film) August 2, 2020

It’s not just Mexicans who love El Hombre Araña, though. Right now, Spider-Man is at an all-time commercial high.

“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” has been the most commercially successful blockbuster of the year so far. As of writing, the movie has generated more than US $923 million globally, beating out “Toy Story 5” and “The Odyssey” as the highest-grossing film of 2026, to date. In July, the movie’s star cast members even visited Mexico City to promote the film.

A futuristic webslinger with Mexican roots

Add to that a newly reinvigorated generation of Spider-Man fanatics with the children’s animated series “Spidey and His Amazing Friends” — a show that currently ranks as the third-most-watched show for kids between ages 2 and 5 (including my son, who is obsessed), with billions of streaming hours on Disney+.

Across every metric, Peter Parker is a tried-and-true hit.

But what about Marvel Comics’ other Spider-Man? The one who lives in a futuristic 2099 version of New York City (creatively renamed Nueva York) and is of Mexican Irish descent? I’m talking about Miguel O’Hara.

Created by Marvel in 1992 as part of a larger effort to refresh the brand and reconfigure its legendary characters with a larger “Marvel 2099” wave of alternate-universe storylines, O’Hara is a geneticist working for a mega-wealthy corporation, Alchemax. Rather than being bitten by a radioactive spider as the original Parker is, O’Hara is researching the by-then-archaic Spider-Man of former New York City (fourth-wall meta stuff, I know) and attempting to replicate that Spider-Man’s powers for the greedy Alchemax corporation, a private entity that happens to govern the United States through its wealth and militant force.

The unusual origin of the Day of the Dead suit

Like any true superhero origin story, O’Hara is unexpectedly turned into Spider-Man 2099 when a villainous Alchemax colleague throws O’Hara into the mutation machine that is conveniently set to the original Spider-Man’s specifications. O’Hara gets zapped. He transforms. He learns how to wield his powers and manage his personal relationships across hundreds of issues. The usual.

Here’s the unusual part, though: O’Hara — or rather, his alter ego Spider-Man 2099 — is equipped with a Day of the Dead costume rather than a traditional Spider-Man onesie.

Early on, the comics (created by Peter David and Rick Leonardi) establish that not only is O’Hara of Mexican descent, but that he took a trip down to Mexico City for a “The Jetsons”-style Day of the Dead.

There are multiple allusions to it in the opening issues of the series, with a backstory that goes something like this: A pre-superpowers O’Hara returns to his mother’s homeland south of the border (her name is Conchata, and she also appears as a character early on). There, he attends a festive Day of the Dead celebration. In this dystopian future, there is a special fabric referred to as “UMF” — or Unstable Molecule Fabric, as explained in the series — that is both indestructible and highly versatile, something O’Hara deems necessary for the rowdy Día de Muertos crowds and festivities in 2099.

Dystopian fashion and geometric design

I know all of this because I ordered a 1,384-page omnibus of “Spider-Man 2099” and have been reading it for weeks.

“Only thing I own made from UMF is this death’s head costume I brought when I went to Mexico last year for the Day of the Dead festival,” O’Hara says in issue No. 2. In the background, silhouettes of festivalgoers dressed as skeletons and demons wander as he recalls: “Festival can get pretty wild. I wanted something extra sturdy.”

The suit itself is futuristically cool, for lack of a better description, though not overly Day of the Dead-themed. It features a bright red skull-like design at the center of the chest, which extends into stripes that flare down and outward in the opposite direction, wrapping around the shoulder in a shape that loosely resembles a spider’s many legs with a geometrically balanced aesthetic. The base of the suit retains a much deeper shade of blue than the original webslinger.

In all, it retains the essence of Spider-Man’s original garb, with subtle nods to Day of the Dead aesthetics.

Reincarnation and honoring the fallen heroes

O’Hara’s suit and abilities are rounded out with razor-edged retractable talons for climbing surfaces and annihilating his foes, and spikes protruding from his forearms, which seem to be a menacing suit accessory. Though not overtly Mexican or Day of the Dead in its presentation, if you squint, you can sense minor inspirations from Mexico’s Indigenous past and geometric design work.

Simple, but striking. Creative, but balanced.

The Day of the Dead theme does, however, emerge in the storyline — with additional references to Mexico, and even an entire issue titled “Day of the Dead.” In it, O’Hara takes a trip to Mexico City, where he battles zombies who have been mass-reincarnated by Fernando Morgez, a Mexican character who had hoped to revive his late sister, Anita, but brought back more than he anticipated.

Mexico’s Day of the Dead is a series undercurrent

The idea of life and death, reincarnation and honoring the deceased is an undercurrent throughout the entire series. In the 2099 timeline, the Avengers are more myth than reality, with previously indestructible characters like Thor and Peter Parker’s Spider-Man being remembered as deceased gods who are revered and worshiped by cultish hordes of followers.

That is, the world’s heroes of yesterday have fallen, and the living must find ways to cope with that remaining void.

In that sense, the series certainly has touches of Mexico’s Day of the Dead — a remembrance of those who are no longer physically present, but perhaps offer spiritual hope and a connection to, if not preservation of, the past.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Shirley Manson’s Garbage to headline free Zócalo show next month
World.content:
Garbage in the Zócalo! And for free?

No, we’re not talking about a sanitation worker’s revolt or some weird twist to recycling and reusing household waste.

The American rock band Garbage will play a free concert in the Zócalo on Saturday, Nov. 14, the final show of their North America tour which kicked off back in September 2025.

Lead singer Shirley Manson, aka “The Godmother of Rock,” said the show will mark the close of 30 years of traditional, continuous bus-touring for the band, saying long-term heavy touring has become economically and personally unsustainable.

Shortly after the Mexico City mayor’s office jumped the gun (officials shared the announcement through the government’s official X account before deleting the post), Garbage confirmed the gig on Instagram.

“Well. The news got leaked so here we are — a little off balance and rushing to catch up,” the band wrote. “We were going to announce this show tomorrow, but someone has beaten us to it.”

Overcoming the spilled beans, Garbage — which has sold 17 million albums worldwide — declared they were enthusiastic about the invitation.

“We are so immensely proud and deeply honoured to have been invited by the Mexican Government to play in Mexico City on the 14th of November at Mexico City’s most prestigious venue – The Zócalo,” the band said.

Manson also heaped praise on the band’s Mexican fans for supporting the group since their first visit in 1996. Since then, Garbage has played in Mexico 16 times, including three shows last year (April 4 in Zapopan, Jalisco; April 6 in Monterrey and Nov. 14 in Mexico City).

“We are one of the most fortunate bands in the world to have enjoyed playing in Mexico since we first arrived on the scene but this is the absolute cherry on the top of what has been a passionate and 30 year long love affair,” the Instagram post said.

Formed in 1993 in Madison, Wisconsin, the band’s four-member line-up has remained unchanged: the Scottish lead singer Manson and American musicians Duke Erikson (guitar, bass, keyboards), Steve Marker (guitar, keyboards) and Butch Vig (drums, percussion).

With reports from El Financiero, Consequence, Chilango and Billboard

World.title: Brazil Court Rejects Novo Bid on Artist Acts
World.content:
A results screen at the Electoral Court (TSE) in Brasília shows the first-round count by state on 4 October 2026. (Photo: Agência Senado, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

BRAZIL · ELECTIONS

Published Sunday, 18 October, 9:13 a.m. ET · Source: Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE) ruling, as reported by Jovem Pan and Revista Fórum

Key Facts The country Brazil, Latin America’s largest country, elects its president in a runoff on Sunday 25 October between President Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

What happened On Saturday 17 October, Electoral Court (TSE) minister Ricardo Villas Bôas Cueva rejected a request by the Novo party to suspend pro-democracy concerts with artists planned for Sunday 18 October.

The dispute Novo, a conservative party, argued the events were disguised campaign rallies for Lula, which Brazilian law bans, and targeted Copacabana (Rio de Janeiro), Salvador and Porto Alegre.

The ruling Cueva found no proof at this stage that the events were campaign rallies, and said artists’ political preferences alone are not an electoral offence.

Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

Prediction markets Polymarket gives Flávio Bolsonaro an 80.8% chance and Lula 19.5% of winning the 25 October runoff (18 October, 9:10 a.m. ET). Polymarket puts Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning at 81% and Kalshi at 80% (Lula: 20% and 22% ), as of 18 October, 9:00 am ET ; prices are bets, not polls.

Still open The court kept the power to punish concrete violations, so the events themselves can still be reviewed.

Brazil’s electoral court has rejected a request by the Novo party to stop pro-democracy concerts with artists on Sunday 18 October, a week before the Brazil election 2026. The ruling by minister Ricardo Villas Bôas Cueva came on Saturday 17 October, according to Jovem Pan.

Novo had claimed the shows in Copacabana, Salvador and Porto Alegre were disguised campaign rallies for President Lula, which matters because court fights over campaign rules can shape the final days of the race and, with it, Brazilian markets. The Brazil election odds on Polymarket still favour Flávio Bolsonaro, the conservative senator for Rio de Janeiro.

What the Electoral Court Decided

Cueva, a minister of the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), denied Novo’s injunction request, the party’s plea for an immediate order, Jovem Pan reported.

The minister said the public political preference of artists is not, by itself, an electoral offence, Jovem Pan reported. He added that ideological closeness between organisers and a candidate does not prove a legal, financial or organisational link.
