World.title: Integrity advocates support State funding for CAFFE, but with guardrails
World.content:
MUNROE... it is essential for Jamaica’s taxpayers to provide a budgetary allocation to help sustain CAFFE, possibly through a line item in the budget for the Electoral Commission of Jamaica

SOME governance integrity advocates believe that the Jamaican Government could provide a financial lifeline for Citizens Action for Free and Fair Elections (CAFFE), but offered differing positions on how State subvention should be administered.

As the electoral watchdog group continues to seek private sector assistance amid financial challenges following the withdrawal of US funding, Dr Trevor Munroe, founding director of National Integrity Action and former vice-chair of CAFFE, argued that Government funding could be a crucial source of support to its survival.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer last Monday, Munroe noted that CAFFE plays an integral role in safeguarding the integrity of Jamaica’s polls, and warned that inadequate funding could undermine the country’s democratic process.

“The recent narrowing of the funding base of CAFFE potentially weakens our citizens’ critical role in maintaining the electoral foundation of Jamaica’s democracy. It also undermines the important role that the organisation can and is seeking to play in building public awareness on the importance of voting as well as in the exercise of our other democratic rights,” he said.

CAFFE, established in 1997, has monitored seven general elections, seven local government polls, and several by-elections and re-run elections. Since 2025, however, the watchdog group has faced severe financial challenges following the Donald Trump Administration’s withdrawal of United States Agency for International Development (USAID) funding from non-governmental organisations globally.

The frozen funding has heightened concerns about CAFFE’s capacity to monitor future elections.

“In these circumstances it is essential for Jamaica’s taxpayers to provide a budgetary allocation to help sustain CAFFE, possibly through a line item in the budget for the Electoral Commission of Jamaica (ECJ),” Munroe reasoned.

While acknowledging that ethical concerns could arise from the executive arm of government interfering in the operations of neutral bodies, Munroe argued that CAFFE’s integrity depends on its ability to maintain impartiality towards political affiliations.

“For example, alertness to ethical concerns is always demanded when neutral regulatory bodies, like the NEPA [National Environment and Planning Agency] and the judiciary — the latter an independent co-equal branch of the Jamaican State — are financed by the Jamaican taxpayer through the Government budget,” he pointed out.

“If and when Government oversteps its bounds, it is an alert citizenry and robust neutral bodies’ resistance that deters and blocks interference, thereby putting Government back in its proper place,” said Munroe.

He added that he does not anticipate CAFFE facing such complications, noting that its funding from USAID had been channelled through the executive branch of the US Government without influencing the organisation’s performance.

“It was up to CAFFE and USAID to ensure that the conditions of, and the actual dispensation of funds did not violate CAFFE’s independence nor neutrality in the exercise of its responsibilities. So it must [also] be with funding provided by other international partners [eg the European Union] or by the Jamaican Government,” he argued.

“In this latter case the funding would come through the ECJ budget, and CAFFE would have to ensure that its utilisation would be consistent with independent election monitoring — excluding political considerations and being mindful of ethical concerns,” Munroe said.

Meanwhile Jeanette Calder, executive director and founder of the Jamaica Accountability Meter Portal, argued that while Government subvention to neutral agencies is not a foreign concept, it must be instituted at no risk to CAFFE’s autonomy.

Calder argued that if Government funding is considered, then it should not be the observatory group’s main or only source of financing.

“CAFFE serves an important, independent monitoring role of the State’s elections processes. State funding can assist but [should] not be [the] sole or primary source, in order to protect and preserve independence. State funding would best be for CAFFE’s discretionary use where it determines best,” she said.

Attorney and former politician Ronald Thwaites shared similar sentiments, stating that it is “perfectly reasonable” for the Government to subsidise CAFFE’s monitoring and surveillance operations.

Expanding on his position, Thwaites told the Sunday Observer that it was embarrassing for CAFFE to have relied on international funding rather than support of the Government and private sector.

“I would also want to hope that Government’s interests would not be singular, and that the private sector and all of us, in different ways, would want to support CAFFE.

“I’ve been a little embarrassed that we were depending on foreign sources to help us to keep our elections clean and fair, so the moment has come now where we have to take care of our own interests. And that should be a combination of Jamaican donations — no doubt including people from the Diaspora and also, very appropriately, a subvention from Government,” he argued.

Addressing concerns that State funding could compromise a neutral body, Thwaites said other independent public interest organisations receive Government support while remaining autonomous, provided that proper accountability safeguards are maintained.

“The Integrity Commission does that. Various other bodies that are for the public good but are not connected with any State agency also receive those monies. The question of the ethical considerations would only apply in terms of the use of the private sector, and it is not beyond us to ensure that we give proper accounting,” he said.

World.title: Larry McDonald’s journey
World.content:
Larry McDonald

FOR nearly seven decades, the heartbeat of Jamaican music has echoed through the hands of one extraordinary musician: Lawrence “Larry” McDonald.

A master percussionist, cultural ambassador, and living legend, McDonald has devoted his life to preserving, celebrating, and sharing the rich rhythmic traditions of Jamaica with the world.

On Monday, October 19, 2026 his remarkable journey will receive national recognition as he is awarded the Badge of Honour for Meritorious Service in the field of Entertainment, acknowledging his tremendous contribution to Jamaica’s musical heritage and cultural identity.

For McDonald, whose hands have helped shape the sound of ska, rocksteady, reggae, jazz, and countless other musical traditions, the honour represents more than personal achievement. It is a celebration of Jamaican culture, its ancestral rhythms, and the generations of musicians who have carried those traditions across the globe.

Born on June 11, 1937, in Port Maria, St Mary, McDonald’s musical journey began long before he stepped onto an international stage.

Growing up immersed in Jamaica’s vibrant cultural traditions, he was deeply influenced by the powerful African-derived rhythms of Kumina, Burru, and Jonkannu. These traditions, rooted in the island’s history and ancestral heritage, became the foundation of his musical identity.

As Jamaican popular music evolved through the 1950s and 1960s, McDonald emerged as one of the percussionists helping to define its distinctive rhythmic character.

Working alongside pioneering musicians such as Carlos Malcolm, Count Ossie, and Toots and the Maytals, he brought the expressive power of traditional hand drumming into the developing sounds of ska, rocksteady, and reggae.

At a time when the drum kit, bass, and guitar were becoming central to Jamaican popular music, McDonald helped establish the conga as an equally compelling musical voice. His playing added depth, texture, and a connection to Jamaica’s African heritage.

After relocating to the United States in 1973, he became an influential presence in an international musical community, collaborating with some of the most celebrated names in reggae, jazz, blues, soul, and spoken-word performance.

His remarkable list of collaborators includes Bob Marley and the Wailers, Peter Tosh, Bunny Wailer, Lee “Scratch” Perry, Taj Mahal, The Skatalites, and the groundbreaking poet and musician Gil Scott-Heron.

His association with Scott-Heron, spanning nearly three decades, was particularly significant. Together, they helped create music that combined rhythm, poetry, social consciousness, and powerful cultural commentary.

Whether performing before thousands or contributing the subtle rhythmic details that elevate a recording, McDonald has always approached percussion as something greater than accompaniment.

In 2009, after decades of lending his extraordinary talents to the music of others, McDonald released his first album as a leader, Drumquestra.

The album was both a musical achievement and a cultural statement.

Bringing together an exceptional gathering of Jamaican musicians and vocalists, including Sly Dunbar, Toots Hibbert, Mutabaruka, Bob Andy, Bongo Herman, and members of the Mystic Revelation of Rastafari, Drumquestra placed percussion at the centre of the musical conversation.

Rather than treating the drum as a supporting instrument, McDonald presented it as the foundation of an entire orchestra of rhythm.

The project celebrated Jamaica’s African musical inheritance while demonstrating the extraordinary possibilities of traditional percussion in contemporary music.

At 89 years old, he continues to embody the spirit of creativity, resilience, and cultural pride that has defined his life’s work.

Far from slowing down, McDonald remains an active and dynamic presence on the international music scene, continuing to tour and perform with The Skatalites, David Hillard and the rocksteady 7, The NYC Ska Orchestra and Subatomic Sound System.

Whether introducing new generations to the infectious rhythms of ska and reggae, or sharing the stage with musicians decades younger than himself, McDonald continues to demonstrate that great music knows no age limits.

In January 2026 he was selected to deliver the keynote address at the University of California, Santa Cruz’s 42nd annual Martin Luther King Jr Convocation, a recognition of his extraordinary artistic journey and his enduring connection to music, history, and social consciousness.

Although his name may not always have appeared in the brightest lights, his rhythms have been heard alongside some of the most important voices in modern music.

He belongs to that exceptional generation of Jamaican musicians whose artistry helped transform a small Caribbean island into one of the world’s most influential musical nations.

World.title: New private high school in St James working to create global citizens
World.content:
Founder and Director Natalie Morris speaks with students (from second left) Marissa Hylton, Natoya Williams and Zavoya Forbes at the recently opened Integrated School of the Arts Jamaica.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Founder and director of Integrated School for the Arts Jamaica (ISAJ) — the newest educational institution in the western end of the island — Natalie Morris says the plan is for the school to develop global- ready students.

Just weeks after the private high school opened its doors for the 2026/2027 academic year, Morris told the Jamaica Observer in an interview that it is already making progress towards that goal.

“Global citizens, that’s our motto. It means regardless of your ability, we want you to — even if you’re living locally — you should be thinking global…As we are living in a world where artificial intelligence is shaping the way we do business and the way we learn, I want our students to be thinking in that realm,” said Morris.

She said the varied nature of the student population is already helping to bring that vision to life.

“We have a diverse school even though it’s so small. We have Spanish speakers, we have Mandarin speakers, we have English speakers,” explained Morris, who pointed out that the school has already started establishing international connections — including one expected to provide students with opportunities to travel overseas.

“Just right now, we were identified by Marnix College in Curaçao…they are coming… to Jamaica next year to partner with us as a language exchange programme.

“We want to get the students to be thinking that we are not just in a local space, we are in a global space, and that’s how we have been pushing the school,” Morris told the Sunday Observer.

Located at the Blue Diamond Shopping Mall in Ironshore, on the outskirts of Montego Bay, ISAJ currently has 45 students enrolled in grades seven to 10.

The grade 10 cohort will progress to grade 11, in which students will be guided in preparing for the Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) examinations.

Morris shed some light on the school’s origin.

“I was a consultant to Naz Children’s Centre where I actually assisted them to implement a high school programme,” she explained.

Naz Children’s Centre offers tailored learning programmes for children who may have special educational needs.

“Naz, as most persons would know, it would be from preschool to elementary, and I implemented a high school programme there in 2018,” Morris explained.

“Fast-forward to 2026, on February 28 this year, the owner of Naz Children’s Centre called me and said… the programme is doing well there, but she really wants to refocus and go back to core —and that is how she said, ‘I am giving you back your baby,’ “ she recounted.

Taking a leap of faith, Morris said she stepped down from her corporate job at Harbour City Mall in Montego Bay to establish the school. Nearly 30 students from Naz Children’s Centre were transferred to her care to continue their secondary education.

Morris said she felt prepared to take on the challenge, given her background in teaching.

“My journey started about 20-something years ago in the classroom as a primary school teacher. I have taught in Jamaica and in The Bahamas,” she said.

Despite her experience, she admitted that she was uncertain about how things would unfold, particularly as she had to find suitable premises to accommodate the school.

“I am saying it’s nothing short of a miracle, because I’ll tell you this, when I got that call, I didn’t have a building. I didn’t have any idea how anything was going to work, and this moment has been a faith walk for me.

“I remember the day when we were looking for a venue and we’re looking at another venue, and it was not approved by the Ministry [of Education], and the same day I called the owner of Blue Diamond and he said, ‘You know, ironically, one of our tenants is moving,’ “ she told the Sunday Observer.

The tenant was Nexus Tours, a tourism-based company that was relocating its operations to the grounds of Sangster International Airport.

“I can say that Nexus Tours was here and they were our first funding partner. Nexus contributed a large percentage of our furniture. They started us with everything, most of the things that you’re seeing here are from Nexus Tours,” said Morris.

“All of what you are seeing in form, is like God placed all of this and so we were able to organise to start school in six months. We met the students on June 1, and from June to September we were able to transition and to start school with 44 children here,” she stated.

Despite the progress, Morris said the school’s long-term goal is to secure premises of its own, although she remains grateful for what has been achieved so far.

She explained that the small class sizes were intentional, allowing teachers to provide greater support to students, particularly those who require additional assistance.

“Our class right now is standard 10 to 15 [students], but our largest class right now is 12, and we are able to do a more personalised learning or differentiation learning experience and that is part of the unique nature of this,” said Morris.

She pointed out that although ISAJ has a focus on the arts, its curriculum extends beyond that field.

“We do try to use a STEAM [science, technology, engineering, the arts, and mathemat-ics] based approach. So, in the mornings, mostly, we do all the academic stuff, but in the afternoon we do arts-based subjects. We have drumming as a part of the curriculum, we have robotics, we have all of those things,” said Morris.

World.title: BEYOND THE LENS
World.content:
In this file photo Samantha Hall competes in the women’s discus throw Group B qualification during the World Athletics Championships in Tokyo . (Photo: AFP)

WHEN Dominica’s Olympic champion Thea LaFond and Trinidadian journalist Dennis Allen first discussed the new European broadcast guidelines, they pointed out a tricky puzzle: While tight, suggestive camera angles objectify female athletes, those same viral moments often help competitors build a following and secure paying sponsor deals.

Published by the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) and European Athletics, the Raising the Bar guidelines instruct camera operators to avoid extremely low-angle shots from behind, limit unnecessary slow-motion replays during athlete preparations, and use wider shots that focus on technical execution over physical body parts.

For the women inside and around the sport every day, this debate goes much deeper than camera angles. It touches on what they describe as a frustrating double standard — a female athlete’s financial survival often depends on her looks, even when her hard work and talent should be doing all the talking.

Reigning Commonwealth Games champion and national discus thrower Samantha Hall knows this struggle first-hand. She sees a clear gap in how male and female athletes are treated.

“I understand both sides of the argument,” Hall told the Sunday Observer. “As athletes we do like to see ourselves — especially for field events, we can see where we went wrong with our technique based on pictures — but at the same time, we don’t want to be seen as sexual figures. I hate that for women, this is how we have to earn money — that we have to look sexy, and not for our talents. For men, they don’t really have to do much; it’s just about their talents. They’re getting paid for their talents but for women, it’s not enough. You have to have that image with it.”

Hall’s words point to a wider issue in sports. While male athletes build their careers purely on distances, times and medals, women are expected to win medals and meet a specific standard of beauty.

Long before the cameras zoom in on the field, female track stars face non-stop public criticism over their appearance—from make-up and hair to body art. Criticism male athletes rarely hear.

“I’ve seen it for other athletes, especially like Elaine Thompson-Herah and Ashanti Moore, because they have tattoos in various places on their bodies,” Hall said. “I’ve seen comments like, ‘Why do they have these tattoos? It’s the reason why they can’t perform well.’ And I’m like, ‘That has nothing to do with their performances.’ But yeah, you always have people criticising females based on how they look — like their make-up is off, ‘Her hairstyle doesn’t look neat on her’, ‘Her outfit doesn’t fit her’. They’re always judging female athletes based on their looks.”

Even off the screen, off-hand comments can be intrusive. Hall shared that people sometimes approach her to talk about her physique rather than her throws.

Yet Hall handles this pressure with incredible grace. Rather than letting outside noise get to her, she chooses to own her style and feel confident on her own terms. “It does affect me, but not in a negative way,” she said. “I want to impress my fans, so if this is what the fans want then I have to dress to impress them. At the end of the day, it’s all about fashion; they like your sense of style. For Shelly-Ann [Fraser-Pryce], it’s all about her wigs; they like her style of wigs. For me, if they talk about my bottom it doesn’t really affect me in any way. I don’t feel bad about it. I try to dress appropriately, but at the same time I want to feel sexy as well.”

Hall says other broadcasters around the world will eventually adopt Europe’s cleaner camera rules by 2028, to keep athletes respected and comfortable. But media experts say changing camera angles won’t fix deep-rooted cultural habits overnight.

Melena Helias, a Kingston based French sports journalist who has covered track and field for both local Jamaican outlets and France’s premier sports newspaper L’Équipe, welcomes the new European guidelines as a solid first step.

“My first reaction was quite positive,” Helias told the Observer. “That said, it’s a shame that it has come to the point where a guide on this is needed but I commend EBU Sport for their work. It won’t solve the problem of the sexualisation of sportswomen, or of inequality and stereotypes in sport, but it’s a good start.”

Helias reminds us that women have had to fight for basic space in sports history. Because track and field doesn’t offer massive multimillion-dollar contracts like football or basketball, athletes often have to rely on their public image to survive financially.

“A male athlete attracts sponsors thanks to his results and his personality, among other things,” Helias said. “A female athlete, on top of her results, needs to be perceived as beautiful. That’s precisely the paradox: There isn’t that much money in athletics compared to other sports so you have to capitalise on what sells. And I certainly don’t blame female athletes who use their assets or their beauty on social media to attract sponsors; it’s actually quite logical. I’d just like appearance to be a less omnipresent criterion in the way women are perceived.”

Speaking up against objectification isn’t always easy, either. Even inside the press box Helias admits that as a woman in a heavily male-dominated career, finding the courage to call out inappropriate remarks can be a challenge.

“Unfortunately, no,” Helias said when asked if she feels she has a safe platform to speak out. “I’d even say that I’ve heard, more than once, remarks that outraged me — comments about female athletes — but I didn’t dare say anything. It’s not always easy to find your place in sports journalism; we’re still very much a minority. It’s one thing to have confidence in your abilities and knowledge but it’s another to assert yourself, stand up for yourself, and express your opinions. I’m hopeful that all of this will improve, but it won’t happen overnight.”

When asked if Caribbean broadcasters will follow their European peers, Helias says protecting young athletes — especially minors competing in high school meets — should be a top priority. Ultimately, she believes that while better camera rules help, the real change has to happen inside the minds of the people watching.

“We can change the guidelines but social norms, mentalities, what is or isn’t acceptable, that’s another matter.”

World.title: Manchester dad charged in suspected revenge killing of two men over daughter’s murder
World.content:
File photo of the crime scene in Land Settlement, Manchester where two men were gunned down in March 2026.

MANCHESTER, Jamaica – A Manchester father has been charged with conspiracy to murder in relation to the killing of two men in the parish in March that is believed to have been a reprisal for the shooting death of his daughter a month earlier.

Charged is 37-year-old Kumar Obrien, otherwise known as ‘Frazzle’, of Melrose Drive, Land Settlement.

The deceased have been identified as 29-year-old farmer Yakieni Shaw, also known as ‘Yankee’, of Comfort District, Manchester, and 21-year-old Damien Edwards, otherwise known as ‘Damie’, of Melrose Gardens, Williamsfield, in the parish.

Reports from the Mandeville Police are that Obrien allegedly conspired with other men to kill Edwards and Shaw, who were gunned down about 3:50 pm on Saturday, March 14, 2026.

The shooting is believed to have been a reprisal for the fatal shooting of Obrien’s four-year-old daughter, Saniyah Obrien, on Sunday, February 8, while they were seated in his Voxy motor car in the parish.

An investigations led to Obrien being apprehended, interviewed, and subsequently charged. He is scheduled to appear before the Manchester Parish Court on Wednesday, October 21.

World.title: Adam Stewart, Sheryl Lee Ralph honoured at AFJ Hummingbird Gala
World.content:
Sandals Resorts Executive Chairman Adam Stewart and Emmy Award-winning actress Sheryl Lee Ralph pose with their awards after being honoured at the American Friends of Jamaica (AFJ) Hummingbird Gala at The Plaza in New York on Friday, October 16, 2026.

Sandals Resorts Executive Chairman Adam Stewart and Emmy Award-winning actress Sheryl Lee Ralph were honoured at the American Friends of Jamaica (AFJ) Hummingbird Gala, held at The Plaza in New York on Friday,

Stewart received the International Achievement Award in recognition of his contribution to Caribbean tourism, business and philanthropy, while Ralph received the International Humanitarian Award for her achievements in entertainment and longstanding advocacy, particularly in HIV/AIDS awareness.

Prime Minister Andrew Holness and Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett were among the guests at the annual fundraising gala, which brought together business leaders, philanthropists and members of the Jamaican diaspora in support of AFJ’s work across Jamaica, including ongoing Hurricane Melissa recovery efforts.

World.title: DIRTY COWARDS
World.content:
Police personnel at the scene where one of their colleagues was fatally shot and another left with lifethreatening injuries in the Five Miles area of St Catherine on Friday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

THE police have identified one of three men killed in a firefight in the Five Miles area off the Sligoville main road in St Catherine, Friday morning, during which gunmen used a child to draw cops closer before opening fire, killing one law enforcer.

He is Malique Hussey, otherwise called Mal Boss, from Spanish Town, St Catherine, with connections in Five Miles.

According to the police, Hussey was a known associate of a high-risk target identified as Kenroy Willis, who operates out of the St Andrew North Police Division and is wanted for four murders.

Up to news time the police had not determined the identities of the other two men who were fatally shot in the gun battle which also resulted in the death of Corporal Trevoy Shaw, who was assigned to the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s (JCF) Special Operations Unit, and the injury to a constable who, up to press time, was in hospital in critical condition.

A third cop suffered minor injuries, not gunshot-related, during the incident.

A 10-year-old child was also shot in what Jamaica Observer sources say was a deliberate attack by Hussey, who was her father.

According to the police, about 5:15 Friday morning members of its Special Operations Unit went in search of Willis, Hussey, and their cronies.

On arrival, the police were met with gunfire by men who had barricaded themselves in a house with a woman and three children, including a monthsold baby.

During the stand-off the men indicated that they wanted to surrender, and used one of the children to signal their willingness to lay down their illegal firearms.

“I can confirm that a child was held out the door, and it was declared that they were willing to surrender, and when the police approached, seeking to retrieve the child, fire was opened upon those policemen,” senior communications strategist at the Jamaica Constabulary Force Dennis Brooks told journalists metres from the shooting scene.

“The gunmen shot from behind the child, which placed the police in a precarious position, even in accessing the building, because of the presence of children,” Brooks said.

He explained that they were met by heavily armed men, and a woman declared from inside the building that she and two children were inside.

The woman, the injured 10-year-old, and the baby were allowed to leave the building by the gunmen, who kept a child inside the house as they continued to fire at the cops who were supported by members of the Jamaica Defence Force.

According to Brooks, the men manipulated the presence of the children in the house and the police’s willingness to accept their surrender, pretending to wave the ‘white flag’ multiple times.

“It is the intention of the police on every operation to bring persons to justice, place them before the court, and so it is not our intention to proceed marauding into a building — whether or not there are children and women in there.

And if there is an indication, even the slightest indication, that they are willing to surrender then we are going to engage that possibility,” Brooks said.

He lamented the death of the corporal who was trying to retrieve the child, describing it as heartbreaking.

“I left several policemen and women in tears in Kingston because they knew him well… He was promoted to the rank of corporal about a month ago, which speaks to his own dedication and the recognition of his work.

“I mean, imagine at this time he is just enjoying this new development in his career, and he is [the] pride of his family in this moment, and for his life, his light to be put out in such a manner in seeking to make this country a safer place — it is heartbreaking,” Brooks said.

The pain of Shaw’s colleagues was palpable at Spanish Town Hospital as news spread that two of their colleagues had been rushed there with gunshot wounds.

It became worse when it was confirmed that he had died while the constable had been rushed into surgery.

Shortly after 10:00 am a policeman was seen leaving the hospital’s Accident and Emergency Department (A&E), with sources indicating that he was the person who had suffered the non-gunshot-related injury.

The cop appeared to be in some discomfort as he limped towards a police vehicle parked on the grounds of the hospital.

The vehicle was quickly surrounded by other cops.

Shortly after 11:00 am, people who appeared to be related to the shot cops stormed onto the facility, with cries of grief, as they sought to enter the A&E Department seeking answers.

About five minutes later a black police vehicle raced onto the compound, with cops carrying what appeared to be the bodies of the three slain criminals.

For a minute chaos unfolded as several people hurried to the van to observe what was happening.

But this curiosity was stopped in its tracks by police personnel, who chased away civilians trying to capture videos or photos.

In his immediate reaction to the attack on the men and women under his command, Police Commissioner Dr Kevin Blake, who visited the scene, described the gunmen as murderous.

He said while death is always a possibility for a cop, “We prepare, we equip, so that every single member after an operation goes home to his or her family safe and injury-free.

Unfortunately this morning, that hope and that preparation was shattered.” Blake told the police on the scene that the best way to honour their fallen comrade would be to remain relentless.

“Because we are who we are, because we would rather take them in to face the court, we lost a member… let not that define how we operate going forward,” said Blake.

“I know it is a tough time, and for the colleagues of the officer killed and the officer injured, I understand,” added Blake.

The attack on the police was condemned by political representatives during Friday’s sitting of the Senate, human rights group Jamaicans For Justice, and several other organisations

World.title: France says Israel must ‘stop these acts of terror’ following attack on EU diplomats
World.content:
The incident took place in Taybeh, a mainly Christian town north of Jerusalem, where diplomats and other officials from France, Poland and Belgium were watching local people harvest olives. Video footage of the attack showed settlers confronting a convoy of diplomats and a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a car.

“The mayor of the commune of Aulnoye-Aymeries was violently assaulted by extremist settlers in the West Bank,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on X, adding that that Israel “must urgently put an end to these criminal acts.”

Belgian Foreign Minister Maxim Prévot said that in addition to the assault on the French mayor, a Belgian vehicle was damaged in the incident. He added that “Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice,” and said Belgium “will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them.”

On Sunday morning, an EU spokesperson said that the bloc “strongly condemns” the attacks by violent settlers in the West Bank, “including on European diplomats.”

The spokesperson added: “We take positive note of statements by several Israeli representatives who condemned the attacks but we expect full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians, including during the ongoing olive harvest season, as well as against journalists.”

Writing on X, the Israel Defense Forces strongly condemned “the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters.”

The IDF added that “according to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack”.

However, the office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu urged caution “before drawing conclusions” from reports of the attack, while noting that “any violence against diplomats is unacceptable.”

World.title: Ukraine strikes oil facility in St. Petersburg as part of ‘massive’ drone attack
World.content:
Smoke rises above the city following an air attack on the oil terminal in Saint Petersburg on October 18, 2026, amid the ongoing Russian-Ukrainian conflict. | AFP via Getty Images

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last week he had ordered the resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries following a three-day pause.

Ukraine struck an oil terminal in St. Petersburg Sunday morning in what Russian state media called “one of the biggest drone attacks of the year.”

Alexander Beglov, governor of St. Petersburg, said on Telegram Sunday that the city underwent a “massive” overnight attack from Ukrainian drones. “The Ministry of Emergency Situations continues to extinguish fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses in the Kolpino district,” he said, adding that one person died and several others were injured in the incident.

The drone strikes come as Kyiv and Moscow ramp up attacks on each other’s infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last week he had ordered the resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries following a three-day pause after U.S. President Donald Trump declared he had brokered an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia.

World.title: Starlink restrictions in Ukraine a ‘planned operation’, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
The restrictions have revived questions on Ukraine’s reliance on the satellite system operated by a U.S. company amid escalating tensions between Kyiv and the White House. “This will cost many of us our lives,” an experienced Ukrainian officer told POLITICO and the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network earlier this week.

“We’re reaching out to everyone at the military level, at the Ministry of Defense level, and at the diplomatic level, including to SpaceX. Right now, no one is responding to our military or the Ministry of Defense,” Zelenskyy told reporters.

The European Union is under increasing pressure to provide Ukraine with an alternative to Starlink. But negotiations between Brussels and Kyiv over access to the bloc’s Govsatcom program — which gives participating governments secure communications capabilities— have been stalling. And IRIS², the EU’s in-house planned network to match Starlink, is only expected to come online in 2030.

“The Europeans are now raising the question of alternatives themselves. And they’re already working on them. They’re already making progress, and they’ll succeed in this area. I can already see that,” Zelenskyy said.

SpaceX did not immediately responded to a request for comment.

Earlier on Saturday, Zelenskyy accused Russia of looking to create a blackout across Ukraine, amid attacks on energy infrastructure and the waiver of U.S. sanctions on Moscow.

World.title: Police, demonstrators clash on sidelines of mass French protests
World.content:
“A very large majority of people are protesting without violence,” Paris’s police prefecture said on Saturday afternoon.

Around 4,500 secondary school pupils and university students involved in the Yellow Vests movement demonstrated side by side against the cost of living in Pau, south-west of France on 17 October 2026. | Jean-Christophe Chartre/AFP via Getty Images

Saturday’s demonstrations grew out of the student protests that began last month with school blockades and calls for better study conditions, more teachers and more funding. The movement has since spread nationwide — and become a political issue as the campaign for next year’s presidential election heats up.

In recent weeks, the government has struggled to deal with the crisis — which Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu described as “urban violence” — and is hoping the student movement will now fade because of a two-week school holiday that started Friday evening.

“The mobilization is marked by a very strong involvement of the ultra-left movement, which is only looking to cause disorder,” Nuñez’s office said Saturday, adding that the minister reiterated his “instructions of utmost firmness” to local prefects and police forces.

Footage showed Lyon’s tourist board office engulfed in flames on the city’s Place Bellecour. A police station was vandalized in Marseille, where a group of “rioters” also entered city hall, Mayor Benoît Payan said. He told BFMTV that “damage was objectively fairly limited,” although the act of vandalism was “unacceptable.” The headquarters of right-wing TV channel CNews in Paris was also targeted , authorities said.

World.title: Spain’s far left fails to unite ahead of November vote
World.content:
The Broad Front is made up of Sumar, the current junior partner in the Socialist-led government, the Catalan Comuns, the Communist-led United Left and Más Madrid. Some smaller local parties have also joined the ticket. The lead candidate for prime minister will be Ada Colau, the former mayor of Barcelona.

Sumar, the dominant force in the alliance, has seen its vote share more than halve since 2023, to 5%, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls.

Although Podemos has only been polling at 3%, its full involvement in the Broad Front would have meant a greater overall share of seats for the far left, according to analysts.

The PSOE has been trailing the conservative People’s Party and would need a strong performance by parties to its left in order to keep Sánchez in office. The more likely scenario, polls show, is that the PP will be able to form a majority with the far-right Vox, whose support has been rising.

“The Spanish left is caught up in a game of thrones that demobilizes [voters],” said Irene de Miguel, coordinator of Podemos in the western region of Extremadura, as the deadline loomed.

World.title: EU leaders clash over migration, Ukraine and budget in Brussels — but delay big decisions
World.content:
Speaking to journalists during a packed news conference, Ukraine’s wartime leader urged his European counterparts to come up with a financial plan or risk facing an unprecedented migration crisis with “20 million Ukrainians” fleeing to Europe.

“The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion more from you — for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience,” Zelenskyy said. “This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back.”

But two diplomats told POLITICO that capitals would continue exploring a range of options to meet Kyiv’s needs, including a potential further loan from the EU.

Luc Frieden and Emmanuel Macron speak ahead of a round table during the EU summit in Brussels on Oct. 15, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images

A debate over whether to mobilize some €300 billion in Russian frozen assets to help Ukraine is a case in point. Nearly a year after EU leaders rejected using the assets amid objections from Belgium, France and Italy, several countries have asked for the option to be revisited, and top EU diplomat Kaja Kallas had said frozen assets would be on the table when leaders met in Brussels.

But after hours of talks about Ukraine, “nothing has changed,” said Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. “The money is not lost but in my belief nothing has happened since we had the discussion last time.”

“In the short term, money to support Ukraine must come from other sources than the frozen assets,” he concluded.

World.title: EU faces growing pressure to plug Ukraine’s Starlink gap
World.content:
"It is unacceptable for Ukraine’s defense — and therefore Europe’s security — to depend on the goodwill of a single American billionaire or on Donald Trump’s decisions," French centrist Member of the European Parliament Christophe Grudler told POLITICO.

Ahead of Thursday's high-level meeting, European lawmakers had been calling on the EU executive to fast-track Kyiv's access to satellite capabilities already pooled under the bloc’s Govsatcom program — which gives participating governments secure communications capabilities.

Negotiations between the EU executive and Ukraine over this access have been ongoing since March, with no breakthrough. Norway and Iceland secured such an agreement earlier this year.

"What I don’t understand is why the European Commission and the Member States have not done everything possible to quickly reach an agreement that would allow Ukraine to benefit from it," added Christophe Grudler, who wrote to EU leaders.

He also called on them to speed up work on IRIS² — the EU’s in-house, planned satellite network and full-fledged match to Starlink, which is only expected to come online in 2030.

Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed in a statement that it is "currently in talks with Ukraine to fully associate" the country with the EU's Govsatcom program. "The war in Ukraine shows that our security also depends on space. And the EU has been doing quite a lot. We are ready to support Ukraine where we can support Ukraine," he added.

World.title: 21 things we learned at the EU leaders’ summit
World.content:
1) Energy stole the show right out of the gate

The summit’s first major clash came Thursday morning, with EU leaders split over whether to delay ETS2, the bloc’s second phase of carbon pricing, to address high energy prices, triggering a three-hour-long standoff.

Italy and Greece joined the Visegrád Four — Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia — in calling for a delay, a push rejected by the majority of countries.

The debate dragged on, delaying lunch (spare a thought for our hungry leaders!) and leading to the cancellation of a press conference on Thursday night.

2) Budget negotiations are a marathon…

Negotiations on the bloc’s next long-term budget were expected to be one of the summit’s most contentious topics. But they were a nothingburger, with most leaders repeating positions they have held for months. The summit brought them no closer to a breakthrough.

Many countries, of course, want a smaller budget, with Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson telling reporters that his country is “not an ATM for the EU.”

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, meanwhile, said he had no choice but to be frugal at the European level, arguing he is used to tightening his belt at home because his wife is Dutch. Think of Bart next time your Dutch friends ask you to pay them back for that coffee.

World.title: Businesses and shopkeepers pick up the pieces after protests in France spiral into looting
World.content:
Major businesses and local shop owners are recovering from widespread looting across France on Saturday, after cost-of-living protests spiralled into scenes of violence that saw masked individuals force their way into stores and make off with goods.

 

French authorities say shops were looted across cities including Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux, Rennes, Strasbourg, Grenoble, Nice, and Limoges, as well as in the French capital, Paris.

Among the targets were major supermarket chains including Carrefour, Franprix, and Monoprix, as well as luxury boutiques, bars, and vape shops.

Groups of masked individuals, many dressed in black, paraded the streets, smashing windows and pulling at metal shutters until they gave way, before grabbing items from the shelves.

On Sunday morning, broken glass and litter filled the streets as Parisians emerged from their apartment blocks to be greeted by the aftermath of the destruction.

Protesters emerge from a looted store during a demonstration against rising living costs, joining students' grievances, in Paris, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Alexandre Bompard, the Chairman and CEO of the Carrefour Group, said on Sunday that a "total of 50 shops" had been targeted, "including 19 Carrefour convenience stores and supermarkets."

He said the affected locations included premises in Paris, Rennes, Lille, and Bordeaux, among others.

"My thoughts are also with the 1,500 shops belonging to all the other retail chains and with all the shopkeepers who have suffered the same unacceptable violence," Bompard continued, adding that the destruction would have "considerable human and economic consequences.

"Dozens of employees at our franchise partners will be forced onto short-time working," he said. "The cost of the repairs will run to well over ten million euros."

One store owner near the Place de la République whose shop had been wrecked by rioters told the Brut outlet that he had put all his savings into the business and that he felt like he'd lost everything.

"I don't know how I'll get by or how I'll live with my family," he said.

Brut said a neighbour had decided to set up a fundraiser to help the man get back on his feet.

A man takes photos of a looted store after a demonstration against rising living costs, joining students' grievances, in Lyon, France, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire has also pledged to offer his full support to businesses affected in the capital and announced that he had requested the creation of an "emergency task force to support shopkeepers who have been victims of vandalism."

"Its role will be to assess the damage, support affected shopkeepers, and assist them with administrative and insurance procedures," he said. "You bring Paris to life every day. Today, it's Paris' turn to stand by your side."

Looters assault Euronews crew

A Euronews crew were assaulted by looters in Paris on Saturday, near the Place de la République, as they reported on the situation.

Protesters scuffle with police during a demonstration against rising living costs, joining students' grievances, in Paris, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

The crew were making their way to another location when they were confronted by masked individuals looting a nearby Intermarché Express supermarket.

"We were standing on Boulevard de Magenta, not far from a supermarket that was being looted by young people, young adults, teenagers. When they saw we were filming, they started hitting my cameraman and attempted to take his microphone and they encircled us," Estelle Nilsson-Julien, Euronews’ correspondent in Paris, said.

"They then pushed him against the wall and started hitting and punching him. They also hit me. They punched him in the face, but because he was wearing goggles and a mask, he was not harmed," she added.

A march moving along the Boulevard de Clichy towards the Place de Clichy across the other side of Paris remained peaceful, another Euronews journalist on the ground reported.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said in an update on Sunday that more than 600 police officers, gendarmes, and firefighters had been injured on Saturday, with more than 2,000 people arrested.

World.title: Ukrainian forces strike St Petersburg and Leningrad region
World.content:
An oil terminal and a data centre belonging to the VK social networking service were reportedly among the targets of a drone attack on St Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad region overnight into Sunday.

 

The attack is being described by Russian media as one of the largest on the area since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. One person was killed and 15 people were injured in the strikes, local officials said.

A total of 144 drones were shot down over the Leningrad region, regional governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said.

According to Drozdenko, drone debris fell on houses in Gatchina and other districts, causing fires and damaging 55 vehicles.

"Emergency power cuts were recorded; specialists are carrying out emergency work and the electricity supply is being promptly restored. At the moment, two transformer substations in Yanino remain switched off, and 50 apartment blocks, home to around 20,000 people, are in the outage zone," he said.

The VK press office reported an attack on its data centre in the Leningrad region but said the company's services remained available to users as normal.

In St Petersburg, governor Aleksandr Beglov said fires broke out at civilian infrastructure facilities in the Nevsky, Krasnoselsky, Krasnogvardeisky, and Moskovsky districts and on the grounds of the St Petersburg oil terminal.

Preliminary information indicated that no one was injured. The oil terminal is located in the Great Port of St Petersburg.

The terminal is capable of receiving and shipping 1.1 million tonnes of fuel a month, using four berths for sea-going vessels and tankers. Its 32 storage tanks occupy an area of 442,000 square metres.

One of the fires broke out at an Ozon warehouse. According to the company, staff were evacuated. Smoke is rising above the warehouse complex, and several roads have been closed in the area.

Due to the attack, flights were suspended at Pulkovo airport for more than seven hours. Rosaviatsia, Russia's aviation authority, lifted the restrictions at 10 am Moscow time.

Russian strikes on Ukraine

It comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Russian forces had carried out further strikes against Ukraine's energy sector on Saturday night, targeting substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions.

"Tens of thousands of families remain without power. Energy workers and repair crews are working virtually around the clock to restore electricity supply," he wrote in a post on X.

Zelenskyy said attacks on residential buildings had also left two people dead and 12 others reportedly injured.

According to the Ukrainian leader, Russia hit Ukraine with close to 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles over the last week.

World.title: Burnt bicycles, smashed windows and looted shops: Trail of destruction across Paris
World.content:
Paris woke up to widespread damage on Sunday after violence overshadowed Saturday’s protests over the cost of living. Streets were littered with debris, burnt bicycles and damaged vehicles, while shops across the city had smashed windows and signs of looting.

 

Businesses including Nike, Sephora and Burger King were among those left damaged, and windows at the Paris Opera ticket office were also shattered. Cleaning crews worked to clear the streets as workers began repairing shopfronts.

The unrest came amid nationwide demonstrations against rising prices.

World.title: Lyon wakes up to scenes of destruction after violent protests
World.content:
Central Lyon was left littered with debris, shattered shop windows and looted stores on Sunday morning after violence erupted during Saturday’s cost-of-living protests.

 

The city’s tourist office was also left burnt out, while graffiti appeared on nearby streets. Cleaning crews worked to clear the wreckage along Rue de la République, and workers boarded up damaged shopfronts.

The unrest came amid nationwide demonstrations over rising prices, with France’s presidential election scheduled for next year.

World.title: Off the Record: Trump blames Zelenskyy to cover up his own mess in a dramatic week for Ukraine
World.content:
Welcome back to Off the Record after another hectic week.

 

I like to joke with our Deputy Head of EU News, Maia de la Baume, that things cannot get crazier with each passing week. Every time, I’m proved wrong. It’s bad news for my immune system, which has finally succumbed to a cold.

This week, I spent some time in Warsaw before the European Council summit in Brussels, which wrapped up as I sat down to file this newsletter next to my Kleenex.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was in Brussels for the summit on Friday, looking to shore up support after a brutal week for Kyiv. The mood in Ukraine heading into the winter couldn't be grimmer.

Fears of abandonment mounted this week after the US announced a shocking deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel in a desperate attempt to bring down fuel prices. The deal is deeply flawed. It gives Russia a fresh revenue boost with no strings attached and little to show for it beyond temporary relief.

By now, it should be clear that President Donald Trump is freaking out about the US midterm elections. Petrol prices have surged since the start of the year, pushing up the cost of living for Americans. Across the Atlantic, the US national average for gas prices hit $4.27 a gallon this week.

If you know anything about Americans, they expect cheap energy – and plenty of it. Prices at the pump and fears of an economic downturn will prove decisive in the midterms.

Much of the pain stems from the collateral effects of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Now, you could argue that Tehran poses a real threat to the world's security and, as Trump himself has suggested, that the country is led by a bunch of crazy people. They are. But they are not dumb.

Iran has successfully weaponised the Strait of Hormuz, choking off the passage of roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil supply. That's a problem for everyone. And someone is going to have to take the blame. Trump has picked Zelenskyy.

Sure, Ukraine is knocking out Russian refineries, hitting Moscow where it hurts and reducing global refining capacity. But that is not the root of the problem. The situation in the Strait of Hormuz is - and Trump doesn't have a quick solution for it.

Instead, the US president has sharply escalated his rhetoric against Zelenskyy, accusing him of creating “problems for our ranchers, our farmers, and the world”. He also suggested Zelenskyy, whom he once described as “a modestly successful comedian,” claims to want peace with Russia while working against it. Ukraine should therefore get a new leader.

This is a shocking statement to make about a country that is surviving daily missile strikes and, coincidentally or not, has encountered serious operational difficulties this week with critical intelligence and infrastructure needed to prevent more people from dying.

Trump has never used that kind of language towards Russia’s Vladimir Putin. He has never called on Putin to hold free elections, either. His words reveal a striking bias that is inappropriate for a country seeking to mediate between the two sides. There is also an element of personal animosity.

The US president has criticised everything about Zelenskyy: his military attire (he now wears a black jacket), his manners (remember the “you don’t have the cards” episode?) and his refusal to budge. Trump’s frustration seems to stem from his perception of Zelenskyy as an obstacle to peace.

Much can be said about Zelenskyy’s tactics, his diplomatic faux pas and the serious corruption allegations involving his senior staff. But when it comes to the war, he is right to stand his ground: the quick deal Trump wants is bad for both Ukraine and Europe.

Zelenskyy also makes a fair point: refineries become legitimate military targets when they help fund the Russian war machine. You could argue that pressure is necessary in any negotiation to force tough decisions – but it has to go both ways. Trump seems intent in applying it in only one direction.

That reflects the US administration’s calculus. Washington appears convinced that the war is unlikely to change much: the conflict has become a war of attrition, the frontline is largely frozen, and Ukraine cannot win back the territories Russia occupies while inflicting brutal damage on civilians. The human cost will go up, but little will change on the ground.

The US also seems to believe – wrongly, in my view– that Putin can be coaxed back to the negotiating table through business deals and economic incentives, and by persuading Moscow that ending the war is in its own interest. But this approach risks fundamentally misreading Putin’s motivations.

Don't just take my word for it.

In 2021, Putin published an essay titled “On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians”. He argued that the two were one people, effectively denying the historical legitimacy of Ukrainian independence. The full-scale war broke out a year later.

For Ukrainians, this is a war of survival – the survival of an independent nation.

Zelenskyy has not budged on territorial concessions, and understandably so, because what is at stake goes beyond a piece of land.

No one has yet explained what would happen after a hypothetical territorial swap, which Kyiv would never recognise de jure anyway. Is the US prepared to offer ironclad security guarantees in return? And what would those guarantees look like in practice?

No country would willingly give up part of its territory – including land Russia does not even control – in exchange for promises that, for now, amount to little more than words. And what would happen to the wider European security architecture, which has gone up in flames as a result of the invasion?

Zelenskyy arrived in the Belgian capital on Friday with a message of gratitude. He thanked the institutions and EU leaders, who he described as “real leaders” in an apparent dig at Trump. But he also showed up with a list of unresolved issues.

Ukraine is heading into a rough winter, with much of its energy infrastructure destroyed by Russia, an urgent need for air defence and billions in fresh funding for 2027.

In his address to leaders, he said the war next year would cost €155 billion, of which €70 billion would have to be financed by the Europeans. He urged them to find the resources, arguing that his estimate is realistic.

Two things stand out. Ukraine is working on the basis that the war will last at least another year, so it has to budget for it. And Europeans will have to foot a substantial part of the bill, with the US no longer providing any assistance.

Last December, European leaders signed off on a €90 billion loan that was supposed to cover two years of financial needs. By now, we know it won’t be enough. And Ukraine will probably never be able to repay it.

The question of financing may be a crude one, but it is a critical one.

European leaders know that cash is tight. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, told me in an interview this week that it is palpable that European public opinion has changed compared with four years ago, as there is an element of fatigue.

The mega election cycle in Europe over the next 12 months doesn’t play into Ukraine’s hands, and the EU should be clear-eyed about it.

In France, Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, used a visit to Brussels this week to send a message to both Brussels and Zelenskyy: she ain’t paying.

On the basis that France is “on the brink of default”, Le Pen said the country could no longer afford to contribute to the common pot for Ukraine. If others want to pay, she said, that is fine, but France won't.

She seems to be taking a cue from the Trumpian playbook: Ukraine is not her taxpayers’ problem. In Germany, the AfD says Berlin shouldn’t either. To be sure, this is a minority position within the EU Council, and it is not even clear that these parties will come to power. But that doesn’t mean they should be ignored.

These parties are successfully tapping into a growing social and economic malaise in Europe. It doesn’t work in Ukraine’s favour. And there is also a legitimate question at the heart of this debate: where will the European Union find €70 billion to €90 billion, potentially every year?

Issue more debt? Tap the frozen Russian assets? Open up the pool of international donors? Use its leverage over third countries to increase their contributions? And what is the strategy behind this massive war effort?

As leaders gathered in Brussels, they instructed the European Commission to come up with options to plug the financing gap by November. Privately, diplomats agree that it will be up to Europe to keep Ukraine in the fight or give Russia the upper hand. But it is not clear how they will get there.

Emmanuel Macron told reporters it was much too soon to talk about €70 billion, but several diplomats told Euronews that Brussels would probably have to raise fresh debt. While there has been talk of reviving the idea of using the Russian frozen assets, it remains a long shot, close to wishful thinking.

The hour is grave for Ukraine. Difficult decisions will have to be made.

World.title: Looting and buildings ablaze: France's violent Saturday protests in 10 pictures
World.content:
Cost-of-living protests descended into violence across parts of France on Saturday as demonstrators clashed with police officers and set buildings and vehicles alight.

 

More than half a million people are thought to have joined the demonstrations, including 110,000 in the French capital, Paris. Violence also broke out in cities such as Lyon, Marseille, Bordeaux, Rennes, Strasbourg, Grenoble, Nice, Toulouse, and Limoges, where the town hall was almost completely destroyed in a fierce blaze.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said on Sunday that more than 500 police officers, gendarmes, and firefighters were injured during the protests, with 1,800 people arrested.

Euronews has put together 10 of the most dramatic images from the day.

World.title: France reels after cost-of-living protests see widespread violence
World.content:
Between 550,000 and 800,000 people took to the streets of France on Saturday, mostly peacefully and often unaware of the unprecedented violence breaking out in some of the country's major cities.

 

Limoges city hall went up in flames, as did the iconic tourist office on Place Bellecour in Lyon. Vandals also forced their way into town halls in Marseille, Lille, and Angers, whilst in Bordeaux, the prefect's residence was ransacked.

Lyon tourist office, 17.10.2026 (AP Photo/Laurent Cipriani) AP Photo

Widespread destruction

"Scenes of insurrection," reads the front page of Le Parisien.

In Paris, Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said "entire streets" had been "systematically devastated" after the French capital saw violent clashes between protesters and police.

The French capital quite literally went up in flames on Saturday. By midday, Place de la République was littered with projectiles, police were clashing with rioters in clouds of tear gas, and a thick column of black smoke rose above the city's iconic rooftops as emergency service vehicles burned.

After nightfall, in several districts, Parisians watched in fear from restaurants and café terraces as groups of young people continued to rampage through the city.

Dressed in black and wearing masks, the groups moved either in their dozens or in small, scattered bands.

Each time, they used the same tactic: several would approach a shop and attack its metal shutters until they give way, before people rushed in to loot the premises.

They left behind smashed storefronts, charred bicycles, and stolen goods scattered on the ground.

Riot police units, who were charged with maintaining public order, followed alongside firefighters as the groups moved on to find more targets ahead.

The looters did not spare the Champs-Élysées, and clashes with the police moved closer to the Élysée Palace and the National Assembly.

The government has said around 1,200 arrests were made across France and that 150 police officers and gendarmes were injured over the course of the day.

Politicians react

Addressing the protests in a post on social media on Saturday evening, French President Emmanuel Macron said there was "no place for violence" in France.

"Those who have vandalised and attacked prefectures and shops alike, and even looted our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished," he wrote.

People look at charred cars the day after a demonstration against rising living costs, joining students' grievances, in Paris, Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

For his part, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has spoken of "groups of several hundred or even thousands of rioters, very clearly instigated by the far left."

Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen said "legitimate social demands" had been "taken hostage by the far left and by the speeches of Jean-Luc Mélenchon's MPs who, by legitimising violence, by seeing order as oppression and disorder as a right, are trying to plunge the country into chaos."

According to Mélenchon, the far-left presidential candidate, the "absurd leadership has opened the door to chaos.

"The leaders no longer know what to do; the rank and file are afraid and running amok," he wrote on X.

"I do not know who will hear my voice in such circumstances, but my message is clear: those who share our struggle have no place in looting and vandalism," he added.

World.title: Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea
World.content:
A wave of deadly attacks on cargo ships in the waters of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania has jolted the alliance into calling an emergency meeting on Black Sea security. Yet any move to send NATO ships hinges on Turkey reversing its steadfast refusal to allow warships into the Black Sea.

Advertising

Thursday saw two chemical tankers struck by drones close to a Romanian port.

It follows two similar attacks in Bulgarian waters in the past week. More than 20 sailors have been killed or remain missing.

“The war has come in full force to the Black Sea now,” said Yoruk Isik, a maritime analyst who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. “With the change in technology compared to the beginning of the war, drones really disrupted maritime traffic.”

According to Isik, the latest attacks underscore the growing spread of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. “Russian ports and Ukrainian ports are heavily targeted, but now even in NATO waters ships are getting hit, in Bulgarian waters, Romanian waters.

“We are at a point where there is no safe place.”

The latest strikes targeted vessels along a key Ukrainian shipping route, casting Russia as NATO’s prime suspect as Moscow intensifies its assault on Ukrainian trade.

After meeting on Thursday with the leaders of Bulgaria and Romania, both NATO members, Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the military alliance would “continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed”.

Romanian President Nicușor Dan said NATO would hold a crisis meeting next week to discuss the situation.

Gatekeeper to the Black Sea

NATO could deploy air defence systems against drones to protect Bulgarian and Romanian waters.

But any deployment of naval ships will depend on NATO member Turkey, which controls access to the Black Sea through the Turkish Straits under a long-standing international treaty, the 1936 Montreux Convention.

Since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Ankara has blocked entry of Russian and Ukrainian warships or military vessels belonging to NATO members without a Black Sea coast, arguing for a diplomatic solution.

In recent weeks the Turkish government has sought to broker a ceasefire on commercial shipping, without success. Isik claims that failure, coupled with the latest escalation in attacks, is increasingly calling into question Ankara’s reliance on diplomacy alone.

“Either they’re going to have a breakthrough and the Kremlin is going to de-escalate, or Ankara is going to accept the reality that there needs to be a more credible force here – bigger vessels have to come,” the analyst said.

He pointed out that the navies of Romania and Bulgaria are not equipped to handle such an operation alone, with Cold War-era ships nearing the end of their lifespan.

“So Turkey's engagement is key to any successful NATO planning in the Black Sea.”

Russian leverage

Despite Turkish-owned cargo ships coming under attack in recent weeks, and Turkey’s deep reliance on Black Sea trade, Ankara has so far kept its powerful navy on the sidelines.

International relations expert Huseyin Bagci, of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University, says Turkey fears an escalation in the conflict and will be wary of allowing NATO ships into the Black Sea.

“I do not think the government would dare,” said Bagci. “Probably the government considers this a provocation to drag Turkey into the war... Turkey is afraid of getting involved in the Black Sea against Russia, this is somehow a trauma in the Turkish mind.”

Moscow also retains powerful leverage over Ankara, he suggested.

Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom is about to complete a multi-billion-dollar nuclear power station in Akkuyu, southern Turkey. Ankara sees it as vital to the drive to reduce its heavy dependence on imported energy. “It is illogical to oppose Russia now while you let the Russians complete the nuclear plant,” said Bagci.

Erdogan hints at larger nuclear partnership with Russia, unsettling Turkey's allies

Ankara also knows that letting NATO vessels in while barring Russian warships could provoke Moscow into contesting Turkey’s prized status as the gatekeeper to the Black Sea.

However, retired Turkish diplomat Selim Kuneralp, an expert on the Montreux Convention, warns Turkey’s control over Black Sea access is likely already in Russian President Vladimir Putin’s sights.

“This has probably had an impact on Russia’s ability to conduct the war, and I doubt that Putin is very happy with the situation,” said Kuneralp. “So if he were to win the war, there is a very strong risk that he will take the initiative of saying: ‘this is unacceptable and we want to have free passage of warships from now on, regardless of whether there is a war’.”

As a signatory, Moscow has the right to call for a revision of the Montreux Convention every five years.

For centuries, Russia fought repeated wars with the then Ottoman Empire for control of the Turkish Straits. In the early years of the Cold War, even Joseph Stalin tried his hand, but the United States intervened and thwarted him.

Now Ankara walks a tightrope between Moscow and its NATO partners to avoid a resurrection of those historical rivalries.
