World.title: France: Young voters blase about Glucksmann's Socialists
World.content:
Raphael Glucksmann wants to lead France's Socialists to power without working with the left-populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, who is particularly popular with young voters. How can the center-left candidate win them over?

The historically working-class Parisian neighborhood of Belleville has gentrified in recent years. It was here that Raphael Glucksmann, a member of the European Parliament for France's center-left Socialists, celebrated his victory in the party's presidential primary on October 11.

Two rounds of voting had been anticipated, but the 46-year-old son of philosopher and essayist Andre Glucksmann triumphed in the first round with a convincing 66% of the vote and will be the Socialist candidate in France's 2027 presidential election.

As he left the Cantine de Belleville restaurant, Glucksmann was flour-bombed by an unidentified assailant. The following morning, he called on his rival, the left-wing French populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, to condemn attacks carried out by his supporters, though it is not clear that the attacker was indeed a supporter of Melenchon's La France Insoumise (LFI).

The incident has highlighted the issue set to dog Glucksmann's presidential candidacy over the coming weeks: How can he win over Melenchon's supporters if he refuses to work with their candidate?

Glucksmann was flour-bombed while leaving his victory celebration Image: Raphael Lafargue/abaca/picture alliance

Gluckmann's rapid rise

"Where do you stand on Melenchon?" That was the question that dominated much of the Socialists' primary campaign. Party leader Olivier Faure spoke in favor of leaving the door open for cooperation with the LFI, but Glucksmann called for a clear break with the far left. His decisive victory is therefore also seen as a vote in favor of a clear demarcation.

The other primary candidates questioned Glucksmann's political experience. Segolene Royal, a previous presidential candidate, compared his bid for the Elysee with that of an "intern" wanting to take charge of a company. She said Glucksmann had no experience in government or even running a local authority.

Despite Glucksmann's victory in the primary, his starting position is a difficult one. A poll by Toluna Harris Interactive, published the day after his win, projects that he would win 10–11% of the vote. The same poll put Melenchon on 18%, meaning the far-left man would be much more likely to reach the runoff. But the survey was conducted before Glucksmann won the primary, and so does not take into account any potential boost the nomination may give him. Still, 10% would be an improvement on the Socialists' performance in the last presidential election in 2022, when their candidate Anne Hidalgo won just 1.75% of the national vote.

There is also the complication that the Socialists are banking on a man who is not even a party member to lead them from irrelevance. Raphael Glucksmann actually belongs to a small center-left party called Place Publique.

France students demand better schools To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Melenchon's youth appeal

Glucksmann has his work cut out for him — especially with young people. In an Ipsos survey in September, which posited Glucksmann as the social-democratic candidate and Edouard Philippe as the only candidate from the political center, Melenchon scored 41% among the under-25s. Meanwhile, 20% of this age group supported the far-right nationalist Marine Le Pen. France's young electorate is politically divided, but Melenchon still dominates on the left.

The 75-year-old is currently rallying alongside the students whose protests have drawn international attention. At a rally near Clermont-Ferrand in central France , he expressed solidarity with their movement and reiterated his calls for lowering the voting age to 16 and abolishing Parcoursup, France's national admissions procedure for higher education.

In an analysis for the Fondation Jean-Jaures, a Socialist-aligned think tank, the political scientist Antoine Bristielle distinguishes between a core group of committed LFI voters and the broader left. Melenchon's most loyal supporters, he says, are often young, educated city-dwellers, and many are under a lot of financial pressure. Four in ten households in this group live on a net monthly income of less than €2,000 ($2,200).

Bristielle estimates that just under a third of the left-wing electorate in his study care more about a left-wing victory than their allegiance to any particular party. Almost half of the people in this group are younger than 35, and would consider voting for the Socialists, the Greens, or LFI. Redistribution and an active government are important to them, but most would prefer politicians who are willing to compromise.

Melenchon in Paris during a public sector strike on September 29 Image: Tom Nicholson/REUTERS

Glucksmann's youth efforts

The pattern recently observed in Germany, where young women are more likely to vote for the left and young men for the right, does not apply in France. Political scientists Anja Durovic, Nonna Mayer and Noemie Piolat found that in the 2024 European and parliamentary elections, young French women were not significantly more likely to vote for the left, or less likely to vote for the far right, than men of the same age. It remains to be seen whether this pattern will be replicated in the 2027 presidential election.

Glucksmann says he would ease the burden on earned income by reducing France's CSG social security tax while increasing taxes on inheritances worth more than €2 million. He also presents himself as a committed supporter of European integration, while Melenchon has called the EU a neoliberal institution. Glucksmann's political profile combines social policy demands with foreign policy positions that could also appeal to voters from the camp of the current president, Emmanuel Macron.

France's Ukraine policy is one such issue. Glucksmann favors decisive support for Kyiv. Manon Aubry, a member of the European Parliament for Melenchon's LFI, says her party supports military assistance only under certain conditions, namely: The provision of aid to Ukraine must first be subject to democratic debate; it must not enable attacks deep inside Russian territory; and it must not weaken France's own defense capabilities. In 2024, LFI MPs voted against the French–Ukrainian security agreement.

The tension between the parties of the left was once again apparent in the aftermath of the flour attack in Belleville. The LFI MP Sebastien Delogu posted a declaration of support on X for the taxi driver who was going to have to clean his car.

Glucksmann must win over a lot of voters from Melenchon's camp if he is to have a chance of winning the presidency. This is likely to prove a much more difficult task than simply distancing himself from Melenchon.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?
World.content:
Would you work 12 hours straight? The CDU/CSU and SPD are locked in a dispute over reforms to the Working Hours Act. Workplace flexibility, collective bargaining agreements and worker protection rules are at stake.

The town of Leuna, in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, is one of the country's largest chemical industry hub, where more than 100 companies have established operations. Among them is the Finnish biotechnology group UPM, which has recently built a biorefinery for wood-based chemicals in Leuna. It's now hiring.

One of the job listings is for a chemical technician to oversee the rollout of new facilities. But to qualify, candidates must be willing to work 12-hour shifts. Is that legal? According to German law, standard working hours are limited to eight hours per day. It is permissible to extend this to ten hours, provided that workers receive compensatory time off for the overtime, and there must be at least 11 hours of rest between two shifts.

Twelve-hour shifts? What German law permits

Business associations and the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties have long called for these rules to be made more flexible.

Rainer Dulger, president of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), points to the European Working Time Directive, which allows for a maximum weekly working time of 48 hours. "The allowance is being taken advantage of almost everywhere else — except here," Dulger told the dpa news agency in August.

Companies say they often find the existing rules too rigid, particularly in industries with seasonal fluctuations — such as tourism — or in project-based work, or during irregular peaks in workload, such as in the restaurant industry. They could deploy their staff more efficiently, says Dulger: "The Working Hours Act dates back to the era of fax machines and rotary-dial phones. It knows nothing of laptops or daycare hours."

4-day workweek: A model for the future? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

CDU and SPD divided on working hours

In their 2025 coalition agreement, the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) agreed to reform the Working Hours Act. "In keeping with the European Working Time Directive, we want to allow for a maximum weekly rather than daily working time — also and especially to promote a better work-life balance," the agreement said.

The SPD would have preferred to leave the law unchanged, but had to accept the conservative parties' plans. The Social Democrats pointed out that longer working hours are already permitted in exceptional cases, such as in emergency services, the health care sector and security services. Workers in power plants, refineries and the chemical industry are also allowed to work up to 12 hours at a time.

A surprise for Chancellor Friedrich Merz

Even Chancellor Friedrich Merz himself seemed unaware of this exception until quite recently. After visiting the UPM refinery in Leuna in September, he recounted to business leaders at the German Employers' Day in Berlin that he was "completely surprised" to learn that the facilities operate on a continuous 12-hour shift schedule, thanks to the approval of the works council.

Merz recounted the shift supervisor describing the work schedule as "really great" — with three-day work weeks. "He said we have plenty of time for our families — it's a great way to organize things." Merz went on to conclude that this demonstrates the benefits of relaxing the Working Hours Act.

"Working more than eight hours is not exploitation. Rather, it can be a good opportunity to organize working hours more flexibly — both for businesses and for the people working there," the chancellor said. "We should do it."

SPD agrees to longer working hours, but with conditions

But there is resistance from within the SPD and from trade unions opposed to amending the Working Hours Act. The trade union Verdi argues that significantly longer workdays would have negative consequences for employees' health and would disadvantage people with family and caregiving responsibilities. In certain industries, employees could also be put under pressure to accept longer shifts.

An initial reform draft was drawn up in June 2026 by the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry, headed at the time by Bärbel Bas, an SPD politician who has since resigned for personal reasons.

The draft includes some conditions, including a collective bargaining agreement between employers and unions if any schedule changes were made, as well as health and safety regulations, and working hours to be tracked electronically.

Bärbel Bas' reform plan had the CDU up in arms Image: Christophe Gateau/dpa/picture alliance

Dispute over collective bargaining rights and worker protection

Annika Klose, spokesperson for labor and social policy for the SPD parliamentary group, explained the thinking behind the idea. Flexibility, she said, is "not a one-way street." The coalition agreement explicitly aims to promote a better balance between family and work. "So that it's sometimes possible to take your child to football practice in the afternoon and then continue working afterward — but not that my boss tells me against my will: 'You're working the shift from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. tomorrow.'"

The CDU/CSU immediately rejected the draft. Businesses were also up in arms. "This draft must be withdrawn and completely revised," demanded Dulger in a statement, saying it was "steeped in mistrust." The German Confederation of Skilled Crafts (ZDH) spoke of a "breach of the commitments agreed to in the coalition agreement." The reform has been on hold ever since.

Why the reform stalled

At the Employers' Day event, Merz held out the prospect of progress. "This is indeed long overdue. I believe we can accomplish this relatively quickly and create flexibility in the labor market."

It remains to be seen, however, whether the new SPD Labor Minister, Alexander Schweitzer, shares this view. In early October, his party released a paper on reforming working hours that read like a declaration of war against the CDU. "Self-determination, Not Deregulation" is the title of the seven-page document that was signed by the SPD working group on labor, the youth organization Jusos, the "60plus" working group and the women's wing of the SPD.

In the paper, the Social Democrats not only reiterate the points that already appeared in Bas' draft back in June. They also demand that, in the future, employers and employees should decide on working hours "jointly and by mutual agreement." They argued that it is not "in the spirit of a modern reform of working time law" if only employers can determine when employees finish work.

From a political perspective, the dispute over reforming work hours has long become more than just a debate over legal provisions. It is a fundamental dispute over how much flexibility workers should be expected to tolerate in the future and to what extent the state should protect them. And it is yet another stumbling block for the already beleaguered government in Berlin.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: France reports more than 1,800 arrests after riots, looting and arson during cost-of-living protests
World.content:
Rioters torched public buildings and looted shops across France, destroying Limoges' historic town hall. The violence erupted during nationwide cost-of-living protests.

More than 1,800 people were arrested across France following riots, looting and arson during cost-of-living protests, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said Sunday.

The unrest on Saturday has sharpened tensions ahead of France's 2027 presidential election, as anger over living costs collides with tight limits on government spending.

What happened during the protests?

Clashes, fires and looting broke out in several cities during Saturday's demonstrations. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 150 police officers had been injured and blamed what he described as a highly organized, violent far-left group.

Paris police reported 855 arrests, describing the figure as a record. Prosecutors said 517 people remained in custody, including 171 minors. Those figures were provisional, with arrests continuing until early Sunday.

Most arrests in the capital were linked to suspected handling of stolen goods, participation in a group intending to commit violence, and vandalism.

In central France, rioters set fire to Limoges' historic town hall, leaving much of it gutted. Mayor Guillaume Guerin condemned the destruction.

Rioters set fire to Limoges' historic town hall during nationwide demonstrations over living costs Image: Pascal Lachenaud/AFP

"There are no words to condemn what happened, so appalling is it," he told broadcaster LCI. "The country is in chaos."

Authorities reported attacks on public buildings and shops in Marseille, Lyon, Avignon and Grenoble. Police used tear gas, batons and water cannon in several cities.

Demonstrators were also reported injured. The newspaper Le Figaro reported that a 17-year-old lost a hand to a grenade fired by police in Saint-Etienne.

What have leading French politicians said?

President Emmanuel Macron vowed that those responsible would be prosecuted and punished.

"No room for violence in our Republic," he wrote on X, condemning attacks on government buildings, businesses and town halls.

The Elysee Palace said French President Emmanuel Macron would address the nation at 8 p.m. local time (1800 UTC) on Sunday.

France protests escalate as unrest spreads across cities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Opposition politicians seeking to succeed Macron in presidential elections in April and May also responded to the unrest.

Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen accused the party of her far-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon of having "legitimized the violence." She pledged to protect the French "from the violence of the extreme left."

Melenchon, who had backed the demonstrations and preceding student protests, urged demonstrators to stay away from looting, calling it "contrary to our methods."

The demonstrations brought together grievances over fuel prices, low wages and problems facing farmers and firefighters. School and university students demanding better learning conditions also participated.

The interior ministry put nationwide turnout at 550,000, including 110,000 in Paris. The CGT trade union gave a higher national estimate of 800,000.

France's high debt and budget deficit limit the government's ability to meet demands for additional spending.

Online calls to revive the yellow vest movement have added to government concerns that student demonstrations could grow into broader unrest.

The yellow vest movement began in 2018 over planned fuel tax increases and grew into wider protests over living costs and inequality. Named after the high-visibility vests worn by demonstrators, it brought months of nationwide demonstrations, some marked by violent clashes with police.

World.title: Vietnam signs free trade deal with four European countries
World.content:
Vietnam has signed a deal with four non-EU members that covers trade in goods and services, intellectual property rights, and sustainable development, among other areas.

Vietnam and four European countries signed a free trade agreement in Hanoi on Sunday.

The deal was announced by the governments of Vietnam and Norway.

Vietnam's Trade Ministry said it signed the deal with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), which is made up Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

The four European countries are not part of the European Union (EU).

The official talks between Vietnam and the EFTA began in 2012. The talks were interrupted in 2018 and only resumed last year.

How does the deal benefit Vietnam?

The agreement between Vietnam, which is Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economy, and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) waives or reduces customs duties, including on imports of industrial, fish and agricultural products.

Is Vietnam set to replace China as the world's factory? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Under the deal, around half of Norway's exports ​to ‌Vietnam will be tariff-free, with more than 98% ‌to be tariff-free within seven ‌years, ​the Norwegian government said in a statement.

According to the signing parties, the deal covers trade in goods and services, intellectual property rights, trade remedies and sustainable development, among other areas, both parties say.

Last year, the trade value between the EFTA and Vietnam stood at €4.8 billion ($5.4 billion), according to the association.

Vietnam said the agreement showed the parties' resolve to "reinforce the rules-based trading system amid continued volatility in the global economy," according to a government statement.

It was also expected to help Vietnam "diversify its import and export markets" and "integrate more deeply into global value chains," the government said.

World.title: How reliant is Ukraine on the US-controlled Starlink internet service?
World.content:
Kyiv keeps issuing warnings that the satellite internet system Starlink is being restricted in Ukraine. How dependent is the country on the system, and what would happen if it went down?

Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink, central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use.

How Starlink enables communications

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down.

According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage.

The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis , the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative.

Starlink and Starshield: civilian versus military use

When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably.

There are around 50,000 Starlink terminals in Ukraine Image: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications.

This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.

The role of Starlink in drone warfare

Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones.

This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines.

According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations.

What throttling Starlink would mean

According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph).

Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.

Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.

More than just satellite internet

However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.

This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.

The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.

This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.

Strategic dependence

Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.

Starlink terminals enable mobile internet connection on the battlefield for the operation of drones Image: Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP

The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Germany news: Police probe security incident at Leipzig/Halle airport
World.content:
Söder spoke on the last day of the two-day gathering Image: Marc John/IMAGO

Bavarian Premier Markus Söder has slammed the Left Party's plans to socialize housing in Berlin and spoken of a "red front" in the German capital as a leftist coalition seems likely to take power there (see earlier entry in this blog).

Speaking at a gathering of the youth wing of Germany's coalition alliance (JU) in Bonn, Söder said that "such absurd expropriation fantasies by socialists" had to be stopped.

He called on the government to quickly put in place a planned law against putting private property into public ownership.

Söder, who leads the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party to Chancellor Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), even suggested that payments to Berlin under Germany's financial redistribution scheme be cut if the Left Party plan is put into practice.

"The others [other federal states: Ed.] can have the money. But it is just not right that we even end up paying" for such things, he said.

Söder's speech at the meeting followed one by the chancellor on Saturday Image: Chris Emil Janßen/IMAGO

Allegations of antisemitism in Left Party

Söder also described an "antisemitism agreement" reached by the Left Party, the Greens and the Social Democrats (SPD) during exploratory negotiations as apparently "not worth the paper it is written on," saying that the Left Party held stances that were unacceptable.

"Germany must not be identified with such forces in leading positions," he said, saying "firewalls" like that against the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) were needed against the left as well.

He backed a resolution put forward by the JU that calls for any such leftist coalition in Berlin to be refused access to information from the BfV domestic intelligence agency and the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA).

Along with allegations of antisemitism, the Left Party has faced accusations of having links to clan criminality in the capital, leading some conservatives to suggest it might abuse such information.

Elif Eralp of the Left Party (C.) could become governing mayor of Berlin Image: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

Pre-coalition agreements

During exploratory coalition talks, the three left-leaning parties agreed to socialize properties belonging to real-estate companies possessing more than 10,000 apartments.

Under the agreement, a fund of up to €16 billion ($17.98 billion) is to be prepared to pay out compensation for the expropriations.

Before the exploratory talks even began, the three parties reacted to accusations of antisemitism levelled at the Left Party with an agreement in which Israel's right to exist was enshrined as "non-negotiable."

The agreement also foresees penalties for party members who do not act in accordance with this stipulation.

The Left Party emerged as the strongest force from September 20 elections in the city-state of Berlin, with its lead candidate Elif Eralp well set to become the governing mayor.

World.title: Populist Czech PM Babis goes empty-handed in Senate elections
World.content:
Opposition parties still control the Czech Senate, in a major blow to Prime Minister Andrej Babis' and his governing coalition.

The ruling coalition of populist billionaire Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis has failed to win a single seat in elections in the Senate.

The result means pro-Western opposition parties control the chamber, the upper house of parliament.

The election on Saturday was the first electoral test for Babis after he won parliamentary elections in October 2025 that returned him to power after a break of four years since his first term as premier.

What happened in the Czech Senate elections?

Final results from the two-day ballot showed that candidates directly linked to the opposition parties won 22 of the 27 seats up for grabs in the 81-member Senate, retaining a previous opposition majority.

The centrist ANO (or YES) movement led by Babis failed to win any more seats, leaving it with 14 Senate lawmakers.

Babis called the result "catastrophic."

"We certainly didn't expect that we wouldn't win a single Senate seat in this election," he said, but vowed to nonetheless go ahead with his government's agenda.

That includes an unpopular plan to revamp funding for the country’s public broadcasters.

Czech journalists warn of dangers of public media reform To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

His euroskeptic coalition has also ended direct military support for Ukraine as it defends itself against a Russian invasion, and opposed European Union policies to combat global warming.

Although the lower house of the Czech parliament plays the main legislative role, the Senate has a big say in passing constitutional amendments and approving Constitutional Court judges.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: India: CJP leader Abhijeet Dipke released after detention
World.content:
Two other prominent CJP leaders are set to be released on Sunday. India has seen huge rallies calling on the country's top election official to step down over alleged manipulation of voter rolls.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), was released on Saturday, a day after he was detained by the Delhi police during protests against the election authority in India.

The 31-year-old youth leader was detained while he was trying to join the protest rally which the CJP movement had called in the capital's central Connaught Place district.

The movement published a photo of him on X in which it referred to Dipke as "a free man."

"Abhijeet Dipke released," CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh said on social media.

Singh said Dipke was released after agreeing to certain conditions. She did not provide details about the terms.

In a post on Instagram, Dipke said he "knew going to jail was inevitable" and that he was ready to face "whatever comes my way."

"Because the day I decided to come back to India, I placed my fate in the hands of the people of India and the Constitution of this country."

What are the protests about?

All India Students' Association (AISA) President Neha Bora, who was also detained during a protest in New Delhi on Friday, was released later on Friday evening.

Bora has emerged as a prominent face in the protests against India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged manipulation of voter lists.

A widespread review exercise — called Special Intensive Revision (SIR) — has struck off over 130 million names from India's electoral rolls since it began last year.

Opposition leaders and critics say that those removed from the voter lists include a large proportion of minority voters. They accuse Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist BJP of using the exercise as a tool to secure future electoral gains.

The neutrality of the Election Commission of India (ECI) is also being questioned.

The ECI denies favoring any party. It says the SIR removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also helps in preventing the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."

Youth being made 'pawns' — BJP



Modi's party has slammed its opponents for undermining democracy and has denounced the protests as attempts to create "anarchy".

BJP's Rajnath Singh — who is also India's defense minister — addressed the protests at a press conference on Friday.

Singh accused the opposition, led by the Congress party, of wanting to bring a "regime change along the lines of Bangladesh" and using Indian youth as "pawns in the politics of disorder."

"It appears that the Congress and its political allies, both directly and through their affiliated organisations, are attempting to channel the energy of young people not into constructive activities and nation-building, but into instruments of political confrontation and the spread of chaos," he said.

India: Protesters jailed amid election row To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka's custody ends Sunday

Two other senior CJP leaders, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, were arrested on October 14 for entering Jantar Mantar.

Jantar Mantar had been a prominent protest site in the heart of Delhi for decades. However, Delhi police blocked it amid heavy barricading and deployment.

The two leaders were sent to five days of judicial custody, which ends Sunday. The CJP has warned of legal action if Das and Ranka are not released.

"Now just waiting for my brothers to be free", Dipke said in a post on X that included a photo of Ranka and Das.

For the latest coverage of news from India on Sunday, check out our blog.

World.title: Información genética para una medicación más segura y eficiente
World.content:
Con una simple muestra de saliva, la farmacogenética permite el análisis de decenas de genes y cientos de fármacos de uso habitual y revela por qué un simple analgésico quita el dolor a una persona y a otra le produce una reacción adversa

Según estima la Agencia Española de Medicamentos y Productos Sanitarios, entre el 3% y el 6,5% de la población tiene una variante genética que provoca que su hígado transforme la codeína (un compuesto presente en medicamentos o soluciones tan frecuentes como las pastillas para la tos) en morfina. Este proceso, que se produce a gran velocidad incluso si la dosis administrada es normal, puede desembocar en una sobredosis accidental, que en algunos casos termina en el fallecimiento del paciente.

El ejemplo lo pone Javier Suela, director técnico del laboratorio de genética de Sanitas (Madrid). Él mismo pertenece a este pequeño grupo poblacional de riesgo: “Hay mucha evidencia acumulada de la toxicidad de ciertos medicamentos en ciertos pacientes. Estas reacciones adversas van desde un brote cutáneo hasta la muerte en casos extremos, como este mismo de la codeína”, explica.

Suela trabaja para reducir esa peligrosidad al mínimo. En el laboratorio que dirige, desde el pasado mayo, se extrae el perfil genético de quien lo solicite para “determinar si tiene un componente genético, una proteína, que produce que determinados fármacos se procesen de una forma que no es habitual”, sintetiza.

El perfil genético, en tres pasos 1 Recepción de las muestras e identificación de cada paciente El paciente lleva una muestra genética (basta la saliva, por ejemplo) en un tubo. Este tubo va a una primera máquina que realiza una preanalítica y transforma las muestras en placas que identifican a cada persona: en la posición A1 está la muestra de un paciente concreto y en la B1, otro, y así sucesivamente. 2 Procesado del material genético El material genético de la placa, que contiene muestras de hasta 96 pacientes, se prepara y depura (se corta, se colorea...) en otra máquina para el análisis final. Lo que se obtiene, tras cuatro horas de refinado, es la placa definitiva (en la imagen) que se usará para extraer el perfil genético. 3 Obtención del perfil genético La placa, con el material genético ya refinado, se introduce en un escáner que analiza cada celda, que contiene más de un millón de variables (cada una asociada a un genotipo) que procesar. Cuando este escáner finaliza se obtiene el perfil genético del paciente, el resultado final del proceso.

Esta disciplina se conoce como farmacogenética y en Sanitas está disponible para todos sus asegurados bajo el nombre de Mi Farmagen. “Un ser humano puede metabolizar todos los fármacos, pero en función de ciertas variables genéticas los metaboliza a distintas velocidades; entonces el medicamento puede funcionar demasiado bien o demasiado mal. Esto es lo que da lugar a reacciones adversas o reacciones inexistentes, es decir, cuando el fármaco no funciona”, detalla.

29 genes y 125 fármacos analizados

Mi Farmagen analiza hasta 29 genes y más de 125 fármacos de uso habitual, y ofrece un informe con las reacciones a cada uno de estos medicamentos. Y siempre es útil, tanto si se obtiene antes o después de la prescripción, ya que “permite ajustar la medicación sin perder efectividad, pero evitando posibles efectos adversos y aumentando la seguridad”, incide Suela.

Hay casos en los que un cambio anticipado de medicación puede salvar la vida del paciente, pero también situaciones más cotidianas en las que esta información es de mucha utilidad. Así lo explica Andrea Azcárate, jefe de servicio de Endocrinología del hospital Sanitas de La Moraleja (Madrid): “Es el ejemplo de un paciente con colesterol alto al que le sienta mal un tipo de estatina, que es el tratamiento habitual para esta patología. Para corroborarlo, se le hace la prueba farmacogenética. A partir de ahí, probablemente escojamos otro tipo de estatina que vaya a tolerar mejor”. Sin embargo, cada caso, en opinión de Azcárate, no es blanco o negro: “Lo que el análisis nos da es una predisposición de respuesta, una información probabilística que nos permite individualizar el tratamiento”, puntualiza.

0:00 ANDREA AZCÁRATE, jefe de servicio de Endocrinología del hospital Sanitas de La Moraleja (Madrid)

Azcárate y Suela inciden, precisamente, en la importancia de la interpretación facultativa de esta información, que por sí sola vale poco. “Es fundamental la interpretación y el ajuste, algo que siempre se ha hecho: la medicación, en función de las características clínicas del paciente, las casuísticas y las edades, se individualiza”. Y eso mismo se hará a partir de ahora, subraya: “Ajustaremos caso a caso, pero con más información. Es una herramienta más, muy buena y útil, pero hay que tener prudencia a la hora de incorporarla”.

En esa misma línea se expresa Suela: “El informe son páginas de metabolización, nada más. No vale de nada sin facultativo detrás que las interprete. Y, sobre todo, hay que combinar toda la información: igual tienes un paciente del que el análisis dice que el fármaco le va a sentar muy bien, pero esa misma persona tiene unas condiciones físicas complicadas o es un paciente polimedicado, en el que es fundamental medir las interacciones entre fármacos”. Es una cuestión de personalización, como dicta la tendencia actual en la medicina, pero con un conocimiento más preciso.

Así funciona Mi Farmagen Mi Farmagen analiza cómo las variantes genéticas influyen en la respuesta a determinados medicamentos.

influyen en la respuesta a determinados medicamentos. Permite conocer cómo metabolizamos determinados fármacos para aumentar su eficacia y reducir posibles efectos adversos.

y más de de uso habitual, y ofrece un informe con las a cada uno de estos medicamentos. En Europa ya se han hecho más de 1.000 perfiles farmacogenéticos con este sistema.

Hacia un pasaporte genético

En el futuro, coinciden los especialistas, se abre paso la idea de que todo ciudadano cuente con un carnet genético. Esta posibilidad existe gracias a la tecnología, explica Suela, que ha multiplicado el poder de las técnicas de genotipado: “Antes hacíamos un solo caso, un solo paciente, con cientos de marcadores. Ahora procesamos hasta 96 casos y en cada uno analizamos millones de marcadores. El salto es impresionante”.

0:00 JAVIER SUELA, director técnico del laboratorio de genética de Sanitas (Madrid)

El objetivo es que la farmacogenética sea útil, no un mero postulado teórico. Y ya lo es, pero todavía a pequeña escala. Mi Farmagen acumula ya mil análisis farmacogenéticos a pacientes con aplicación real. “Necesitamos que poco a poco todos tengamos un carnet farmacogenómico. En la actualidad esa información que tenemos ya nos salta a la historia clínica de forma automática como alerta a la hora de prescribir medicamentos con un programa propio, Farmacheck, y esta información también está a disposición del paciente en su app para poder ajustar e individualizar el tratamiento. En pocos años será un estándar”, señala Azcárate. Suela añade: “Nuestro sueño sería que en más del 90% de las prescripciones se tuviese en cuenta esa información genética de manera previa”.

Todo con un fin: obtener la mayor seguridad para el paciente, ya que, hasta hoy, “a la hora de prescribir algunos fármacos, operábamos con un método prueba-error: si no funcionaba uno, o si funcionaba mal, se probaba otro. Pero con la farmacogenética se abre otro camino, de máxima seguridad, basado en evidencias clínicas rigurosas”, afirma Suela.

World.title: Cómo un buen café puede cambiar un negocio hostelero
World.content:
Entre el café de batalla y la fiebre por su refinación, cada vez más hosteleros abandonan los automatismos a la hora de preparar esta bebida para formarse en su preparación. Un ejemplo es la cafetería Formentor, en Madrid. Tras 70 años en activo, ha transformado su servicio con la ayuda de un experto cafetero

¿Por dónde empieza un buen café? ¿Por los ingredientes, por la forma de prepararlo, por la exigencia del cliente? “El primer paso es convencer a los hosteleros de que cambien su forma de prepararlo”, responde Raúl Villanueva, barista y formador de la marca Café Saula. Él, con dos décadas de experiencia en el sector hostelero, reconoce que deshacerse de las manías y automatismos puede ser complicado. Villanueva forma parte del equipo de seis formadores de Saula, la marca premium de café de Grupo Pascual, que recorren distintos locales del país para enseñar a los hosteleros a servir una bebida equilibrada, rica y estable; para que todas las tazas de café que sirvan tengan la misma calidad. “La resistencia al cambio impide sacar el máximo provecho del producto”, reflexiona. “La idea es culturizar a nuestros alumnos para que entiendan el café y sepan tratarlo mejor. Esto beneficia a todos: a nosotros como marca, a ellos como negocio y a su cliente final”, sostiene.

La cultura del café ha crecido, insiste el experto. Percibe que los consumidores también se preocupan más por lo que consumen. Han pasado a interesarse por el origen, la calidad y la elaboración. A este fenómeno lo impulsa, además, el factor económico. “La diferencia de precios entre un café de alta calidad y otro normalito es ridícula”, añade el barista.

Raúl Villanueva, barista y formador de la marca Café Saula. Cedida por Saula

Villanueva atribuye el cambio de paradigma a la profesionalización del sector y a la labor pedagógica de tostadores, baristas y marcas. Después de cuatro años trabajando para Saula, aún encuentra nudos en los negocios. Cada vez son menos, pero todavía hay algunas personas que ven el café como un producto secundario, tienen poco interés por aprender nuevas técnicas y “no cuidan la receta”. Ni siquiera la prueban. “Preparar un café es un cocinar”, insiste. “Cualquier cambio en molienda, dosis, temperatura, agua o tiempo altera el resultado final”. Por eso, en sus cursos aborda desde la materia prima hasta el funcionamiento de la maquinaria o la texturización de leche.

Los cinco errores cafeteros más comunes del hostelero Según Raúl Villanueva, barista y formador de la marca 'premium' Café Saula Utilizar café viejo Los granos molidos pierden aroma, cuerpo y sabor a medida que se oxidan. Un mal control del 'stock' puede mermar la calidad.

Priorizar la rapidez sobre la calidad La premura puede llevar a desatender la atención a los detalles que marcan la diferencia.

No cuidar correctamente la máquina La acumulación de restos de café y suciedad afecta a la presión y la temperatura de extracción, esenciales para el buen sabor.

No considerarlo una receta (y no probarlo) Muchos hosteleros controlan cocina, vino o cerveza, pero olvidan beber el café que venden. Es un error pensar que basta con pulsar un botón; la preparación depende de múltiples variables.

No formar al equipo Si cada empleado elabora el café de una manera distinta, repercute en la experiencia del cliente. Se vuelve inconsistente.

La calidad acaba por imponerse

La pastelería Formentor abrió sus puertas en Madrid hace 70 años, cuando un matrimonio que regentaba en Mallorca un local llamado el Forn de Santa Eulàlia decidió traer a la capital española el sabor de las ensaimadas. Eran los abuelos de Ane Forteza (San Sebastián, 31 años), que hoy, como tercera generación, está al frente del negocio. “Algunos clientes que nos visitaban junto a sus abuelos llegan ahora acompañados de sus nietos”, se enorgullece.

Tienen dos locales, uno en Chamberí y otro acristalado en el barrio de Salamanca, desde donde Forteza recuerda que cambiar su marca de café fue una difícil decisión. “Muchos nos decían que venían porque les gustaba el sabor”, admite. La mayoría de habituales lo desayunan acompañado de una ensaimada ―las lisas, sin relleno, se hornean continuamente en el local―. A pesar de todo, el pasado julio decidieron dar el paso. “Fue una evolución natural. Somos una empresa que intenta dar productos de la mejor calidad y pensamos que el café tenía que ser acorde”.

De entre todas las marcas, se quedaron con Saula por la formación presencial, el seguimiento constante, la facilidad a la hora de pedir el café (junto a su pedido de leche Pascual), la sustitución de la maquinaria y el esmero en los detalles. La respuesta de los consumidores, al final, ha sido mayoritariamente positiva: “Algunos notaron que era un café más suave y menos tostado”. Tampoco les preocupa los que aún no se adaptan: “Es una cuestión de hábito, la calidad acaba por imponerse”.

Ane Forteza representa la tercera generación al frente de la Pastelería Formentor, fundada por sus abuelos en Madrid. INMA FLORES

Al otro lado de la barra, Andrés Vidarte (Tesalia, Colombia, 30 años) se encarga de servir los cafés con una sonrisa extensa ante unos clientes exigentes que ya le conocen y saludan. Él, que cumple con precisión lo aprendido en las formaciones de Saula, reconoce que algunas pautas le sorprendieron, como la colocación de las tazas (boca arriba, para que se caliente la base y no el borde, donde se apoyan los labios), la cantidad de agua que había que utilizar o la importancia de una limpieza minuciosa y frecuente. “Aprendimos que cualquier resto puede influir en el sabor del café”, señala. El barista, que nació en una zona cafetera de Colombia, dice que la aportación de Saula le ayudó a ser más consciente de todo el ritual de preparación: “Ahora prestamos más atención a aspectos que antes pasaban desapercibidos”, admite.

Los cuatro pasos para servir un buen café Por Andrés Vidarte, barista de la cafetería Formentor (Madrid) 1 Limpiar bien la maquinaria entre servicio; sobre todo, el portafiltros. Además, realizar purgas diarias y lavados profundos periódicos.

2 Controlar la receta con la ayuda de dos máquinas. La primera tiene programada la dosis exacta de café y la segunda, el tiempo de extracción (que suele ser de unos 25 segundos) y la cantidad de bebida que debe salir.

3 Comprobar la temperatura y la presión. La cafetera debe alcanzar y mantener una temperatura estable, que marque aproximadamente 116 ºC, para que se extraigan los aromas y sabores.

4 Finalmente, trabajar la leche (si la lleva), calentar media jarra e introducir la lanza de vapor solo parcialmente para texturizarla (transformarla en una crema suave). Después, girar levemente la taza para una integración proporcionada. FOTOGRAFÍA: Inma Flores

Tueste lento y conservación en lata

Desde sus inicios a finales de los 50 en Cataluña, la filosofía de Saula se basaba en la obsesión por mantener la calidad del producto y del proceso. Lo define Javier Peña, director general de Café del Grupo Pascual, quien precisa que entonces la mayor parte del mercado estaba orientada hacia cafés más amargos y con mayor cuerpo, elaborados principalmente con variedades robustas. “El fundador de esta marca, Lluís Saula, detectó una oportunidad para ofrecer un café de mayor calidad: el café arábica, que es más aromático, complejo y delicado”, añade.

Para alcanzarlo, elaboran una selección muy rigurosa desde el origen, la altura de cultivo, el tamaño o el procesamiento. Peña compara el café con una cereza: “Una vez recolectado, es necesario separar correctamente la pulpa exterior para evitar que la fermentación no controlada afecte al grano”. Su tueste es lento y controlado y permite desarrollar notas achocolatadas y especiadas. La conservación se realiza en lata, con una maduración de tres o cuatro semanas antes de salir al mercado. “Los envases incorporan válvulas unidireccionales que permiten la salida de los gases sin que entre oxígeno, para evitar la oxidación”, expone.

Pascual adquirió hace un par de años Café Saula porque “estaban en sintonía”; ambas se esmeran en un cuidado “extremo”, define Peña. El propósito era expandir este café; a comienzos de 2026 llegó a Madrid y desde este verano a Galicia, Asturias y Cantabria. Peña explica que el crecimiento de esta área dentro de Pascual ha sido significativo en los últimos años: “El objetivo era alcanzar 100 millones de euros en café en 2027, pero podría lograrse antes. En unos siete años se ha duplicado el valor del negocio del café dentro del grupo”. En la actualidad, esta vertical supera los 300 empleados, de los cuales 80 están dentro de Saula.

Javier Peña, director general de Café del Grupo Pascual. Cedida por Saula

Quieren desplegarse, pero con conciencia; sin perder sus estándares de calidad. “Solo trabajamos con establecimientos que se comprometan a tratar bien el producto”, apunta Peña, y pone el ejemplo de Formentor: “Cuando entras, ya se percibe. El olor a pastelería y a un buen café te enganchan”. Por ello, Saula cuida permanentemente de que los empleados estén actualizados en conocimientos, gracias a Raúl Villanueva y otros seis preparadores.

Estos expertos encuentran indicadores inmediatos para saber si el café es de calidad. Por ejemplo, Villanueva lo hace a través de tres sentidos. Por la vista, al observar el color de la crema, la cantidad, la uniformidad: “Las figuras en la leche no garantizan que el café sea bueno, pero sí refuerzan la experiencia”, incide. Por el olfato, ya que el aroma puede revelar los defectos: “Si hay un exceso de extracción, se perciben notas quemadas. O, al contrario, si ha sido insuficiente, falta aroma”, continúa. Por último, el más evidente: el sabor y su regusto: “Un buen café debe tener equilibrio, dulzor, aroma, acidez y cuerpo”, resume.

World.title: Viaje a la remota isla escocesa de Islay y a la aún más inaccesible Jura, donde Orwell terminó ‘1984′
World.content:
Una escapada entre destilerías, turba y ciervos donde el paisaje se mete en el cuerpo, las canciones guardan la memoria de quienes se fueron y aún parece posible perderse entre acantilados e historias

Cuando George Orwell llegó a la isla escocesa de Jura para aislarse del mundo en 1946, escribió en su diario: “Este es un lugar extremadamente inaccesible”. Basta con intentar llegar hasta su casa en Barnhill para comprender que no exageraba: Jura está al otro lado de Islay y, una vez en esa isla, todavía hay que seguir avanzando hacia el norte por carreteras y caminos que parecen empeñados en devolver al viajero al punto de partida. Tengamos en cuenta este dato: en Jura viven 250 personas y 5.000 ciervos. Jura es la hermana pequeña de Islay, una de las islas más narcóticas de las West Highlands escocesas (las tierras altas del oeste) y donde viven 3.000 personas que gozan del lujo medioambiental yendo a donde el viento quiera, un viento con propiedades altamente saludables, que despeja y ventila como una verdad incómoda y con el que uno acaba empatizando porque, al fin y al cabo, él también parece tener prisa por detenerse a contemplar.

Para llegar hasta estas dos islas de las Hébridas Interiores, lo primero es aterrizar en Glasgow (bendito problema), la ciudad más divertida del Reino Unido, y si hay que pasar la noche, mucho mejor, porque los bares Nice ‘N’ Sleazy y Stereo no cierran nunca.

Más información En la isla de Rügen, un patrimonio entre lo mitológico y lo real

Observando la silueta de Islay por la ventanilla de la avioneta antes del aterrizaje, uno ya intuye que lo mejor será ser presa de la isla, un grano de arena entregado al aislamiento. Islay tiene algo de territorio que se ha quedado al margen por vocación. El mar, el viento y la turba han definido el carácter de las cosas, y hasta el silencio tiene una textura particular. Es una isla de horizontes bajos, carreteras estrechas en las que más de una vez hay que echarse atrás para dejar pasar al que viene, playas que cambian de humor con la marea y pequeños pueblos donde la vida transcurre como debería transcurrir la vida en todas partes. El whisky parece estar flotando en el aire, en las bodegas y en una forma de entender el paisaje. Islay no se visita, se entra en ella para dejarse llevar.

Vista de Portnahaven, un pequeño pueblo situado en el extremo sur de la isla de Islay. Paul Carroll Y Mhairi Carroll (GETTY IMAGES)

Veamos cinco puntos fuertes para hacernos una composición de lugar y extraerle el mayor partido más allá del tópico de las destilerías y apostar por el paisaje, la fauna, el bienestar, la gastronomía y la hospitalidad local.

1. La costa de Islay desde el mar

Una manera de acercarnos a esa hospitalidad de sus gentes y de su territorio es dejar las cosas en el hotel y acudir a la localidad de Port Ellen para sumarse al recorrido en bote de tres horas con comida (inolvidable) incluida de Islay Sea Adventures. El capitán Harold nos recibe empuñando una gaita cuyos fogonazos conmovedores consiguen caldear el viento.

La destilería de whisky Lagavulin, y los restos del castillo Dunyvaig, en la isla de Islay. Patsy Davies (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

Desde el mar se contemplan las tres grandes destilerías del sur —Laphroaig, Lagavulin y Ardbeg— y, delante de cada una, la tripulación sirve un trago de whisky para que cada marca se fije en la memoria con el pegamento de haberla probado allí donde nace. Así continuamos hacia el Área Especial de Conservación de Islay, un espacio protegido al que solo se puede acceder para contemplarlo desde el agua. Mientras los simpáticos patrones van contando historias de la isla, su pasado y su patrimonio, recorremos la costa sudeste, entendiendo uno de sus paisajes más hermosos y también uno de los más ricos en fauna. Aquí vive una importante colonia de focas, además de delicados ciervos rojos que te miran con una pureza con la que mira un niño a su rey mago. Con un poco de suerte, durante la travesía pueden aparecer incluso águilas de cola blanca y delfines.

Parte de la actividad organizada por Islay Sea Adventures consiste en un pícnic de marisco tras un paseo en barco. Ben Shakespeare (Islay Sea Adventures)

El momento más extraordinario llega al alcanzar las aguas tranquilas de los islotes del sudeste de Islay (South-East Islay Skerries), porque es entonces cuando empieza el festival del marisco fresco capturado prácticamente a la puerta de la mesa: del mar al plato apenas hay unos pocos kilómetros. Langosta, bocas de buey de mar, salmón ahumado y, aparte, las vieiras, que son las protagonistas. Porque es un placer ver cómo Harold las cocina a bordo, sobre una barbacoa, con mantequilla, ajo y chile. Se agradecen el pan fresco, la ensalada y las salsas caseras, pero como decoración. Comer así es la experiencia que mejor explica la isla. Ningún folleto, ningún libro, ninguna foto puede superarlo. El único problema de esta actividad puede ser el precio: 115 libras (unos 135 euros, al cambio actual)

2. Vida de isla: tartán, ‘fish and chips’, folclore, Hollywood y Port Charlotte

Con un clima tan contradictorio, en el que un amanecer soleado puede transformarse en cinco minutos en un chubasco pasajero, conviene vestirse correctamente. Se explica así que la lana y el tartán sean tan importantes y se hayan convertido en una de las señas de identidad de las Highlands. Para hacerse una idea de hasta qué punto forman parte de su cultura, merece la pena visitar Islay Woollen Mill, una fábrica con una historia estupenda: allí se diseñó y produjo el tartán utilizado en la película Braveheart. La propia fábrica conserva y comercializa la colección Braveheart y ha trabajado también para otras producciones cinematográficas. El tartán es ese tejido de líneas de distintos colores que se cruzan en ángulo recto formando una trama de cuadros y que acabó convirtiéndose en uno de los signos visuales de Escocia. El que aquí se fabrica lo hemos visto también en Rob Roy, Highlander, Harry Potter (forma parte del uniforme de Hogwarts) e incluso en Forrest Gump, aunque en esta película el tartán juega ya como estampado universal y no tanto como emblema escocés.

El taller de Islay Woollen Mill, que trabaja con los tejidos de forma artesanal. Kenny Lam (VISIT SCOTLAND)

Al hilo de la tradición y para ver esas vestimentas, nada como una noche en el pub del Port Charlotte Hotel, en el pueblo de Port Charlotte, uno de esos rincones dulcemente extendidos frente al mar, reconocibles por sus casas blancas de dos alturas, tan bien conservadas. El local es un punto de reunión donde convergen la nostalgia y la identidad. Su fish and chips es tan interminable como irresistible. La sala tiene el encanto de los negocios eternos que abren fuera de temporada. La cerveza acompaña la llegada de los músicos, que se van sumando como si bajaran a la calle para encontrarse con sus amigos. El fiddle (violín tradicional), el acordeón, las guitarras, las mandolinas y la gaita van llenando el pub de canciones y viejas melodías de las islas, como si cada una trajera consigo un pedazo de memoria o una lágrima que se disuelve en el vaso. Cuando suena Westering Home, no hay nada ni nadie que pueda deshacer el nudo del estómago.

Esas canciones, esa música tradicional gaélica o folk, parecen creadas por la naturaleza, el viento, la lluvia, en ese mar que se lleva a la gente de aquí a probar suerte en otros mundos que difícilmente serán mejores. Y es que cuando uno se va, lo único que de verdad se lleva encima, incrustado, es la música: la canción de cuna que le cantaba su madre, las canciones que moldearon su infancia. Es la prenda mayor.

3. Excursión a Jura

Si Jura no es una isla inventada para perderse, no lo es ninguna. Lo que decíamos antes —250 vecinos rodeados por unos 5.000 ciervos— se comprueba nada más cruzar en ferri el kilómetro —apenas cinco minutos— que separa ambas islas. Bienvenidos a las montañas, las turberas, las costas solitarias y los Paps de Jura, esas tres cumbres que dominan el horizonte como una presencia casi mitológica.

Tres ciervos junto a la costa de la isla escocesa de Jura. Chris Morson (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

Hacia el norte está Barnhill, la remota casa donde George Orwell se refugió para terminar 1984. Pero la historia del escritor británico y Jura había empezado antes. Él y su mujer, Eileen, llevaban tiempo pensando en abandonar Londres y marcharse a las Hébridas. Tanto era así que Orwell ya había iniciado las gestiones para encontrar allí una casa cuando, en marzo de 1945, Eileen murió inesperadamente durante una operación. Tenía 39 años. Orwell se quedó viudo y con Richard, el hijo que ambos habían adoptado pocos meses antes.

Un año después, David Astor, su amigo y editor del periódico The Observer, le sugirió que se marchara a Jura. La familia de Astor tenía propiedades en la isla y conocía Barnhill, una granja aislada en su extremo norte. Orwell llegó en mayo de 1946 y acabó alquilando la casa. Lo que había sido un proyecto compartido con Eileen se convirtió así en su refugio: un lugar donde alejarse de Londres, del periodismo y del ruido del mundo. En Barnhill, sin electricidad, teléfono ni vecinos a mano, encontró el aislamiento que buscaba y terminó escribiendo 1984.

Más amable es la parada en Lussa Gin, donde la ginebra se elabora con botánicos recolectados en la isla. Georgina y Claire nos enseñan su huerto, donde crecen algunos de sus ingredientes: enebro, rosas y tomillo limonero. Allí nos presentan su licor, extraordinariamente botánico, antes de mostrar su nueva creación, una ginebra homenaje a George Orwell llamada Nineteen Eighty Four, con notas de té Assam, cardamomo y rosas. El licor sirve también para hablar del escritor, que nació en la India en junio de 1903, hijo de un funcionario del Imperio británico. Con apenas un año, su madre se lo llevó a Inglaterra. Luego participó en dos guerras, experiencias que acabarían alimentando buena parte de su obra.

Parte del equipo de la destilería Lussa Gin. Lussa Gin

Cuando nos vamos, le digo a Georgina que pensamos comer en The Antlers. Su respuesta llega inmediata:

-Oohh, The Antlers... Desde que abrió, la gente de Jura está más gorda y es más pobre.

Le sobra razón. Esta bakehouse (panadería) roba el corazón hasta a la persona más evitativa con su pastrami y sus sausage rolls (rollos de salchichas). En The Antlers, la gastronomía vuelve a poner los pies en la tierra después de tantas millas de paisaje. En Jura todo parece estar desproporcionado: hay más ciervos que personas, más naturaleza que habitantes y una sensación de espacio que hace que incluso el silencio parezca perdido.

4. El imprescindible paseo al American Monument

Hay que dejar el coche en el aparcamiento de la reserva natural de The Oa, al final de la carretera que atraviesa esta península del sur de Islay. Desde allí comienza el camino hacia el American Monument, un paseo de unos treinta minutos, aunque lo razonable es hacer la ruta circular completa, de unos tres kilómetros y medio, sin ninguna prisa. Y, sobre todo, reservar otra hora para quedarse allí.

El camino es un abrazo constante de la naturaleza: la hierba, el viento del Atlántico, el salitre y esa sensación de ir dejando atrás el mundo... Hasta que aparecen los acantilados, el mar y el monumento, levantado en memoria de los soldados estadounidenses que murieron en los naufragios del Tuscania y el Otranto en 1918, que desde lejos parece suspendido sobre el océano.

El faro de Carraig Fhada, situado en la isla de Islay, es un faro emblemático en forma de torre cuadrada. Catherine Gilbrook (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

Hay algo de templo en este lugar: un santuario sin techo ante el que uno acaba pidiendo deseos al mar, como quien deja una ofrenda y confía en que alguien, o algo, se encargará de ella. Y luego está el viento, que aquí parece tener permiso para hacer lo que quiera. Empuja, despeina, zarandea, te da la vuelta y te hace gritar al vacío. Un grito que mezcla la alegría y el dolor, la satisfacción de estar allí y la emoción que uno carga.

Después de este paseo solo quedan dos opciones: volver al whisky o entregarse al hotel. La primera pasa por Bowmore, una de las destilerías históricas de Islay, fundada en 1779 y una de las más antiguas de Escocia. Está a orillas del Loch Indaal y conserva uno de los elementos que mejor explican su carácter: sus almacenes de maduración, algunos de ellos situados prácticamente al nivel del mar. Aquí el whisky sigue teniendo algo de paisaje: turba, agua, sal y años de espera convertidos en una bebida.

La segunda opción es bastante más peligrosa para el presupuesto: irse al hotel, pero, en fin, tampoco todos los días se despierta uno en Islay.

5. The Machrie, un hotel convertido en galería

El hotel The Machrie está frente al Atlántico, entre dunas y junto a una playa de siete millas, pero quizás lo más sorprendente está dentro. La colección de arte, reunida y comisariada por su fundadora, Sue Nye, convierte el alojamiento en una especie de galería habitada: las obras aparecen en los pasillos, las habitaciones, el restaurante, la recepción o el gimnasio. Hay artistas escoceses como John Bellany, Pat Douthwaite, Peter Howson o Elizabeth Blackadder, junto a nombres como Tracey Emin, Antony Gormley, Peter Blake, Picasso, Miró, Dalí o Banksy. El arte forma parte de la vida cotidiana.

El hotel y campo de golf The Machrie. KEVIN MURRAY (THE MACHRIE)

Y luego está el paisaje, la ubicación. The Machrie recibe también a muchos jugadores de golf, que encuentran aquí un tapete verde frente al Atlántico. Para quien disfrute dándole a una pelota con un palo y persiguiéndola después por la hierba, probablemente no se pueda pedir más. Para los demás siempre queda sentarse frente al mar. Porque las vistas de la hierba y el océano son de esas que consiguen que uno se quede un rato sin hacer absolutamente nada. Uno mira cómo el viento mueve la hierba y cómo la isla continúa con su vida. Quizá ese sea el lujo verdadero de The Machrie. Y, puestos a confesarlo todo, quizá también el único que importa, junto a la poesía, porque ante este paisaje por fuerza vuelven a la cabeza aquellos versos de Wislawa Szymborska: “Comprendo que mi tristeza no frenará la hierba. Si los tallos vacilan será sólo por el viento”.

World.title: Midterm melee: Americans in the Netherlands gear up to vote
World.content:
Americans living abroad can often feel like they’re stuck on the political sidelines of their native land. With one of the most contentious midterm elections in US history coming up next month, we spoke with the Netherlands’ American community about how they’re getting involved in the race and the challenges they face.

For the past two years, Donald Trump has dominated headlines around the world. It seems like there’s little the divisive president and his administration haven’t disrupted within and well beyond US borders.

There’s no denying that much is riding on the country’s midterms on November 3 and that the result will have a defining impact on the course of global politics over the next few years.

As with prior elections, Americans living in the Netherlands may feel there’s little they can do besides mail in their absentee ballots – and even that is an often complicated process that many fail to complete.

Each state sets its own deadlines and decides whether ballots can go back by email, fax or post. A ballot posted from the Netherlands also has to cross the Atlantic in time to be counted.

Some don’t bother at all, and some feel they shouldn’t. “One of the reasons why many in the Netherlands don’t vote is because they’ve been here for a very long time,” said Tre’ Shawn Griffin-Noordermeer, vice chair of the Netherlands chapter of Democrats Abroad. “They feel like they shouldn’t be voting because they’ve lived outside the US for so long.”

In fact, federal law lets US citizens abroad keep voting in federal elections in the state where they last lived, however long they have been away.

To help get that message out, various groups here have been volunteering and hosting events in the days leading up to the midterms.

Reaching out to voters

Members of campaign group Democrats Abroad in the Netherlands have spent recent weeks running an email campaign and arranging “Vote From Abroad” gatherings on Zoom.

They’ve also been hosting lunches and other events in cities around the country to discuss the midterms along with putting up fliers and getting the word out on social media and via phone banking.

“We’ve got hundreds of volunteers here in the Netherlands who have been helping with this,” Griffin-Noordermeer told Dutch News. “A few weekends ago, we called over 13,000 people.”

Originally founded in 1964, Democrats Abroad serves as the Democratic party’s official organisation for American citizens living overseas. One of its primary tasks is encouraging its members and other voters, who are spread across 197 countries, to cast their ballots.

And that’s more difficult than it might seem.

Counting the voters

Nobody knows exactly how many Americans in the Netherlands can vote. The US does not require citizens to register with the government when they move abroad, and some states drop overseas voters from their rolls when they stop responding to election mail. That leaves neither the State Department nor voter lists with a reliable count.

The national statistics office CBS puts the number of US nationals living in the Netherlands at just over 27,000 in 2026 – though not all are old enough to vote, and Dutch-Americans with both passports are counted as Dutch, so aren’t included.

Worldwide, about 2.2 million Americans of voting age live abroad, according to the Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP), the US defence department office that helps military and overseas citizens vote. FVAP estimates only about 11% of them voted in the 2024 presidential election. Even fewer typically take part in midterms.

FVAP says 14.8% of eligible voters in Europe voted in 2024.

Preparing for the worst

Despite Trump’s low approval ratings, the path to a “blue wave” for the Democrats won’t necessarily be an easy one.

His administration also continues to meddle with the midterms. In August, the Pentagon, which runs FVAP, made last-minute changes to the Federal Post Card Application (the form overseas voters use to register and request ballots), removing the checkbox for US citizens who were born abroad and have never lived in the US. The Democratic National Committee has gone to court over the change.

That followed a March 2025 executive order in which Trump sought to add proof-of-citizenship requirements to the same form, parts of which federal courts have blocked. The order also aimed to stop states counting mail ballots that arrive after Election Day.

In June, the US Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that states can keep counting ballots postmarked by Election Day that arrive later. That matters for voters whose ballots travel by international post.

Hayley Hughes, the co-founder of the Netherlands chapter of Indivisible, admitted she’s worried about how things might go.

She has already had discussions with the leads of other chapters about what to do if the administration interferes with ballot counts or sends government agents to polling stations.

Trump has said Republicans should “take over the voting” in at least 15 places, and his former adviser Steve Bannon has welcomed the idea of immigration agents at the polls.

“We’re already thinking we might have to mobilise,” Hughes told Dutch News.

“We’re looking at a protest here that week, if needed. In the US, there could be a mass mobilisation of peaceful protests and a general strike where people don’t go to work or school. We all hope that won’t be needed.”

The week of the midterms

Several midterm events are scheduled for the week of the elections. The Atlantische Commissie in The Hague is hosting an “American midterm election breakfast” on 4 November.

In Amsterdam, the commission is also helping with the John Adams Institute’s “Midterm Madness” event on November 6. It’s set to serve as an afterparty with a ‘festival-style experience’ featuring live music along with discussions and lectures about the results featuring Mark Leibovich, a staff writer at The Atlantic, and others.

Comedian Greg Shapiro is once again teaming up with Pep Rosenfeld for an Election Night Party at Boom Chicago. They’ve hosted these events since the ‘00s and are once again prepared to stay up late. The comedy club has vowed to remain open past 4:00 “if things get crazy.”

“How late, well, we’ll wait and see,” Shapiro told Dutch News. “I’ve got performances the next day. At some point I’ll have to get some sleep.”

Shapiro will be taking a break from his ongoing ‘KING ME: 250 Years of Donald Trump’ comedy tour for the Boom Chicago gathering. He’s worried about how much rewriting he’ll have to do for subsequent performances after the midterms.

“There’s no telling what could happen,” he said. “It could become January 6th on a national scale.”

If you’re an American living overseas and haven’t voted yet, there could still be time based on where you’re registered. Visit votefromabroad.org for further assistance.

World.title: US ambassador to the NL gave $1m to Trump ballroom
World.content:
The US ambassador to the Netherlands, Joe Popolo, donated $1 million towards president Donald Trump’s new White House ballroom, according to a leaked list of project donors.

The Washington Post, which obtained the list, said the gift was made late last year, around two months after the businessman was appointed ambassador. Popolo declined to comment further to the paper.

The list runs to the end of September and records 67 donations of $10,000 or more, with a total of $333 million pledged. Tech, AI and arms manufacturers made up a large share of the donors. Some, who asked to stay anonymous, accounted for $77 million.

According to the paper, about half of the money came from companies or individuals with business before the federal government. Democratic politicians had previously asked for the donor list without success.

The fund managing the money agreed with the government not to reveal the identities of its backers, which US non-profits are generally not required to do.

Trump said last year the ballroom would be paid for entirely by himself and a few friends, but the list shows no contribution from the president. The Washington Post reported earlier this year that half the construction costs, now estimated at $600 million, are being met from public funds.

The White House snubbed the criticism, saying the same critics would complain if taxpayers were paying for the renovations.

The ballroom, which the president says will hold nearly 1,000 guests, is being built on the site of the White House east wing, which Trump had demolished last year. The plans include a military bunker underneath.
