World.title: Menopause is normal, suffering through it shouldn't be
World.content:
Is menopause in women treatable?

Indian Journal of Preventive & Social Medicine

Menopause can bring a range of physical, emotional and urogenital symptoms, affecting womenâs sleep, mood and everyday lives.

When menopause symptoms are dismissed as âjust ageingâ

Treatment options for menopause range from hormone therapy and non-hormonal medicines to lifestyle changes

Menopause Symptoms Experienced by Women in India,

The doctorâs dilemma: recognising symptoms, choosing treatment

Is Indiaâs healthcare system prepared for menopause?

Treatments available in India

How social stigma plays a role

Dr Soy talks to TOI

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

She lies awake at night. The next morning, she struggles to concentrate at work, snaps at loved ones over things that never bothered her before, or wonders why her own body suddenly feels unfamiliar.For some women, menopause arrives quietly; for others, it brings a wave of physical and emotional changes that can leave them exhausted, anxious and searching for answers.And often, the hardest part is not just dealing with the symptoms, but getting someone to take them seriously.Menopause is a natural biological transition, but the symptoms can be disruptive enough to affect everyday life. While some women dismiss them as stress or ageing, others find their concerns brushed aside or are unsure where to turn for help. Despite growing conversations around women's health, gaps in awareness, medical guidance and access to appropriate treatment continue to shape their experiences.A quantitative descriptive survey involving 150 women from urban areas assessed the impact of menopausal symptoms on quality of life. The study, published in the, was authored by Somibala Thokchom and David Ratna Paul Talagathoti.Participants aged 40 to 55 years completed the 11-item Menopause Rating Scale (MRS) to assess their symptoms and a modified 32-item Menopause-Specific Quality of Life Questionnaire (MENQOL) to evaluate how menopause affected their daily lives.The study found that 58.7% of participants were aged 40â45 years, while 75.3% had already experienced menopause. Overall, 92% reported moderate to severe symptoms, 4.7% experienced mild symptoms and 3.3% reported very severe symptoms. Nearly all participants (99.3%) reported changes in their daily routines.Although the findings cannot be generalised to all Indian women, given the small, urban sample, they highlight the potential impact of menopause on everyday life.The question is not simply how women experience menopause, but why so many may struggle to recognise their symptoms, seek medical advice or access appropriate care.Many women continue to experience menopause symptoms without seeking medical help, often assuming that fatigue, anxiety, disturbed sleep and mood changes are an inevitable part of ageing.Doctors say this can delay assessment and treatment, particularly when women prioritise family and work responsibilities over their own health.âMenopause is a natural condition, but that does not necessarily imply that symptoms cannot be treated,â said Dr Mitul Gupta, senior consultant, obstetrics and gynaecology, Cocoon Hospital, Jaipur.Dr Gupta cautioned against attributing symptoms to ageing without proper examination. Fatigue, irritability and poor concentration can also occur with conditions such as thyroid disorders, anaemia, sleep disorders and anxiety, making a detailed medical assessment important.Maya, a Uttar Pradesh native who now lives in Delhi, said, âI started experiencing menopause when I was 51. I did face difficulties, but back then, we didnât really talk about these things at home. I used to feel hesitant."âI thought it was just a normal part of aging, and no one in my family really knew what I was going through. Even today, many families are unaware of what women experience during menopause, and often, women end up dealing with it on their own,â she adds.Menopause care extends beyond irregular periods and hot flashes. Hormonal changes can affect sleep, mood and sexual health, while the menopausal transition is also an important time to discuss longer-term health concerns, including bone health.A systematic review titledexamined 23 studies reporting symptoms among menopausal women in India. The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and included eligibility criteria, a literature search, screening and data extraction.The review found that somatic symptoms were the most frequently reported category, with an average of 73.66% across the studies. Joint and muscular pain and fatigue were the most commonly reported complaints, followed by hot flashes.Psychological symptoms were reported in an average of 63.03% of women in the studies assessing this category. Eighteen studies reported psychosomatic symptoms, while five did not report psychological symptoms.Urogenital symptoms were reported in 13 studies, with an average prevalence of 51.40%. Ten studies did not report symptoms in this category. Although urogenital symptoms were the least frequently reported, the review noted that women who experienced them reported greater symptom intensity.The findings highlight the range of symptoms associated with menopause and the importance of recognising them rather than dismissing them as an unavoidable consequence of ageing. The percentages are averages reported across the reviewed studies and should not be interpreted as prevalence estimates for all Indian women.Menopause symptoms can vary considerably from one woman to another, making individual assessment essential before deciding on treatment.Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) can help women experiencing troublesome symptoms, including hot flashes and night sweats, but it is not suitable for everyone. Decisions about treatment must take into account an individual's symptoms, medical history, age, time since menopause and potential risks.âHRT is neither universally dangerous nor suitable for everyone. The right treatment is the one that is carefully chosen according to your individual needs, with proper medical guidance and regular follow-up,â said Dr Bharti Soy, consultant, obstetrics and gynaecology, Fortis O.P. Jindal Hospital & Research Centre.Doctors emphasise that consultations should cover the potential benefits and risks of hormone therapy, as well as non-hormonal alternatives where appropriate. Women should be able to discuss their concerns and make informed decisions with their healthcare providers.Symptoms should not automatically be attributed to menopause, as other medical conditions may require separate investigation and treatment. A thorough consultation can help distinguish between menopause-related changes and other possible causes, allowing care to be tailored to the individual's needs.Awareness alone may not be enough if women cannot access appropriate and affordable care. Gaps in menopause-specific knowledge, counselling and healthcare access can leave women without adequate guidance on managing their symptoms.The challenge is not limited to the availability of gynaecologists, but also whether consultations address menopause-related concerns beyond menstrual changes. Symptoms affecting sleep, mood, sexual wellbeing and bone health may require a broader discussion of a woman's physical and emotional health.âWomen need a complete evaluation not a consultation for the issues related to menstruation,â said Dr Priyanka Sharma, senior consultant, obstetrics and gynaecology, Cocoon Hospital, Chandigarh.Barriers such as the cost of travel, time away from work, lack of awareness and limited access to healthcare facilities can make seeking care more difficult. Strengthening primary-level assessment, training healthcare workers and establishing referral pathways could help women receive appropriate support.Education in local languages and more affordable treatment options are also important to ensure that women can understand their symptoms, discuss available choices and access care when needed.Making menopause a routine part of women's healthcare could help shift the focus from simply enduring symptoms to identifying and managing them appropriately.Medical care is only part of the picture. Family attitudes and social expectations can influence whether women feel comfortable discussing menopause or seeking help.âIn many Indian households, menopause is still not discussed openly because of social stigma, lack of awareness, and the belief that it is simply a natural process. As a result, many women suffer silently rather than seeking medical help,â said Dr Bharti Soy.When symptoms such as disturbed sleep, irritability or discomfort are dismissed as inevitable consequences of growing older, women may begin to question whether their concerns deserve medical attention.âIf relatives tell her that discomfort, irritability or sleep problems are simply part of growing older, she may question whether her concerns deserve medical attention,â said Dr Swati Sinha, senior consultant, obstetrics and gynaecology, Rosewalk by Rainbow Hospitals.Families can help by making menopause a subject that can be discussed without embarrassment or judgement. Listening without dismissing symptoms, offering practical support and encouraging medical consultations when problems affect daily life can make the transition easier to navigate.Partners, children and other family members need not have all the answers. Understanding that menopause affects women differently, and that help is available when symptoms become disruptive, is an important first step.Menopause may be a natural stage of life, but that does not mean women should have to endure its more difficult symptoms without support. Better awareness, informed medical consultations, accessible treatment and understanding families can help ensure that women are heard and their concerns taken seriously.

World.title: The Dimple factor: Can she crack BJP's women-voter fortress & deliver UP to Akhilesh?
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Like many women who marry into political families,

âs entry into politics was more a matter of circumstance than choice. She made her electoral debut in 2009 after her husband,

chief

, vacated the Firozabad Lok Sabha seat, choosing to retain Kannauj after contesting from both constituencies.

Despite a star-studded campaign, Dimple lost to Congress candidate Raj Babbar. Since then, however, she has contested five Lok Sabha elections, winning four.

Yet, her electoral record did little to dispel the perception that she was a relatively passive player in politics. Within the Samajwadi Party, she was seen as a low-profile figure who complemented her husband from the background. In Parliament, she was often spotted sitting behind Akhilesh, thumping her desk in support of his speeches.

For years, Dimple appeared unable (or perhaps unwilling) to step out of her husbandâs political shadow.

That may now be changing.

With the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections approaching, Dimple, who has largely accompanied Akhilesh at party meetings and public gatherings, has been entrusted with an independent political responsibility. The move signals a possible shift in her role as Akhilesh prepares for another bid to return to power at 5, Kalidas Marg, after a decade out of office.





From Akhileshâs shadow to SPâs second-in-command

Ahead of the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections, Dimple Yadav is stepping into a more prominent role in the Samajwadi Party. Since Mulayam Singh Yadavâs death in 2022 and the decline of Shivpal Yadavâs influence within the party, she has increasingly emerged as one of its most visible campaigners and a key figure in its leadership.

During the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, Dimple addressed rallies across more than a dozen constituencies.

She also retained Mainpuri, the family stronghold, by a margin of nearly two lakh votes. Her media appearances and social media presence have grown considerably, reflecting a more assertive public role than in the past.

Her growing political visibility has extended beyond election campaigns. During the protests over the NEET paper leak in June and July, she emerged at the forefront of the partyâs outreach to student protesters.

She also led delegations to meet climate activist Sonam Wangchuk during his hunger strike, expressing support for his demands.

On July 20, she joined the student-led âSansad Chaloâ protest in New Delhi and was seen tending to injured students after clashes with Delhi Police.

While Akhilesh was inside Parliament, Dimple was out on the streets.

She has also become a more vocal representative of the partyâs position on issues ranging from womenâs safety to the alleged embezzlement of donations made to Ayodhyaâs Ram temple.

Both inside and outside the Lok Sabha, she has sharpened her attacks on the BJP, challenging its claims on governance and social justice.

Dimple has also accused the BJP of deliberately delaying the implementation of womenâs reservation, despite Parliament passing the legislation in 2023.

âWhen the Bill was tabled in 2023, all political parties supported it and it was passed, which explains that the opposition was in no way against the Bill.

If the BJPâs sole intention was reservation to women, they would have implemented the Bill passed in 2023,â she said.

âThey have other motives behind moving the amendment Bill,â the Mainpuri MP added.

Her latest initiative is the proposed Stri Samman Samriddhi Yojana, a scheme aimed at the economic and social empowerment of women that the Samajwadi Party says it will introduce if voted to power in 2027. The proposal promises eligible women an annual payment of Rs 40,000.

âWomenâs power will develop not merely by talking about it, but by giving women true representation. Respect and prosperity of every woman included in the PDA as âAadhi Abadiâ (women) is our resolve,â Dimple said.

âShe deserves respect simply because she is a woman. Social empowerment and strengthening her position require respect even before prosperity,â she added.

The announcement also places the Samajwadi Party in direct competition with the BJP over women-focused welfare.

It came amid reports that the Yogi Adityanath government was considering a direct cash-transfer scheme offering women Rs 50,000.

Why Akhilesh needs Dimple

The PDA formula â Pichada, Dalit, Alpasankhyak (backward classes, Dalits and minorities) â helped the Samajwadi Party stage a remarkable comeback in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections.

After winning just five of Uttar Pradeshâs 80 seats in 2019, the party secured 37 in 2024, emerging as the stateâs largest party in the Lok Sabha.

It expanded beyond its traditional Muslim-Yadav support base by fielding candidates from non-Yadav OBC and Dalit communities.

But replicating that success in an assembly election will require more than maintaining caste arithmetic. As Akhilesh prepares for the high-stakes polls scheduled for early 2027, he is looking to preserve the partyâs momentum and widen its appeal further. Women, who cut across caste and religious boundaries, are central to that effort.

The scale of the opportunity is considerable. Women account for 45.46% of Uttar Pradeshâs electorate, with 6,09,09,525 registered voters, according to the figures cited by the stateâs electoral authorities.

They have also consistently turned out in greater numbers than men in recent elections. In the 2022 Assembly polls, womenâs turnout stood at around 62.2%, compared with 59.6% among men. The pattern continued in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, when turnout among women was 57.22%, against 56.46% among men.

Yet women voters have historically been a weak spot for the Samajwadi Party.

According to the Lokniti-CSDS post-poll survey for the 2022 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections, the BJP enjoyed a 13-percentage-point lead over the SP-Rashtriya Lok Dal alliance among women voters.

The BJP has also repeatedly invoked the law-and-order record of previous SP governments to portray the party as insensitive to womenâs safety.

Recalling the period before 2017, chief minister Yogi Adityanath said during a public address in Gorakhpur: âA saying had become popular: âDekh Sapayi, bitiya ghabrayiâ.â

He alleged that criminals and strongmen under the then government had created an atmosphere of fear, leaving families worried about their daughtersâ safety.

This is where Dimple could prove politically valuable.

Her growing prominence gives the Samajwadi Party a recognisable woman leader who can take its PDA pitch beyond caste coalitions and make aadhi abadi â women, or half the population â a more visible part of its political strategy.

She can serve as the face of its outreach to women, amplify its welfare promises and challenge the BJPâs claim to be the more women-friendly party.

She also offers the SP a way to counter its longstanding image problem on law and order. Unlike the partyâs male leadership, which continues to face the BJPâs allegations of mafia-gunda raj, Dimple has no comparable political baggage. Her public persona is less confrontational, potentially allowing the party to project a more measured and inclusive image without abandoning its attacks on the ruling party.

Her role could also help the SP challenge the BJP on womenâs representation and welfare on more equal political terms.

Rather than relying solely on Akhilesh to make the case, the party now has a prominent woman leader with electoral credibility, national visibility and a place within its inner circle.

Dimpleâs Rajput background could offer another avenue for outreach beyond the partyâs traditional support base.

Whether that translates into wider support among Rajputs, however, remains uncertain.

Poll Vote & Share your view Which issue should Dimple Yadav prioritize to appeal to women voters? Women's safety. Economic empowerment. Political representation. Education and employment opportunities. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

How an SP win could reshape Dimpleâs role

A return to power in Uttar Pradesh could further transform Dimpleâs position, both within the Samajwadi Party and in national politics.

If Akhilesh becomes chief minister, Dimple could assume a more substantial role in Parliament and potentially take on greater responsibility for coordinating the partyâs parliamentary strategy.

A stronger organisational position could also put her at the centre of the SPâs outreach to women and communities beyond its traditional support base.

Such a shift would mark a significant departure from the role she occupied for much of her political career: a low-profile MP whose public identity was closely tied to her husbandâs.

But greater visibility does not automatically translate into electoral gains. Dimpleâs prominence could help the SP soften its image, challenge the BJPâs women-centric welfare politics and give its promises on representation and economic empowerment a more credible public face.

Whether she can materially alter voting patterns, however, remains an open question.

Uttar Pradesh is expected to vote in February-March 2027 to elect a 403-member assembly, though the Election Commission has yet to announce the official schedule.

In the 2022 assembly elections, the BJP won 255 seats, securing a second consecutive term in power. The BJP-led NDA won 273 seats, while the Samajwadi Party secured 111, a significant improvement on its tally of 47 in 2017.

The Congress was reduced to just two seats, down from seven in the previous election.

For Akhilesh, the next election will be a test of whether the coalition he built in 2024 can be sustained and expanded. For Dimple, it could be an opportunity to establish herself as more than a trusted political companion and emerge as an independent force in the partyâs bid for power.

World.title: Sudden rain, poor crowd management likely led to Kolkata Durga Puja stampede: What we know so far
World.content:
Locals blame sudden rain, narrow space and lack of police personnel for stampede

High-level committee reviews pandals

7 arrested

Victims' bodies handed over to kin

12 patients stable

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Amit Shah visits injured

NEW DELHI: At least 19 people died and 25 others were injured in a stampede at Kolkata's Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal on Saturday evening.The stampede occurred after a sudden downpour triggered a crowd surge, with hundreds of visitors rushing into the pandal for shelter and trapping those already inside.West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari blamed the incident on the organisers' callousness and appealed to puja committees across Kolkata to adopt safety measures.âItâs a painful incident and extremely heartbreaking,â Adhikari said.âAs per initial information received, the incident happened due to an announcement made by the puja committee. Right now our priority is to treat the 25 people who have been injured. Among them, 24 are stable but one is critical. We are standing by the affected families. The Chorbagan puja pandal has been handed over to forensic teams, STF and fire brigade,â he added.Here's what we know so far about the incident.Locals, who were among the first responders, said sudden rainfall, narrow lanes, a heavy rush of visitors and a lack of adequate volunteers and police personnel for crowd management contributed to the stampede.They said heavy rain forced people inside the pandal to wait for the weather to improve, while visitors outside grew restless and tried to rush into the already crowded marquee.Pramod Gupta, who lives near the Chorbagan puja pandal on Radha Madhav Lane, said the queue of visitors to the marquee had stretched to Mahatma Gandhi Road, about 700 metres away."Everything was fine till the rain started," he told news agency PTI."Standing in front of my house, I could hear screams as people rushed out. I and my daughters helped four girls and asked them to stay in our house till the situation eased," he said.Locals also said narrow lanes and a lack of police personnel and volunteers inside the pandal hampered the swift rescue of the injured."Ambulances could not reach the spot, and the injured had to be carried out to the main thoroughfare some distance away," a woman told PTI."We started the rescue work by breaking the bamboo structures and barricades of the pandal," another local man alleged.A high-level committee formed to review safety arrangements at major Durga Puja marquees across West Bengal began visiting community puja pandals on Sunday.The panel includes disaster management secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh and director general of fire services Anuj Sharma.The panel members will visit several crowd-puller Durga Puja pandals across Kolkata to review safety and security norms and crowd management plans, sources told PTI.The administration has stressed the need for wider exit points, adequate lighting and the removal of bottlenecks caused by temporary rope enclosures.Kolkata Police have arrested seven people, including organisers of the Chorbagan Durga Puja, a senior officer said.Police have also registered a suo motu case of culpable homicide not amounting to murder."We have arrested seven people. They were among the 14 detained last night. More arrests may be made," the IPS officer told PTI."Rajkumar Seoda and Shantanu Dubey were the secretary and vice-president, respectively, of the Chorbagan Puja committee. Biplab Mukhopadhyay was responsible for installing the bamboo structure at the pandal, while Kaushik Saha and Pintu De were in charge of crowd management," the officer said.Those arrested include the puja committee's secretary and vice-president, as well as two employees of a private security agency, among others, he said.Authorities handed over the bodies of those killed in the stampede to their family members on Sunday.Among the victims was a 27-year-old nurse whose mortal remains were taken to her native place in Hooghly. Her relative told news agency ANI that she had gone to the pandal after completing her duty."After doing her duty, she went to watch the puja (worship/festival) with her friend," he said.The West Bengal government has announced compensation of Rs 25 lakh and a job for the family of each deceased person. The Special Task Force (STF) has also initiated an investigation to establish accountability.Twelve of the 14 patients admitted to Apollo Hospital in Salt Lake following the stampede are stable, with most expected to be discharged on Monday, Dr Narayan Banerjee said.Providing an update on the patients' condition, Dr Banerjee told ANI that five were in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), while the remaining patients were being treated in the ward. He added that two patients continued to require closer monitoring.âAmit Shah ji came; it's a very good thing because the government has done whatever is possible. Except for two patients, all the others are stable. Of the 14 patients admitted, five are in the ICU, and the rest are in the ward," Dr Banerjee said."I think most of them will be discharged tomorrow, and a few who require surgery will remain here. Except for one patient who has a fractured pelvis and urethra, the others do not have very serious injuries or internal injuries so far. A young child, aged 13, was also admitted. She is fine,â he added.Union home minister Amit Shah and Suvendu Adhikari visited the injured undergoing treatment at Apollo Hospital earlier on Sunday.Shah had earlier expressed condolences to the families of those killed, describing the stampede as âextremely distressingâ. He also said he had spoken to Adhikari to take stock of the situation.Following the incident, Kolkata Police imposed prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, in parts of the city from October 18 to October 20 to maintain law and order and prevent untoward incidents.The order was issued amid concerns over possible demonstrations, rallies and meetings that could affect public order and safety.

World.title: Gwalior temple tragedy: CM Mohan Yadav orders removal of City SP, suspension of 8 others after 14 killed
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

Mohan Yadav on Sunday ordered the removal of Gwaliorâs City SP and eight others over alleged negligence that left 14 dead and 28 injured as a truck rammed into the devotees in a temple.

âInstructions have been issued to immediately remove the CSP from his post and suspend three station house officers, one traffic inspector, one head constable, and three constables,â Yadav said in a post on X.

Around 1.30 am on Sunday, a truck, with a Punjab registration number, entered the prohibited zone near a slope on Chinor Road and ran over devotees outside the Sheetla Mata temple, in Gwalior district, eventually ramming into its entrance gate.

14 people were killed in the incident; 28 were injured, with seven in critical condition, officials said, as per PTI. Two police personnel were also among the injured.

A wall of the temple reportedly collapsed under the impact of the collision.

The impact caused a temple wall to collapse, trapping people beneath the debris. The bodies of the deceased and the injured were taken to various hospitals, including the trauma centre in Gwalior.





"The accident occurred because the truck entered a prohibited area," Yadav told reporters in Indore, PTI reported.

The CM also ordered a detailed investigation into the incident to find those responsible and ensure strict action against the guilty.
