World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] China’s envoy: Sounds like a threat, walks like a threat
World.content:
The reality on the ground and at sea is that a 'peace-loving' China can still inflict harm — economically and physically

Since 2026, the Chinese embassy in Manila has made it normal to issue strong, sometimes incendiary, statements against Philippine agencies and officials, including the nationally-elected kind. It’s language that has teetered close to gutter-level, particularly when it’s the exchanges between its deputy spokesperson Guo Wei and Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela, who speaks for the Philippine Coast Guard on the West Philippine Sea.

Yet it was still quite surprising — even if it was arguably expected — for Beijing’s top diplomat in the Philippines, Ambassador Jing Quan, to say the Philippines “should feel fortunate” that China doesn’t use force in its maritime disputes. If it did, the veteran diplomat said, “we may easily win.”

“But no, we will not choose to use force. We love peace,” he told reporters on October 15, on the sidelines of a forum.

Jing went on to mention regions in the world — Gaza and Venezuela — where conflicts launched by Israel and the United States, respectively, have triggered instability in the region. The ambassador conveniently left out two other major conflicts in the world: the Israel and US war on Iran, and Russia’s war on Ukraine.

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), in a rare strongly-worded but terse statement, chastised Jing for his remarks.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is expected to summon the Chinese envoy for the second time in less than a year over the same remarks, which he characterized as a “threat.”

The Chinese embassy has pushed back against the DFA through a statement and against Marcos through a vaguely-worded tweet (“Is this a threat?” to caption a longer clip of the chance interview with the media).

In the five-minute interview, Jing goes on about the importance of dialogue in Asia, including within Southeast Asia, which is negotiating a South China Sea code with China.

But the minutes preceding and succeeding that one line about the use of force doesn’t really take away from how out-of-pocket it was — to insist that Manila should be grateful that its superpower neighbor “loves” peace because, if it did not, it would handily win.

Because the reality on the ground and at sea is that a “peace-loving” China can still inflict harm — economically and physically. Filipino personnel have been injured, to varying degrees, from the water cannons the China Coast Guard (CCG) uses to drive away maritime missions to key features in the West Philippine Sea.

Literal blood has been shed by soldiers inadvertently injured during confrontations — a finger was severed in Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal in June 2024, and one soldier sustained a head injury just in July 2026. Earlier in October, the medical evacuation of a soldier with appendicitis took 10 hours because the CCG insisted on their way of doing things during the mission.

Fisherfolk in Zambales, Palawan, and other fishing communities that have historically relied on the West Philippine Sea speak of dwindling catches or the lack of any opportunity to fish at all.

During embeds in Navy warships on West Philippine Sea missions, I’ve come to almost expect the presence of a Chinese navy warship. I have to actively remind myself that while this has become the norm, it should not be accepted as such.

Such is the “reset” that Marcos signalled and Filipino diplomats have aspired for since the beginning of 2026.

The information ecosystem when it comes to discussions on the West Philippine Sea and the disputes between the Philippines and China is, no doubt, full of noise — many of it the manufactured kind that’s designed to obfuscate from the facts on hand.

Information and influence operations want to wear down the Filipino soldier and civilian’s spirit to wanting to defend what is the Filipinos’ by spotlighting Chinese narratives: that resistance is futile, or that it’s a binary choice between war and peace.

I sometimes find myself having to discern whether a statement from either the embassy or a Philippine government official ought to be highlighted and amplified. He-said-he-said and tits-for-tats are easy and fun to draw out, sure. But they don’t always help readers make sense of what’s going on between the two countries in terms of maritime, political, or diplomatic issues.

Recently, journalism students interviewed me for a school project. At one point, they asked me: How do you sift through the noise in diplomacy when, in some cases, either side has their own truth that they want amplified?

The answer can be simple, I told them. You go back to what international law, including the 2016 Arbitral Award, says. In reconstructing events that are not available for the public or even journalists to see, you talk to the widest range of sources, including those who could be adversarial to your personal beliefs.

You probe, you ask — and then you second-guess yourself. Rinse, repeat.

In conversations with sources, there have been worries that, in all the noise, advocates and experts — even the most earnest ones — are in danger of losing the plot.

The burden then falls onto the bureaucrats, the credentialed experts, and journalists who’ve done their homework to sift through propaganda, spin, and political noise, and stay laser-focused on key truths: that Manila must defend its entitlements and claims in the West Philippine Sea while also trying to keep okay ties with a sometimes-renegade Beijing.

For the military, that means keeping vigilant, especially with the 2028 presidential elections forthcoming, while still keeping itself free of partisan and electoral politicking. It means amping up its external defense posture, which, 15 years since the revised AFP modernization act, means focusing on logistics and supply chains. What good are new and shiny military toys when there’s little space to service them?

We recently published a two-part report on the military’s modernization and defense self-reliance efforts. Because as we keep close track of both escalating rhetoric and confrontations in the West Philippine Sea, it’s important to keep an eye on how the Philippines’ maritime frontliners are preparing for any and all eventualities, including scenarios they would never wish on themselves.

(If you want access to more exclusive content and briefings on security affairs, you can sign up to Rappler+, our membership program.)

World.title: Zelenskyy criticizes Trump’s waiver of sanctions on Russia as ‘wrong’
World.content:
TRUMP AND PUTIN. File photo shows US President Donald Trump and Russia's President Vladimir Putin during the G20 leaders summit in Buenos Aires, Argentina on November 30, 2018.

WASHINGTON DC, USA – US President Donald Trump‘s decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday, October 17, predicting even more US sanctions relief.

“The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me,” Zelenskyy wrote on X. “It definitely helps only the Russians.”

An executive order issued by Trump on Friday night, October 16, waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs — including duties on the country’s goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas — that had been scheduled to start next week under the legislation known as the Graham Act that he signed into law last month.

Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the US

The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming toward Moscow while publicly criticizing Zelenskyy, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.

Zelenskyy said Trump’s latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin.

“It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people,” wrote Zelenskyy, who said Russia struck more than 15 Ukrainian power generation and transmission sites on Friday. “This certainly does not stop the war.”

The Ukrainian leader accused Russia of planning to ramp up strikes in western Ukraine. “Is Russia preparing for this? I think so,” Zelenskyy wrote.

Russian envoy praises waiver

Russia’s investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, called the Trump waiver “a truly historic moment,” posting on X on Friday that had the penalties taken effect, they could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a halt.

Weeks before US midterm elections in which Trump’s Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked further raising oil prices as Americans face increased costs largely attributed to the US-Israeli war with Iran, analysts have said.

Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.

The legislation’s primary backer in Congress was the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican. It would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.

Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to fill his Senate seat after he died in July, and Trump endorsed her for a full term heading into the midterm elections. At a campaign stop on Saturday, she did not directly criticize Trump for waiving sanctions, but she said she would not have made that choice.

“Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia,” she told reporters, according to multiple news outlets. “Because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia.”

China and India, which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, however, had raised concerns about the Graham Act.

Beijing has said it “consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law” while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties.

But the Graham Act also allows the president to waive sanctions by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest. Friday’s executive order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that “further action is appropriate.”

US Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said Trump was giving in to Putin.

“Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression,” Beyer said in a statement on Friday.

Lindsey Graham, who died in July, strongly supported US assistance to Ukraine. The passage of the bill named for him had provided hope of continued bipartisan support for Kyiv, wrote Zelenskyy.

But with Graham gone, the US under Trump will continue sanctions relief for Russia beyond Friday’s waiver and the diesel export agreement announced earlier this month, the Ukrainian leader predicted.

“I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately,” wrote Zelenskyy, who lamented Graham’s absence. “It’s unfortunate because we all had great respect for Lindsey … It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest.” – Rappler.com

World.title: For chefs Joanna Ledesma and Jeremaine Sze, success is on the menu — but so is learning
World.content:
Food entrepreneurs Joanna Ledesma and Jeremaine Sze head back to the classroom, proving that even successful chefs still have more to learn

Bolinao, Pangasinan wakes to the sounds of water.

Before the first guest opens the door at Birdland Beach Club, the sea has already been at work all day, dragging itself up the sand and letting go over and over, the slow percussion of a shore town that has never known silence.

By the time the sun clears the treeline, the roast smell from the coffee bar is pushing its way out the open windows, warm and nutty, drifting across the lot where Joanna Ledesma’s Kopi Kubo Kollective stands on the highway: a coffee shop built on land with a rice field view, where the evening fog lifts.

Joanna Ledesma at Kopi Kubo Kollective. Contributed photo

Two hundred kilometers south, in a small dining room on D. Tuazon, Santa Mesa Heights in Quezon City, a different pot has been at work since morning.

At Nam Jai Thai Noodle House, khao soi is a study in contrast: soft egg-wheat noodles below, crisp ones on top, all meeting in coconut-curry broth.

The broth takes six to eight hours to prepare. Jeremaine Sze makes the curry paste from scratch, imports ingredients from Thailand, and works with local farms to source herbs and spices.

Just like in most things she does, there is no shortcut: no pressure cooker and no premade paste.

Jeremaine Sze with her staff at Nam Jai Thai Noodle House. Contributed photo

Two women head these two kitchens. Ledesma owns the Birdland Beach Club and runs the Kopi Kubo Kollective in Bolinao, while Sze leads as the executive chef and owner of Nam Jai in Quezon City

The businesses are different. But the question that brought the two owners to the same culinary school was the same.

Although both have long been passionate about cooking, they always get the the question: “Are you a culinary graduate?”

Ledesma heard it while running a restaurant and coffee shop in Malaysia.

“Everybody’s telling me, ‘Are you a culinary graduate?’…I felt like there’s something missing on my side,” she recalled.

Ledesma knew how to cook and create menus, but the question left her feeling inadequate.

When culinary terms meet credentials

Working with a staff who had formal culinary training also brought the knowledge gap into focus.

For Ledesma, the hardest part was memorization — the terminologies refusing to stick to a 40-year-old brain.

She recalled hearing terms such as “mise en place” and “bouquet garni” and realizing she could not explain them, even as the head of the kitchen.

Joanna Ledesma prepares meals for 50 people in her resort. Contributed photo Joanna Ledesma meticulously prepares her pastry for a nine-course degustation. Contributed photo

It’s the same for Sze, who found herself having to look up certain words that her assistant, who is a culinary school graduate, would often use in the kitchen.

Both women had learned cooking by doing.

This time, both wanted the formal grounding to match what they already knew.

Taste of home

Before the resorts and the noodle houses, Ledesma and Sze were just two girls who had something to sell.

For Sze, learning to cook began with learning to taste. At home, her parents would ask what a dish needed: more salt, more sweetness, a better balance.

She was often asked to try the dish, identify what was missing, then add it herself. That early practice of testing and adjusting became a way of thinking about food.

Sze was eight when a move to Davao had her wanting to help earn money for tuition and personal expenses.

She made yema and polvoron, learning to craft these sweets through family and necessity. While this was her first foray into the culinary world, she attests that they aren’t really considered cooking.

Jeremaine Sze checks her food creation. Photo by: Jade Tan/Rappler

Years later, under the name Manila Flavorful Asian Favorites, Sze would run catering services and work on party trays and food carts from a studio condominium.

In peak periods, she cooked 40 to 80 trays a day, starting as early as 2 or 3 am.

It was a lot to prepare all on her own. Her husband would come home from work and face the pile of dishes at the sink, waiting to be washed.

The work filled the small space. Sze recalled cooking until late at night, with dishes and cookware covering the floor from 3 in the morning until 10 at night.

A familiar community

Ledesma’s first kitchen memories had her standing beside her parents and grandmother, watching them cook, tasting the food and being handed broth while the pots were still going.

In second grade, like Sze, she made sweets to sell to her classmates.

“When I was in Grade 2, I started making yema, I started making polvoron, I started making turon. I learned how to make money at a very young age because I love making food, also so I could sell them.”

Later on, while living independently with housemates who did not cook, she made a dish of ampalaya with eggs and shared it with them.

Her housemates would tell her that it tastes different, and their enjoyment encouraged her to keep experimenting with food.

“So there, when people eat my food, it makes me feel different and happy,” Ledesma shared.

Joanna Ledesma cooks for her family. Contributed photo

Her love for cooking grew from family. Ledesma’s grandmother had a restaurant; her parents ran businesses, including a grocery and salon, and cooked at home.

In Bolinao, seafood, sea salt, and fermented fish are part of their local food landscape.

So early on, Ledesma built food businesses in the Philippines and Malaysia. She also traveled through Southeast Asia, taking short cooking courses and seeking local families who could teach her the food of their communities.

In Malaysia, she also put up a Kopi Kubo in Kuala Lumpur after staying there for two years.

In Bali, Indonesia, she went to a village in 2023 and asked her driver’s mother to show her how they made babi guling, which is similar to the Philippines’ lechon. She wanted to understand not only the recipe, but the traditions behind it.

But Ledesma graduated in finance from St. Louis University, shaped by a family that’s strongly into commerce.

In Makati, she sold healthy juices, then built Simone’s original snacks, fruits, vegetables, and meat dried into jerky. She worked the market for two to three years until she knew every vendor in the aisles and navigated the crate-stacked chaos.

Ledesma did it all, running two businesses in two countries, while raising two children.

Still learning

Sze’s decision to open Nam Jai came while she was in her first trimester of pregnancy, tired of managing tray orders alone.

“The only thing that I craved during the pregnancy was having my own restaurant,” she joked.

Ledesma, meanwhile, shared it was her husband’s idea to put up a coffee shop on a lot they had bought along a highway, partly so he could have his coffee on long drives.

Amid their growing success, both Sze and Ledesma felt the need to go back to school.

At 40, with two kids and multiple businesses, Ledesma initially hesitated until she found the Center for Culinary Arts’ (CCA) professional weekend program, which had people around her age.

She traveled to Manila from Bolinao every week. During the finals, she lived in Manila for an entire month to fully focus.

Chef Marco critiques the dishes prepared by students Joanna and Jeremaine at CCA. Photo by Jade Tan/Rappler

Sze had already taken introductory courses at CCA, but wanted more depth.

Her progression included signing up for Kitchen Discovery, Food and Culture Appreciation, Fundamentals of Culinary, and ProChef.

The credential question followed her there.

“Being a good cook is not enough,” Sze said. “People will still ask you, ‘Culinary graduate ka?’ San ka nag-aral? (Are you a culinary graduate? Where did you study?)”

The school experience tested Sze and Ledesma in various ways.

The pressure weighed in for Sze as she juggled culinary school and her business along with her pregnancy.

During classes, Sze kept her phone so she could check the CCTV and monitor the restaurant’s staff and customer flow.

Jeremaine Sze opens Nam Jai Thai Noodle House.Contributed photo Jeremaine Sze and her husband pose for a maternity photo shoot during her CCA graduation. Contributed photo

For Ledesma, the lesson of formal technique arrived through heat. She was not used to a kitchen with many stoves running at once, or to washing and cleaning her own station, after being accustomed to directing operations and focusing on menu development and recipe research.

“Hindi ako sanay, mainit sa kitchen (I’m not used to it, it’s hot in the kitchen),” Ledesma shared.

But completing the work gives her a sense of accomplishment: “Oh, kaya ko pala (Oh, so I can actually do it).”

Back to the kitchen

At Nam Jai’s kitchen, Sze’s culinary school habits became evident, from the color-coded cutting boards to sanitation practices and house rules.

Sze feels fully stepped into her role as a chef, confident enough to direct experienced staff, lead training, and instill cooking discipline.

“Yung seven to eight hours na broth [of khao soi], I don’t do shortcuts,” she said. “So, parang in life, I’m also that kind of person, that I don’t do shortcuts.”

(The seven to eight hours of cooking the broth of khao soi, I don’t do shortcuts. So, like in life, I’m also that kind of person, that I don’t do shortcuts.)

CCA graduate Joanna Ledesma learns that culinary education complements food entrepreneurship. Photos from CCA

Ledesma’s kitchens also had school imprints: knife skills, ingredient evaluation, seafood technique — all of them also taught to staff and family, quietly correcting provincial habits, like how shrimp shouldn’t be boiled too long or else they turn rubbery.

Her signature dishes involve the fresh seafood of her beach town; her philosophy: all healthy, organic, pesticide-free, MSG-free, non-GMO cooking.

For Ledesma, one of the satisfying moments at graduation was when she could finally call herself a chef.

“Don’t hesitate,” Ledesma said. “If you have the means of doing culinary, please do it. It will improve you a lot, physically, mentally, and emotionally.” – Rappler.com

Jade Tan is a Rappler intern studying AB Journalism at University of Santo Tomas, Manila.

World.title: When the Cordillera danced down Session Road
World.content:
DAZZLE. Baguio performers bring Panagbenga to Session Road during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals 2026, with this yearu2019s presentation drawing from the story of Bangan and the Benguet pine.

The Festival of Festivals turns Session Road into a showcase of the region’s diverse cultural traditions

BAGUIO CITY, Philippines — The gongs came first, then the colors.

Then came women balancing clay pots on their heads, men carrying shields and spears, dancers in woven skirts and feathered headgear, baskets of grain, bamboo, chants, prayer movements, and stories that usually live several mountain roads apart.

On October 17, they all met on Session Road.

The 5th Cordillera Festival of Festivals brought together the region’s six provinces and two cities, turning downtown Baguio into a living picture of the Cordillera’s diversity.

BELIEF. Tabuk City performers present Gabbok, a traditional Kalinga thanksgiving associated with the birth of a first child, during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals in Baguio City on October 17, 2026. The performance used chants, music, dance, and scenes of family life to express gratitude, blessing, and hopes for the child’s future. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

More than 500 performers joined the parade and cultural showcase, moving from the Melvin Jones area through Harrison Road, Magsaysay Avenue, and Session Road before gathering near Post Office Park.

Abra brought the Kawayan Festival, while Apayao presented Say-am. Benguet was represented by Kabayan’s Bindiyan, Ifugao by Gotad ad Ifugao, Kalinga by Pasil’s Tachok-Salip, Mountain Province by Lang-ay featuring Pasuk-ey, Baguio by Panagbenga, and Tabuk City by Gabbok.

It was easy to be dazzled. The more interesting part was figuring out what everyone was actually dancing about.

TRADITION. fugao performers showcase Gotad ad Ifugao during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals 2026, bringing chants, traditional dances, agricultural symbols, and stories of ancestry, abundance, and community to Session Road. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

Eight communities, eight ways of remembering

Abra’s performance highlighted bamboo craftsmanship, resilience, and the intersection of the province’s lowland and Tingguian, or Itneg, traditions.

Apayao’s Say-am was about thanksgiving, community, gongs, song, dance, and shared celebration.

Kabayan’s Bindiyan brought the pulse of the gangsa and a circle dance tied to victory, thanksgiving, and communal life.

Ifugao’s Gotad turned part of Session Road into a scene of ritual and daily life, with chants, rice, agricultural tools, baskets, woven objects, and movements tied to ancestry and abundance.

Pasil’s Tachok-Salip featured gongs, chants, Banga dancing, and movements that spoke of joy, unity, and connection to the land.

Mountain Province presented Lang-ay through Pasuk-ey, a Central Bontoc thanksgiving tradition rooted in Manerwap, an ancestral rain-calling ritual.

Tabuk’s Gabbok celebrated the birth of a first child.

Baguio’s Panagbenga performance drew on the story of Bangan, an Ibaloy woman whose offering to Kabunian is linked to the Benguet pine.

Put all eight together and one thing becomes obvious.

Mayor Benjamin Magalong said that even people who have lived in the region for years still have plenty to learn about one another.

“We may be neighbors, but our customs, celebrations, languages, traditions, and histories are not all the same,” he said.

Baguio itself, Magalong noted, has long been shaped by people from across the region who came to the city and eventually called it home.

“So much of the region is already present here in our city,” he said. “And today, that becomes even more visible.”

DANCE. Mountain Province performers present the Lang-ay Festival featuring Pasuk-ey: The Thanksgiving Summer Fest during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals 2026, bringing chants, prayer dances, and a Central Bontoc tradition rooted in Manerwap, an ancestral rain-calling ritual, to Session Road. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

More than something pretty to photograph

There were, naturally, phones everywhere. Session Road gave people plenty of reasons to point them.

But the Festival of Festivals was never meant to be reduced to a reel of costumes, choreography, and pretty pictures.

Department of Tourism (DOT) – Cordillera Regional Director Jovita Ganongan said the dances, garments, and traditions on display should be understood for what they are.

“Our festivals are not merely performances of our culture,” she said. “They are expressions of our identity, living stories of our ancestors, and a legacy we must carry forward.”

Ganongan also said the region’s cultural differences should not be mistaken for division.

“We may be different in our traditions and expressions of culture, but we are united through our heritage and our pride in who we are,” she said.

It is easy to turn culture into something decorative on a festival stage. But Cordillera traditions are tied to land, kinship, farming, ritual, memory, peace, conflict, survival, and belief. Strip away those meanings and what remains may still look beautiful, but it is no longer the whole story.

Baguio Representative Mauricio Domogan said the harder part comes after the applause.

“When the music subsides and the parade has passed, our responsibility to our heritage must endure,” he said.

ABRA. Abra performers showcase the Abrenian Kawayan Festival during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals 2026, bringing bamboo traditions and the shared heritage of the province’s lowland and Tingguian or Itneg communities to Session Road. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

Tourism without losing the plot

The Festival of Festivals is also a tourism event, and nobody was pretending otherwise.

DOT Secretary Judilyn Quiachon said the Cordillera has a distinct place in Philippine tourism because of its mountains, rice terraces, food, crafts, and living cultural traditions.

But she said more visitors should not be the only goal.

Tourism should create opportunities for local businesses, farmers, artisans, guides, accommodation providers, and other workers while respecting Indigenous cultures and protecting the environment.

The point, she said, is for communities to “participate meaningfully in and benefit from tourism development.”

Ganongan put it more plainly during an earlier briefing. Tourism should “entertain and educate, not exploit,” create livelihoods without sacrificing identity, and welcome visitors without pushing communities to the margins of their own stories.

How do you invite people to look without turning culture into spectacle? How do you make traditions visible without reducing them to content? How do you welcome tourism without asking communities to perform a version of themselves that outsiders find easier to consume?

But for that morning, the people carrying the traditions remained in the middle of the frame.

TRADITION. Kalinga performers from Pasil showcase the Tachok-Salip Festival during the Cordillera Festival of Festivals 2026, bringing gongs, chants, Banga dancing, and traditions of celebration, unity, and connection to the land to Session Road. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

A Cordillera too big for one photo

Women moved in measured steps beneath foliage headdresses while young men struck gongs behind them.

Rice was winnowed in the middle of Session Road. Farming tools became props but also reminders of where many of these traditions begin. Clay pots rose above dancers’ heads. Wooden bulul figures sat among grain and baskets. Men crouched low with gongs, then sprang back into movement.

Elders danced beside students. Older women carried traditions beside younger performers learning to inherit them.

Some spectators knew exactly what they were seeing. Others were encountering these practices for the first time.

The festival did not ask Abra to look like Kalinga, Ifugao to move like Benguet, or Mountain Province to tell the same story as Apayao.

Domogan summed it up in one line: “Identity does not require uniformity.”

By noon, the gongs had quieted. Performers were resting, spectators were drifting away, and Session Road was slowly becoming Session Road again.

After five years in Baguio, the Festival of Festivals will leave the city for the first time in 2027, with Kalinga set to host. – Rappler.com

World.title: Lean Alejandro and climate justice: Why Lidy Nacpil now believes in living for a cause
World.content:
A key lesson from our time as Martial Law babies is top of mind for Lidy in the battle for climate justice: You have to keep pushing — even when the odds seem overwhelming.

The devastating floods in Thailand and Nepal turned the spotlight on a familiar name for those of us who lived through Martial Law and dictatorship.

Lidy Nacpil was one of the leaders who fought the Marcos regime, a cause she and many from our generation were ready to die for. Now she’s a leader in the global battle against climate change, when the romance of dying for a cause has been overshadowed by the pressing need to stick around as long as possible for a struggle for future generations.

“Those who contributed the least to global emissions continue to shoulder the heaviest costs without prospects for a resilient future,” she said in an essay co-written with two prominent climate activists from Europe and Africa.

For Lidy, the stakes are higher than half a century ago when we faced off with the Marcos regime. We didn’t expect to live long back then. Dying young was possible.

We grew up under a dictatorship so brutal and with so little respect for life that many of us from the Martial Law generation believed that if we want to help end it, we would have to give up a lot for the fight — including our lives.

The death of Lean

For Lidy, that became real on September 19, 1987. What was painfully ironic was that the dictatorship had already been overthrown then. But the fascists were still around and there were still forces who shared the dictator’s disdain for democracy and who targeted those who were fighting to preserve and expand it — like her husband, Lean Alejandro.

On that day, Lidy returned home to find the sitter of their 6-month-old daughter Rusan waiting for her at the door. She said Lean had been ambushed.

“My first thought was that she said ‘ambush’ So I was really hoping that it did not mean he was dead. So I said, ‘Where was he taken?’ I was so afraid of asking point blank: ‘Buhay pa ba? Is he still alive?’”

But the sitter confirmed her worst fear. Lean was dead.

Lean had just led a press conference before the attack to share plans for the upcoming 15th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law. He and several companions were about to drive into their office on Rosal Street in Cubao, when a van pulled up next to the car. Then the assassins opened fire.

Rosal Street is about a mile away from our house in Cubao. I actually remember hearing the shots, though I did not think much about it initially. Only an hour later did I realize its significance when a friend called and said she heard a radio report about the ambush.

I drove to the office which had been abandoned by the time I arrived. There was blood on the driveway. The staff, including friends of mine, had retreated to a nearby office of a major human rights coalition in New Manila.

We were in shock. A brilliant leader, the most inspiring symbol of the Martial Law generation, was gone.

Friends and family joined Lidy at the morgue for what she recalls as “a nightmare into the night.” Lean’s face was shattered in the attack. “What I did was not look at where he was badly damaged and just concentrated on looking at parts of his body and his face that were intact,” she said. “My memories of that day are still vivid. I don’t think I’ll ever forget.”

I last saw Lidy in person in 2007 when we commemorated Lean’s 20th death anniversary in Quezon City. By then, her activism had expanded in scope, focused not only on social justice and human rights issues in the Philippines, but also on a grim global concern: climate change.

In 2012, when I posted a Facebook note celebrating Barack Obama’s reelection despite misgivings about some of his policies, Lidy posted a comment: “Boying, hope he will have a far, far better position on climate change and US cuts on its emissions than he took during his first term.”

When we talked four years ago for my series on Martial Law Babies, the urgency of the climate change battle clearly informed her own updated view of activism — and the sacrifices one must be willing to make in the fight for change. (READ: The Martial Law babies’ turn)

We were in our late 20s when Lean was assassinated nearly 40 years ago. Most of us are now in our late 50s or early 60s. When we were younger, being prepared to die for the cause, for the struggle against dictatorship was a given. But things are different now, Lidy told me.

“The sacrifices and what we are willing to give up, nag iiba iba iyan (it changes),” Lidy said. “At that time for us, the biggest is you were willing to risk your life.”

“The challenge for me today is: you have to live long because there’s so much to do — and to pass on. We cannot recklessly risk our lives today. That’s not what is being asked for. The times are different. The needs are different.”

Play Video

Lean’s Rado watch

Lidy was a high school freshman at UP High when Martial Law was declared in September 1972. After a long break from school after Marcos seized power, she returned to a campus where there were “whispers” of students and teachers who had been arrested. But she had been vaguely aware of the protests and the unrest. She and her schoolmates didn’t have a clear idea of what was going on.

“That’s why we were called Martial Law babies. We were just babies, not literally in age but in consciousness.”

Although she would later be known as a UP student leader, it was actually through her church and groups like the Student Christian Movement that she became exposed to political activism.

In fact, she was initially unimpressed with the first student activists she encountered in Diliman. “I used to see small groups of students marching down the corridors of Palma Hall, sloganeering. I used to think, ‘Ano ba naman iyan, ang babaw. Paano mo mababago ang lipunan kung nagsisigaw ka lang diyan? (It was shallow. How will you change society by just yelling slogans?).”

She laughed at the memory, adding, “If that’s all we were going to do as students, do marches and shout slogans, I wasn’t interested. I was looking for something deeper and more profound.”

Eventually, she found it.

The marches and the slogans turned out to be just one part of a broader and more dynamic activist movement that was at that time starting to push back against the dictatorship. And these efforts, the years of testing the limits and pushing back against the regime — which had led to arrests and even the death of Philippine Collegian editor Ditto Sarmiento — eventually produced victories. By the time Lidy entered UP Diliman, students, after years of struggle, had reclaimed their right to elect their own student councils and other campus rights.

It was around that time that she met Lean. They would later share a scary experience — though one that they would later talk about lightheartedly.

It happened in 1980 when Lidy and Lean joined a major student demonstration at Liwasang Bonifacio. The rally was violently dispersed. “I fell during the dispersal. I vaguely remember someone helping me get up and then I ran.”

She didn’t see and had no idea who helped her up. But Lean later told her that it was him — and he actually paid a price for it. “I was about to get hit with a truncheon when he blocked it with his hand.”

Lean was wearing a Rado watch which got smashed in this act of chivalry. “His father had given it to him so it was valuable. Kaya sabi niya, ‘Ikaw ang dahilan kung bakit nabasag. (You’re the reason it got smashed.).”

Remembering that made Lidy laugh.

I still fondly remember Lean as a brilliant, inspiring activist — intelligent, articulate, charismatic. He was a young leader brimming with confidence who could give a firebrand speech at a rally at Mendiola Bridge and also engage in serious political discussions with established political figures like Lorenzo Tañada and Jose “Pepe” Diokno.

He was also a humble, patient young leader who I saw several times up close. During a rally shortly after the Aquino assassination, when he was not yet a nationally known figure, I saw Lean defuse a situation in the crowd where some impatient protesters started throwing little stones at other protesters who decided to stand up to see what was going on at the main stage.

“Huwag po. Magkakainitan lang po tayo niyan. (Sir, please don’t do that. It will just make things worse.),” Lean said calmly, successfully convincing the irritated rallyists to settle down.

I also remember Lean for his quirks and unorthodox style. He used to walk around Diliman in faded jeans and flip flops. He was known as a computer geek and an avid fan of chess, The Lord of the Rings, and Fiddler on the Roof.

Like many of us back then, he was a chain smoker — perhaps because many of us didn’t expect to lead long lives. So why not smoke our lungs away. We were prepared to go all in so to speak.

In fact, Lean famously said: “The line of fire is the place of honor.” The day he was assassinated, Lean was reading Antonio Gramsci, the Italian revolutionary who is also famous for the quote, “The old world is dying and the new world struggles to be born.”

For Lidy, it is the first sentence of what Gramsci said that truly resonates more than 30 years later. The world indeed is dying — and there is much to be done.

Climate justice

Lidy became involved in the climate justice movement about 15 years ago. As one of the leaders of the Asian People’s Movement on Debt and Development, she has emerged as one of Asia’s leading voices in the movement.

That fight has become harder.

When the UN Climate Change Conference was held in 2021 without the participation of countries in the Global South, she was among those who spoke out. “The conference has long been dominated by wealthy governments and corporate interests, thus it’s always an intense effort to raise the voices, perspectives and calls of people and communities, especially those from the Global South,” she said.

When the Nepal tragedy hit, Lidy spoke out in a Bangkok Post op-ed: “Declarations can no longer substitute for action, and excuses can no longer be allowed. Behind every discussion of temperature thresholds, emissions pathways and international obligations are communities losing lives, homes, livelihoods and ecosystems.”

It is a different kind of struggle — one that poses a host of unique tougher challenges.

“You’re fighting for things not to get worse in terms of the climate. On the other hand, you want to establish systems where there’s more equality and where people will have a better chance of a good livelihood. “

“The real impact of climate change can no longer be reversed. What we’re telling people is we cannot go back to the past. We’re working to prevent things from getting worse.”

It would be hard to imagine a time when there are no super typhoons, she said. There is, in a way, the element of making people fearful of what could happen.

“That’s not the easiest thing to do. Mas madaling sabihin sa tao, ‘Lumaban tayo dito para mawala iyan’ imbes na ‘Lumaban tayo para hindi lumala.’ (It’s easier to tell people, ‘Let’s fight to make this go away,’ instead of ‘Let’s fight so things don’t get worse.’)”

But today’s generation of climate change activists also are “blessed,” she said. Activists from earlier generations had laid the foundation for the fight — similar to the way our generation learned a lot from the experiences of earlier activists and leaders like Tañada and Diokno.

Lidy became involved in the climate justice movement a decade after the 1992 international conference which helped make clear the dangers the world faced and establish basic principles on how nations should respond.

“I was surprised and wondered how they were able to win progressive provisions and principles, because they are really helping us now.”

Her past as a Martial Law baby, and a veteran of the struggle that overthrew the Marcos dictatorship has also helped. A key lesson from our time as Martial Law babies is top of mind for Lidy in the battle for climate justice: You have to keep pushing — even when the odds seem overwhelming.

“From our experience in the fight during the dictatorship, you learn to widen and push the edges of these platforms and these opportunities. Hindi ka pwedeng magkasya doon sa ito lang iyong binigay sa iyo. (You must never settle and accept what they say they can offer you.) You push for more so you can have more space to raise your voices.

“The discipline we developed as activists in the Philippines was helpful. We were very broad-minded in terms of tactics, strategies, and alliance work… What we experienced during martial law, what we learned about struggle, about strategies and tactics, these are very useful in taking on all these global problems and fights and institutions and arenas.“

For example, she said, with movements in some countries, there is a dichotomy between “those who just believe in mobilizations, mass actions and radical slogans and those who just do policy advocacy and do the nitty gritty of negotiations.”

That’s not how she was trained as an activist. In a way, the lesson goes back to her initial reaction to UP activists, those who held loud marches in Diliman — which she subsequently realized were just one part of a broader and deeper movement. Marches and pickets were just as important as other tasks, from studying an issue to formulating a policy and position and engaging negotiations to achieve a goal.

“Para sa Pinoy, lahat yan kasama. (For Filipinos, that’s all combined.) Those are all needed.”

There’s another lesson Lidy shared and it’s related to how we all remember Lean. “Lean had extraordinary and outstanding traits,” she said. But in honoring his memory, we shouldn’t idealize who he was.

“Ang hirap kasing naghohold up tayo ng icons minsan kasi baka ma-frustrate lang. (Holding up people as icons is sometimes not helpful. It may just lead to frustration.) Not everybody can be a Lean Alejandro.”

And not everyone has to be a Lean Alejandro, she said. That’s a key lesson from the Martial Law generation. Many of us weren’t. But that didn’t matter.

“I think the most important story of our generation is that most of us were just your average youth. The thing that was extraordinary about us is that we rose to the occasion. We weren’t particularly more intelligent. Mas sharper pa nga sila ngayon e. (Young people today are even sharper.) The knowledge base is much larger now. The technology is there. They are faster in dealing with all the technology.

“But we rose to the occasion. We realized that we had more than ourselves to live for.”

And that’s what she hopes young Filipinos today will keep in mind, she said — that “they realize that they have to live for more than themselves. And that they rise to the occasion, whatever the occasion demands, whatever the times now demand from them. It doesn’t take extraordinary things. It’s your willingness and readiness and there are many ways that you can contribute.”

In a way, the idea of “giving your life” for the cause — “medyo abstract na. (It’s a bit abstract now.),” Lidy said. “That means many different things.”

“I want to last as long as it takes until there is a fresh resurgence of movements and struggles so we can pass on whatever knowledge and wisdom we gained from our experiences.” – Rappler.com

This essay is based on an article first published in 2022.

Benjamin Pimentel is the author of ‘U.G. An Underground Tale: The Life and Struggle of Edgar Jopson’ published by Anvil Publishing which just released the 2nd printing of the 3rd edition. He is also a journalist and technology editor based in the San Francisco Bay Area, California, USA. Royalties from ‘U.G.’ are donated to Bantayog ng Mga Bayani.

World.title: Super Typhoon Champi to enter PAR on October 20
World.content:
CHAMPI. Satellite image of Super Typhoon Champi outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility as of October 18, 2026, 10:30 am.

As of Sunday morning, October 18, Super Typhoon Champi is located 2,090 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon, still outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility

MANILA, Philippines – A tropical cyclone with the international name Champi is expected to enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) on Tuesday, October 20.

Champi had intensified from a typhoon into a super typhoon as of 2 am on Sunday, October 18, and it is projected to enter PAR as a super typhoon.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said in an advisory that Champi was located 2,090 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon as of 10 am on Sunday.

The super typhoon is moving west at 25 kilometers per hour (km/h), while over the sea near the United States island territory of Guam.

Champi did not make landfall in Guam, but still lashed the island with heavy rain and damaging winds during its closest point of approach in the early hours of Sunday, according to Guam Homeland Security. Guam is just two hours ahead of Manila.

So far, Champi has maximum sustained winds of 185 km/h — the minimum threshold for classification as a super typhoon by PAGASA — and gustiness of up to 230 km/h.

The weather bureau sees Champi strengthening further and possibly reaching a peak intensity of 205 km/h before its entry into PAR, but it may start gradually weakening on Tuesday.

Once it enters PAR on Tuesday morning or afternoon, Champi will be given the local name Rosal. It would be the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October.

Champi only has a slim chance of making landfall in the Philippines, as it is more likely to head for Taiwan. Taiwan, located above the northernmost province of Batanes, is within PAR.

Although landfall is less likely in the country, PAGASA warned the public that Champi may still bring heavy rain to extreme Northern Luzon, or the Batanes-Babuyan Islands area.

The weather bureau might also raise tropical cyclone wind signals for the northern and eastern portions of Northern Luzon and even parts of Bicol as early as Monday evening, October 19, or by Tuesday morning, since winds from Champi could reach these areas. The highest wind signal may be Signal No. 3 or 4.

PAGASA added that most parts of Luzon and the Visayas, as well as portions of Mindanao, are likely to experience gusty conditions beginning Tuesday or Wednesday, October 21.

Also on Tuesday, moderate to rough waters are expected in the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon and the eastern seaboards of the Visayas and Mindanao.

Starting Wednesday, very rough, high, or very high waters may affect the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon.

ALSO ON RAPPLER

For now, the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ) and the easterlies are the weather systems affecting the country on Sunday.

The ITCZ is a belt near the equator where the trade winds of the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere meet, while the easterlies are warm winds from the Pacific Ocean.

The ITCZ is causing scattered rain and thunderstorms in the Zamboanga Peninsula, Basilan, Lanao del Sur, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Occidental, and Palawan, as well as isolated rain showers or thunderstorms in the rest of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao and Soccsksargen.

Meanwhile, the easterlies are bringing scattered rain and thunderstorms to Quezon and Camarines Norte, and isolated rain showers or thunderstorms to the rest of the country.

The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

World.title: US Holds Second Round of Talks With Myanmar Regime as Concerns Grow Over Policy Shift
World.content:
U.S. officials held a meeting with Myanmar miliary regime officials in Tokyo last week, Reuters reported on Friday, citing sources familiar with the meeting.

It was the second round of talks between the two countries within a month. A U.S. delegation led by Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance visited the regime’s capital Naypyitaw in mid-September.

Vance also led the delegation in Tokyo, which included over a dozen U.S. officials, while the identities of regime representatives and the issues discussed remained undisclosed, according to Reuters.

At the September talks, the U.S. delegation met with coup leader Min Aung Hlaing and secured the release of American businessman Adam Castillo, who had been detained upon returning to Yangon in June 2026 over a lawsuit filed against him.

The U.S. outreach led by Vance has focused on shutting down scam centers that target Americans, but could lead to broader engagement, including on Myanmar’s rare-earth mineral deposits, Reuters reported, citing current and former officials as well as others familiar with the U.S. policy shift.

The Irrawaddy has learned that during the Naypyitaw meeting, the U.S. side urged the regime to reduce attacks on civilians, crack down on money-laundering gangs, engage with ethnic armed groups, release political prisoners and allow unfettered distribution of humanitarian assistance.

Observers noted that the Trump administration has shifted its policy from isolating the Myanmar military-installed government to engaging with it.

The National Unity Government (NUG), a leading anti-regime revolutionary organization, said it was not overly concerned by the increasing engagement between the U.S. and the military junta.

Speaking to The Irrawaddy, NUG Foreign Affairs Minister Zin Mar Aung said the U.S. is engaging with both sides—the military regime and the revolutionary groups—purely based on promoting its own interests, without granting legitimacy to anyone.

“Its [U.S.] policy is already clear. They are taking a transactional, practical approach to tackle issue like TOC [transnational organized crime]. They will discuss matters that are crucial to U.S. interests,” she said.

“So, this is nothing unusual. Nor is it a shift in policy. Since the Trump administration took office, this is how the U.S. has been dealing with [all] countries, not just Myanmar.”

Banya Khung Aung, Secretary 2 of the Interim Executive Council of Karenni (Kayah) State, which largely controls the eastern Myanmar state, told The Irrawaddy he is concerned that increased U.S. engagement with the regime will harm the country’s federal democracy and human rights movements, whether financially, technically or operationally. As evidence, he pointed to the Trump administration’s recent cuts to USAID funding for Myanmar.

“If you look carefully at Donald Trump’s policies, everyone knows that he engages with all [sides] and highly considers his national interests. So, I am not surprised with [the administration’s ongoing] engagement with the regime,” he said.

He noted that foreign governments are no longer prioritizing democracy and human rights, and are instead focusing on their national and common interests.

“Because of that, whether it is a government or a dictatorship, if there are benefits for America, it is almost certain they will engage.”

Bertil Lintner, a Swedish journalist, author and strategic consultant who has been writing about Asia for more than four decades, echoed Banya’s comments.

“I am not surprised. Democracy has never been a top priority for the Trump administration. And more countries are starting to acquiesce to a fait accompli. The military-dominated government is there to stay for the foreseeable future.”

Following the 2021 coup, the U.S. under Joe Biden imposed sweeping sanctions against top regime generals—including Min Aung Hlaing and his family—as well as military-owned conglomerates.

But Trump has shifted U.S. policy from isolating the regime to engaging with it, including delisting junta cronies accused of aiding and abetting regime war crimes and crime against humanity committed against their own people.

Meanwhile, the country, whose economy has collapsed under the regime, has become a hotspot of transnational organized crime. Chinese-run scam syndicates under the protection of several armed organizations, including regime-controlled or aligned militia groups, defraud huge sums from victims globally, including Americans, who have lost billions of dollars annually in recent years.

Regarding U.S. engagement with the regime, Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative Asean Network on Burma, said, “It looks like President Trump has been scammed by sham President Min Aung Hlaing. Trump is rewarding a criminal for committing more crimes.”

She warned that U.S. engagement with the regime not only poses risks to the country’s pro-democracy movement, but also endangers civilians in Myanmar and across the region. She noted that Min Aung Hlaing has escalated the country’s conflicts, causing mass displacement, while also driving a boom in transnational crime that targets victims regionally and globally.

“Embracing Min Aung Hlaing is embracing a nest of vipers. He has been intensifying threats to regional human security and economic stability,” Stothard said.

The U.S. State Department said it engages will all groups in Myanmar on issues affecting U.S. interests and has raised the need to cease violence and release political prisoners, according to the Reuters report.

World.title: Chinese Jet-Fuel Refinery to Bypass Sanctions, Myanmar’s Blood Timber Flows to China, and More
World.content:
China‑backed refinery lets regime bypass jet fuel sanctions

Myanmar’s military regime has restarted the Thanlyin No.1 Oil Refinery near Yangon, allowing it to bypass jet fuel sanctions and sustain its deadly air raids on the civilian population. According to Nikkei Asia, Phase 1 is designed to produce 150,000 metric tons of jet fuel annually, roughly equal to Myanmar’s import volume last year.

The refinery, operated by Myanma Petrochemical Enterprise (MPE), was taken offline in 2017 but rebuilt after the 2021 coup. The engineering, procurement and construction contract was awarded to Peiyang Chemical Engineering Service Corporation (PCCS), a Singapore-registered subsidiary of Peiyang Chemical Equipment in Tianjin.

Anhui Tiankang Group supplied nearly 400 measuring devices for the various chemical processes, coordinated by Tianjin Sainuo Oil & Gas Technology. Some modules were fabricated in China and shipped via Singapore to Thilawa Port.

The regime says the project will reduce foreign currency outflow and stabilize supply. It has heavily relied on air power since 2022, killing thousands of civilians, and this dependency has only increased as the territory it controls continues to shrink. In the most recent atrocity, 50 civilians died and nearly 60 were injured when the regime bombed a busy market in Rakhine’s Kyauktaw.

China becomes biggest buyer of Myanmar’s blood timber

China has become the dominant buyer of Myanmar’s timber since the 2021 coup, according to UN Comtrade data cited by Australia’s Wood Central.

Last year, China’s purchases climbed to US$147.3 million, nearly double the pre-coup total of $78 million, while Western imports collapsed from roughly the same amount to just $1.2 million worth, according to Forest Trends, a Washington‑based non‑profit that monitors global forest trade and conservation finance.

The group’s analysis shows China’s share of Myanmar’s reported wood exports rose from 25.5 percent in 2019 to a peak of $228.7 million in 2024, nearly 80 percent of the total, before settling at 74.1% in 2025. Nearly three‑quarters of China’s imports since the coup were bound for companies registered in Yunnan Province.

Myanmar’s total reported wood exports rose from $304.3 million in 2019 to $370.6 million in 2022 but then fell to $198.9 million last year after the regime lost control over most of the border with Yunnan in Shan and Kachin states. But China continues to import timber through border crossings now controlled by ethnic armed groups.

Western buyers’ share now accounts for just 0.6 of Myanmar’s blood timber, but Forest Trends warns that the decline does not necessarily mean sanctions are working. Instead, the group believes much is “re-exported” to the West after “transiting through China,” though the flow is harder to trace.

Kokang scam warlord sentenced to death

A Chinese court on Tuesday sentenced three leaders of Myanmar’s notorious Wei clan to death as Beijing continues its public reckoning with the Kokang scam syndicates. The Quanzhou Intermediate People’s Court convicted Wei Huairen and two others of running violent fraud compounds that trafficked Chinese nationals, forced them into online scams, and murdered at least two victims.

According to Chinese state media, the Wei family’s network generated 12.2 billion yuan (US$1.8 billion) through online scams, drug trafficking, illegal casinos, and prostitution. Courts also handed life sentences to three associates and prison terms to 55 others, describing the gang as the “most violent criminal force in northern Myanmar.”

The Wei clan was one of four family crime syndicates in Kokang, which is now controlled by the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA). Wei Huairen was the chief of the regime-aligned Kokang Border Guard Force (BGF), in which capacity he created a much-emulated model of quasi-official armed protection of online fraud parks. The ruling follows earlier executions of Ming and Bai clan members.

Beijing renews outreach to Myanmar’s party leaders

The director‑general of the Chines Communist Party’s International Liaison Department, Peng Xiubin, met leaders of nine Myanmar political parties in Yangon on Tuesday, though none associated with the bona-fide opposition.

Present at the meeting were the usual suspects from the ruling Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) as well as a few co-opted ethnic political parties like the Arakan Front Party (AFP) and Shan and Nationalities Democratic Party (SNDP). Discussions focused on “bilateral ties” and Myanmar’s “peace and reconciliation,” according to participants.

SNDP chair Sai Aik Pao told the Popular News propaganda outlet that he urged Peng to help the central regime regain control over the Muse–Mandalay trade corridor, pushing out the MNDAA and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA).

“China has influence” over those armed groups, he was quoted as saying.

While the USDP remains at the center of party-to-party ties, China also often flies other party leaders to Kunming and Beijing for “study tours” and “cooperation forums.” Shortly after the regime announced its planned elections last year, the department hosted a delegation of several Myanmar political parties in Beijing.

Shan groups warn against MNDAA’s ‘Sinicization’

Eight Shan civil society and youth groups published an open letter to the MNDAA on Oct. 9, warning that its boorish cultural and administrative practices in northern Shan State threaten ethnic coexistence and China–Myanmar border stability.

The letter warns that the MNDAA’s military control is only temporary and urges it to respect local ethnic traditions, languages, and rights. The groups accuse the Chinese-speaking group of erasing Shan, Ta’ang and Burmese scripts from public signboards and replacing them with Chinese characters. They argue that imposing Chinese-style governance and financial systems without consultation undermines trust and risks fueling resistance.

Such actions could even jeopardize the future of the China–Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC), the letter warns, referring to the pet project of the MNDAA’s paymasters in Beijing.

Ta’ang civil society groups have similarly condemned the MNDAA’s actions. In April, six Ta’ang organizations said replacing Ta’ang signs with Chinese amounted to erasing an ethnic identity—a violation of international human rights law.

The MNDAA is busy consolidating its control of all major trade corridors linking to Yunnan Province.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Regime Turns to Belarus for High Interest Loans as Fiscal Crisis Deepens
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime, squeezed by a worsening fiscal crisis, has turned to its ally Belarus for high‑interest loans, with its rubber-stamp parliament granting approval to borrow at rates nearing 10 percent.

On Wednesday, lawmakers endorsed coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s proposal to secure loans from Belarus just eight days after he submitted the request to the Union Parliament. The loans will be used to purchase goods from Belarus.

The loans will come from the state-controlled Development Bank of the Republic of Belarus (DBRB) and Belinvestbank JSC, with maturities ranging from one to five years. The regime has not disclosed the total amount, but the high interest rates have already drawn criticism.

Deputy Finance Minister Than Than Lin told parliament on October 6 that rates would range from 2.25 to 9.33 percent. Her colleague Kyaw Htin argued on October 14 that the short‑term nature of the loans — capped at five years — would limit exposure to market volatility.

The loans can be denominated in Russian rubles, Belarusian rubles, yuan, US dollars, or euros, with interest rates varying by currency type and commodity group. The regime says it will pre‑screen payment channels to avoid currencies subject to sanctions.

Authorities plan to use the loans to import capital goods (machinery), intermediate goods (raw/semi-finished products), consumer products, and other commodities. Purchases of Belarusian‑made goods, machinery, technology, and services will be financed through Belarusian banks, with Myanmar ministries, agencies, or private firms acting as buyers. In effect, Belarusian exporters will supply the goods while Myanmar entities serve as importers.

Three state‑owned banks, Myanmar Economic Bank, Myanmar Foreign Trade Bank, and Myanmar Investment and Commercial Bank, have already signed banking arrangements with Belarus, and talks are underway to open accounts.

During Min Aung Hlaing’s August trip to Minsk, the regime signed nine agreements, including a loan framework deal between Myanmar’s Ministry of Finance and JSC Development Bank of Belarus.

While the junta chief has repeatedly insisted Myanmar must rely on domestic resources rather than foreign loans, his regime’s rush to secure Belarussian credit underscores the depth of its fiscal crisis. The loan approval came the same day that lawmakers nodded through the regime’s proposal to “borrow” up to 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to fill its 2026-27 budget deficit.

“Myanmar’s public will suffer from the high-interest loans, which will be repaid at the expense of education and health budgets,” said a Myanmar analyst.

Myanmar’s ties with Belarus were once limited to arms sales, but since the 2021 coup cooperation has expanded into politics, economics, and now finance. Belarus has emerged as a key ally alongside Russia, with Min Aung Hlaing visiting Minsk frequently while also hosting Belarusian strongman Alexander Lukashenko in Naypyitaw.

Lukashenko was the first foreign leader to visit Myanmar after Min Aung Hlaing installed himself as head of state in April.

Reports suggest the regime may next lean on Russia for credit, with President Vladimir Putin pledging financial sector cooperation in August while hosting Min Aung Hlaing in Moscow.

Meanwhile, the junta has cut imports of basic goods including fuel, cooking oil, and steel to save foreign currency, while squeezing revenue through tax hikes, natural resource sales, and tighter remittance rules for migrant workers.

After the World Bank, Asian Development Bank, and Western governments suspended aid and imposed sanctions following the coup, Min Aung Hlaing’s regime has been increasingly dependent on loans and support from his authoritarian allies, analysts say.

World.title: China’s Shrinking Politburo Has a Diversity Problem
World.content:
China’s Communist Party chose 24 men for its Politburo in October 2022, all of them Han Chinese. It was the first Politburo without a woman in 25 years, and it included nobody from any of China’s 55 officially recognized ethnic minority groups. After four years, the group is even more exclusive.

In October 2025, the party expelled Central Military Commission Vice Chairman He Weidong. Former Xinjiang Party Secretary Ma Xingrui followed in July 2026, and top general Zhang Youxia last month. Official notices accused all three of serious violations; the notice on Zhang also alleged disloyalty, “faction-building” and a remarkably large number of bribes. Their removal leaves an active Politburo of 21—a concentration that tells us something important about power under Xi Jinping. Diversity exists farther down the political system, often through quotas and administrative rules. It disappears where the most consequential decisions are made.

A narrowing funnel

The contrast starts with the membership. At the end of 2025, women accounted for 31.5 percent of the Communist Party of China’s 101.3 million members, while ethnic minority members made up 7.8 percent. Among people admitted in 2025, women made up 46.5 percent and ethnic minorities 10.2 percent, according to the Central Organization Department.

Representation was also visible at the 20th Party Congress. Its 2,296 delegates included 619 women or 27 percent, and 264 ethnic minority members or 11.5 percent, drawn from 40 minority groups. Then the funnel thins. Only 11 of the 205 full members elected to the 20th Central Committee were women, while nine came from ethnic minority groups. At the Politburo level, both figures fell to zero.

This isn’t a simple story of too few qualified candidates. Shen Yiqin, an ethnic Bai woman, had served as Guizhou governor and provincial party secretary before the 2022 congress. She became a state councilor in 2023 and later president of the All-China Women’s Federation, yet never entered the Politburo. Her current brief covers civil affairs, human resources, social security, veterans, sports and liaison with the ethnic affairs bureaucracy. Those duties matter, but a state councilor ranks below the Politburo members.

Rules stop below the top

China has spent decades building representation requirements. A 2001 party directive called for at least one woman in provincial and prefectural party, government, legislature and political advisory leadership teams, as well as in county party and government teams. It gave early priority to women in education, culture, health, family planning, civil affairs and similar departments. The 2021-2030 national program for women calls for more women in local government leadership, more female principal officials and better access to training, rotation and key posts.

Yet many targets use the phrase “gradually increase” without a numerical floor for the Central Committee, Politburo or its Standing Committee. The result is presence without a reliable route to the top.

A peer-reviewed study of every prefectural mayor and party secretary serving between 2003 and 2020 found that women followed faster but more restricted careers. Female officials were younger and better educated, but more often came through the Women’s Federation, Communist Youth League and other less powerful portfolios. Men had greater access to finance, development and core party offices. Women held only 135 of 1,987 mayoral posts and 88 of 1,694 party secretary posts.

The study also found a revealing pattern: about 20 percent of women mayors were ethnic minority members, compared with 13 percent of male mayors. One appointment could therefore satisfy expectations for both gender and ethnic representation, while leaving more positions open for Han Chinese men. The evidence supports this “tandem quota” effect at the prefectural mayor level, but it doesn’t establish that top leaders consciously use the same calculation when selecting the Politburo.

Ethnic glass ceiling

Ethnic minority cadres face a parallel divide. China’s ethnic autonomy law reserves the head-of-government in autonomous areas for a member of the relevant minority, but the more powerful party secretary post has generally gone to a Han Chinese official. For decades, minorities held roughly 10 percent to 11 percent of full and alternate Central Committee seats, yet most sat in the alternate tier.

No ethnic minority official has ever joined the Politburo Standing Committee. A handful reached the wider Politburo: Zhuang general Wei Guoqing and Mongolian leader Ulanhu served there during the Mao and early reform years; Hui Liangyu later served in the body and became a vice premier. Those cases show the barrier isn’t formal, but they also highlight how rarely it has been crossed.

Under Xi, official ethnic policy increasingly centers on “forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation.” At the 2021 Central Ethnic Work Conference, Xi linked good cadre standards to firm support for centralized party leadership and commitment to his national community project. The policy stresses political unity, shared identity and security more than representation by distinct groups.

Perhaps this policy did not directly cause the all-Han Politburo. Public records don’t reveal the bargaining, vetting or rejected candidates behind elite appointments. Still, the roster fits a system where minority identity can warrant representation in congresses and autonomous governments but offers little access to the center.

Diversity and decision quality

An all-male, all-Han Chinese Politburo doesn’t mean every member thinks alike. Nor does adding women or minority officials guarantee different policies. Officials who rise through the same selection system may share its priorities. But there is evidence that representation can affect what institutions do. Women held about one-fifth of the seats in China’s 12th National People’s Congress but sponsored 44 percent of legislative bill proposals and more than half of proposals concerning women’s rights and interests. That finding comes from the first systematic study of female legislators’ behaviour in the national legislature.

The useful question isn’t whether one woman or minority official would transform policy but whether the leadership is drawing on the country’s full pool of political experience. The body, after all, makes decisions on birthrates, employment, Xinjiang, Tibet and social welfare.

The practical tests are clear. Party authorities could publish measurable targets for women and ethnic minority officials at each rung of the promotion ladder, report compliance and place more candidates in finance, security, organization and provincial party secretary jobs that feed Politburo selection. They could also stop treating one minority woman as sufficient evidence that two representation goals have been met.

Watch the 21st Party Congress, expected in 2027. Count who enters the full Central Committee, who receives powerful provincial and central portfolios, and who reaches the Politburo. Speeches about equality are easy to issue. Twenty-one occupied seats provide the harder evidence.

Chandu Doddi is an Assistant Professor at the Centre for Chinese Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi.

World.title: New ID Rules Tighten Regime’s Grip on Migrant Remittances From Thailand
World.content:
Desperate for revenue, the Min Aung Hlaing regime is again using the Certificate of Identity (CI) process to extract money from undocumented Myanmar migrants in Thailand, forcing them to shoulder even greater financial hardship.

The regime recently added new rules to the CI process, requiring migrants to use the regime’s official channels for 25 percent of their remittances before applying for the certificate.

The CI is a temporary document intermittently issued by Myanmar that serves as an alternative to a passport for migrant workers in Thailand, allowing them to secure a legal work permit.

Regime Labor Minister Maung Myint told Parliament on Thursday that five centers issuing CIs started operating on Wednesday in Thailand’s Samut Sakhon, Samut Prakan, Chiang Mai, Chon Buri and Surat Thani.

The new order requires workers to provide proof of remitting 6,000 baht (about US$180) through official channels, equivalent to 25 percent of three months’ wages calculated on a fixed monthly salary of 8,000 baht, as well as proof of payment of 2 percent income tax. Newly appointed regime Labor Minister Maung Myint said remittances are a matter of “national interest,” and workers should consider them “a donation” to the country.

The move is part of the regime’s longstanding effort to extract foreign currency from overseas workers, including through the income tax and mandatory 25-percent remittance rule introduced in 2023.

Groups assisting migrant workers said the new requirements would complicate the employment process, potentially leading to higher costs for workers.

“Many workers do not have stable jobs,” a member of a migrant assistance group told The Irrawaddy. “How can they transfer the money, when they are already struggling with the cost?”

Complicating the process by requiring more documents would create space for service providers to charge more money, he said.

The CI application costs around 3,600 baht, but workers must rely on service providers or agents, who normally charge between 7,000 and 15,000 baht, including service fees, though precise costs under the latest rules remain unclear.

A migrant worker in Thailand told The Irrawaddy that the agent who managed his CI application process charged around 15,000 baht.

The amount is paid in installments to his employer through deductions from his monthly wages, reducing the amount he could send home.

“I send less money to my family. Everyone around me has to do the same thing,” he said.

Meanwhile, service providers said families of some workers in Myanmar do not have access to the banking system, making it more difficult to obtain proof of remittance transfers.

“Some workers’ families live in remote areas. It is not easy for them to withdraw the money,” a service provider told The Irrawaddy. He added that the regime was also likely to introduce stricter checks on applicants and their supporting documents.

U Set Aung, an economist and former deputy minister of planning and finance under the ousted civilian government led by Aung San Suu Kyi, wrote on his Facebook page on Thursday that low-wage Myanmar workers in Thailand were struggling to cover their living expenses and could not afford to remit 25 percent of their wages.

“The amount workers send home should be their own decision,” he said.

He added that the policy was designed solely to benefit the regime, rather than to support families and formal banking use.

“When remittances are converted at exchange rates below prevailing market rates, workers and their families suffer additional financial losses,” he said. “It raises serious concerns about freedom of movement, the right to pursue a livelihood, and fundamental labor rights.”

As the Myanmar regime steps up efforts to squeeze remittances from overseas workers, workers in Thailand are a prime target. Thailand hosted nearly 3 million Myanmar workers as of November 2025, according to official Thai figures. But the real number is likely to be much higher as many workers are undocumented.

Labor Minister Maung Myint said on Thursday that remittances from Myanmar migrant workers abroad totaled $5.6 billion in 2025. Experts say the regime’s remittance controls have cut a vital financial lifeline for the Myanmar population, which has been badly affected by conflict and economic collapse triggered by the 2021 coup that brought the regime to power.

World.title: Kyat Slides Again as Regime Wins Approval for 2.1 Trillion-Kyat Borrowing Plan
World.content:
The kyat lost value again this week after the regime-backed parliament on Wednesday approved borrowing of up to 2.1 trillion kyats (approximately US$1 billion at the fixed official rate) for a junta struggling with ballooning defense costs.

The kyat has weakened drastically since the 2021 coup plunged Myanmar into a dollar crisis, with economic sanctions, the withdrawal of foreign investment, declining exports and fighting in border trade zones taking a toll on the regime’s coffers.

On Wednesday, the rubber-stamp parliament approved the regime’s proposal to “borrow” up to 2.1 trillion kyats from the Central Bank of Myanmar to fill its budget deficit for fiscal year 2026-27. The legislature has already approved the regime’s plan to borrow money from major arms supplier Belarus, which will be used to import goods from Minsk.

Prior to Wednesday’s parliamentary approval, the regime had already raised nearly 14 trillion kyats through multiple treasury bill and bond auctions to finance its budget deficit for fiscal year 2026–27, according to Central Bank Deputy Governor Thet Htun Aung. He admitted the regime had also relied on treasury bond issuances and borrowing from the Central Bank to address budget shortfalls in previous years.
