World.title: Jordon Steele-John says he has been falsely accused of inappropriate conduct
World.content:
Greens senator Jordon Steele-John has denied allegations of inappropriate conduct raised in a letter to the Greens, which he says included false allegations of sexual assault, and blamed the public fallout from the allegations against him on party "factionalism".

The Greens have been in crisis management since the existence of a 47-page dossier surfaced about how the WA Greens would manage media coverage of allegations made about Senator Steele-John.

It was previously reported Senator Steele-John had taken leave from the party room last week after a letter from seven party members was sent to the office of Greens leader David Shoebridge.

According to media reports the letter alleged the writers were aware of "multiple allegations" about his behaviour in the presence of women, although none of the writers was said to have direct knowledge of "the matters involved", according to Senator Shoebridge.

In a public statement on social media, Senator Steele-John said, among the false allegations made against him, was an allegation of sexual assault, which police had investigated and made no adverse findings against him, with a finding of no charges.

He said that, with respect to that complaint, he had faced abuse and threats before the original complaint to police was made.

Senator Steele-John addressed several other allegations which he said were put to him by a journalist, which are now the subject of an internal Greens investigation.

Jordon Steele-John says false allegations have been made against him. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

He said a nickname others used to refer to him, "Feels on wheels", had grown from its original meaning to something "more sinister".

"Other parties started using [the name] to refer to me after I became emotional early in my career while giving speeches about the Royal Commission into Violence, Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation of Disabled People," he said.

" This phrase, which mocked my disability and my emotions, had taken on a new, more sinister meaning: that I had treated women inappropriately. "

The senator said his experience as a victim of abuse had collided with "political games", and denied he had taken leave after the allegations surfaced.

"I had hoped to be able to share all of this when I was ready, but because of a political clique in Greens WA and a leader facing his first serious test of leadership, I feel that the silence of self-protection will be [and has been] perceived as the silence of guilt," he said.

The senator claimed an "unofficial faction" of the Greens WA branch had released a letter detailing the allegations against him.

"This is not accountability. It is factionalism, and it has no place in the Greens," he said.

In a statement, a Greens WA party spokesperson said they were "putting together an independent process to assess the allegations".

"To ensure the integrity of that process, we will not be commenting further at this time," the spokesperson said.

Greens see red-hot anger as an opportunity David Shoebridge has big ambitions for the Greens, but his party is still wrestling with how to turn voter disillusionment into greater support.

Senator Steele-John said he had asked Senator Shoebridge "not to announce that I had requested leave" as it would appear to validate the allegations against him.

"I had expected him to recognise that absent any specific allegations, there was no procedural need for me to take leave of any kind," Senator Steele-John said.

"It was a bad call from David. We've all made those in politics.

"So, to be clear, I am not on leave and did not agree to the inclusion of that line within David's statement."

Senator Shoebridge's office has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Aussies survives dramatic collapse to beat New Zealand in first women's T20
World.content:
Australia has survived a dreadful collapse to claim a tense two-wicket victory over New Zealand in the opening Twenty20 International at North Sydney Oval.

The reigning T20 World Cup champions won with seven balls to spare, scoring 8-165 in reply to New Zealand's 2-162 on Sunday night.

Number 10 Kim Garth faced eight balls without scoring before hitting a boundary to give Australia a 1-0 lead in the three-match Rose Bowl series, with the remaining matches at North Sydney Oval on Tuesday and Thursday.

Australia overcame the early LBW loss of Georgia Voll and were charging towards victory when star veteran Beth Mooney and Ellyse Perry were involved in a dreadful mix-up.

They had taken the score to 86 in just 8.2 overs when Mooney was struck on the pad and charged off for the most ambitious of runs.

Perry sent her back, Mooney was slow to turn, and was run out well short of her ground.

The loss of Mooney for 38 from just 25 balls prompted a collapse.

Perry raced to her equal fastest T20 half century in just 27 balls but on 52 dragged a short ball from Jess Kerr to deep backward square, where she was well caught by Issy Sharp running to her right.

Georgie Wareham (10 from 7 balls) sliced a leg-spinner and Kerr's younger sister Amelia straight to point.

Ash Gardner (23 from 17) gave Jess Kerr her third wicket on review and Annabel Sutherland (9 from 5 balls) became her fourth, pulling a short ball to deep square leg.

Nicole Cary (4 from 3 balls) was run out by the recalled Tahlia McGrath and when captain Sophie Molineux (11 from 5 balls) fell, Australia had lost 7-62.

But the home side hung on for their 11th T20 win in a row, while the White Ferns have now lost six of their past nine matches.

Not even a record partnership and a record-equalling total in Australia could secure New Zealand victory.

After a difficult start by the White Ferns, Georgia Plimmer and Maddy Green combined for an unbeaten 127 in 80 balls.

Plimmer made a career-high 85 off 68 balls and Green 56 from 37 balls.

It was a breakout innings for the 22-year-old Plimmer, her fourth T20 half-century in 54 matches for New Zealand.

Going into the game she had an average of 16 and a strike rate of 104.

She was the beneficiary of two difficult chances, a stumping and catch from wicketkeeper Beth Mooney standing up to seamers Sutherland and Hamilton.

World.title: Australia claims second silver at track cycling world championships
World.content:
Australian cyclist Leigh Hoffman has claimed silver in the individual sprint at the UCI World Championships in Shanghai.

Hoffman, who won the bronze medal at the world championships 12 months ago, was beaten by Dutch legend Harrie Lavreysen in the gold medal race.

"To come away with a silver is still pretty amazing," Hoffman told AusCycling.

"But it is bitter sweet to be so close to getting a world title and having it slip away."

It was Australia and Hoffman's second medal of the world championships, after the men's team sprint squad won silver to the Netherlands on the first night at the spectacular Shanghai Velodrome.

Lavreysen won both sprints in the gold medal match, but there is little doubt that the 29-year-old five-time Olympic champion was still made to work for it.

Hoffman was the fastest qualifier for the sprint, the South Australian laying down a stunning 9.285 for his flying 200m on Saturday, and progressed comfortably through to the final.

Leigh Hoffman was always underdog against Harrie Lavreysen. (Reuters: Kacper Pempel)

Leading off in their first match up, Hoffman appeared to be in control before briefly dipping off the racing line.

That momentary lapse washed the Whyalla man's speed and allowed Lavreysen to power past him in the home straight.

The Dutchman made no mistake in the second race, leading from the front with brutal power to stay away and win a record-extending 23rd world title.

"Obviously wanted to win it but just didn't come away with it," Hoffman said.

"Lavreysen, he's won 23 world titles so he's got a ton of experience whereas for myself, that's my first gold-silver [race] at world champs."

No rider has managed to beat Lavreysen in an individual sprint at a world championships since Australian Matthew Glaetzer won gold in 2018.

But Hoffman showed once again that he is getting closer to becoming the first man to wrest the rainbow jersey from Lavreysen shoulders in almost a decade.

"I had a lot of confidence going through the rounds yesterday and today," Hoffman said.

"Beating [Japan's] Kaiya Ota in straight sets [in the semifinal], someone who has beaten me at the Olympics and beaten me at Copenhagen Worlds as well, it was good to get some runs on the board against him."

Leigh Hoffman got one over Japan's Kaiya Ota in the semifinal. (Reuters: Kacper Pempel)

Missing from the sprint field at these world championships was former Australian rider and world record holder in the flying 200m, Matt Richardson.

Richardson was withdrawn from the British squad earlier in the week over alleged misconduct, with the 27-year-old writing on social media that he both understood the seriousness of the allegations and would cooperate with any investigation.

"I understand the seriousness of what has been raised in recent reports about my withdrawal from the 2026 UCI Track Cycling World Championships," Richardson wrote.

"British Cycling has said it looks into matters like this through its established procedures. I will cooperate fully with its processes.

"I assure everyone that I will do so properly, and appropriately and with contrition for the feelings of anyone who might be affected.

"Out of fairness to everyone involved, and on advice, like British Cycling, I will not be commenting further until any process is complete."

The UK-born, Perth-raised rider won three Olympic medals for Australia before switching allegiance to Great Britain after the 2024 Paris Games.

World.title: Fatalities as 'serious incident' causes fire at Canadian military base
World.content:
People have been killed and injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire, according to Canada's defence minister, while the media is reporting that large numbers were being transported to hospitals.

Fire crews scrambled late into the night as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area.

It was not immediately clear how many people were killed or injured, but a doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180km north-west, told Canada's national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as healthcare facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing treatment.

Doctors called the disaster a "one in every 15- to 25-year event". (AP: John Ulan/The Canadian Press)

"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News.

" It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster. "

The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.

Defense Minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate."

He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information soon.

The RCMP said officers were called shortly after 4pm on Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base.

Firefighters faced a volatile situation.

Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts of up to 100 kilometres an hour.

Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. (Reuters: Camden Scott/Canadian Forces)

The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.

By 11pm, the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held, and that property and critical infrastructure were protected.

There was no evacuation order for residents.

Mr McGuinty, speaking to reporters in Ottawa, confirmed the casualties but had no other details to share.

"I cannot recall such an incident in my short time for sure as a minister, but I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory," Mr McGuinty said.

"We will have more to say in the coming hours and days."

He said armed forces members were at the scene and that RCMP were also involved.

"This is an active and delicate situation and soon to be an active and delicate investigation," he said

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.

"Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier in a social media post.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel.

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations.

It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.

Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Mr Carney and the defence minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.

"Pray for Wainwright, everyone," Mr Poilievre said.

Canadian province's breakaway push Alberta's separatist movement is exposing deep fractures inside one of the world's most stable federations and shares striking similarities with WA's historical secession attempts.

He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.

The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday's referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada.

Elections Alberta said two polling locations, in Lloydminster and Vermilion, closed early on Saturday and the ballots were transported securely.

AP

World.title: Two teenagers arrested after fight involving dozens of youth at Glenelg
World.content:
Two teenage boys have been arrested following an alleged fight at Mosely Square in Glenelg, after reports of a disturbance involving a large group of youths.

SA Police said they were called to the beach after 3:50pm on Sunday.

"Two youths who were fighting each other were arrested at the scene and charged with disorderly behaviour," police said in a statement.

Police said a nearby patrol was on scene about four minutes after the initial call was made for police assistance.

"No police officers were injured during the incident," police said.

"Police are actively patrolling all coastal areas in the metropolitan area.

" Police would like to advise the public that there is no tolerance of bad behaviour by members of the public and police will be taking a proactive approach and taking positive action against those who behave in a disorderly manner in public. "

Patrols responded to reports of a disturbance at Glenelg Beach on Sunday. (Supplied)

Police said dozens of youth witnesses gathered to watch the fight, officers dispersed the crowd and are patrolling the area.

It comes more than two weeks after police said they were investigating several public brawls that occurred at Glenelg and Henley Beach.

Police said they would examine the "level of organisation" of the fights after numerous social media videos emerged online.

Several videos posted of the September brawls showed people in separate fights on the Glenelg shore and at Henley Square, watched on by hundreds of young people.

Other clips showed large groups of youths running across roads in front of traffic.

Earlier this month, police launched Operation Jericho which will focus on addressing anti-social behaviour, criminal activity and road safety issues throughout the warmer months.

The operation will run until April 2027.

The two teenagers will appear in court a later date.

Police are urging anyone who witnesses disorderly behaviour to call the Police Assistance Line on 131444.

World.title: Kangaroos flick switch to kill off Bombers' resistance
World.content:
Ash Riddell has starred through the midfield and Tahlia Randall kicked three goals as North Melbourne unleashed a second-half masterclass to thrash Essendon by 52 points at Windy Hill.

Essendon led by seven points at quarter time and was still within striking distance at the main break, with North Melbourne holding a 29-20 lead after two terms.

But the reigning AFLW premiers flexed their muscles, scoring eight goals to two in the second half to win 12.13 (85) to 5.3 (33).

Riddell was prolific with 32 disposals, six clearances and two goal assists.

Jasmine Garner (27 disposals, two goals) and Eilish Sheerin (25 disposals, one goal) were also influential.

Madison Prespakis battled valiantly for Essendon on the way to 32 disposals, Bonnie Toogood kicked two goals from 18 possessions, while Stephanie Wales (23 hit-outs, 13 disposals, four clearances) was important in the ruck.

The Kangaroos (9-1 win-loss record) will snare the minor premiership if they win their remaining two matches against Adelaide and Richmond.

The Bombers (1-9) are among three one-win teams vying to avoid the wooden spoon.

Earlier at Windy Hill, Chloe Molloy and Cynthia Hamilton unleashed an early goal barrage to lead Sydney to a 51-point victory over Collingwood.

Molloy and Hamilton had three goals apiece by the opening minute of the second term against Collingwood, before forward-turned-ruck Taylor Smith chipped in with three of her own, as Sydney cruised to a 12.8 (80) to 4.5 (29) triumph.

The result kept seventh-placed Sydney (7-3) in the hunt for a home final with two rounds remaining.

Giants stun Hawks

Hawthorn's finals hopes are on thin ice after its forward Aine McDonagh missed a snap with just 18 seconds remaining as GWS pulled off an upset one-point win at Sydney's Henson Park.

The Hawks (5-5) slipped to ninth after falling 7.13 (55) to 7.12 (54) to the 15th-placed Giants (2-8).

Tilly Lucas-Rodd (left) enjoyed the Giants' win in their milestone match. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

They trailed by eight points with 2 minutes remaining before Jacqueline Dupuy took the ball out of the ruck and snapped truly to make it a two-point game.

With just 25 seconds remaining, McDonagh took a mark in the pocket, giving her the chance to clinch victory.

McDonagh played on but sent her snap wide, allowing GWS to hang on for a rare victory in what marked the perfect way to celebrate Tilly Lucy-Rodd's 100-match milestone.

Dockers survive Saints scare

In Perth, Fremantle's finals hopes were hanging in the balance as St Kilda surged to a two-point lead with less than nine minutes remaining.

But 19-year-old Noa McNaughton, who kicked a remarkable checkside goal earlier in the match, turned the contest on its head with a magical few minutes to lead her side to an 11-point win, 7.9 (51) to 6.4 (40).

First, McNaughton got the lead back for Fremantle by shaking a tackle and snapping truly.

Then from the next centre bounce, her surge forward resulted in a mark and easy goal to Eden Zanker.

And she killed off the contest a few minutes later when she combined with a teammate for a one-two play before dribbling the ball to Hayley Miller in the goal square.

The win lifted the Dockers (5-5) into eighth spot, but they face an uphill battle to make the finals given they finish their campaign with tough games against second-placed Geelong and seventh-placed Sydney.

AAP

World.title: Live: Boland's double lights up rain-affected first day in Gqeberha
World.content:
(Getty Images)

There's nothing I like better than a classic cricket ground, and St George's Park definitely fits that bill.

St George's Park is the oldest Test venue in South Africa, hosting the 31st Test in history back in March 1889.

It was the first Test to ever be held outside of Australia or England and just the seventh Test venue ever used after the MCG, The Oval, Lord's, SCG, Adelaide Oval and Old Trafford.

England won that first Test by 8 wickets, the match finishing inside two days.

England were the first four opponents to play at the ground, and won all of those matches, which were played in 1896, 1914 and 1949.

Australia played there for the first time in 1950 and won by an innings and 259 runs, Arthur Morris (157), Neil Harvey (116) and Lindsay Hassett (167) all scoring big in their first innings total of 7-549 declared.

Keith Miller than took 4-42 to help bowl the South Africans out for 158, before they were bowled out again following on for 132.

South Africa won their first match at the ground in 1954, beating New Zealand by 5 wickets and, in 1957, beat England there for the first time by 58 runs.

Trevor Bailey bowled Neil Adcock (Getty Images)

The lowest team total ever scored at the ground was 30 all out by South Africa against England in 1896, with the next lowest coming much more recently, Zimbabwe bowled out for just 68 in 30.1 overs in 2017, and Bangladesh falling for 80 in 2022.

Herschelle Gibbs' 196 against India in 2001 is the highest ever score at the venue, while Keshav Maharaj possesses the best innings figures of any bowler in recent years with a 7-40 against Bangladesh in 2022.

World.title: Teenage boy rescued from Brisbane stormwater drain
World.content:
Firefighters have rescued a teenager from the "maze" of stormwater drains under Brisbane.

Emergency services received reports that the boy was caught in the underground waterway system in the Kangaroo Point area about 2pm on Sunday.

Five firefighting crews were involved in the rescue effort. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

It took five firefighting crews about half an hour to find the boy, who was with his brother. The other boy did not need to be rescued.

Queensland Fire Department station officer Clint Pilon said he was found about 20 metres from the entrance of a stormwater drain and fire crews were able to bring him to safety on an inflatable rescue boat in a "pretty smooth" rescue.

Emergency services after the successful rescue. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

He said the teenager was uninjured and did not need to be taken to hospital.

Mr Pilon said that "playing in stormwater drains" was never a good idea, particularly after a bit of rain.

"The stormwater drains venture ... all over the city. It's like a little maze and they exit throughout the whole river," he explained.

He described the rescue as a positive outcome.

World.title: Australia vs South Africa LIVE: Boland takes two wickets in two balls before the rain sets in
World.content:
Eight years after Sandpapergate, reverse swing is again playing a “crucial” role in Australia’s Test series in South Africa, with old-ball movement a key to both Josh Hazlewood’s outstanding first Test and the looming recall of Kagiso Rabada.

After what has felt like years of green, seaming surfaces, Hazlewood spoke openly on Friday of the importance of generating reverse swing this series, with all matches being played on traditional cricket grounds with wicket squares that can scuff the ball.

There’s no question about the legality of the methods being used this time to achieve it.

Hazlewood’s 6-49 was punctuated by several moments of sharp movement once the ball had lost its shine, including David Bedingham’s lbw dismissal and Wiaan Mulder’s leg glance into Alex Carey’s gloves. According to CricViz, it was the most old-ball movement Hazlewood had achieved in a Test match since the corresponding Durban Test in 2018.

World.title: ‘Nasty political games’: Steele-John claims rumours were weaponised, denies taking leave
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership ‘Nasty political games’: Steele-John claims rumours were weaponised, denies taking leave Natassia Chrysanthos October 18, 2026 — 11:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Senator Jordon Steele-John has accused factions within the Greens of weaponising rumours about him for political reasons, and said he was not on leave from the party despite leader David Shoebridge saying so last week. In a near 2400-word statement posted to social media on Sunday night, the WA Greens senator responded to complaints made about him in a letter by Greens members and maintained he would take part in an investigation about its contents. “Because these references have been widely reported as allegations in their own right, I want to address each one fully and directly,” he wrote. Greens leader Senator David Shoebridge and Senator Jordon Steele-John in the Senate last Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen “And I will explain how my experience of family violence collided with nasty political games, and why, despite what you’ve heard, I’m not on leave.”



Steele-John’s response came after this masthead reported that seven Greens members wrote to Shoebridge last week regarding “multiple allegations” about the senator’s “behaviour in the presence of women” between 2017 and 2025. This masthead also revealed the Greens had kept a 47-page dossier that catalogued allegations against Steele-John and set out ways to shut down media coverage and monitor members who raised concerns on social media. Shoebridge commissioned an investigation last week and said Steele-John was taking leave from the party room. Steele-John strongly denied the claims against him, describing them as non-specific. In his statement on Sunday, the senator elaborated with a lengthy post that said the original letter sent to Shoebridge did not detail any allegations, only said that the authors were aware that allegations existed.



Steele-John responded to three elements contained in last week’s letter before criticising the way Shoebridge handled the situation. He said that rumours had been weaponised by factions in the WA Greens who were unhappy he joined the Senate 10 years ago, and that he was not on leave as the leader claimed. The senator’s response to claims in Greens letter The letter to Shoebridge last week said Steele-John was referred to in parliament as “feels on wheels”. This masthead chose not to report the nickname in the original story. In his statement, Steele-John said he had been called “feels on wheels” by staff within parliament because he became emotional early in his career while giving speeches about the disability royal commission. “Eventually, I was informed that this phrase, which mocked my disability and my emotions, had taken on a new, more sinister meaning: that I had treated women inappropriately,” he said.



“And now, in this letter, the existence of the nickname itself is the allegation.” Related Article Greens Steele-John probe should examine Greens processes, publish key findings: WA MPs Second, Steele-John responded to a reference in the letter to an alleged incident at a Greens event in 2024 that the writers claimed had not been reported because of fears the alleged victim would not be believed. “I’m really concerned to read this. No details were provided in the letter, so unfortunately, at this point, I don’t know how I could respond, or how anyone would begin to investigate it,” Steele-John said. The third element of his response concerns allegations made about him by a woman that he had previously dated. The statement elaborated on his initial comments last week about being a victim of family violence himself.



Steele-John claimed that his original election to the Senate in 2016 had upset some Greens members “who felt that their personal political ambitions had been upended” and pressured him to resign for another candidate. He claimed those people “couldn’t move on” and recruited more members to form an unofficial faction in the WA Greens. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership How to kill a story: The secret dossier the Greens used to protect Steele-John He also said that group had heard rumours of an interpersonal conflict between him and two other people in 2017, and tried to “shop them to journalists as part of a smear campaign”. “In the lead-up to the 2019 election, the rumours resurfaced. This led to the creation of a Google Doc so that Greens staff and the party office all had the same accurate information to give anyone who had heard the rumours and was concerned. One of its main purposes was to ensure journalists didn’t bombard these two women again. Neither woman made a complaint.”



Steele-John said it was “no coincidence” the letter was sent to Shoebridge “the day after we agreed on the timeline for the next preselection”. “It is my opinion that this is an attempt to influence forthcoming party pre-selections by deliberately leaking out of context or misleading information to smear potential candidates and myself.” Steele-John says he is not on leave Steele-John said he did not ask to take leave from the party room, as Shoebridge said during press conferences last Thursday and Friday. “I very much understand the tremendous scrutiny David was under in his first week in Parliament as leader, and I have compassion for that. I also feel that he let me and my team down,” he said.



“On the morning the story was about to break, we had a series of meetings about how we would respond. I understand that he was stressed. So was I. But I feel that he used those meetings to repeatedly pressure me to say that I would take leave. I was stunned by this.” Steele-John said he told Shoebridge he would need time off to look after himself but explicitly requested the leader “not to announce that I had requested leave, because I knew it would be read as validating a story where there isn’t one”. “And that is exactly what has happened,” he said. “It was a bad call from David. We’ve all made those in politics. So, to be clear, I am not on leave and did not agree to the inclusion of that line within David’s statement.” He said Shoebridge, as federal leader, did not have the power to place a Greens MP on leave from parliament, the party or the party room. “I will continue to do my job in a way that supports my staff team, my family and my community. I believe that is what the community would expect,” he said.



“I do not know who signed this letter, and I suspect many did so out of a genuine commitment to people who experience violence. I share that commitment. That is exactly why I am so angry that it has been used this way. “When processes meant to protect victims are turned into weapons in preselection contests, everyone loses. Survivors become less likely to be believed. Real complaints are treated with suspicion. And the people who did this know it. That is not accountability. It is factionalism, and it has no place in the Greens.” Steele-John said he had “bitten his tongue” for years but owed it to the party and community to speak out against “a political clique who have now done so much harm to so many”. “I genuinely welcome the opportunity to participate in the Greens WA investigation process,” he said. “I trust it will be robust, independent and timely – and I will not be drawn into factional rhetoric that relies on distressing rumours with a total disregard for genuinely addressing the male violence epidemic across Australia.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: RBA’s worst nightmare as oil pushes up inflation threat
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalInterest rates RBA’s worst nightmare as oil pushes up inflation threat Shane Wright October 18, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There are growing concerns within the Reserve Bank that the fallout from the war against Iran means inflation will remain elevated and force it to push up interest rates higher, even if it means more people may end up unemployed as the Australian economy slows. Ahead of two critical meetings in the run-up to Christmas, the bank is wrestling with the trade-off between bringing down inflation – which has remained above its 2-3 per cent target for three of the past four years – and the broader economic damage that would be caused by tighter monetary policy. Oil tankers and cargo vessels anchored off Port Sultan Qaboos in Muscat, Oman, in late June. Getty Senior sources within the bank, not authorised to comment publicly, have expressed growing concern that oil prices – which finished last week at $US106 a barrel – are showing no sign of falling as the war in the Middle East broadens to Saudi Arabia and the Gulf of Aden. While there is ongoing concern that spending by state and federal governments is also fuelling inflation, the RBA’s own economic forecasts – due to be updated next month – were based on oil prices being as much as $US20 a barrel lower.



Related Article Interest rates ‘Cost-of-living nightmare’: Consumer confidence slumps to historic low Diesel prices are much higher – around the level they hit at the start of the Russia-Ukraine war. Diesel is a major concern for every central bank, as it feeds into transport, manufacturing and food production costs. Australian inflation, which rose by 0.4 per cent in August, would have fallen but for the increase in petrol prices that month. It’s not just oil with prices for almost all commodities climbing due to the war and weather conditions. LNG prices are around $US28 per unit more than double they were before the war.



Food commodity prices are also being pushed higher, by both the increase in oil and fertiliser prices and the impact of this year’s “super” El Nino. Wheat prices have climbed by 37 per cent this year, soybeans are up by 24 per cent, sugar prices have soared by 42 per cent while cocoa beans have more than doubled. After weaker-than-expected job figures last week, which showed unemployment climbing to a five-year high of 4.7 per cent in September, financial markets sharply wound back expectations of a further interest rate increase. Ahead of the figures, markets believed there was a one-in-three chance the RBA would push the cash rate to 4.85 per cent at its November meeting. Markets now put the chance at closer to one in five. But the bank, and its counterparts overseas, continue to fret over the inflation pressures largely caused by the war and the global AI construction boom. On Friday, the RBA released papers from a conference on “monetary policy trade-offs” it held earlier this month.



Bank governor Michele Bullock, with senior RBA researcher Anthony Brassil, noted the problems caused by a supply shock to the economy such as the current surge in oil prices. They said that a supply shock coupled with the bank’s dual mandate – low inflation and full employment – meant it faced a difficult choice between supporting the economy or taking sterner action to control prices. Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has noted interest rates could go higher if inflation pressures did not abate. Louise Kennerley “If prices are rising faster than nominal incomes, households experience a direct loss of purchasing power. At the same time, weaker activity may mean that unemployment and underemployment are already increasing,” they said. “The costs on both sides of the mandate are then visible together, and monetary policy cannot eliminate the real economic loss caused by the shock. It can only influence how that loss is distributed over time.”



The bank has already come under fire for taking official interest rates to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent, prompting complaints that this is putting borrowers under extreme pressure. Despite higher rates, most borrowers remain well ahead on their repayments, with many holding large balances in offset mortgage accounts. In the three months to June, Australian home borrowers paid a record $21 billion in interest on their loans, but the share of household disposable income servicing mortgages is lower than in 2024, when the cash rate peaked at 4.35 per cent. But there are concerns that high inflation is doing more damage to low-income earners who are unlikely to hold a mortgage. These people have been the hardest hit by the ramp-up in rents over the past three years. “High inflation makes budgeting and planning harder, increases uncertainty and distorts price signals,” Bullock and Brassil said. “High inflation also tends to impose the most significant burdens on households with limited financial buffers.”



It’s not only a problem for the Reserve Bank. Central banks around the world have lifted interest rates over the past three months as inflation has climbed. The International Energy Agency last week noted that global diesel prices, while easing from the all-time high of $US200 a barrel reached in September, are still almost double their pre-war levels and are now starting to affect “real incomes, economic activity and inflation”. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said at the weekend that the war against Iran and the ongoing Russian-Ukraine conflict was hurting the global economy through oil prices. “Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, have driven up the cost of refining crude into end products,” he said. Last week, the International Monetary Fund’s chief economist Silvana Tenreyro noted that the global economy had shown surprising resilience in the face of the turmoil unleashed by the war against Iran.



Related Article Editorial

Australian economy Tough choices needed to keep Australian economy on track for growth The Herald's View Editorial She revealed that the global economy would have been much weaker, and inflation higher, but for the re-routing of oil supplies, an increase in energy efficiency and the shift in some countries towards renewable energy. But there are concerns the ability to mitigate the drop in oil production out of the Middle East has almost run its course. A squeeze on global supplies through 2027 is increasingly expected by analysts. Tenreyro noted not only the fallout from the war on oil supplies, but the pressure being put on the world economy by the surge in activity by tech companies as they build new data centres for their AI plans. World.title: Walkman down memory lane
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

David Leary of Newtown, intrigued by how much the HSC may have changed since he completed it in 1983, looked at this year’s exam timetable and noticed smartwatches and mobile phones on the list of banned items. “But in 2026, students are still allowed to use last-century technology such as a pair of compasses, a protractor, set square and even a piece of string for exams like geography. That got me thinking about things that students were allowed to bring into exams in my day. I remember the weirdest one was in a midterm exam at UNSW when a student was allowed to bring in a Sony Walkman to listen to a tape of bird noises to help her concentrate in the exam. Anyone else born last century remember anything weird like that from their exams?”

Donald Hawes of Peel noted “that students with very immigrant-style names were taking up Advanced English. Hopefully, some of the fourth-generation Australian illiterates might adopt their example.”

“To keep my brain active as I approach a nice old age, I’ve been teaching myself to fluently say Mark Nawaqanitawase,” admits Geoff Goodfellow of Moss Vale. “Three weeks on and I’m doing a beautiful Mark.”

“Yes, Edward Loong (C8), I did attend school at Marist Brothers, Parramatta, in the late fifties,” reports Barry Wooldridge of Harden. “I think you were a year ahead of me, and perhaps a classmate of one of my three brothers, Bill, Peter and Terry. Your family was well known and regarded in the district. Your contributions to Column 8 and Letters are always an enjoyable tonic.”

“If Janice Creenaune (C8), takes food to her daughter’s bogong-themed Halloween party, will she be carrying the moth-er load?” asks Caz Willis of Bowral.

World.title: ‘Beyond thankful’: How $1 million tech gave five-year-old stroke survivor her childhood back
World.content:
NationalWAHealthcare ‘Beyond thankful’: How $1 million tech gave five-year-old stroke survivor her childhood back Indigo Lemay-Conway October 18, 2026 — 9:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Riley Shawcross is five years old, a time of life that ought to be measured in lost baby teeth, scuffed knees, and primary school milestones. Instead, the last two years of her childhood have been calibrated in hospital monitors and dozens of silent brain injuries. Riley Shawcross is a five-year-old from Margaret River who has a rare genetic mutation which causes the blood vessels throughout her body to behave abnormally, leaving her particularly vulnerable to stroke. Kylie Plunkett Photography Born with a gene mutation so rare that there are only one in four cases in Australia and 80 worldwide, it causes the blood vessels throughout her body to behave abnormally, leaving her particularly vulnerable to stroke. Since suffering her first transient ischaemic attack (TIA) in July 2024, she has experienced more than 25 mini strokes. Her family has watched her suddenly lose her speech, struggle to move parts of her body and, at times, be unable to get words out at all.



“[After her first stroke] we ended up being in and out of Perth Children’s Hospital for about three months. Riley ended up having upwards of 10 TIA’s in a three-month period, and that’s when the doctors decided that they needed to do something intervening,” Riley’s mum Stephanie Shawcross said. But a $1 million leap in surgical precision gave doctors the ultimate vantage point that has left the Margaret River youngster stroke-free for more than four months. Riley was born with multisystemic smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome (MSMDS), caused by a mutation in the ACTA2 gene. The condition affects smooth muscle throughout the body, including the heart, lungs, digestive system and blood vessels. In Riley’s brain, smaller blood vessels can narrow or close over time, restricting blood flow and increasing her risk of stroke. After extensive consultation with specialists, Riley’s medical team determined that a highly specialised revascularisation surgery could help improve blood flow to her brain.



The first surgery on the right side of Riley’s brain was performed in July 2025. Just before her second surgery, the hospital was given a new state-of-the-art neuro-microscope that would help surgeons navigate the complex brain surgery even more precisely. The technology, funded by Perth Children’s Hospital Foundation (PCHF) led surgeons to discover that Riley’s brain had begun growing its own new blood vessels. Dr Snigdha Saha and the microscope during a live brain surgery procedure at Perth Children’s Hospital. Kylie Plunkett Photography Riley’s surgeon, Dr Edward White said the technology had been incredibly valuable in helping the team understand Riley’s changing brain anatomy and tailor the surgery to her individual needs. “Blood vessels are around half a millimetre wide, so these are structures that are incredibly difficult to see with the naked eye,” White said.



“The technology gives us a much clearer view of what we are working with and, in Riley’s case, allowed us to tailor the surgery to preserve the blood vessels already supplying her brain.” Following the surgeries, Riley has been stroke free, and her family is hopeful that the new blood vessels growing in her brain will continue to improve blood flow and protect her from future strokes. “Parenting a child with a complex medical condition, there will always be a worry in the back of your mind of what is next,” Shawcross said. “However, we will take all the good days we can get and right now, Riley is stroke-free since April, and we are beyond thankful for that!” Riley is one of the first kids in WA to benefit from the new neuro-microscope, following its arrival at the hospital earlier this year.



The device combines advanced magnification and illumination with AI-powered and robotic features to give surgeons greater precision and visualisation when operating on the brain and spine. Riley Shawcross had two complex brain surgeries to help reduce her risk of stroke. The neuro-microscope also incorporates fluorescence imaging, allowing surgeons to use a contrast dye to visualise vascular structures in real time, alongside voice controls and robotic assistance that automate microscope adjustments during surgery. PCHF chief executive Carrick Robinson said the investment in technology would help ensure the hospital remained at the forefront of paediatric healthcare. “Our $1 million investment is about giving PCH surgeons access to the very best tools available as they care for children like Riley with incredibly complex conditions,” Robinson said.



“As the first children’s hospital in Australia to have this technology, we’re proud to be leading the way in bringing next-generation surgical technology to WA kids and their families.” PCH neurosurgeon Dr Snigdha Saha said the technology was already proving valuable across the hospital’s neurosurgical services. “Better visualisation can help make surgery safer and more accurate for patients,” Saha said. “We’ve already used the microscope for brain tumour resection and the additional features such as voice command and robotic assistance, automating adjustments and visual workflows, were highly useful and has facilitated good outcomes.” The microscope is expected to be used in more than half of neurosurgeries at PCH, including neurovascular, brain cancer and spinal cases.

World.title: ‘I couldn’t account for it’: Sue Neill-Fraser opens up on lies to police after partner vanished
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Tasmanian grandmother convicted after a high-profile murder trial of killing her partner on their yacht has spoken for the first time, revealing why she lied to police about her whereabouts on the day he died and how she now fears for her life as she attempts to clear her name. In her first interview since being convicted and serving 13 years in jail, Sue Neill-Fraser has told 60 Minutes she maintains her innocence and fears for her safety for speaking out about the 2009 death of her partner, Bob Chappell, in Hobart. “There are huge vested interests in keeping this quiet,” Neill-Fraser tells 60 Minutes. Sue Neill-Fraser speaks publicly for the first time since a gag order imposed as part of her parole conditions was lifted. 60 Minutes Fearful for her safety, Neill-Fraser says she wants it known she’s “not depressed” and if she was to die in suspicious circumstances, no one should believe it was self-harm. The unlikely murderer Sue Neill-Fraser is a softly spoken and extremely articulate lady, with kind but tired eyes. She’s also one of Tasmania’s most notorious, cold-blooded killers.



At 72, she’s strikingly beautiful, although she insists her face is weathered from her years working in paddocks with horses. When Neill-Fraser talks about her grandchildren over a cup of tea, it’s almost impossible to reconcile the person in front of you with the violent murder she was convicted of committing. “I’ve never physically harmed anybody, ever,” Neill-Fraser says in the exclusive interview. Sue Neill-Fraser and Bob Chappell had been a couple for nearly 20 years before he was killed. 60 Minutes It’s the first time she’s spoken publicly since leaving jail in 2022, and Neill-Fraser admits she’s nervous about finally telling her version of events. But she’s determined to explain herself. Because four years into her parole, Neill-Fraser says she feels far from free. “Sitting with a wrongful conviction is like having an infected thorn in your mind,” she says quietly.



“Never in my wildest dreams did I imagine that I could be convicted in Australia if I hadn’t done anything.” Body overboard It was Australia Day 2009, and Neill-Fraser and Chappell, her partner of nearly 20 years, were pottering about the 53-foot yacht they’d bought months earlier with plans to spend their retirement sailing. The Four Winds was moored at Hobart’s Sandy Bay, and Chappell was fiddling with the electrical wiring when Neill-Fraser decided to head back to land, to the home they shared. Chappell planned to spend the night onboard, as he regularly did, and Neill-Fraser says their last words, down in the boat’s saloon, were the sort of idle chit-chat you’d expect between long-term partners. “He said, ‘yep, all right, bye!’ And that was it,” Neill-Fraser says. According to Tasmania Police, Neill-Fraser picked up a large wrench, bashed Chappell to death, and winched his body up two sets of stairs to the deck before manoeuvring him over the edge of the vessel into an inflatable dinghy below.



She then dumped his body somewhere in the Derwent River. “I can’t make it real, even now,” Neill-Fraser says. Released from prison, Sue Neill-Fraser says she will fight to clear her name. 60 Minutes “I don’t understand how you would get somebody up two flights of stairs … I have a slipped disc that I’ve had for about 35 years, and I would’ve had trouble lifting anything over about 10 or 12 kilos.” The police case was circumstantial; Chappell’s body nor a weapon were ever found. But there were signs of foul play; the Four Winds was found sinking and sabotaged the following morning and Chappell’s blood was splattered about the saloon. In the absence of witnesses or suspects, police quickly narrowed in on Neill-Fraser. As the victim’s partner and the last person to see him alive, she was the obvious culprit.



Investigators claim she stood to inherit Chappell’s assets and was motivated by money. Neill-Fraser disputes this, and while usually private about finances, wants to set the record straight. “When Bob went missing, I had over $80,000 in cash in a bank account,” she says. Bob Chappell was last seen onboard his yacht Four Winds. 60 Minutes “I paid for my half of the yacht outright. I had two rental properties and a farm. I didn’t need money.” But she did nothing to dispel police suspicions. In fact, in the days following Chappell’s disappearance, Neill-Fraser gave authorities every reason to believe she had something to hide.

Stringer is a proven goalkicker, with 440 goals to his name from 250 matches at three clubs – the Western Bulldogs, Essendon and the Giants for the past two seasons. Two industry sources, who preferred to remain anonymous when discussing contract matters, said the Saints were moving towards securing Stringer. World.title: ‘Nasty political games’: Steele-John claims rumours were weaponised, denies taking leave
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership ‘Nasty political games’: Steele-John claims rumours were weaponised, denies taking leave Natassia Chrysanthos October 18, 2026 — 11:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Senator Jordon Steele-John has accused factions within the Greens of weaponising rumours about him for political reasons, and said he was not on leave from the party despite leader David Shoebridge saying so last week. In a near 2400-word statement posted to social media on Sunday night, the WA Greens senator responded to complaints made about him in a letter by Greens members and maintained he would take part in an investigation about its contents. “Because these references have been widely reported as allegations in their own right, I want to address each one fully and directly,” he wrote. Greens leader Senator David Shoebridge and Senator Jordon Steele-John in the Senate last Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen “And I will explain how my experience of family violence collided with nasty political games, and why, despite what you’ve heard, I’m not on leave.”



Steele-John’s response came after this masthead reported that seven Greens members wrote to Shoebridge last week regarding “multiple allegations” about the senator’s “behaviour in the presence of women” between 2017 and 2025. This masthead also revealed the Greens had kept a 47-page dossier that catalogued allegations against Steele-John and set out ways to shut down media coverage and monitor members who raised concerns on social media. Shoebridge commissioned an investigation last week and said Steele-John was taking leave from the party room. Steele-John strongly denied the claims against him, describing them as non-specific. In his statement on Sunday, the senator elaborated with a lengthy post that said the original letter sent to Shoebridge did not detail any allegations, only said that the authors were aware that allegations existed.



Steele-John responded to three elements contained in last week’s letter before criticising the way Shoebridge handled the situation. He said that rumours had been weaponised by factions in the WA Greens who were unhappy he joined the Senate 10 years ago, and that he was not on leave as the leader claimed. The senator’s response to claims in Greens letter The letter to Shoebridge last week said Steele-John was referred to in parliament as “feels on wheels”. This masthead chose not to report the nickname in the original story. In his statement, Steele-John said he had been called “feels on wheels” by staff within parliament because he became emotional early in his career while giving speeches about the disability royal commission. “Eventually, I was informed that this phrase, which mocked my disability and my emotions, had taken on a new, more sinister meaning: that I had treated women inappropriately,” he said.



“And now, in this letter, the existence of the nickname itself is the allegation.” Related Article Greens Steele-John probe should examine Greens processes, publish key findings: WA MPs Second, Steele-John responded to a reference in the letter to an alleged incident at a Greens event in 2024 that the writers claimed had not been reported because of fears the alleged victim would not be believed. “I’m really concerned to read this. No details were provided in the letter, so unfortunately, at this point, I don’t know how I could respond, or how anyone would begin to investigate it,” Steele-John said. The third element of his response concerns allegations made about him by a woman that he had previously dated. The statement elaborated on his initial comments last week about being a victim of family violence himself.



Steele-John claimed that his original election to the Senate in 2016 had upset some Greens members “who felt that their personal political ambitions had been upended” and pressured him to resign for another candidate. He claimed those people “couldn’t move on” and recruited more members to form an unofficial faction in the WA Greens. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership How to kill a story: The secret dossier the Greens used to protect Steele-John He also said that group had heard rumours of an interpersonal conflict between him and two other people in 2017, and tried to “shop them to journalists as part of a smear campaign”. “In the lead-up to the 2019 election, the rumours resurfaced. This led to the creation of a Google Doc so that Greens staff and the party office all had the same accurate information to give anyone who had heard the rumours and was concerned. One of its main purposes was to ensure journalists didn’t bombard these two women again. Neither woman made a complaint.”



Steele-John said it was “no coincidence” the letter was sent to Shoebridge “the day after we agreed on the timeline for the next preselection”. “It is my opinion that this is an attempt to influence forthcoming party pre-selections by deliberately leaking out of context or misleading information to smear potential candidates and myself.” Steele-John says he is not on leave Steele-John said he did not ask to take leave from the party room, as Shoebridge said during press conferences last Thursday and Friday. “I very much understand the tremendous scrutiny David was under in his first week in Parliament as leader, and I have compassion for that. I also feel that he let me and my team down,” he said.



“On the morning the story was about to break, we had a series of meetings about how we would respond. I understand that he was stressed. So was I. But I feel that he used those meetings to repeatedly pressure me to say that I would take leave. I was stunned by this.” Steele-John said he told Shoebridge he would need time off to look after himself but explicitly requested the leader “not to announce that I had requested leave, because I knew it would be read as validating a story where there isn’t one”. “And that is exactly what has happened,” he said. “It was a bad call from David. We’ve all made those in politics. So, to be clear, I am not on leave and did not agree to the inclusion of that line within David’s statement.” He said Shoebridge, as federal leader, did not have the power to place a Greens MP on leave from parliament, the party or the party room. “I will continue to do my job in a way that supports my staff team, my family and my community. I believe that is what the community would expect,” he said.



“I do not know who signed this letter, and I suspect many did so out of a genuine commitment to people who experience violence. I share that commitment. That is exactly why I am so angry that it has been used this way. “When processes meant to protect victims are turned into weapons in preselection contests, everyone loses. Survivors become less likely to be believed. Real complaints are treated with suspicion. And the people who did this know it. That is not accountability. It is factionalism, and it has no place in the Greens.” Steele-John said he had “bitten his tongue” for years but owed it to the party and community to speak out against “a political clique who have now done so much harm to so many”. “I genuinely welcome the opportunity to participate in the Greens WA investigation process,” he said. “I trust it will be robust, independent and timely – and I will not be drawn into factional rhetoric that relies on distressing rumours with a total disregard for genuinely addressing the male violence epidemic across Australia.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: RBA’s worst nightmare as oil pushes up inflation threat
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalInterest rates RBA’s worst nightmare as oil pushes up inflation threat Shane Wright October 18, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. There are growing concerns within the Reserve Bank that the fallout from the war against Iran means inflation will remain elevated and force it to push up interest rates higher, even if it means more people may end up unemployed as the Australian economy slows. Ahead of two critical meetings in the run-up to Christmas, the bank is wrestling with the trade-off between bringing down inflation – which has remained above its 2-3 per cent target for three of the past four years – and the broader economic damage that would be caused by tighter monetary policy. Oil tankers and cargo vessels anchored off Port Sultan Qaboos in Muscat, Oman, in late June. Getty Senior sources within the bank, not authorised to comment publicly, have expressed growing concern that oil prices – which finished last week at $US106 a barrel – are showing no sign of falling as the war in the Middle East broadens to Saudi Arabia and the Gulf of Aden. While there is ongoing concern that spending by state and federal governments is also fuelling inflation, the RBA’s own economic forecasts – due to be updated next month – were based on oil prices being as much as $US20 a barrel lower.



Related Article Interest rates ‘Cost-of-living nightmare’: Consumer confidence slumps to historic low Diesel prices are much higher – around the level they hit at the start of the Russia-Ukraine war. Diesel is a major concern for every central bank, as it feeds into transport, manufacturing and food production costs. Australian inflation, which rose by 0.4 per cent in August, would have fallen but for the increase in petrol prices that month. It’s not just oil with prices for almost all commodities climbing due to the war and weather conditions. LNG prices are around $US28 per unit more than double they were before the war.



Food commodity prices are also being pushed higher, by both the increase in oil and fertiliser prices and the impact of this year’s “super” El Nino. Wheat prices have climbed by 37 per cent this year, soybeans are up by 24 per cent, sugar prices have soared by 42 per cent while cocoa beans have more than doubled. After weaker-than-expected job figures last week, which showed unemployment climbing to a five-year high of 4.7 per cent in September, financial markets sharply wound back expectations of a further interest rate increase. Ahead of the figures, markets believed there was a one-in-three chance the RBA would push the cash rate to 4.85 per cent at its November meeting. Markets now put the chance at closer to one in five. But the bank, and its counterparts overseas, continue to fret over the inflation pressures largely caused by the war and the global AI construction boom. On Friday, the RBA released papers from a conference on “monetary policy trade-offs” it held earlier this month.



Bank governor Michele Bullock, with senior RBA researcher Anthony Brassil, noted the problems caused by a supply shock to the economy such as the current surge in oil prices. They said that a supply shock coupled with the bank’s dual mandate – low inflation and full employment – meant it faced a difficult choice between supporting the economy or taking sterner action to control prices. Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has noted interest rates could go higher if inflation pressures did not abate. Louise Kennerley “If prices are rising faster than nominal incomes, households experience a direct loss of purchasing power. At the same time, weaker activity may mean that unemployment and underemployment are already increasing,” they said. “The costs on both sides of the mandate are then visible together, and monetary policy cannot eliminate the real economic loss caused by the shock. It can only influence how that loss is distributed over time.”



The bank has already come under fire for taking official interest rates to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent, prompting complaints that this is putting borrowers under extreme pressure. Despite higher rates, most borrowers remain well ahead on their repayments, with many holding large balances in offset mortgage accounts. In the three months to June, Australian home borrowers paid a record $21 billion in interest on their loans, but the share of household disposable income servicing mortgages is lower than in 2024, when the cash rate peaked at 4.35 per cent. But there are concerns that high inflation is doing more damage to low-income earners who are unlikely to hold a mortgage. These people have been the hardest hit by the ramp-up in rents over the past three years. “High inflation makes budgeting and planning harder, increases uncertainty and distorts price signals,” Bullock and Brassil said. “High inflation also tends to impose the most significant burdens on households with limited financial buffers.”



It’s not only a problem for the Reserve Bank. Central banks around the world have lifted interest rates over the past three months as inflation has climbed. The International Energy Agency last week noted that global diesel prices, while easing from the all-time high of $US200 a barrel reached in September, are still almost double their pre-war levels and are now starting to affect “real incomes, economic activity and inflation”. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said at the weekend that the war against Iran and the ongoing Russian-Ukraine conflict was hurting the global economy through oil prices. “Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, have driven up the cost of refining crude into end products,” he said. Last week, the International Monetary Fund’s chief economist Silvana Tenreyro noted that the global economy had shown surprising resilience in the face of the turmoil unleashed by the war against Iran.



Related Article Editorial

Australian economy Tough choices needed to keep Australian economy on track for growth The Herald's View Editorial She revealed that the global economy would have been much weaker, and inflation higher, but for the re-routing of oil supplies, an increase in energy efficiency and the shift in some countries towards renewable energy. But there are concerns the ability to mitigate the drop in oil production out of the Middle East has almost run its course. A squeeze on global supplies through 2027 is increasingly expected by analysts. Tenreyro noted not only the fallout from the war on oil supplies, but the pressure being put on the world economy by the surge in activity by tech companies as they build new data centres for their AI plans. Riley Shawcross is a five-year-old from Margaret River who has a rare genetic mutation which causes the blood vessels throughout her body to behave abnormally, leaving her particularly vulnerable to stroke. Kylie Plunkett Photography Born with a gene mutation so rare that there are only one in four cases in Australia and 80 worldwide, it causes the blood vessels throughout her body to behave abnormally, leaving her particularly vulnerable to stroke. Since suffering her first transient ischaemic attack (TIA) in July 2024, she has experienced more than 25 mini strokes. Her family has watched her suddenly lose her speech, struggle to move parts of her body and, at times, be unable to get words out at all.



“[After her first stroke] we ended up being in and out of Perth Children’s Hospital for about three months. Riley ended up having upwards of 10 TIA’s in a three-month period, and that’s when the doctors decided that they needed to do something intervening,” Riley’s mum Stephanie Shawcross said. But a $1 million leap in surgical precision gave doctors the ultimate vantage point that has left the Margaret River youngster stroke-free for more than four months. Riley was born with multisystemic smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome (MSMDS), caused by a mutation in the ACTA2 gene. The condition affects smooth muscle throughout the body, including the heart, lungs, digestive system and blood vessels. In Riley’s brain, smaller blood vessels can narrow or close over time, restricting blood flow and increasing her risk of stroke. After extensive consultation with specialists, Riley’s medical team determined that a highly specialised revascularisation surgery could help improve blood flow to her brain.



The first surgery on the right side of Riley’s brain was performed in July 2025. Just before her second surgery, the hospital was given a new state-of-the-art neuro-microscope that would help surgeons navigate the complex brain surgery even more precisely. The technology, funded by Perth Children’s Hospital Foundation (PCHF) led surgeons to discover that Riley’s brain had begun growing its own new blood vessels. Dr Snigdha Saha and the microscope during a live brain surgery procedure at Perth Children’s Hospital. Kylie Plunkett Photography Riley’s surgeon, Dr Edward White said the technology had been incredibly valuable in helping the team understand Riley’s changing brain anatomy and tailor the surgery to her individual needs. “Blood vessels are around half a millimetre wide, so these are structures that are incredibly difficult to see with the naked eye,” White said.



“The technology gives us a much clearer view of what we are working with and, in Riley’s case, allowed us to tailor the surgery to preserve the blood vessels already supplying her brain.” Following the surgeries, Riley has been stroke free, and her family is hopeful that the new blood vessels growing in her brain will continue to improve blood flow and protect her from future strokes. “Parenting a child with a complex medical condition, there will always be a worry in the back of your mind of what is next,” Shawcross said. “However, we will take all the good days we can get and right now, Riley is stroke-free since April, and we are beyond thankful for that!” Riley is one of the first kids in WA to benefit from the new neuro-microscope, following its arrival at the hospital earlier this year.



The device combines advanced magnification and illumination with AI-powered and robotic features to give surgeons greater precision and visualisation when operating on the brain and spine. Riley Shawcross had two complex brain surgeries to help reduce her risk of stroke. The neuro-microscope also incorporates fluorescence imaging, allowing surgeons to use a contrast dye to visualise vascular structures in real time, alongside voice controls and robotic assistance that automate microscope adjustments during surgery. PCHF chief executive Carrick Robinson said the investment in technology would help ensure the hospital remained at the forefront of paediatric healthcare. “Our $1 million investment is about giving PCH surgeons access to the very best tools available as they care for children like Riley with incredibly complex conditions,” Robinson said.



“As the first children’s hospital in Australia to have this technology, we’re proud to be leading the way in bringing next-generation surgical technology to WA kids and their families.” PCH neurosurgeon Dr Snigdha Saha said the technology was already proving valuable across the hospital’s neurosurgical services. “Better visualisation can help make surgery safer and more accurate for patients,” Saha said. “We’ve already used the microscope for brain tumour resection and the additional features such as voice command and robotic assistance, automating adjustments and visual workflows, were highly useful and has facilitated good outcomes.” The microscope is expected to be used in more than half of neurosurgeries at PCH, including neurovascular, brain cancer and spinal cases.

World.title: ‘I couldn’t account for it’: Sue Neill-Fraser opens up on lies to police after partner vanished
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A Tasmanian grandmother convicted after a high-profile murder trial of killing her partner on their yacht has spoken for the first time, revealing why she lied to police about her whereabouts on the day he died and how she now fears for her life as she attempts to clear her name. In her first interview since being convicted and serving 13 years in jail, Sue Neill-Fraser has told 60 Minutes she maintains her innocence and fears for her safety for speaking out about the 2009 death of her partner, Bob Chappell, in Hobart. “There are huge vested interests in keeping this quiet,” Neill-Fraser tells 60 Minutes. Sue Neill-Fraser speaks publicly for the first time since a gag order imposed as part of her parole conditions was lifted. 60 Minutes Fearful for her safety, Neill-Fraser says she wants it known she’s “not depressed” and if she was to die in suspicious circumstances, no one should believe it was self-harm. The unlikely murderer Sue Neill-Fraser is a softly spoken and extremely articulate lady, with kind but tired eyes. She’s also one of Tasmania’s most notorious, cold-blooded killers.



At 72, she’s strikingly beautiful, although she insists her face is weathered from her years working in paddocks with horses. When Neill-Fraser talks about her grandchildren over a cup of tea, it’s almost impossible to reconcile the person in front of you with the violent murder she was convicted of committing. “I’ve never physically harmed anybody, ever,” Neill-Fraser says in the exclusive interview. Sue Neill-Fraser and Bob Chappell had been a couple for nearly 20 years before he was killed. 60 Minutes It’s the first time she’s spoken publicly since leaving jail in 2022, and Neill-Fraser admits she’s nervous about finally telling her version of events. But she’s determined to explain herself. Because four years into her parole, Neill-Fraser says she feels far from free. “Sitting with a wrongful conviction is like having an infected thorn in your mind,” she says quietly.



“Never in my wildest dreams did I imagine that I could be convicted in Australia if I hadn’t done anything.” Body overboard It was Australia Day 2009, and Neill-Fraser and Chappell, her partner of nearly 20 years, were pottering about the 53-foot yacht they’d bought months earlier with plans to spend their retirement sailing. The Four Winds was moored at Hobart’s Sandy Bay, and Chappell was fiddling with the electrical wiring when Neill-Fraser decided to head back to land, to the home they shared. Chappell planned to spend the night onboard, as he regularly did, and Neill-Fraser says their last words, down in the boat’s saloon, were the sort of idle chit-chat you’d expect between long-term partners. “He said, ‘yep, all right, bye!’ And that was it,” Neill-Fraser says. According to Tasmania Police, Neill-Fraser picked up a large wrench, bashed Chappell to death, and winched his body up two sets of stairs to the deck before manoeuvring him over the edge of the vessel into an inflatable dinghy below.



She then dumped his body somewhere in the Derwent River. “I can’t make it real, even now,” Neill-Fraser says. Released from prison, Sue Neill-Fraser says she will fight to clear her name. 60 Minutes “I don’t understand how you would get somebody up two flights of stairs … I have a slipped disc that I’ve had for about 35 years, and I would’ve had trouble lifting anything over about 10 or 12 kilos.” The police case was circumstantial; Chappell’s body nor a weapon were ever found. But there were signs of foul play; the Four Winds was found sinking and sabotaged the following morning and Chappell’s blood was splattered about the saloon. In the absence of witnesses or suspects, police quickly narrowed in on Neill-Fraser. As the victim’s partner and the last person to see him alive, she was the obvious culprit.



Investigators claim she stood to inherit Chappell’s assets and was motivated by money. Neill-Fraser disputes this, and while usually private about finances, wants to set the record straight. “When Bob went missing, I had over $80,000 in cash in a bank account,” she says. Bob Chappell was last seen onboard his yacht Four Winds. 60 Minutes “I paid for my half of the yacht outright. I had two rental properties and a farm. I didn’t need money.” But she did nothing to dispel police suspicions. In fact, in the days following Chappell’s disappearance, Neill-Fraser gave authorities every reason to believe she had something to hide.
